holdings.what_they_did: Jim Haynes was one of three candidates, with Leonard Heydt and John Lovett, who presented their views to the Herald in the race for the first presidency of the Associated Students in May 1966, days after the student body ratified the new constitution. Haynes captured the presidency the following week, becoming the first president of the Associated Students of Western Kentucky University. The same issue carried a skeptical editorial titled 'We Do Not Deserve Student Government,' a measure of the doubts his administration set out to answer. Haynes's term closed in May 1967, when the Herald summed up the government's first year as one of organization, progress and apathy and carried president-elect William Menser's plans for 1967-68.

holdings.what_they_did: Menser headed the Associated Student Government from the start of the 1967-68 year, appearing alongside President Kelly Thompson in a 14 September 1967 Herald article welcoming students back to campus. That fall the idea of a student seat on the Board of Regents was already circulating: a 2 November 1967 Herald article headlined 'Ward Favors Student on Board of Regents' reported support for the idea four months before an enabling bill reached committee. That December the Herald reported an Associated Students survey of student activity preferences and, in the same 8 December 1967 issue, ran a piece by Dennis Jaffe commending the government's efforts; the same issue covered the Kentucky Intercollegiate Press Association backing a proposal for student representation. In February 1968 Western sent lobbyists to Frankfort for a bill to seat a student on the Board of Regents; on 4 April 1968 the Herald reported Menser had assumed duties as the board's first student regent, a non-voting seat. As his term closed, the Herald's 29 April 1968 issue - the same one covering the Straeffer-Whitley presidential race to succeed him - carried both a piece headlined 'Menser Discusses Head Fee' and a separate retrospective, 'Past Performance of Associated Student Government Analyzed'. The archive does not yet hold the text of either article, only their headlines. Menser opened his year in office in September 1967 sharing the front page with President Kelly Thompson, in a piece headlined "Dr. Kelly Thompson, William Menser Welcome Students." The same first issue of the year set out the Associated Student Government's schedule of events. Menser's correspondence with President Kelly Thompson survives in the WKU Archives, filed under student fees. The file is described as correspondence about the assessment of student fees and the Associated Student Government budget for 1968-1969.

Heads the 1967-68 officers and congressmen roster and its Executive Committee list. The 1968 Talisman's Associated Students page describes the body in its second year of existence pushing student proposals through legislation and expanded activities.

Claudia Fowler served as secretary of Associated Students for 1967-68, under president William Menser, and sat with him on the Executive Committee. The 1967-68 officers roster and the 1968 Talisman's caption of the year's officers, which names her Claudia Fowler, secretary, are the only records the archive has found of her term.

Larry Heishman returned as treasurer of Associated Students for 1967-68, the office he had held on the founding Congress the year before, and sat on the Executive Committee under president William Menser. He was the only one of the four 1966-67 founding officers kept in the same post for a second year; his full record is under his first term, in 1966-67.

Ronald Beck was elected vice president of Associated Students for 1967-68 and sat on the Executive Committee under president William Menser. He had served the year before as junior class president in the first Congress, elected in May 1966; the 1968 Talisman's officer photograph captions him as Beck, vice president, closing out the record the archive has found of his term. The memo reporting the May 1968 election results is itself signed 'Ron Beck, Vice-President,' independent confirmation that he was still the sitting 1967-68 vice president that spring. A different Ron Beck, an assistant dean of student affairs who clashed publicly with Associated Student Government officers over concert booking in the 1970s, is not the same person and is not part of this profile.

holdings.what_they_did: Straeffer ran for the Associated Students presidency against Charles Whitley in the 2 May 1968 election, the organization's second contested presidential race. He won 1,732 votes to Whitley's 1,098. Terry Gilpin was elected vice president in the same election, beating Bob Van Corbach 1,516 to 1,206. Total turnout was 2,894 votes, about 34 percent of the roughly 8,500-student enrollment - a turnout the Herald's coverage of the result treated as a persistent problem, running an editorial in the same issue headed 'Elections Illustrate Faults, Indifference'. A year later, the Herald's 8 May 1969 issue carried Straeffer and Gilpin's own review of their year in office, headlined 'Associated Students Produces Year of Advancement,' alongside a companion piece, 'Bill Straeffer, Terry Gilpin Review Their Year with Associated Students.' The archive does not yet hold the article text itself, only its headline and byline (Ellen Bennett), so the specifics of what the administration counted as advancement are not yet confirmed. Bill Straeffer vied with Charles Whitley for the Associated Student Government presidency in the spring 1968 election, the Herald carrying both hopefuls' ideas before the balloting, in a campaign that also saw Terry Gilpin and Bob Van Corbach contest the vice presidency. Straeffer won the presidency in the May 1968 vote, and in the same issue the Herald reported the new president making plans for 1968-69. Closing his term in May 1969, Straeffer and vice president Terry Gilpin reviewed their year with the Associated Students for the Herald, which credited the administration with a year of advancement.

Paul Gerard first appeared in the Herald's campus politics coverage in April 1968, when the paper reported him battling Mike Collins for a senior class post in that week's election. A Paul Gerard of Bowling Green appears on the 1967-68 Associated Students committee roster, appointed to the Rules and Elections Committee that fall; nothing on that roster confirms the two are the same person, but the hometown and the timing, a year before this campaign, are circumstantially consistent. By February 1969 Gerard held the student seat on the Board of Regents, and Herald writer Bruce Tucker profiled him as the student regent. He followed William Menser, who in April 1968 had become the first student to sit with the board.
holdings.source: UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Results of Election, Ron Beck, 3 May 1968

holdings.what_they_did: Lyne first ran for Associated Students office in the March 1969 election, contesting the vice-presidential ('second spot') race against David Porter and losing; Porter went on to serve as Larry Zielke's vice president for 1969-70. A year later, no one filed against Lyne for the 1970-71 presidency, and the Herald reported on 13 March 1970 that he had 'won the presidency before the race begins.' Doug Alexander won the vice presidency the same election cycle, beating Steve Tichenor, in a vote held the following week. The term began against the backdrop of the Kent State shootings that May: the Associated Student Congress's October 1970 resolution on the women's curfew ran in a Herald issue whose letters page was dominated by students arguing about Kent State, and the same fall the Board of Regents seated eight students on the Academic Council. Beyond the curfew resolution, the Congress passed a lecture bill on 6 November 1970 funding campus appearances by William Kunstler and Bernadette Devlin, and separately endorsed a proposed new constitution two weeks later; a study committee kept refining it, reaching judicial-reform provisions by February 1971. John Lyne was one of the most visible students on the Hill before taking office, writing a steady stream of Herald columns through 1969-70 and representing Kentuckians in the national draft lottery drawing in December 1969. Lyne won the Associated Students presidency in March 1970 without opposition, the Herald reporting that he had captured the office before the race began. Through 1970-71 Lyne fought his administration's corner in the Herald's letters column, complaining in January that he had been kept in the dark about an appointment and defending the Associated Students lecture series against attack that April, in the issue that reported W.S. Moss taking the oath as regent.
holdings.source: Herald 49:35, 13 Mar 1970 - "John Lyne Wins Presidency Before Race Begins"

holdings.what_they_did: Unopposed.

Before running, Alexander had already been active in student government: the Herald of 12 December 1969 reported him named the student member of the University's Athletic Committee. During his term, Alexander shared a byline in the Herald of 16 October 1970 with Brett Butler, that year's treasurer, over a piece headlined "Heads You Win . . .". A 1973 Talisman profile, occasioned by his selection as Sigma Nu's national Man of the Year, said he had also been president of the fraternity's chapter and, the profile said, its scholar for three years; it named him commander of WKU's ROTC program the year before, where he produced a training film about the program that the Army paid to have copied and shown around the country. Jones was elected the first woman president of the Associated Student Government on 6 April 1971; the Western Alumnus photographed her being sworn in with faculty regent Lowell Harrison by Georgia Bates. That fall, on 14 September 1971, the Herald reported the Associated Students affiliating with a wider student association, though the article index alone does not identify which body. By 1 February 1972, four years after the student regent seat was created, the Herald was still reporting the seat had no vote. Through February and March 1972, Jones's Congress pushed a rewritten constitution: it voted section by section on 22 February, when the Herald printed the executive branch's full text, and the Herald reported the executive branch accepted on 29 February. The same 29 February issue reported the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union planning court action connected to Associated Students and The Fly, a separate WKU underground newspaper, and carried Jones's own piece, 'Associated Students Corrects Herald', a public correction of the paper's coverage of the organization. The archive does not yet hold the text of either the KCLU piece or Jones's correction, so the underlying dispute and what she corrected both remain unconfirmed. Days earlier, the Herald's 25 February 1972 issue ran under the headline 'Chaos Reigns at Associated Students Meeting', alongside a separate piece arguing that student interest in the organization had collapsed and the Associated Students had followed it down. The constitution went to referendum at the end of March: the Herald's 28 March issue urged students to 'Vote Yes' ahead of a two-day vote, and Associated Students formally endorsed the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union's lawsuit in the same issue. The archive does not yet show the referendum's result or turnout. Her term closed on 28 April 1972 as a Mass Action Committee called for a strike over dorm visitation and the Associated Students installed its next officers; the same issue reported students had won six votes on a university council, and carried Jones's own reflection on her year in office.

Reginald Glass was elected vice president of the Associated Students for 1971-72 under president Linda Jones, becoming, the 1972 Talisman says, the first Black vice president of the body and the first Black student to hold a top student leadership post at Western. As vice president he sat on the Academic Council as one of its two voting student members and chaired the activities committee; a yearbook caption shows him signing a speaker contract, placed beside the note that Dr. Benjamin Spock was A.S.'s first sponsored speaker, though the volume does not state outright that this was Spock's own contract. Glass was also active in Black campus life outside ASG: he belonged to Alpha Phi Alpha fraternity, chartered nationally at Western on 31 October 1971, and the Herald reported him named the campus's outstanding Black Greek that November. He remained involved in student government after his year as vice president ended. By the fall of 1973 he sat in the ASG Congress as the representative from the Graduate College, and the Herald reported him pressing for better representation of minority students in student government and on the Academic Council. On 4 December 1973 the Herald reported that he had resigned that seat in protest; the 1974 Talisman records his reasoning as the harm he said the absence of Black and foreign students from ASG and the Academic Council did to the minorities and to the University.

Jordan ran for the Associated Student Government presidency on a platform the Herald's Roger Miller labeled progressivism, profiled a week before the vote. Congress had separately voted to place his opponent, Bob Hatfield, on the ballot after a dispute over Hatfield's eligibility. Jordan beat Hatfield in the 20 April 1972 election; the Herald reported his win on 25 April under the headline 'Ed Jordan Wins Top Office,' in the same issue as an editorial by Pence and Carter arguing the new ASG president needed cooperation and support. Edward Jordan's name entered the Herald's letters columns on November 7, 1972, when he and Charles Boteler urged readers to restore ideals. The digitized index does not label the ASG office Jordan held. On April 10, 1973, as top ASG offices went on the line in the spring election, a letter praising Ed Jordan ran in the Herald. Jordan stayed in student politics after his year: in April 1974 he wrote to the Herald judging Steve Henry the most qualified candidate in that spring's races.

In September 1972 the Herald profiled Michael Fiorella, the Associated Student Government vice president, under the headline that he was anti-apathy. A week later the Herald reported that Fiorella had won the student seat on the Board of Regents. Fiorella was sworn in on September 26, 1972, alongside Gerald Edds and Chalmer Embry, the board's two other new members.

Charles Boteler was elected administrative vice president of the newly renamed Associated Student Government for 1972-73, the first year the vice presidency was split in two under a revised constitution; Boteler held the administrative half while Mike Fiorella, later that year's student regent, held the activities half. Boteler was also prominent in campus electoral politics that year. The 1973 Talisman records him co-leading, with Pat Long, the student effort behind George McGovern's 1972 presidential campaign at Western, running a voter-registration drive and organizing for the Warren County Democratic caucus. He served as an alternate delegate pledged to McGovern at the Democratic National Convention, and helped lead a McGovern-Shriver teach-in on the Vietnam War alongside faculty members Jim Wayne Miller and Nick Kafoglis.

Pat Newton served as treasurer of the Associated Student Government for 1972-73, under the constitution that remade the Congress to include ten representatives at large and two from each academic college alongside the class officers and Academic Council delegation. The 1973 Talisman's Who's Who feature profiles Newton separately from her ASG role: an accounting and economics major, she was a member of the business games team and was named to Who's Who Among Student Leaders of America. She also served as both treasurer and president of Alpha Delta Pi sorority.
holdings.source: 1973 Talisman, Associated Students, and Who's Who, p. 227

holdings.what_they_did: Debby Clark served as secretary of the Associated Student Government for 1972-73, the year the body adopted that name in place of the earlier Office of Associated Students, under president Ed Jordan alongside vice presidents Charles Boteler and Mike Fiorella and treasurer Pat Newton.

This archive's leader record names Michael Fiorella only as the 1972-73 student regent, but the sources say he held both offices at once. The 1973 Talisman states that the newly revised ASG constitution created two vice presidents, one for administrative duties and one for activities, and that Charles Boteler and Mike Fiorella held them respectively; the Herald of 1 September 1972 likewise calls him vice president for activities, and the 1974 Talisman says he was elected ASG activities vice-president in his junior year and was also student regent. As activities vice president he headed the Activities Committee, which the 1973 Talisman credits with the greatest number of nationally known groups yet booked at Western, naming Chicago, Jethro Tull and the Beach Boys among five concerts that year. The same volume records him arguing for a higher student activity fee than the $1.50 a semester then charged. Fiorella went on to the voting student seat on the Board of Regents that year; the 1973 Talisman's own account of how he came to hold it is not fully consistent, crediting his selection in one place to Ed Jordan's disqualification as an out-of-state student and in another to election by the student body. He was sworn in on 26 September 1972.
holdings.source: 1973 Talisman, Associated Students, pp. 74-75, and Profile, p. 237

holdings.what_they_did: Don Carter chaired the ten-member Judicial Council in 1972-73, the body Associated Student Government used as its final court for appeals of campus rule violations, including parking tickets, dorm-campusing penalties and election disputes. The 1973 Talisman, describing the council's work that year, notes that student rights on campus were also handled through disciplinary boards set up in each residence hall to rule on in-hall cases. The archive has found no further record of Carter's time in office.

Congress unanimously elected Pat Long parliamentarian at its first meeting of the 1972-73 year, 31 August 1972; the Herald described him as a senior speech major from Franklin, Ohio. The 1973 Talisman also names him, together with Gary Whitfield, as head of the Legal Rights Committee, which worked on a bail-bond fund for arrested students, on the appeal of the 'Fly' movie-censorship case, and pressed the university over the expulsion of students charged but not convicted of drug violations. Long had run for ASG president that spring and lost. A 31 March 1972 Herald feature profiled him under the headline "Pat Long: Activism is Associated Student Government," and on election day the paper urged support for Ed Jordan over him, while a student action group declined to endorse Long. Jordan won and served as president for 1972-73, the year Long instead held the parliamentarian post and the Legal Rights co-chairmanship. That same spring, Long and Charles Boteler led a group of Western students into the McGovern-for-president campaign, running a voter-registration drive and taking part in the Warren County Democratic caucus that chose delegates to the party's national convention; the 1973 Talisman later names Long president of Western's Young Democrats club. Long ran for ASG president again in April 1973, one of four candidates -- with Henry Davis, Mike Fiorella and Steve Yater -- whose platforms the Herald covered that spring. Yater won and served as president for 1973-74. The archive has found no further record of Long's activity in student government after that election.
holdings.source: Herald 52:3, 1 Sep 1972, 'New appointments win ASG approval'

holdings.what_they_did: Louis Berman was elected freshman-class representative at large in fall 1971, one of five officers chosen at the class's first meeting. The following spring he was elected sophomore class president, a post that under ASG's constitution carried an automatic Congress seat; Congress then approved him as sergeant-at-arms on 31 August 1972, in the same vote that made Pat Long parliamentarian. A Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity brother, the 1973 Talisman's chapter page lists 'ASG Sargeant-at-Arms Louis Berman' among its members' honors that year, and its class-of-1974 section, headlined 'Louis Berman Led Sophomores During a Quiet Year,' names him sophomore class president alongside vice-president Michael Inman. The archive has found no further record of his time in the post.
holdings.source: Herald 52:3, 1 Sep 1972, 'New appointments win ASG approval'

holdings.what_they_did: Congress approved R. G. Meade as chairman of the Rules and Elections Committee at its first meeting of the 1972-73 year, 31 August 1972; in the same issue, speaking as co-chairman, he told the Herald that filing was so thin that four colleges had only one candidate each running for their Academic Council seats. The 1973 Talisman describes the committee, headed by Meade and Fred Price, as the body that set campaign guidelines and heard election disputes, and says it drew particular attention that autumn over a disputed Homecoming Queen election and re-election. The Herald itself is inconsistent on his name, printing him as both R. G. Meade and Robert Meade in stories from the same page; the archive keeps both spellings rather than silently choosing one.
holdings.source: Herald 52:3, 1 Sep 1972, 'New appointments win ASG approval'

holdings.what_they_did: Joe Cheak chaired ASG's Environmental Committee in 1972-73, which the 1973 Talisman calls the year's most notable achievement in student services: the committee's first year of active involvement in campus ecology. ASG's own newsletter of 3 November 1972 names Cheak committee chairman and reports he had already proposed to the university's Physical Plant that it supply containers for a campus paper-recycling drive; the newsletter's January 1973 issue records that the first two weeks of collection brought in more than a ton and a half of material, mostly newsprint, before the project nearly collapsed when the paper company that had agreed to buy it, the Alton Box Board Co., could not collect it. The Talisman adds that the committee went on to add can and bottle recycling, with proceeds funneled back into expanding the program, and that ASG separately began researching banned toys sold by local merchants toward organizing a Kentucky Student Public Interest Research Group. Cheak also represented the senior class in the Associated Student Congress that year as its vice president, alongside class president Terry Miller; the 1973 Talisman notes the two felt their main duty was representing the class in Congress, and that beyond sponsoring a Homecoming queen candidate the class held no other activities that year. In April 1973 Cheak wrote to the Herald praising outgoing president Ed Jordan. A Herald story from the same autumn also lists a 'Joe Cheek' among ten members approved to the Rules and Elections Committee; the archive does not reconcile the two spellings.
holdings.source: ASG Newsletter, Vol. 1 No. 1, 3 Nov 1972 (WKU SGA collection)

holdings.what_they_did: The 1973 Talisman names Gary Whitfield, together with Pat Long, as head of ASG's Legal Rights Committee in 1972-73 -- the yearbook uses the word 'headed' rather than a formal title. The committee worked to set up a bail-bond fund for students who were arrested and pressed the university over three issues: the expulsion of students charged but not convicted of drug violations, the refusal to show X-rated films in the student center, and the appeal of the 'Fly' movie-censorship case. The archive has found no further record of Whitfield's time in office.

Gail Emberton was elected junior class vice-president for 1972-73, serving under president Fred Price. The 1973 Talisman recorded that the revised Associated Students constitution had cut the class slate to two officers, and that the class's Homecoming float, entered with Debby Clark as its queen candidate, won the Red Towel Award. The class also planned a dinner for its active members. The 1974 Talisman named her to Who's Who among students, listing her as personnel chairman of Chi Omega, 1972-73 junior class vice-president, first runner-up in the Miss Three Alarm contest, and a President's Scholar. A Gail Emberton bylined Herald housing and academic-affairs reporting through the same year, from dormitory occupancy in January 1973 to the Housing Committee's proposed policy revisions on 1 May. The archive has not confirmed from any source that the reporter and the class vice-president are the same person, and records the byline without asserting it.

Michael Inman entered the Associated Students Congress by the class-officer route. The 1973 Talisman records the sophomore class electing Louis Berman president and Inman vice-president the previous spring, and the same volume's account of the revised constitution places class presidents and vice-presidents on the roll of Congress with a vote. The yearbook's account of the class year is thin: a large class that took part in few class projects and put its effort into a single Homecoming queen candidate, Elaine Leftwich. Later volumes give his home as Harrodsburg.

Terry Miller held class office in two consecutive years. The 1972 Talisman lists him as junior class vice-president for 1971-72, one of five class officers headed by president Ed Jordan, who became Associated Students president the following year; that volume says the class structure carried no separate power of its own and left its officers to direct their attention at the A.S. Congress. For 1972-73 Miller was elected senior class president, with Joe Cheak as vice-president. The 1973 Talisman recorded that the number of class officers had been cut to two that year, and that Miller and Cheak understood their responsibility as representing the class in the Associated Students Congress; the yearbook reported that class activity was otherwise nil, the only class project being to sponsor Lee Davis as a Homecoming queen candidate.

holdings.office: junior class president; co-head, Rules and Elections Committee
holdings.what_they_did: Fred Price was elected junior class president for 1972-73 with Gail Emberton as vice-president. The 1973 Talisman noted that under the revised Associated Students constitution only the top two class officers were retained, and that class presidents and vice-presidents had previously been allowed to vote in Congress. The yearbook recorded the class's Homecoming float as winner of the Red Towel Award, with Debby Clark as its queen candidate. The same yearbook recorded the Rules and Elections Committee, which handles campus elections and hears election disputes, as headed by R. G. Meade and Fred Price. That committee was tested in the first week of November 1972, when a voting discrepancy forced a special election for Homecoming queen; the Herald of 4 November 1972 carried the story alongside an item headlined that Fred Price said the committee would investigate the election. Price stood for Associated Student Government administrative vice president in the spring of 1973. The Herald of 6 April 1973 printed the platforms of the two hopefuls for the office, Glenn Jackson and Fred Price. Jackson took the post for 1973-74. The 1973 Talisman pictures Price in the Pi Kappa Phi colony, and the 1974 volume records the chapter receiving its national charter with Price still a member.
holdings.source: 1973 Talisman, Classes (Juniors), p. 397, and Student Government section

holdings.office: Academic Council representative, College of Education
holdings.what_they_did: The 1973 Talisman recorded Carl Stoltzfus as a member of the Associated Students Government, the student member of the Academic Council from the College of Education, and a member of both the College of Education Curriculum Committee and the University Academic Complaint Committee. He and fellow Sigma Phi Epsilon member Mike Brandenberg represented their fraternity at the National Leadership Methods Convention. The 1974 volume gives his home as Cochranville, Pennsylvania, and his major as elementary education. The Herald of 13 April 1973, the issue that carried the Associated Student Government election returns and a report on the installation of officers at the Congress party, printed a letter under his name headlined as thanking his supporters. The archive has not read the letter and cannot say whether he had stood, or for what office. For 1973-74 he was elected senior class president, with Hamp Moore as vice-president; the 1974 Talisman recorded the pair supervising the class's Homecoming activities and its Gone with the Wind float. That yearbook also listed him as chairman of the Associated Student Government's Rules and Elections Committee, public relations chairman of the Student National Education Association, Talisman Greek editor and a member of Who's Who. The archive holds his surname in two spellings. Every appearance in the 1973 and 1974 Talisman — the fraternity pages, the Who's Who entry, the senior class pages and both name indexes — gives Stoltzfus, as does the Herald's index of his own 4 December 1973 letter. The single Stolzfus is the Herald's index of his letter of 13 April 1973, which is the spelling the 1972-73 Congress record was built on. The difference is flagged, not resolved.

Ronda Talley sat in the Associated Students Congress in 1972-73 as the student representative from the College of Education. The 1973 Talisman recorded that she had been voted a representative to the Congress and named to the 1972 edition of Who's Who in American Colleges and Universities, one of two Kappa Delta members tapped that year. The same yearbook recorded her other campus work: membership of Kappa Delta, the Student National Education Association and Lambda Chi Alpha's Crescent Club, which named her its 1972 Outstanding Crescent Girl. She was also one of the student contributors listed on the 1973 Talisman staff page. The yearbook's own pages spell the name two ways: Ronda in the Kappa Delta and Who's Who sections and in the name index, Rhonda in the Crescent Club caption and the Talisman staff list. The archive keeps the spelling its source used and flags the difference rather than settling it.

Pages 264-265 of the 1973 Talisman; the same page notes Ed Jordan was ASG president that year, which matches the archive's 1972-73 entry. The 1971 Talisman index has him as 'Daniel, Larry Wayne'. The colleague's coding of 1975 is wrong; his degree year is 1973 and the evidence is 1972-73.
holdings.source: The 1973 Talisman's Alpha Gamma Rho spread says five of the fraternity's members were 'involved in the Associated Student Government Congress' that year and captions a photograph 'Larry Daniel appears to be deep in'…

holdings.what_they_did: The 1973 Talisman's Who's Who feature profiles her as a senior history and economics major from Cincinnati and records her membership of the Associated Students and its academic council. The feature names no office, so the seat records the yearbook's own wording. The 1971 Talisman carries her as Susan Gayle Stuebing of Cincinnati.
holdings.source: The 1973 Talisman's Who's Who feature (p. 223) profiles her as Sue Stuebing and says: "This senior history and economics major from Cincinnati has been a member of the Associated Students and its academic council, the"…

holdings.what_they_did: Steve Yater led the Associated Student Government through 1973-74. Early in his term he publicly commended the Board of Regents in the Herald, weeks after the board had increased ASG's budget allotment. Yater's win was reported in the Herald's 13 April 1973 election returns; the same issue profiled him as making a good impression in his first contact with Congress and stressing a calm approach to the office. Carter Pence's companion article covered new officers being installed at a Congress party the same week, though the archive index does not yet name who besides Yater took office. In April 1974, stung by election-season criticism, President Yater defended his administration in a letter to the Herald. His final weeks in office stayed argumentative: the Herald of April 30 carried dueling letters under the heading 'Linda Jones vs. Steven Yater' as the student regent race closed out the year. The Herald's own retrospective on his term, by Al Cross, ran 16 April 1974 under the headline 'Presidency Ends for Steve Yater; One Major Program Started' - the archive does not yet hold the article's text, only its headline crediting his administration with a single major accomplishment.

Glenn Jackson was elected administrative vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1973-74, serving under president Steve Yater alongside activities vice president Tom LaCivita, treasurer Lee Goodpaster and secretary Pam Stewart. Jackson was the executive branch's public spokesman for a reorganization of ASG's committee system, which the Herald reported him introducing in the Congress that October and again as formal legislation in January 1974. The 1974 Talisman quotes him saying the old, more numerous committee structure was too rigid, that ideas often fitted no existing committee, and that the result left some committees with nothing to do and others overloaded; the reorganization folded ASG's programs into two broader areas, student affairs and academic affairs. Jackson also coordinated ASG's free university program that year, begun the previous spring, and said afterward that a lack of student interest and difficulty finding people to teach the non-credit courses were its main problems.

Lee Goodpaster served as treasurer of the Associated Student Government for 1973-74 under president Steve Yater, one of the five-member executive branch shown in the year's officer photograph and meeting caption alongside Yater, Tom LaCivita, Glenn Jackson and Pam Stewart. The 1974 Talisman's Who's Who feature profiles Goodpaster separately: an accounting major, she was a member of Alpha Xi Delta sorority and an Alpha Tau Omega Little Sister. The following year's Talisman records that she received Alpha Xi Delta's Frances C. Bloker Pledge Trainer Award at the sorority's national convention in Chicago.
holdings.source: 1974 Talisman, Associated Student Government, p. 56, and Who's Who, p. 95

holdings.what_they_did: Pam Stewart served as secretary of the Associated Student Government for 1973-74 under president Steve Yater. The 1974 Talisman lists her in the year's executive officer roll and pictures her in a meeting caption alongside Yater, activities vice president Tom LaCivita, administrative vice president Glenn Jackson and treasurer Lee Goodpaster.

Thomas LaCivita was elected activities vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1973-74 in what the 1974 Talisman calls one of the most controversial elections in the school's history, serving under president Steve Yater alongside administrative vice president Glenn Jackson, treasurer Lee Goodpaster and secretary Pam Stewart. He was re-elected to the post for 1974-75, one of the few ASG officers of the decade to serve two consecutive years; that second term is recorded under his 1974-75 entry. Early in his first year LaCivita clashed publicly with Ron Beck, the assistant dean of student affairs who administered concert bookings through ASG. LaCivita charged that Beck put too little creativity into the entertainment program, did not weigh LaCivita's opinions, and did not keep up with the music scene; he also argued that concerts should be advertised beyond Bowling Green to draw more ticket revenue. Beck, who at first declined to respond to the specific charges, said cost, student appeal and any tendency of an act to encourage drug use were what determined which acts were booked, telling the Herald's reviewer, 'If I haven't heard of a group, they won't go on this campus.' The dispute eased as the year went on, and the two ran an entertainment program that turned a profit after a rocky start.

Robert Deboe, a brother of Alpha Phi Alpha fraternity, served on Associated Student Government's Judicial Council in 1973-74. The 1974 Talisman's fraternity page named him among the chapter's outstanding brothers, reporting he had been elected to Who's Who Among Students in American Universities and Colleges; the same volume's Zeta Phi Beta sorority page separately records him as that chapter's "Mr. Omega Delta" that year, an honor unconnected to Alpha Phi Alpha. A Robert Deboe had been approved to Congress's Rules and Elections Committee at its first meeting of the year, 31 August 1972, as the Herald reported the following day; the archive has not confirmed this is the same man rather than a returning member from the prior Congress.

holdings.office: representative in the Associated Student Government and on the Academic Council
holdings.what_they_did: Melody Edwards, an agriculture major, was recorded by the 1974 Talisman as a representative in the Associated Student Government and on the Academic Council, and was named to Who's Who. The same entry has her holding that involvement was worth having so long as it stayed moderate. Her other recorded campus work was in her field: she belonged to the Agriculture Club, whose Halloween carnival in 1972 the yearbook credited her with supplying its Great Pumpkin, and to the Agricultural Education Club. Her Who's Who entry argued that agriculture was changing fast and had room for men and women alike.

Debbie Filburn sat in the Associated Student Government Congress as a representative-at-large in 1973-74; the 1974 Talisman named her among the Kappa Delta members who had distinguished themselves on campus, in that office. She had been a student contributor to the 1973 Talisman the year before. The 1975 Talisman recorded that two sisters, Donna and Debbie Filburn, were both in the Associated Student Government. They are two people, and the archive records them separately: Donna Filburn sat in the 1974-75 Congress and was Panhellenic Council president.

holdings.office: ASG representative from the Graduate College
holdings.what_they_did: Resigned from Congress in protest in the section covering 1973-74, having asked for better representation for minority groups in student government and the Academic Council; the text says he argued the lack of black and foreign students in those bodies was harmful to both minorities and the University. His prior 1971-72 Associated Students vice-presidency is not sourced to this citation.

The Sophomores section says active class members included seven sophomores who were members of the ASG congress, and names Steve Henry as class president in text and in a photo caption of Henry and Jeff Wampler checking notes before an ASG meeting.

Michael Inman moved up from sophomore class vice-president to junior class president for 1973-74, with Deborah Locke as vice-president. The 1974 Talisman recorded the pair coordinating the class's activities, which included a Fiddler on the Roof float in the Homecoming parade and a spring dance. He was also a junior ROTC student, photographed by the yearbook helping to ease traffic and assist visiting families as students converged on campus at the start of the year. In April 1974 the Herald ran the contest for the student seat on the Board of Regents over four issues. The issue of 19 April, whose lead reported that five students had filed for the seat, printed a letter under his name headlined "Inman Announces". The archive has not been able to read the letter and cannot say what he announced or whether he was one of the five.

John Donofrio, Jr. was elected freshman class president for 1973-74, with Christy Kay Vogt as vice-president. The 1974 Talisman headed its account of the class "Donofrio and Vogt lead freshman class" and recorded their first major project as a Homecoming float on the theme of Camelot, with Marcia Heckman as the class's queen candidate and a concert-dance planned for the spring. The pair were photographed in the Helm library. His vice-president that year went on to be administrative vice president of the Associated Student Government in 1975-76 and its president in 1976-77, under the name Christy Vogt.

Deborah Locke was elected junior class vice-president for 1973-74, serving with president Michael Inman; the 1974 Talisman recorded the two coordinating the class's Homecoming float and a planned spring dance, and named her among the Kappa Delta members who had distinguished themselves on campus.

Hamp Moore was elected senior class vice-president for 1973-74 under president Carl Stoltzfus. The 1974 Talisman recorded the two supervising the class's Homecoming activities, including its Gone with the Wind float, and listed Moore among the seniors receiving outside honours that year as vice-president of the Southeast Regional Inter-Fraternity Conference. He was a member of Sigma Alpha Epsilon and appears in the yearbook at that fraternity's signing of its scroll before the run to Middle Tennessee, alongside university president Dero Downing. He appears to have been a candidate in the April 1974 election for the student seat on the Board of Regents. The Herald printed letters endorsing him in two of the four issues that covered the race — from Bruce Merrick on 19 April, the issue whose lead reported that five students had filed, and from Gail Getchell on 23 April, the issue in which the candidates listed their qualifications — alongside parallel endorsements of Hank Miles. No source the archive has read names the field outright, and the seat went to Greg McKinney, whom the Herald of 26 April reported vying for the post with Sid Stevens.

His Who's Who entry (no. 16) says he was president of the senior class, a member of the Associated Student Government, a participant in the Academic Council, a member of the Pi Sigma Alpha Government fraternity and Greek editor of the yearbook. The Sigma Phi Epsilon chapter page separately says he was senior class president, chairman of the Rules and Election Committee of the ASG, Talisman Greek editor, and a member of the University Academic Complaint Committee and of Who's Who.
holdings.source: 1974 Talisman, Who's Who no. 16 and Greeks (Sigma Phi Epsilon)

holdings.what_they_did: Named as freshman class vice-president alongside President John Donofrio, Jr. The claim about her 1974-75 representative-at-large seat and January 1975 resignation is not sourced to this citation and is flagged as recorded under that later year, not this one.

Jeff Wampler was elected sophomore class vice-president for 1973-74, serving under president Steve Henry. The 1974 Talisman recorded that seven sophomores sat in the Associated Student Government Congress that year, and photographed the two class officers checking notes before an Associated Student Government meeting; the class's executive committee had tentatively planned a free dance for the spring. The 1976 volume gives him as a pre-med major from Jeffersontown.

Jan Clark was elected a representative for their college in the Associated Students Government elections reported on Alpha Xi Delta's chapter page in the 1974 Talisman, which names them alongside Lee Goodpaster's election as treasurer. Goodpaster served as treasurer through 1973-74. The page does not name the college, and no further record of the term has been found.
holdings.source: 1974 Talisman, Greeks (Alpha Xi Delta chapter page)

holdings.what_they_did: Susan Hahn was elected a representative for their college in the Associated Students Government elections reported on Alpha Xi Delta's chapter page in the 1974 Talisman, which names them alongside Lee Goodpaster's election as treasurer. Goodpaster served as treasurer through 1973-74. The page does not name the college, and no further record of the term has been found.
holdings.source: 1974 Talisman, Greeks (Alpha Xi Delta chapter page)

Goodpaster served as treasurer through 1973-74. The page does not name the college, and no further record of the term has been found.

The archive separately records a Jennifer Rapp among the same sorority's Associated Student Government representatives the following year, in the 1975 Talisman.
holdings.source: 1974 Talisman, Greeks (Alpha Xi Delta chapter page)

holdings.what_they_did: Shrewsbury was described as active in the Associated Student Government in the 1974 Talisman's Who's Who profile of her, which also records a Board of Regents scholarship, Chi Omega and the Talisman staff. The profile gives no office or committee. The archive separately records an Evie Shrewsbury as a graduate college representative in the 1974-75 Congress, pictured at an ASG meeting in the 1975 Talisman.

Siwicki sat on the Associated Students Publicity Committee in 1973-74, according to the 1974 Talisman's Who's Who profile of her, a textile and clothing merchandising major who was also in Alpha Xi Delta and the Home Economics Club. No further record of her committee work has been found.

Gregory McKinney came to campus prominence as a speaker: in March 1974 the Herald reported him winning top honors in competition. That spring McKinney ran for the student seat on the Board of Regents against Sid Stevens, the two candidates' final appeals running side by side in the Herald as an editorial called the race a clear choice for voters. McKinney won the seat and was sworn in on June 19, 1974, becoming WKU's first African American student regent. Midway through the fall 1974 semester, Herald writer Al Cross profiled the new regent under the headline 'Greg McKinney Feels Regents Can Aid Western's Progress,' as McKinney settled into his seat on the Board of Regents. As the academic year closed, the Herald reported 'Student Regent Greg McKinney Calls Year Rewarding,' in the same issue that covered the regents approving a record budget and academic proposals. After his term as student regent, McKinney stayed on at WKU as a graduate assistant in Student Affairs. The university's own file on him, opened in 1983, holds correspondence between McKinney and President Donald Zacharias and a paper he wrote titled "Student Affairs: An Analysis" - the record of a former student regent moving into the administration whose board he had once sat on.

Jeff Consolo won the Associated Student Government presidency in the March 1974 election on a ticket with Steve Henry, in a cycle whose primary the Herald said showed Greek influence. Taking office, Consolo told the Herald he hoped for increased student involvement during his term. Consolo's term closed on April 15, 1975, when new ASG officers were installed at the day's meeting after a spring in which his congress had simplified election procedures and wound down its concert program. Jeffrey Paul Consolo, of Mansfield, Ohio, served as the ninth president of WKU's Associated Student Government for the 1974-75 term, according to the SGA's own roster of former presidents. Early in the fall 1974 semester, Consolo appointed eight students to seats in the ASG congress, reported by Jim Reynolds under the headline 'Jeff Consolo Tabs Eight for Congress.' In early April 1975, as the polls prepared to open to elect his successor, the Herald ran 'Jeff Consolo Notes Progress in His Term' alongside items crediting ASG moves with cutting bookstore prices, gaining parking board input and folding the Volunteer Bureau into the organization.

Paul Nation was administrative vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1974-75 under President Jeff Consolo. The 1975 Talisman's Greek pages record him in the post, and at the close of the year Consolo, crediting each of his officers by name, named Nation first and said all four officers had done a good job.

Ricky Johnson was treasurer of the Associated Student Government for 1974-75. A photograph caption in the 1975 Talisman shows him with activities vice president Tom LaCivita discussing the signing of the rock band War and the Charlie Daniels Band for a Western concert. A Rickie Johnson appears on the ASG Congress attendance roll the 1976 Talisman printed, so he may have stayed active in Congress after his term as treasurer ended, though the spelling differs between the two volumes and the identification is not certain.

Cindy Kirkpatrick was secretary of the Associated Student Government for 1974-75. The 1975 Talisman photographs her checking meeting notes as President Jeff Consolo conferred with Panhellenic Council president Donna Filburn. The 1974 Talisman, covering the year before her term as secretary, already shows her in conversation with activities vice president Tom LaCivita and Vice President for Academic Affairs Dr. John Minton, suggesting she was involved with ASG before she took office.

Thomas LaCivita, elected unopposed to a second consecutive term as activities vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1974-75, chaired the ASG Activities Committee on a roughly $42,000 entertainment budget, of which $27,000 went toward two free concerts. His full account, including the 1973-74 dispute with assistant dean of student affairs Ron Beck over concert booking, is recorded under his first term the year before. After students picketed the poorly received Doc Severinsen Homecoming concert on 11 October 1974, a newly formed Student Action Committee pressed to give LaCivita more say in negotiating with prospective acts; he absorbed the committee into his own rather than cede ground, though Kentucky law kept the activities vice president's role advisory, since a student could not control university funds outright. When a booked Al Stewart mini-concert fell through after Stewart's United States tour was cancelled under immigration law, LaCivita booked the New York hard rock group Kiss to replace him. President Jeff Consolo credited LaCivita afterward with running a more diversified entertainment series that year.

Stan McDivitt was elected to the Associated Student Government Congress, the 1975 Talisman's Sigma Alpha Epsilon chapter pages record, alongside fraternity brother Steve Henry, who went on to be ASG president in 1975-76.

Marc Levy served as an ASG Congress member in 1974-75 and again in 1975-76, and was one of the Herald's most frequent student critics through both years, writing letters attacking Associated Student Government, the Herald itself, the Academic Council and the ASG constitution in issue after issue. In a letter printed in the Herald of 4 October 1974, Levy wrote that he had hoped the year's meetings would differ from what he called the previous year's "invisible congress." He reported that a roll call at the meeting of 1 October 1974 showed a good number of members missing, and that three of the four committee reports were delivered by president Jeff Consolo himself rather than by the committee chairs. In the fall of 1975 Levy brought a complaint against ASG treasurer David Payne over spending ahead of budget approval. The Judicial Council heard the case and cleared Payne of fund misuse, reported in the Herald's 21 November 1975 issue (51:25) under the headline "Judicial Council Clears David Payne of Fund Misuse"; the same issue separately reported Levy had been picked "top legislator" at a recent intercollegiate meeting, without the archive confirming which one.

ASG president Jeffrey Consolo appointed Vern Pulman a representative-at-large in February 1975, filling one of two Congress seats left vacant by Christy Vogt's resignation. The Herald reported the appointment in the same issue that covered the treasurer's budget presentation to Congress. The archive has found no further record of Pulman's time in the seat.
holdings.source: Herald 50:35, 7 Feb 1975, 'ASG congress hears treasurer's budget explanation'

holdings.what_they_did: Beverly Davenport, an Alpha Delta Pi sorority member, served as an ASG Congress representative-at-large in 1974-75, per the 1975 Talisman. In February 1975 the Herald reported she was one of two students appointed to the university's Complaint Committee, alongside fellow student Suzanne Held and assistant professor Ray Biggerstaff of the health and safety department. No further record of her ASG term survives in this archive.
holdings.source: 1975 Talisman, Alpha Delta Pi; Herald 50:35, 7 Feb 1975

holdings.what_they_did: Vogt sat in the ASG Congress in 1974-75 and resigned from it on 28 January 1975. The Herald reported that both the student affairs chairpersonship and a representative-at-large seat were vacated by her resignation and were filled the following week by presidential appointment. She returned the next year as administrative vice president, and the archive already records that term.
holdings.source: Herald 50:35, 7 Feb 1975, 'ASG congress hears treasurer's budget explanation'

holdings.what_they_did: The 1975 Talisman records Ballance as a sophomore class officer who held a seat on the student government, and quotes her arguing that an office amounting to building a float was not worth having and that two people could not represent a whole class. She favoured a student government made up only of representatives from the individual colleges.

holdings.office: representative for the College of Business and Public Affairs
holdings.what_they_did: The 1975 Talisman records Berry founding the Student Volunteer Bureau, which weakened for want of funds and administrators, and then approaching ASG president Jeff Consolo about folding it into ASG; the merger passed at the last meeting of the autumn semester by better than 80 per cent. A Lambda Chi Alpha chapter page in the same volume records him as having set up the bureau and served on student government.
holdings.source: 1975 Talisman, Associated Student Government section; Greeks (Lambda Chi Alpha)

holdings.what_they_did: A Lambda Chi Alpha chapter page in the 1975 Talisman records Blair as serving on student government alongside Rodney Berry and Frank Medaris, and the senior directory gives his home as Bellbrook, Ohio. The volume confirms ASG membership but does not say which seat he held.
A Sigma Nu chapter page in the 1975 Talisman records Calico as a representative-at-large to the student government.

An Alpha Xi Delta chapter page in the 1975 Talisman names DeJarnette, Mary Pat Swift, Jennifer Rapp and Debbie Johnson as representatives for the Associated Student Government. The page confirms ASG membership but does not say which seat she held.

The 1975 Talisman pictures Draheim and Jo Ann Ballance, the sophomore class officers, comparing notes at an ASG meeting, under a caption saying that holding seats in the student government, rather than leading the class, was the main function of class officers.

A Kappa Delta chapter page in the 1975 Talisman records the sisters Donna and Debbie Filburn as both serving in the Associated Student Government, and Donna as Panhellenic president. A separate caption in the same volume names her Panhellenic Council president, conferring with ASG president Jeff Consolo.
holdings.source: 1975 Talisman, Greeks (Kappa Delta); Associated Student Government section

holdings.office: representative for the College of Applied Arts and Health
holdings.what_they_did: Her Who's Who entry in the 1975 Talisman records the Lexington senior as a representative-at-large and a representative for the College of Applied Arts and Health in ASG, and as having served a term as president of the Panhellenic Council. The entry does not date the Panhellenic term.

His Who's Who entry in the 1975 Talisman names him a member of the Associated Student Government, along with chairman of the College Republicans, vice-chairman of the Kentucky College Republican Federation and campus coordinator for Marlow Cook's Senate campaign. He was a senior in 1974-75 and does not appear in the April 1974 returns; the entry summarises his career and does not date the term.

Ran on making the dorms more like home. The first of his reforms, passed by ASG in November 1974, provided a method by which residents could obtain change for vending machines, which resident assistants had not been allowed to give out. He suggested increasing the number of class officers while restricting voting rights to the president and vice-president.

holdings.office: elected member of the Associated Student Government
holdings.what_they_did: A Sigma Alpha Epsilon chapter page in the 1975 Talisman records Henry and Stan McDivitt as elected members of the Associated Student Government. He was elected ASG president the following spring and served in 1975-76.
A Sigma Nu chapter page in the 1975 Talisman records Hooks as a representative for Ogden College.

Mike Inman completed three consecutive years in the Associated Student Government Congress by way of class office, elected senior class president for 1974-75 with Pam Stewart as vice-president. The 1975 Talisman recorded that only the two of them attended the meeting called to organise the class's Homecoming contribution, for a class of 1,865, and that they rented the Harrodsburg Heritage mobile history unit rather than build a float. The yearbook printed his own account of why he sought class office: he said it was the easiest route to a seat in the student government. He held the office itself to be of little consequence, since seniors had little class unity by then, and proposed a bill to abolish class officers and create congress representatives for each class instead. Student government president Jeff Consolo opposed the bill. Inman allowed that class officers carried slightly more standing than representatives-at-large, but argued there should be no distinction among members. He was elected to Who's Who and was president of the Omicron Delta Kappa National Leadership Society. He was a member of the Scabbard and Blade military honour corps, and the same page records him as second runner-up for a national scholarship award the yearbook prints as Mayer-Raebum. Asked to name his chief accomplishment from a list that included the presidencies of his junior and senior classes, the vice-presidency of his sophomore class and a series of military science awards, he chose his involvement in ROTC, and said his campus activities had taught him more than his classes.

An Alpha Xi Delta chapter page in the 1975 Talisman names Johnson among the sorority's representatives for the Associated Student Government. The same page separately lists a D. J. Johnson among the members, so the two names should not be treated as one person without a source that links them.

The 1975 Talisman records Keffer and Tom Hayes as holding the only two freshman seats in the student government, and says both held that including class officers in the student government was essential.

The 1975 Talisman records McNally as junior class vice president and quotes her saying students took no interest in class activities and that nobody came when class meetings were called. She argued that ASG needed more representatives-at-large.

A Lambda Chi Alpha chapter page in the 1975 Talisman records him serving on student government with Rodney Berry and Tom Blair, spelling the surname Medaris, which matches the senior directory's Frank C. Medaris, Jr. The page confirms ASG membership but does not say which seat he held.
The 1975 Talisman pictures Miles with Evie Shrewsbury, both graduate students, considering a programme issue at an ASG meeting, under a passage on college representatives conferring at meetings.

An Alpha Kappa Psi chapter page in the 1975 Talisman records Payne, Andrew Carter and Don Colombero as serving on the Associated Student Government. The page does not say which seat he held. He was elected ASG treasurer the following spring and served in 1975-76 and again in 1976-77.

An Alpha Xi Delta chapter page in the 1975 Talisman names Rapp among the sorority's representatives for the Associated Student Government. She does not appear in the April 1974 returns, so any seat was filled later in the year; no second source has been found.
The 1975 Talisman pictures Shrewsbury with Hank Miles, both graduate students, considering a programme issue at an ASG meeting, under a passage on college representatives conferring at meetings.

The 1975 Talisman records Stewart as senior class vice president alongside president Mike Inman, the only two to turn up at the class meeting called to organise Homecoming. The 1974 Talisman separately records her as secretary of the Associated Student Government the year before.
An Alpha Xi Delta chapter page in the 1975 Talisman names Swift among the sorority's representatives for the Associated Student Government. The page does not say which seat she held.

Jeff Wampler was elected junior class president for 1974-75, moving up from the sophomore class vice-presidency, with Karen McNally as his vice-president. The 1975 Talisman recorded that their main function as officers was to attend meetings of the Associated Student Government. The same account recorded both officers saying there was really no need for class officers, even though they had worked hard to get elected. McNally said students took no interest in class activities and that nobody turned up when meetings were called; she offered no remedy beyond adding more representatives-at-large to the Associated Student Government. The judgement matched that of the senior class president the same year, Mike Inman, who put a bill to abolish class officers altogether. The 1976 Talisman, covering his senior year, named him one of four Sigma Alpha Epsilon members elected to Who's Who, and printed his view that students and the administration both had to move toward each other before student apathy about elections and concerts would lift.

Steve Henry appeared in ASG coverage as early as September 1972, when the Herald reported his view that the Associated Student Government had lost respect. Henry won the spring 1974 election on a ticket with Jeff Consolo, and resigned his post running the student discount program after the victory. As president in 1975-76 Henry moved in November to change ASG's concert proposal after a money-losing fall season, while a student group urged support for his energy awareness plan. At year's end the Herald summed up his tenure with a piece on how the role had required balancing the twin jobs of student regent and ASG president, which he held at the same time. A Wikipedia biography of Stephen L. Henry, later the 52nd Lieutenant Governor of Kentucky (1995-2003), describes an orthopedic surgeon and WKU alumnus who was elected Student Body President on his second attempt after an earlier loss, and who sat on the WKU Board of Regents as president - a career arc that lines up point for point with this record's own Herald sourcing, though no WKU archive document has yet been found that states the identification directly.

Before she became administrative vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1975-76, Christy Vogt had already spent two years working her way up through ASG. A Talisman profile of Vogt recorded that she came to Western from Angela Merici High School in Louisville, where she had served four years on student council and been both its vice president and president; as a Western freshman she ran for and won freshman vice president, then as a sophomore was elected an ASG representative-at-large before President Jeff Consolo appointed her student affairs chairman. She ran for administrative vice president with about a week left before the spring 1975 election and won. In office, Vogt ran the book exchange ASG co-sponsored with Veterans on Campus from 12 to 26 January 1976, reporting that the two groups had covered their expenses by 21 January on sales of more than 600 books at a margin of 25 cents a book. She said the year's executive officers were closer than in any administration she had witnessed, crediting President Steve Henry for not minding which officer brought him ideas directly. She told the Talisman there was a 90 percent chance she would run for the ASG presidency in 1976-77; she did, and won. Her term as president is recorded separately, under 1976-77.

David Payne was treasurer of the Associated Student Government for 1975-76, a job he described to the 1976 Talisman as "simple record keeping": reviewing the past year's records, planning a budget, getting it approved, vouching for payments, advising the ASG president on finances and preparing an expenditure report each semester. Congress member Marc Levy brought charges against him that year for spending before budget approval had been given, and appeared twice before the Judicial Council to press the case; Payne argued the ASG constitution provided for such spending, and the council ruled in his favour. Note for the editor: years.json separately carries a David Payne who succeeded Marcel Bush as ASG president in January 1982, filed under 1981-82 (not 1982-83) with year_confidence "corrected" - Board of Regents minutes of 30 January 1982 already confirm that identification, so he is not simply an unresolved name. This Payne was re-elected treasurer for a second term in 1976-77, recorded there. Whether the 1981-82 president is the same person as this 1970s ASG treasurer is not established by any source found so far, and this archive should not merge them without one that links them.

Nancy Wilk was secretary of the Associated Student Government for 1975-76 and kept the attendance roll the 1976 Talisman printed in full, effective 6 April 1976. She explained the rule to the yearbook: a member received a warning after four absences and was automatically removed from Congress after two more. The printed roll named roughly fifty Congress members and marked Mitchell Deep as resigned.

Rick Kelley was activities vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1975-76, the first of two consecutive terms in the office. In October he introduced a bill creating a student activities committee; members were chosen in December from open applications, and the committee ran three subcommittees covering concerts, lectures, and special events and publicity, meant to bring more student input into the entertainment program after controversy over past concert bookings. The 1976 Talisman credits the Homecoming concert by Linda Ronstadt, on 1 November 1975, with a $4,300 profit for ASG, calling it a tremendous financial success that kept ASG in the black; an earlier concert that September by Kenny Loggins and Jim Messina, by contrast, lost about $7,000 to poor attendance. His surname is printed both Kelley and Kelly in the same volume; the spelling is not settled.

Gerard Faulk, an elementary education major, chaired ASG's Judicial Council beginning in 1975-76, a post the Herald reported carried a two-year term running into the 1976-77 session. Six members of Congress moved to impeach him on 16 March 1976 over his handling of two cases before the council: Tom Blair's allegation that president Steve Henry had obstructed an advisory intramurals committee, and Marc Levy's charge that treasurer David Payne had misused funds. Congress held hearings, postponed a vote once, and acquitted Faulk on 6 April 1976. No later report of a successor has been found in this archive.

Jane Anne Coverdale chaired Associated Student Government's Student Discount Service committee in 1975-76. ASG's own Student Insight supplement to the Herald, published 27 April 1976, credited Coverdale and her committee with contracting 29 local business discounts by the end of December 1975; the 1976 discount cards drawing on that work were then mailed to every Western student. The 1976 Talisman's Kappa Delta sorority page separately named Coverdale among the chapter's outstanding members as an Associated Student Government representative and noted she had been elected to Who's Who Among Students in American Universities and Colleges that year.

Christy Vogt entered the spring 1976 Associated Student Government campaign with an endorsement from Herald columnist John Butchko, in an issue whose front section also covered the start of impeachment hearings against congress member Gerard Faulk and an editorial warning the university's new Faculty Senate away from ASG's own troubles. Vogt and Bruce Smith survived the 2 April primary as the Herald reported 527 ballots cast, then Vogt won the presidency outright, the paper reporting the result on 9 April 1976 under the headline "Christy Vogt Wins Election," with her own note of thanks to voters in the same issue - the same week Faulk was acquitted. In office for 1976-77, Vogt's congress created a constitutional revision committee within its first month (Bill 2, 7 September 1976) and kept revision on its agenda all year. It asked the university for a minimum wage policy for student employees (Resolution, 26 October 1976), recommended preregistration for all students, and opposed a proposed tuition increase (Bill 9, 8 March 1977) while creating a Complaint Committee to field student grievances the same meeting. A resolution on discrimination failed in February 1977 with fourteen members abstaining. The fall Seals and Crofts concert lost the organization $3,800, a recurring sore point ASG had wrestled with under Vogt's predecessors as well. Vogt wrote her own case for the office in the Herald - "Urges Involvement," 12 April 1977, days before Bob Moore won the presidency to succeed her by a 26-vote margin. She closed her term on 26 April 1977 with a letter to Congress thanking its members and recommending four items to the administration: constitutional revision, extended hours for student buildings, open visitation, and advance registration - the same four causes her congress had pushed all year. WKU's own archive later indexes her, alongside her maiden name, as Christy Vogt Mollozzi, and separately as Christy Mollozzi in President's Office records tied to Marketing & Promotions - evidence, though not a documented statement, that she went on to a career on the university's own staff.

Tom Blair was elected administrative vice president of the Associated Student Government on 6 and 7 April 1976, beating John David Evans by 570 votes to 552 in one of the closest races that spring; the 1977 Talisman lists him among the year's officers as already having ASG experience. About a year earlier, the Herald's 1 April 1975 issue had reported that Blair wanted a president's council formed, with no indication in the sources checked that he then held ASG office himself. At the 6 April 1976 Congress meeting, before a vote on the impeachment of congressman Gerard Faulk, Blair moved to drop the proceedings without a vote on removal, then withdrew the motion at the urging of several other congressmen. The Herald's 13 April 1976 issue separately reported that Blair withdrew charges he had brought against President Steve Henry; the archive records those charges, one of the two cases behind Faulk's impeachment, as an allegation that Henry had obstructed an advisory intramurals committee. Blair ran for the ASG presidency himself the following April and lost to Bob Moore, 562 votes to 536.

David Payne returned as treasurer of the Associated Student Government for 1976-77, one of two officers, along with activities vice president Rick Kelley, beginning a second consecutive term that year, the 1977 Talisman recorded. Note for the editor: years.json separately carries a David Payne who succeeded Marcel Bush as ASG president in January 1982, filed under 1981-82 (not 1982-83) with year_confidence "corrected" - Board of Regents minutes of 30 January 1982 already confirm that identification, so he is not simply an unresolved name. Whether the 1981-82 president is the same person as this 1970s ASG treasurer is not established by any source found so far, and this archive should not merge them without one that links them.

Pam Keown was elected secretary of the Associated Student Government on 6 and 7 April 1976, beating Sally Chenault by 731 votes to 501. The 1977 Talisman lists her among the year's officers who came into the term with prior ASG experience, though the archive has not established what that earlier role was.

Rick Kelley was re-elected activities vice president of the Associated Student Government on 6 and 7 April 1976, beating Robert Tackett 705 votes to 496 for a second term running Western's concert program. He presided over the 6 April 1976 Congress meeting in President Steve Henry's absence. A 1977 Talisman feature on his two years in the office, published as his term ended, described how Kelley worked with the concert selection committee and assistant dean of student affairs Ron Beck to book acts. When an agent representing Chicago called offering the band for a $25,000 show, Kelley discussed it with Beck, found a private promoter willing to cover the cost, then took the arrangement to the concert committee for approval; the show, a first for Western with a privately promoted act, set an advance-ticket sales record; Kelley said the show sold out of advance tickets and grossed over $50,000, while the Talisman's own concert report noted that the concert itself was not a sellout despite the record advance sales. The Seals and Crofts homecoming concert that same year drew about 5,200 people but lost roughly $3,800, which assistant dean of student affairs Ron Beck attributed to a Saturday date competing with other homecoming events. Kelley told the yearbook that Beck bore the brunt of student criticism over concert choices, and that students who complained about a show rarely wrote in when one succeeded. His surname is printed both Kelley and Kelly across these volumes; the spelling is not settled.

Faulk continued to chair the Judicial Council into 1976-77, the second year of the two-year term the Herald reported he held, having been acquitted that April of an impeachment brought over his handling of two cases before the council. No later report of a successor has been found in this archive.

Mike Pearson chaired ASG's Rules and Elections Committee in 1976-77 and ran the general election that April. Against complaints about long lines at the polls, he told the Herald that no one had been turned away from voting. The archive has found no further record of his time in office.

Carlson was nominated as a delegate to the Associated Student Government's State Student Government Convention delegation at Congress's 22 February 1977 meeting; the minutes name him as the nominee, but the two convention-delegate seats that meeting elected went to Bill Cortus and Kevin Kinnie, so Carlson was not elected, and his Congress membership itself is not established by that source. A Georgiana Carlson appears elsewhere in this record as the losing candidate for ASG treasurer in the April 1977 election and as an organizer of that year's Rules and Elections committee; whether she and this nominee were the same person, or two members of the same family, has not been established.

Cortus gave a Housing Committee report to Congress and was elected one of two delegates to the State Student Government Convention at the 22 February 1977 meeting, though his Congress membership is not conclusively established by that source. The following spring he ran for Activities Vice President and lost to Brent Shockley, 532 votes to 510, in the April 1977 election.

Evans was named on the Associated Student Government's printed Congress attendance roll effective 6 April 1976. The following year, serving on the Student Affairs Committee, he reported the committee's progress to Congress and moved to waive the rules and vote immediately on Bill No. 12, a motion seconded by Tim Leigh that passed 31 to 0 with one abstention at the 19 April 1977 meeting. The 1977 Talisman separately records a John Evans elected to the student affairs committee before the 1976 summer recess. He is not established as the same John David Evans who lost the 1976 election for Activities Vice President to Tom Blair; no source links the two.

Kinnie served in the Associated Student Government Congress across at least three years. In 1976-77 he was nominated and elected one of two delegates to the State Student Government Convention, and seconded Lynn Moss's motion to bring Bill No. 12 to the floor for an immediate vote, which passed 31 to 0 with one abstention at the 19 April 1977 meeting. The 1978 Talisman indexed him, as a Congress representative, under the fuller name Kevin Robert Kinne. By 1980-81 he chaired both the Academic Affairs and the Student Opinion Poll committees, and at Congress's 11 November 1980 meeting moved that the secretary send Congress's official congratulations to Coach Feix and the football team for winning the 1980 Ohio Valley Conference championship; the motion passed.

Leigh was named on the Associated Student Government's printed Congress attendance roll effective 6 April 1976. The following year, serving on the Academic Affairs Committee, he reported for the committee at Congress's 22 February and 19 April 1977 meetings, brought Resolution No. 24 to the floor (seconded by Gene Saunders, passed 34 to 0 with one abstention), and seconded John Evans's motion to waive the rules and vote immediately on Bill No. 12, which also passed. The 1977 Talisman separately records him taking responsibility for the academic affairs committee.
