holdings.what_they_did: Moore was one of four candidates - with Tom Blair, Kirt Grubbs and Mark McChesney - who opened the 1977 Associated Student Government presidential race on April 1. Moore and Blair survived the primary into the general election; McChesney did not, and by April 12 his letter backing Moore ran in the Herald alongside endorsements for the rest of the ticket, as outgoing president Christy Vogt urged students to get involved. The Herald's April 8 issue had set up the contest alongside the treasurer's race between George Carlson and rivals. Moore won on April 15, 1977, by 26 votes over Blair - one of the narrowest presidential margins in the record - in an issue that also carried the faculty asking for a say in hiring and Western fighting a beer licence for a local pizzeria. That October, as president, Moore publicly questioned how freshman candidates in that fall's class elections were spending their campaign money. The comment drew enough pushback that the Herald ran an editorial the same week headlined 'Bob Moore's Comment Isn't Good Politics.' The archive does not yet show what Moore's administration did over the winter and into the spring beyond the ordinary business of readying his succession - see the 1978 election events below. By September 1978, after his term had ended, the Herald reported that Moore had been found ineligible for another Associated Student Government job; the archive does not yet hold the article's account of why.

Cathy Murphy ran for ASG administrative vice president in the April 1977 election and defeated Jim Keffer, 580 votes to 446, to take the office for 1977-78. The Herald's index for 26 September 1975 lists a report headlined "Roger Phelps, Cathy Murphy Elected to Top Freshman Offices," but the archive does not preserve the report itself, and the 1978 Talisman lists two students of that name, so whether the freshman officer and the ASG vice president were the same person is not established. The year before her election she had written for ASG's own Student Insight supplement about the second cheque-cashing centre that outgoing officers Steve Henry and Christy Vogt had obtained for students at the College Heights Bookstore. In office, the 1978 Talisman's yearbook caption for a March 1978 ASG meeting shows her alongside president Bob Moore, activities vice president David Bass and secretary Sharon May at what the caption calls "a light moment"; the same yearbook page identifies her simply as vice president.

Gary Reed was elected ASG treasurer in the April 1977 election, defeating Georgiana Carlson 554 votes to 437, and served through 1977-78. The archive has not turned up further coverage of his time in the office.

Sharon May ran unopposed for ASG secretary in the April 1977 election. The 1978 Talisman names her secretary in its caption to an ASG meeting photograph and separately indexes her, under a fuller form of her name, as Sharon Gay May. The same yearbook's caption for a March 1978 meeting places her at "a light moment" alongside president Bob Moore, vice president Cathy Murphy and activities vice president David Bass.

Brent Shockley, a Scottsville senior studying government, was elected ASG activities vice president in the April 1977 election, defeating Bill Cortus 532 votes to 510. He does not appear in the office in any later source found in this archive: by 24 January 1978 the Herald was naming David Bass as ASG's activities vice president, and this archive has found no report of when or why Shockley left. The 1978 Talisman explains where he went: that spring he was one of 18 university students who served as legislative interns in Frankfort, and he worked for the Legislative Research Commission preparing bill drafts and summaries and tracking where bills stood in the state Senate. "It's tedious and requires a lot of work," he told the yearbook, recalling being handed his own desk on his first day and thinking back to a sixth-grade field trip to the capitol.

David Bass took over as ASG activities vice president after Brent Shockley left the post; the Herald was naming him to the office by 24 January 1978, and the 1978 Talisman also records him in it. He announced that ASG had signed the Atlanta Rhythm Section and Brick for a 14 February 1978 show and said ASG had decided against giving a free concert that spring, spreading its entertainment funds across the season instead and charging students $3.50 for advance tickets to major concerts. He said ASG might stop offering free mini-concerts so it could book better acts, while trying to keep spending on them between $1,500 and $2,500. Bass handled the year's one free show, the Average White Band and Ramsey Lewis Trio concert of 18 April 1978 and drew about 3,300 people. The 1978 Talisman's caption for a March 1978 ASG meeting photograph places him, president Bob Moore, secretary Sharon May and vice president Cathy Murphy together at what it calls "a light moment."

Tricia Cook served as ASG's interim secretary for part of 1977-78; the 1978 Talisman does not say when or why the office became interim. The yearbook records that a College Heights Herald editorial attacking ASG for inaction cited, among its examples, an inner-office joke at a congress meeting declaring the day "Be Kind to Tricia Day" in Cook's honour. Several ASG members told the Talisman afterward that the actions the editorial had listed were not, in fact, laughable.

Bob Tinsley, of Radcliff, chaired ASG's seven-member Judicial Council in 1977-78. On 17 April 1978 the council, hearing more than an hour of testimony and then deliberating privately, rejected Ed Johnson's challenge to Steve Thornton's 72-vote win in that spring's presidential election; the panel deadlocked, and Tinsley, who had not voted on the first ballot, broke the tie in Thornton's favor on the second. The council's report found it could not be shown that enough illegal votes had been cast to change the outcome, and Johnson said he would take the appeal no further. Tinsley was also a member of WKU's Scabbard and Blade military honor society that year and defended the campus Rifle Corps in a Herald letter published 24 January 1978.

holdings.office: Chairman, ASG Rules and Elections Committee
holdings.what_they_did: Gene Saunders chaired ASG's Rules and Elections Committee in 1977-78 and ran the April 1978 election that produced a formal protest: his committee was the first to hear Ed Johnson's complaint that poll workers had campaigned for candidate Steve Thornton by wearing his campaign buttons. Saunders told the Herald he had seen two workers wearing the buttons and told both to remove them, but found no basis for Johnson's complaint and recommended the election be allowed to stand; his committee rejected the protest, and the Judicial Council under Bob Tinsley rejected Johnson's appeal of that decision on 17 April 1978. Saunders had written the Herald repeatedly in the two years before taking the chairmanship: an April 1976 letter accused the paper of 'yellow journalism' in its ASG coverage, a companion letter the same month credited ASG resolutions with securing better intramural facilities, and a January 1977 letter proposed a student survey on dormitory visitation policy.

John Grizzell chaired Associated Student Government's housing committee in 1977-78, during a year the Herald and the 1978 Talisman both covered as a running fight over dormitory rules. The Talisman's ASG section photographed Grizzell in debate with a representative named Brad Ford over ratifying the Student Rights Alliance's petition on dorm rules, a proposal Congress eventually voted to support; one member argued during the debate that recognizing the alliance posed a potential threat to ASG's own housing committee. The same academic year, the Herald covered the wider dorm reform push in headlines like "American Civil Liberties Union Will Investigate Dorm Reform" (Nov. 1977) and "Dorm Reformers Lose Spirit, But Close Doors" (June 1978); ASG itself tabled and later voted on the dorm petition during this period, the same debate in which Grizzell's committee took part.

holdings.what_they_did: Thornton beat Ed Johnson for the Associated Student Government presidency in the 6 April 1978 election, campaigning on his experience; Johnson contested the result, and the ASG Judicial Council denied his appeal on 18 April 1978 after a long debate. In office that fall, Thornton's ASG tabled an open house bill rather than act on it, the Herald reported on 28 September 1978. By January 1979 the government faced a fight to keep control of student activities funding and was pressing for a student seat on a state-level council, both reported in the same 25 January 1979 issue. In March 1979 the Herald reported Thornton and fellow WKU student Terri Craig elected to the executive council of the Student Government Association of Kentucky, a state-level body - the kind of state seat ASG had been pressing for two months earlier. In the last full week of his term, Thornton's ASG approved resolutions on campus housing and parking policy, reported 26 April 1979, the same week voting closed in the election for his successor. The archive does not otherwise show how the January activities-funding fight was resolved, and no further Herald coverage of the Thornton administration has been found before his successor, Jamie Hargrove, was profiled as the new ASG head at the start of the 1979-80 year.

David Young, a representative from Ogden College in 1977-78, ran unopposed for ASG administrative vice president in the April 1978 election. He told the Herald his main goal as an executive officer would be to start a book exchange for students. In office he helped shepherd a new ASG constitution, approved by congress in November 1978 and ratified by the student body at the April 1979 elections, which created 24 separate races for the 24 representative-at-large seats on congress. Young told the 1979 Talisman the change was meant to "force some heads-up competition" between candidates rather than let them run in blocs.

Steve Shipp was one of four ASG executive officers elected unopposed in the April 1978 election; the Herald's results report names him treasurer for 1978-79. The archive has not turned up further coverage of his time in the office.

Alice Wicks ran unopposed for ASG secretary in the April 1978 election. Before the vote she told the Herald she wanted to make students more aware of what ASG actually did, and that she had joined the organization because she wanted to be more involved in student government.

David Carwell was elected ASG activities vice president unopposed in the April 1978 election and put in charge of the year's concerts and lectures, saying he wanted more mini-concerts and fewer large shows. That fall ASG moved to sign the Indianapolis firm Sunshine Promotions as an outside concert promoter; Carwell told the 1979 Talisman that Sunshine met the university's three tests for such a firm, having an office within 500 miles of Western, having promoted at least 75 major concerts, and having grossed at least $2 million on them. Shortly before the 3 November 1978 Player and Exile concert it emerged that the contract with Sunshine had never actually been signed, because the firm balked at a $100,000 performance bond; Sunshine later posted a letter of credit instead. On 7 December 1978 the Herald reported colleagues' claims that Carwell was neglecting an office that carried an $800 salary, saying he had missed five ASG meetings and that lecture committee members and a Herald reporter had been unable to reach him. President Steve Thornton said one more missed meeting would bring him before the executive council to explain himself; Carwell replied that much of his work was done by telephone from home and defended his record. This archive has found no later report of an executive council hearing, of any removal, or of a successor taking the office before the year ended. That spring the Board of Regents voted to move some responsibility for lecture and concert programming out of ASG's hands and into a rebuilt University Center Board, effective that fall.

Victor Jackson, an accounting major from Clarksville, Tennessee, chaired ASG's faculty evaluation committee in 1978-79. That year ASG approved a questionnaire for a student evaluation of the faculty, called the Purdue Cafeteria System, under which instructors chose questions from a list of several hundred, each form built around a set of core questions common to all of them. Jackson said only the core questions would be published, citing printing costs, and put the first year's cost at about $6,500 and about $5,000 a year after; the evaluations were due to begin in fall 1979. Jackson had earlier been the only Black student to run in a campus election for a seat on the Board of Regents' presidential screening committee, an October 1978 vote called after roughly forty Black students, most of them members of the campus NAACP chapter and the United Black Students, asked ASG to secure minority representation on the committee. Two students were to be chosen for the committee in a campus election, and NAACP chapter president Anita Orr said at the October meeting that Jackson had little chance of winning, since minority students made up only about 6.5 percent of the student body. The regents in the end appointed a Black elementary school principal from Russellville and a female WKU associate professor of home economics and family living to the committee, at the request of ASG president and student regent Steve Thornton. The 1979 Talisman also credits Jackson with serving on several ASG committees that year and being, in the words of Herald reporter Tom Beshear, 'very active.'

Bob Moore, who had just finished a one-year term as Associated Student Government president, was nominated and accepted as Judicial Council chairman at ASG's first meeting of the year, 29 August 1978. The Herald reported on 7 September 1978 that the former president had been ruled ineligible for an Associated Student Government job. By the 12 September meeting, an opening for Judicial Council chairman had appeared and Congress confirmed Steve Wilson in the position, 30 votes in favour with 3 abstaining. Neither source explicitly ties the ineligibility ruling to the chairmanship, but the dates align and no other ASG post for Moore is recorded that year, so his tenure as chairman appears to have run under two weeks.

Steve Wilson was confirmed as chairman of Associated Student Government's Judicial Council at the 12 September 1978 Congress meeting, on a vote of 30 in favour with 3 abstaining, after president Steven Thornton announced the position open. The Herald's 14 September 1978 issue reported the appointment under the headline "Judicial Council Chairman Picked." He took the post from Bob Moore, the former ASG president whose brief hold of the chairmanship that same fall is separately recorded; no source connects Moore's departure to the opening Thornton announced. The archive has not turned up further coverage of Wilson's time in the post.

Whether the Senior Class President position was itself a voting Congress seat under the 1978-79 constitution is not established by that minute alone.

Hargrove, a Milton junior, won the ASG presidency in the 17 April 1979 general election, defeating David Young 1,087-535 on a turnout of 1,725 votes. The same day's balloting elected the rest of his executive slate: Steve Fuller administrative vice president, Dean Bates activities vice president, Betty Thompson secretary and Terri Craig treasurer. All five were sworn in at the outgoing Congress's 24 April meeting, where Congress waived its rules so that Hargrove's first act as president, a resolution asking that Helm-Cravens Library stay open longer, could pass unanimously the same night. By August 30, 1979, at the start of the school year, the Herald profiled him - spelled 'Jamie Hargrove' in the byline - under the headline that he believed students were interested. Beyond the executive roster now on record, the archive does not yet show in detail what Hargrove's administration passed or fought over during 1979-80, beyond the record's general sweep of the year. Further Herald issues from the fall and spring semester have not yet been checked.

Fuller was elected Administrative Vice President on 17 April 1979, defeating Tom Jecker, a Louisville senior, 973 votes to 574, the same election that sent Jamie Hargrove to the presidency. At the Congress's 24 April 1979 swearing-in he urged the incoming members to think about which committees they wanted to serve on. He was elected Associated Student Government president the following spring, taking office for 1980-81.

Dean Bates, a junior from Fairport, N.Y., was elected Activities Vice President of Associated Student Government on 17 April 1979, defeating Ben Bratcher of Louisville 785-761, the closest of the year's four executive races. At the 24 April swearing-in he told Congress applications were open for seats on the University Center Board, the body the Board of Regents had handed control of campus entertainment three weeks earlier. In February 1980 the Herald carried a piece under his byline headlined "Coffee House a Success." The 1980 Talisman's senior class listing records him as an environmental engineering technology major from Fairport, N.Y., confirming the hometown given in the election coverage.

Betty Thompson, a junior from Bowling Green, was elected Secretary of Associated Student Government on 17 April 1979, defeating Lynn Driver of Goodlettsville, Tenn., 1,052-517. She signed the minutes of the 24 April 1979 swearing-in meeting in that office.

Terri Craig, a junior from St. Joseph, Ill., was elected Treasurer of Associated Student Government on 17 April 1979, defeating Darell Pierce of Louisville 937-623. Weeks earlier, the Herald had reported that she and Steve Thornton were elected to the Executive Council of the Student Government Association of Kentucky, a statewide body, ahead of her own ASG win. At the 24 April 1979 swearing-in she moved to waive ASG's rules so that newly sworn-in president James Hargrove's first resolution could be voted on immediately, and told Congress she would be drafting the year's budget.

Steve Fuller entered the April 1980 Associated Student Government presidential race against David Rue and Tim Irons; the Herald covered ASG hopefuls debating the issues at an April 3 candidates' forum before reporting the three-way field on April 10. Fuller won the presidency in the April 24 election, reported under the headline "Persistence Pays Off in Steve Fuller Campaign." Mark Wilson and Greg Zoeller were elected to other top ASG offices the same day; Tim Irons's loss was covered separately. Fuller's fall term was consumed by a running fight over dormitory room inspections. A September 4 inspection measure was voted down amid criticism of how the vote was conducted; a September 11 bill calling for a ban on bugs in the dorms drew a mocking editorial cartoon and an editorial calling the university's protective inspection policy unnecessary; and by November 13 the Herald reported ASG had nearly slept through its own vote before re-endorsing inspections, followed a week later by a bill proposing a stricter room-entry rule. In office, ASG under Fuller also proposed a change to the organization's own title in October 1980 and asked the state to evaluate higher education funding in February 1981, as budget worries dominated the legislative session. His successor, Marcel Bush, was elected that April. Fuller entered the Associated Student Government presidential race in the spring of 1980 as one of three candidates. Michele Wood's Herald report was headlined "3 Running for Associated Student Government President," naming Steve Fuller, David Rue and Tim Irons. During the 1980-81 year the Associated Student Government pressed the state on the condition of higher education, with Robert Pillow reporting in February 1981 that the body had asked the state to conduct an evaluation. The request came as the campus argued over budget cuts, including cuts to athletics.

Steve Fuller held the presidency of the Associated Student Government in 1980-81, elected on 24 April 1980 over David Rue and Tim Irons in a race the Herald reported under a headline about persistence paying off; Mark Wilson and Greg Zoeller took the other top offices the same day. He chaired Congress through the year and made its appointments: Jeff Morris and then Kevin Strader as parliamentarian, M. A. Baker, Charles Bussell, Perry Hines and Jim Payne as representatives, Patti Davis and Lonnie Sears as on-campus representatives, and Margaret Ragan to the University Academic Complaint Committee. The 1980 Talisman records that the ASG president was also sworn in as student regent that year, so Fuller sat on the Board of Regents as well. His term was dominated by the fight over dormitory room inspections, which ran from a defeated measure on 4 September 1980 to Congress's approval of stricter room-entry rules on 4 December, and by the state's cuts to higher education: ASG asked the state for an evaluation of higher education in February 1981, and Fuller circulated a petition to Governor John Y. Brown, finance secretary George Atkins and the Council on Higher Education, saying many students did not realise the cuts meant dismissing faculty. He opened the year telling the Herald that ASG wanted a stronger voice in policy making, and spent much of it complaining of the opposite: he was reported disappointed by attendance at his own meetings in October 1980, and the student opinion poll committee's first survey found 29 per cent of students said they would recognise him while 28 per cent thought the university centre director was the ASG president. Marcel Bush succeeded him in April 1981.

Mark Wilson was elected to a top Associated Student Government office on 24 April 1980, reported alongside president-elect Steve Fuller and Activities Vice President-elect Greg Zoeller. ASG's own minutes name him Administrative Vice President giving officer reports in meetings read from 7 October 1980 through 17 February 1981, and record him chairing the Legislative Research committee, one of two committee chairmanships Congress approved by name at the year's first meeting. The 1981 Talisman, which calls him a Shelbyville junior, records Wilson leading the opposition to a resolution by Michael Baker to abolish the dormitory room inspections, warning that if it passed, "individual rights of those living in dorms would be waived." Congress defeated Baker's resolution 16-13, and after the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union moved toward funding a suit over the inspections anyway, defeated a second attempt 24-9, with three abstentions.

Mark Chesnut served as Associated Student Government Treasurer in 1980-81. He was named 'Treasurer Mark Chesnut' reporting the organization's account balances at the 11 November 1980 meeting, and was among the Congress members recorded absent on 17 February 1981, which suggests the treasurer sat in Congress ex officio.

Marsha L. Sanner signed the minutes of every Associated Student Government meeting read in 1980-81 as Secretary — the signature line reads 'Marsha L. Sanner, ASG Secretary' beginning 2 September 1980 — and chaired the Rules and Elections committee, the other of the two committee chairmanships Congress approved by name at the year's first meeting. The 1981 Talisman, which gives her full name as Marsha Lee Sanner and calls her a senior from Orchard Lake, Michigan, pictures her in that year's Associated Student Government group photograph alongside Wilson, Fuller and Zoeller.

Greg Zoeller was elected to a top Associated Student Government office on 24 April 1980 alongside president-elect Steve Fuller and Administrative Vice President-elect Mark Wilson. ASG's minutes name him Activities Vice-President giving officer reports in meetings read from 2 September 1980 through 31 March 1981. The 1981 Talisman quotes a 'concert chairman Greg Zoeller' — matching name, year and activities-related function, though this title sat with the University Center Board rather than ASG's Congress; the identification rests on the matching name and year, not on a source that states the two are the same person — on that year's concert season: Sunshine Promotions' cancellation of its concert contract with Western over the summer, and the three major shows the university put on, the Statler Brothers, Conway Twitty and John Prine. Zoeller called losing the exclusive promoter contract an advantage, since the university could now "do it with any promoter." Near the end of his term, Zoeller wrote a Herald letter on 2 April 1981 headlined 'Marcel Bush Supported,' backing Bush, who had just won that week's ASG presidential primary, to succeed Fuller.

Morris was appointed parliamentarian of the Associated Student Government by President Steve Fuller, with Congress's consent, at the meeting of 7 October 1980. He moved floor motions that same evening, and on 11 November 1980 he reported to Congress on the Big Red mascot costume under old business. Kevin Strader had succeeded him as parliamentarian by the Congress meeting of 20 January 1981; the record does not say why the post changed hands.

Strader was appointed parliamentarian of the Associated Student Government by President Steve Fuller, with Congress's consent, on 20 January 1981, succeeding Jeff Morris. He moved to dispense with the reading of the minutes at that meeting, and moved adjournment on 17 February and 31 March 1981. The 1981 Talisman also profiles a Kevin Strader as president of the Interhall Council, the residence-hall student government, describing its purpose as making "residence halls a better place to live" and crediting the council with sponsoring that year's Parents' Day and Hall Olympics. The yearbook pictures a Kevin Strader in both the Associated Student Government and the Interhall Council group photographs, and its name index carries one person who could be either, entered as Strader, John Kevin. That is circumstantial, and the archive does not confirm that the parliamentarian and the council president were the same man.

Deom, a junior from Boonville, Indiana, was an Associated Student Government member and Judicial Council representative in 1980-81 when he broke with ASG over the university's dormitory room-inspection policy. After Congress defeated a resolution against the inspections 16-13, he contacted the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union and asked it to investigate, and, working with campus KCLU chapter president Michael Taylor, joined the effort to build a broader Bowling Green chapter of the group drawing in non-student residents. ASG did not follow him. After the KCLU took up the matter, Congress defeated a second resolution against the inspections and re-endorsed the university's policy; the 1981 Talisman's own account of the vote is inconsistent, giving the tally as both 24-9, with three abstentions, and separately as 29-4. Administrative vice president Mark Wilson argued in the debate that fire-safety checks should not be equated with search and seizure, and that if the resolution passed, dorm residents' rights would be waived. By February 1982 Deom was no longer on the Judicial Council. The Herald's 4 February 1982 issue carried a letter from him, headlined "Former Judicial Council Member Irked," and two further letters followed in reply: M. A. Baker's "Paul Deom Honorable" on 9 February and Winston Stevenson's "Paul Deom Defended" on 18 February. The archive does not yet hold the text of any of the three, so what exactly was in dispute is not established beyond what the headlines record.

Marcel Bush won the Associated Student Government presidency in April 1981, defeating David Sturgeon after a campaign the Herald said saw candidates "playing big time politics." Close races elsewhere on the ballot prompted recounts. In office that fall, ASG raised its own campaign spending limit and vetoed a plan to pay an education lobbyist, days after rallying publicly for higher education funding. Bush later listed the fall rally as one achievement of his term. Bush resigned the presidency on or shortly before 14 January 1982, reported the same week as the retrospective on his term. David Payne succeeded him; Board of Regents minutes from 30 January 1982 name Payne the new SGA president.

David Payne first appears in the indexed record in February 1981 with a Herald letter titled 'Apathy Erased.' By October 1981, before he held the presidency, he was writing on the Associated Student Government's behalf, declaring that ASG was rallying for higher education as budget cuts loomed. Payne became ASG's president after Marcel Bush resigned on 14 January 1982; Board of Regents minutes from the January 30 meeting name him the new SGA president. In early February the Herald reported that Payne wanted another adviser for ASG, and its editorial page attacked his judgment, while a report the next week said Payne considered certain resolutions misdirected. Later that month, letter writers to the Herald argued that Payne had been made a victim in the affair; the indexed headline does not state what precipitated it. His name does not appear in the indexed headlines of the April 1982 election that chose Margaret Ragan for the 1982-83 term, nor in the 1982-83 issues examined - consistent with his presidency ending with Bush's original term.

No candidate won a majority on February 9, forcing a runoff, which Norfleet won on February 16. The Herald reported her election as student regent in its February 18 issue. Her initial term was short: by mid-April 1982 the Herald noted that the student regent's 2-month term was nearing its end. She is listed among the 1982-83 student leaders, and in February 1983 the Herald's editorial page was still weighing the office, insisting the student regent must represent everyone. Norfleet reached the student regent seat through a crowded contest. The Herald reported on 2 February 1982 that five students were seeking the student regent spot, and two days later Kevin Francke ran a piece in which the candidates set out their qualities. Kevin Francke reported on 18 February 1982 that Sandra Norfleet had been elected student regent. The same issue carried his story on a group that would speak on the Associated Student Government's behalf. Her time in the seat was short. By mid-April Francke was reporting that the student regent's two-month term was nearing its end, in an issue that also covered voided ASG election results and a joke resolution that nearly passed the congress.
Resigned 14 Jan 1982.
Succeeded Bush; named in Board of Regents minutes 30 Jan 1982.

She was absent from the 9 February 1982 meeting, where Susan Albert filled in for her and announced a new date for the ASG banquet.

Laura Simms was named Public Affairs Vice President in the minutes of 20 October 1981, where she reported on the phone-a-thon and that week's campus events. The year's minutes name her chairperson of the Communications Committee; the 20 October minutes themselves record no committee chairmanship for her, and the attribution rests on the meeting of 9 February 1982, at which another member reported for the committee in her place. holdings.what_they_did: Margaret Ragan survived the April 1982 Associated Student Government presidential primary along with Glenn Sargent, emerging from a five-way field. Endorsement letters for her ran in the Herald through both rounds of the election. After the first general election was voided, Ragan won the presidency in the repeated election held April 20, 1982. She and the other new officers were sworn in before the month was out. Midway through her term Ragan used the Herald's pages to explain that the ASG presidency and the student regent seat were now separate positions. Her spring saw a grade plan, a student shuttle vote, and a contested rewrite of the ASG constitution before Jack Smith was elected to succeed her. Ragan's presidency came out of a disrupted spring. The Associated Student Government repeated its general election on 20 April 1982, after the Herald had reported the previous week that the first round's results were void. She set out her agenda at the start of the fall term. Monica Dias reported in the Herald's second issue of the year that major ASG changes were envisioned by Margaret Ragan, and over the following months the congress took up a campus Wall of Fame, a joint coed housing poll with the Interhall Council, and a coed housing bill it approved in November. Ragan also argued in print for keeping the two student offices distinct. In February 1983 the Herald carried her statement that the Associated Student Government and the student regent position were separate, in the same issue that reported the ASG shuttle service.

No source found ties this Administrative Vice President directly to either the 1982 candidate or the 1983 president, and the archive does not merge them: this record is kept deliberately separate rather than assumed to be the same person.

During that spring's campaign season she wrote a Herald letter supporting Kerrie Stewart, one of the candidates for the ASG presidency who did not survive the primary that Margaret Ragan and Glenn Sargent came through. By the Congress meeting of 29 April 1982, at which Stewart was named chairperson of the Public Relations Committee, Albert herself was serving as Secretary, where she went over the chart for handling motions; the same minutes name her chairperson of the Rules and Elections Committee.

Kerrie Stewart stood in the Associated Student Government elections of spring 1982, a contest run twice after the first general election was voided. This archive's record of the presidential primary places her in the field that Margaret Ragan and Glenn Sargent came through, and her supporters filled the Herald's letters pages from 25 March to 20 April, the last of them, by Melody Murphy, backing Ragan and Stewart together. What office she was seeking by the repeated election of 20 April is not established here. She was sworn in as Public Affairs Vice President for the following year on 27 April 1982, and at the Congress meeting of 29 April was named chairperson of the Public Relations Committee. A LaCenter junior, she described ASG as a liaison between students and the administration, and said its Congress proposed bills in weekly meetings which the administration then voted on once Congress had passed them. The 1983 Talisman's Associated Student Government portrait names her in the vice-presidential role. She also appears in a Phi Mu sorority composite in the WKU Archives' student organizations photograph collection. The Herald marked her death the following year. The index of the issue of 23 August 1983 carries "Saying Goodbye to Kerrie Stewart is Especially Hard" as an obituary, and a remembrance by Jon Norris, "Kerrie Stewart Remembered," followed on 8 September 1983. Neither article was opened for this record, so nothing is said here of the circumstances.

Jack Smith first ran for the Associated Student Government presidency in spring 1982, drawing repeated endorsement letters in the Herald, and though Margaret Ragan won that race, Smith and Lonnie Sears took awards as the year closed. He returned as a candidate in March 1983, when 68 students filed for ASG positions and his supporters again filled the letters pages. Smith won the presidency of the Associated Student Government in the April 12, 1983 election, in which students also approved constitutional revisions. His victory came after roughly 500 students had voted in the primary the week before. His presidency was colorful and contentious: the fall brought a discount card controversy, letters accusing him of partying while committees waited and others defending him, and a December cartoon that he wrote in to protest. In April 1984 the Herald caught him impersonating a bunny as his ASG ran a low-turnout poll on beer and a campus pub. Smith's plaque term runs two years, 1983-85, and the Herald's own account of his exit backs that up: its April 11, 1985 issue reported him ending his term as ASG president in an article headlined 'Jack Smith Ends Term as Associated Student Government President,' alongside a companion piece crediting his enthusiasm with reviving interest in the organization. Smith's 1983 campaign drew an unusual run of supporting letters in the Herald. The issue of 7 April 1983 carried two, from Dorothy Metzmeler and Sarah Hein, following one from Tony Johnson the week before; the same issue reported that about 500 students had voted in the ASG primary. Jamie Morton reported on 14 April 1983 that Jack Smith had won the presidency of the Associated Student Government. The same issue reported that students had also voted in favor of the ASG constitutional revisions worked out that spring. His first term drew heavy comment. In December 1983 the Herald reported that ASG had voided its own procedures even as it saw growth in membership and took up fourteen proposals, and the same issue carried Stanley Reagan's letter headed "Jack Smith, Associated Student Government Thrown Away" along with another Lou Bloss cartoon on ASG. He filed for re-election in February 1984 and stayed in office through a second year, ending his term in April 1985.

Jack Smith held the presidency of the Associated Student Government in 1983-84, the first of two years on a single plaque plate. He won the election of 12 April 1983 after about 500 students voted in the primary the week before, in a campaign carried by an unusual run of supporting letters in the Herald; the same ballot approved that spring's constitutional revisions. He chaired a Congress whose officers were administrative vice president Tony Whalen, treasurer Kelly S. Smith, secretary Teresa Anthony and public affairs vice president Happy Chandler, succeeded during the year by John Holland. The year brought a discount card controversy, letters accusing him of partying while committees waited and others defending him, a December cartoon he wrote in to protest, and a December report that ASG had voided its own procedures even as membership grew and fourteen proposals came forward. Smith filed for re-election in February 1984 and stayed in office a second year. In April 1984 the Herald caught him impersonating a bunny while his ASG ran a low-turnout poll on beer and a campus pub. The paper marked the end of his term on 11 April 1985 with a report headlined that he was ending his term as ASG president and a companion piece crediting his enthusiasm with reviving interest in the organisation.

Smith presided over a productive opening to the 1984-85 year. By the third week of September the Herald reported that four ASG proposals had been made reality, and the congress had begun studying a student book exchange, which became the signature project of his final year. By mid-year the record was mixed. The book exchange venture appeared likely to take a summer pause, and the organization was weighing whether to fight cuts to education funding. His term ended in April 1985. The Herald covered his exit with a news story headlined that Smith was ending his term as ASG president, an editorial crediting his enthusiasm with reviving interest in the organization, and an editorial cartoon. The SGA plaque records him on a two-year 1983-85 plate. Jack Smith first won the presidency of the Associated Student Government in a race the College Heights Herald reported under the headline "Jack Smith Wins Presidency of Associated Student Government," in the paper's fifty-eighth volume. That win put him in the office he would go on to hold across more than one term. Smith and the Herald did not always get along. One issue in the paper's fifty-ninth volume indexed an item headed "Jack Smith, Associated Student Government Thrown Away" together with a letter written by Smith himself under the title "Cartoon Aggravates," showing that he answered the paper's cartoonists in print rather than letting the criticism stand. His time in office closed in April 1985, when Mack Humphreys wrote up Smith ending his term as Associated Student Government president. The Herald ran a second piece in the same issue crediting Smith's enthusiasm with reviving interest in ASG, and Kevin Knapp marked the departure with an editorial cartoon on Smith and the organisation.

Suzie Wilkins served as Treasurer of the Associated Student Government in 1984-85. She reported to Congress on 18 September 1984 that 39 people had signed up and paid for the Weekend in the Woods retreat, discussed the year's budget, and told Congress the vouchers would be ready the following week. That January, while in office, she co-wrote a Herald letter to the editor with Ricki Richmond headlined 'Defends Greeks.'

A Connie Hoffman — almost certainly the same person, given the continuity of interest — was writing about student government before she took office: a September 1983 Herald letter, 'And Old Tricks,' and, ahead of the spring 1984 ASG elections, an April 1984 letter defending a proposal from ASG's own Student Rights Committee (both bylined 'Hoffman' in the Herald's own index, one N; the ASG minutes and a later Herald letter about her spell it with two). The identification rests on the matching name and the continuous ASG involvement, not on a source that states the two are the same; it is recorded here as likely, not certain. As Secretary in 1984-85 she announced the vacancies on Congress week after week and, on 16 October 1984, the openings on the Judicial Council as well; she signed the minutes for the year. She sought further ASG office in the spring 1985 election: the Herald of 2 April 1985 carried a full slate of candidate-endorsement letters, one backing her ('Supports Connie Hoffmann'), alongside letters for Mitchell McKinney, Greg Elder, Loree Zimmerman, and Stan Reagan, plus a joint endorsement of Caroline Miller and Donna Holloway written by Elder himself. The Herald does not say which office any of the letters' subjects were seeking. Only McKinney's result is established elsewhere in this archive; it does not yet record who won the 1985-86 secretary, treasurer or vice-president races, so Hoffmann's absence from the recorded 1985-86 leadership does not establish that she lost — only that which office she sought, and how the race came out, is not yet established here.

John Holland served as Public Relations Vice-President of the Associated Student Government in 1984-85, under President Jack Smith. He confirmed the speakers for that year's Weekend in the Woods retreat at Congress's 18 September 1984 meeting, and the following month announced the date for the Talisman yearbook's student-government photograph and raised the idea of a hayride. Holland co-chaired the student book exchange, ASG's signature project of the year, alongside senior class president Danny Broderick. When the committee sent "ambassadors" out to campus organisations that November to explain the exchange and hand out registration cards, he promised, the Herald reported, to send a speaker "faster than Domino's pizza." Over the Christmas break he and Broderick, together with President Smith and administrative secretary Debra Stahl, keyed roughly 1,400 book listings into an IBM personal computer for the exchange's first printed edition, distributed when students returned for the spring semester.

holdings.what_they_did: Before he was a candidate, McKinney wrote a Herald op-ed on 21 March 1985 headlined 'Associated Student Government Shouldn't Force Bill,' one of a pair of dueling pieces the paper ran on the same question - a sign he was already active in ASG's legislative debates a week before he entered the presidential race. McKinney won the spring 1985 primary on a ticket with Chris Watkins on March 28, the Herald's headline saying the pair rode experience to their primary victory over a field that included candidate Stan Reagan. He was announced as the new Associated Student Government president in the Herald of April 4, in the same issue that reported an unnamed legislative group rejoining ASG. The record found so far does not confirm what office, if any, Watkins went on to hold. In office, the congress abolished its own Finance Committee that September and, the following spring, wrote a Financial Advisory Council into the ASG bylaws in its place. The spring 1986 session was especially active: bills created major/minor college representative seats, revised the membership application process, asked Board of Regents members to attend an SGA meeting, sought chains for Pearce-Ford Tower windows, and pushed for a welcome sign at Normal Drive and University Boulevard. In March 1986 McKinney pulled out of the race for a second term. The same issue carried a piece arguing that student government needed a strong leader, and the field he left behind grew to four candidates before Tim Todd won the presidency that April. The outgoing congress commended McKinney's work in Bill 86-13-S on April 3, and the WKU Board of Regents included a resolution honoring him, alongside outgoing president John D. Minton, at its meeting of August 8, 1986. A 1986 presidential proclamation he signed honoring English professor Thomas Jones survives in the SGA records.

At the year's final Congress meeting on 15 April 1986 she reported the organization's balance as $2,045.59. The 1986 Talisman's Associated Student Government page pictures her among that year's executive officers alongside Greg Elder, Tara Wassom and Loree Zimmerman.

Tara Wassom, a public relations major from Fort Campbell, served as the Associated Student Government's Secretary in 1985-86 and signed the minutes of the year's final meeting, 15 April 1986, at which she thanked the Student Affairs committee for handling the banquet invitations.

Greg Elder, a Glasgow junior, was named the Associated Student Government's incoming Administrative Vice President by the outgoing president on 9 April 1985 and was still in the post at the year's final Congress meeting on 15 April 1986, though he gave no report that day. Describing ASG's work to the 1986 Talisman, Elder said the organization "take[s] students' wants and translate[s] them into action and results," and named moving English 101 to a pass/fail option, reducing the hours required to live in Poland Hall, and starting a book exchange program as the year's accomplishments. Elder filed to run for ASG president in early March 1986. Mitchell McKinney's withdrawal from re-election left Elder and Tim Todd to contest an April runoff, which the Herald reported Todd winning. Elder ran again the next spring: the Herald's 9 April 1987 issue reported him and Todd through to a runoff it called a "deja vu primary," and the following week's issue reported Todd beating him in the re-run general election.

Loree Zimmerman, a senior from Providence, served as the Associated Student Government's Public Relations Vice President in 1985-86 and chaired its Public Relations committee. At the year's closing Congress meeting on 15 April 1986 she thanked her committee, the Executive Council and the Congress membership, and laid out the schedule for the year-end banquet and the organization's anniversary activities.

Donna Pack chaired the Academic Affairs Committee of Associated Student Government in 1985-86. At the Congress's meeting of 15 April 1986 she announced a meeting on 24 April — the minutes abbreviate it only as AC, and do not say which body it was — and asked college representatives to attend to discuss a new English policy; what was decided there is not recorded. She is pictured with that year's other ASG officers and committee chairs in a group photograph in the 1986 Talisman.

Caroline Miller chaired the Legislative Research Committee of Associated Student Government in 1985-86. At the Congress's closing meeting of 15 April 1986 she brought the spring session's last block of legislation to the floor, recommending approval of eight items, including making the Kentucky Intercollegiate State Legislature delegation a standing ASG committee, amending ASG's by-laws, and placing a welcome sign on campus, while recommending against 86-30-S, which would have retained the existing faculty evaluation system. All of that night's legislation passed regardless: the eight recommended items were approved unanimously, by amendment, or viva voce, and Congress also passed 86-30-S unanimously, over Miller's committee's objection. Miller was probably also the Caroline Miller who served as a delegate to the Kentucky Intercollegiate State Legislature, the mock-legislature program ASG made a standing committee that spring. In the 1986 Talisman's account of campus political groups, the delegation's chairman, Lori Scott, named that Miller's election as the group's lieutenant governor one of the year's biggest accomplishments.

Sean Peck chaired the Rules and Elections Committee of Associated Student Government in 1985-86, the year his committee ran that spring's Congress elections. At the 15 April 1986 closing meeting he congratulated the newly elected Congress members and thanked his committee for its work, and he seconded the motion to adjourn, made by Bill Schilling. A year earlier, before he held office, he had written to the Herald arguing that involvement in ASG was the answer to student apathy on campus. The Herald of 27 March 1986 carried a piece from Peck himself, headlined "Thanks A Lot," addressed to Associated Student Government as his chairmanship closed. In the 1986 Talisman, a Sean Peck described as a Gilbertsville senior was quoted on the university's move to coed dormitory housing.

Tim Todd chaired the Student Rights Committee in 1985-86, the year before Associated Student Government elected him president. The one set of that year's minutes the archive holds, from the closing meeting of 15 April 1986, records a single remark of his: he wished the body a good summer.

Reported the Kentucky Intercollegiate State Legislature spring session a success, and was congratulated at the same meeting on being made Speaker Pro Tem of KISL. She became Administrative Vice-President the following year.

Todd reached the April 1986 runoff against Greg Elder after Mitchell McKinney's withdrawal left the presidential field open. The Herald reported the two-man race on 3 April, with the general election the following week. Days after an election week the Herald described as marred by pranks and accusations, the paper identified Todd as the new ASG president in a sharply critical opinion piece headlined that he lacked knowledge of his own issues. Todd answered in print the following issue, criticizing the paper's reporting. His first fall opened with an approved budget of $12,100, a plan to reach students by phone for their ideas and needs, and an ASG retreat featuring university president Kern Alexander. Todd's first year leading Associated Student Government opened with ordinary organisational business. The Herald of 11 September 1986 reported that ASG approved a $12,100 budget, planned to telephone students to collect their ideas and needs, and scheduled a retreat that was to feature Kern Alexander. By the end of the spring term the body was still working through routine legislation, tabling a phone bill after an amendment was raised, while a student government conference was set for that weekend. The same issue of 26 March 1987 covered the election for the following year, in which Todd stood again and Bill Fogle said he had entered the presidential race to help Todd rather than to win it.

Barbara Rush, a senior from Louisville, served as the Associated Student Government's Treasurer in 1986-87 and presented the year's budget to Congress on 9 September 1986, which was accepted by acclamation. The 1987 Talisman pictured her taking notes as ASG treasurer during a lecture by state senator-elect Nick Kafoglis at the organization's Weekend in the Woods retreat that September.

John Schocke served as the Associated Student Government's Secretary in 1986-87. At the first Congress meeting of the year he read the attendance policy to the body and kept the standing list of vacant seats, which by September 1986 covered alternate seats for the Business, Ogden and Education colleges and one on-campus representative; he signed the minutes as John C. Schocke.

Lori Scott, of Princeton, chaired the Kentucky Intercollegiate State Legislature committee for the Associated Student Government in 1985-86, reporting that spring's KISL session a success and being congratulated by Congress on being made KISL's Speaker Pro Tem. She moved up to Administrative Vice President the following year, 1986-87, setting proposed goals for each of ASG's standing committees at the first meeting of the year and taking charge of the student discount card, telling Congress it was being produced strictly by ASG rather than by the Key Line Guide.

Daniel Rodriguez, a senior from Barquisimeto, Venezuela, served as the Associated Student Government's Public Relations Vice President in 1986-87 and chaired its Public Relations committee. At the opening Congress meeting of 2 September 1986 he distributed the year's new ASG brochures and announced the Weekend in the Woods leadership retreat, held at Camp Decker 12-14 September 1986. Rodriguez helped organize that retreat starting in March, lining up speakers and camp reservations, then promoting it with letters to freshmen, newspaper ads and brochures mailed to campus organizations. Rodriguez told the 1987 Talisman that the lower-than-expected turnout, 45 of a possible 75, actually helped attendees participate more. When the closing speaker, university president Kern Alexander, could not make the retreat, he invited the attendees to breakfast at his home the following week instead; Rodriguez called it "a great way to finish."

Chris Millay was nominated from the floor and elected Parliamentarian of Associated Student Government on 2 September 1986; the minutes note he also served as vice-chair of the Legislative Research Committee that year. Two weeks into his term, writing as Christopher Millay, he had a piece published in the Herald on the stereotyping of Christianity.

Dwight Austin was elected Sergeant-at-Arms of Associated Student Government on 2 September 1986, from a field of four nominees, and was appointed to the Judicial Council the following week. The minutes spell his surname both Austin and Austion. No further record of his time in office has been found in the sources searched so far.

Dan Wooten was named chair of the Judicial Council when Congress confirmed the full 1986-87 council on 9 September 1986, an appointment that had been held over from the year's first meeting. No further record of his time in the office has been found in the sources searched so far.

Holger Velastegui, of Bowling Green, chaired the Rules and Elections Committee of Associated Student Government in 1986-87, appointed on 2 September 1986. The year before, he had worked on the legislation asking for a scholarship tied to Bowling Green's sister city, Santo Domingo de los Colorados, work the 1985-86 Student Affairs chairman publicly thanked him for; the minutes do not say which committee, if any, he served on at the time. As chairman himself he campaigned for turnout: the 2 September 1986 minutes record him encouraging freshmen to take part in that fall's elections, and the Herald carried a piece from him that October headlined "Freshmen, Vote Today." He also wrote to the Herald that October urging students to take part in a campus international event. Velastegui had also written to the Herald that spring backing Daniel Rodriguez's campaign for ASG's public relations vice presidency, and a year later, in April 1987, Rodriguez returned the favor, writing publicly to back Velastegui in that spring's ASG elections; the record does not show what office he sought or whether he won. He appears with other ASG members in a 1986 Talisman group photograph.
Appointed chair of Legislative Research on 2 September 1986 and also sat on the Judicial Council that year. He was Administrative Vice-President the following year.

Jeff Key chaired the Student Affairs Committee of Associated Student Government in 1986-87, appointed on 2 September 1986. On 9 September he reminded all class vice-presidents that ASG's rules required them to serve on his committee. In February 1987 he co-wrote a Herald piece with fellow ASG officer Kim Summers on spring break options for students.

Bill Fogle chaired the Associated Student Government's Academic Affairs Committee in 1986-87, appointed at Congress's 2 September 1986 meeting. He had written to the Herald in January 1986, before he joined the cabinet, under the headline "Student Apathy Criticized." In spring 1987 Fogle entered the ASG presidential race himself. The Herald reported on 26 March that he had started his campaign to help fellow candidate Tim Todd rather than to win it, and on 7 April that he had ended his bid for the presidency; Todd went on to win a second term. Using the fuller name William Fogle, Fogle stayed visible in the organization's business afterward: the Herald of 10 December 1987 credited him with explaining Congress's actions in the affair around Administrative Vice President Bill Schilling, after Congress dropped an impeachment proceeding against Schilling and placed him under a watchdog committee instead.

Kent Groemling chaired the Faculty Relations Committee of Associated Student Government in 1986-87, appointed on 2 September 1986, and also sat on that year's Judicial Council, confirmed by Congress the following week. He is pictured with other ASG officers and committee chairs in the 1986 Talisman the year before he took the chairmanship, and is probably the same Kent Groemling the 1987 Talisman elsewhere describes as being from Louisville. Outside ASG that same fall, Groemling served on the University Center Board's special events committee, the year the Homecoming pep rally, Big Red's Roar, moved outdoors to Smith Stadium for the first time. He told the 1987 Talisman the change went over well apart from complaints about the cold, and that organizers expected to keep it outdoors.

Chris LeNeave chaired the Student Rights Committee of Associated Student Government in 1986-87, appointed on 2 September 1986. Several months earlier, in April 1986, he had written to the Herald criticizing the paper's own staff. The Christopher LeNeave listed in the 1987 Talisman's senior class directory as a Mayfield native studying biology is the same man. The yearbook's index carries a single Leneave, Christopher M., and refers him to the directory page and to the two pages carrying the Associated Student Government group photographs, in the first of which he is named in the second row beside William Schilling, with president Tim Todd in the back row. An earlier pass recorded the two as possibly distinct; the index entry closes the gap.

She had run for office earlier: the Herald of 2 April 1985 carries "Elder, Greg. Todd sought a second term in spring 1987 in a rematch against Greg Elder, the man he had beaten the year before. The Herald reported the two would battle again in its 19 March issue. On election day the Herald endorsed Elder as the better choice and indexed the race itself under the headline no contest. The vote was then re-run, and Todd won it: the paper carried the result on 16 April 1987. The SGA plaque lists him on a single 1986-88 plate, and no other president appears in the 1987-88 record. The 1987-88 year under the two-year plate ended with the election of Scott Whitehouse on 7 April 1988, closing out the era of the Todd presidency. Todd stood for a second term in the election held in March 1987. The Herald reported that Bill Fogle had entered the presidential race to help Todd rather than to win it, and the same issue recorded a shortage of candidates across the races and an appeal by a disqualified candidate. His second year drew harder coverage. The Herald of 29 October 1987 reported that Associated Student Government was considering required course evaluations, and carried a separate article saying apathy was killing both ASG and the Residence Hall Association.

Drew DeLozier served as Treasurer of the Associated Student Government in 1987-88, under President Timothy Todd. He issued Congress's monthly voucher summaries through the year, and at the meeting of 15 March 1988 reported that a bill for 1,000 copies had arrived from Kinko's with no explanation of what the copies were for.

Danielle Williamson served as Secretary of the Associated Student Government in 1987-88, under President Timothy Todd. The Herald's coverage of the spring 1987 campaign that put that year's officers in place, in its issue of 14 April, carried a letter backing her under the headline "Danielle Williamson Best" — the same issue in which Kim Summers wrote in support of Todd's re-election as president. As Secretary, Williamson signed Congress's minutes through the year, including those recording the opening of impeachment proceedings against Administrative Vice President Bill Schilling in November 1987. Week after week she read out the same short list of vacancies the body could not fill: the senior class vice-presidency, two off-campus representative seats, and the Business and Potter college alternate seats.

Before he joined the cabinet, Bill Schilling was already the most prolific bill-writer in Congress: a Herald feature by Lisa Jessie on 11 December 1986 named him the one Associated Student Government member who wrote most of Congress's bills, the same season he chaired the Legislative Research Committee. He wrote to the Herald under his own name that year too — a column headlined "Associated Student Government Has New Ideas" in March 1986, a letter backing Tim Todd's first run for the presidency the following month, and a separate letter, "College Heights Herald Abuses Rights." Schilling ran for the Interhall Council presidency in the spring 1987 elections; the Herald covered his signage under the headline "Candidate Using Big Red on Signs," and on 21 April 1987 reported that Delwin Cheek had defeated him for that council's presidency. He was then named Administrative Vice President of the Associated Student Government for 1987-88 under re-elected President Todd, and in that office reported to Congress on the Bowling Green City Traffic Commission and on a rise of more than 20 percent in campus crime, and handed down to Congress an official Judicial Council record to be implemented at the next election. His term turned contentious that fall. The Herald reported on 27 October 1987 that he had lost his Congress seat after the Residence Hall Association refused him a leave of absence — the report did not say which seat — and three weeks later, on 19 November, Congress opened an impeachment process against him. The proceeding did not go the distance: the Herald reported on 3 December that the impeachment request had been dropped, and the following week's issue described Schilling placed under the eye of a new watchdog committee, alongside a page of reader letters divided between defending the outcome and, in one case from Van C. Hodge Jr., insisting the issue was not closed. Schilling asked Congress for a leave of absence on 25 February 1988, and at the meeting of 1 March told the body he had been cleared by the university, that he would run for the ASG presidency, and that he would take leave from his office until after the election. A Herald item two and a half weeks later, on 17 March, reported the arrest of an Associated Student Government officer under the name William Byron Shilling; the surviving index preserves no charge. The Herald of 31 March 1988, the same issue that reported Shannon Ragland and Scott Whitehouse winning the presidential primary, carried the outcome: "Charge Against William Schilling Dismissed." He was not among the two candidates who survived that primary.
holdings.source: ASG minutes, 22 September and 17 November 1987, 1 March 1988

holdings.what_they_did: A Kimberly Summers wrote twice to the Herald's letters pages in April 1986, over a year before Kim Summers's confirmed 1987-88 term in the ASG cabinet: "Appreciates Help – Associated Student Government" ran on 17 April, and "Commends Job Well Done – Associated Student Government" followed five days later. The identification rests on the matching name and the ASG subject matter, not on a source that states the two are the same; it is recorded here as likely, not certain. In April 1987 Kim Summers wrote in support of Tim Todd's re-election as president, in the same issue that carried Danielle Williamson's endorsement and coverage of Bill Schilling's Interhall Council campaign. Summers served as Public Relations Vice-President of the Associated Student Government in 1987-88, under President Todd, after serving as vice-chair of the Faculty Relations Committee the year before. She ran that September's Weekend in the Woods retreat, introduced table tents and a newsletter as new publicity tools, and in March 1988 handed out the year's committee certificates.

Rebecca Hack was accepted by Congress as chairman of the Rules and Elections Committee on 6 October 1987, while the committee was still running that autumn's freshman elections. ASG's own minutes are not consistent on her name: the 22 September 1987 minutes record a Becky Haaek and those of 6 October a Rebecca Hack, and no other source in the archive resolves which spelling is right. No further record of her term survives here.

holdings.what_they_did: Grimly reported for the Associated Student Government's Legislative Research committee at the Congress meeting of 22 September 1987. She spoke to the parliamentary procedure handouts circulated that evening, announced that the committee would run a survey at the freshman elections on whether freshmen should be allowed to bring cars to campus, and set out the changes it wanted in the constitution and bylaws. Those amendments went to a campus vote in November and were ratified by eighty-one students.

Robertson was senior class president in the Associated Student Government in 1987-88 and quit part way through the year; the Herald reported the resignation on 21 January 1988. It opened the run of vacancies that dominated the congress's spring: four positions were filled at a single meeting on 4 February, and on 23 February the body publicly set out its reasons for the empty seats. Only two of the thirty-two positions on that April's ballot were contested.
holdings.source: Herald 63:33, 21 Jan 1988, "Student Government Association Senior Class President Greg Robertson Quits"

holdings.what_they_did: Whitehouse won the March 1988 ASG presidential primary alongside Shannon Ragland, emerging from a field of seven candidates in a year when only two of 32 congress positions were contested. He won the presidency on 7 April 1988, in an election the Herald's own editorial pages said had been marred by oversight and closed minds, and amid coverage of votes for a write-in candidate that the congress was told it could not ignore. The disputed election shadowed his term into the fall: Bruce Cambron, who had demanded a new election in April, took his complaint to university president Thomas Meredith in October 1988, weeks after the congress banned future write-in campaigns. His year also produced ASG's formal written reaction to the General Education Task Force proposal. Scott Whitehouse came through the Associated Student Government primaries in the spring of 1988. Dorren Klausnitzer reported that Whitehouse and Shannon Ragland were the winners, in an issue that also covered what a losing campaign cost candidates in money and in feeling. By the middle of his year in office the Herald had settled on a running characterisation of him. Rebecca Fullen's feature called him the "Peddling President" who sold Associated Student Government to students, and the same issue reported that university president Thomas Meredith had come to speak to the organisation. The following week the paper printed "Scott Whitehouse Selling Good Government" together with a John Chattin editorial cartoon drawing him as a salesman. The salesman image was the Herald's shorthand for a president whose main task was convincing students that student government mattered.

Larry Gumbel served as treasurer of the Associated Student Government for 1988-89. He closed out the 1987-88 books at the start of the year and put ASG onto a monthly voucher system for the 1988-89 budget, and told Congress on 20 September 1988 that the year's congressional retreat had come in under budget.

Mickie Hennig served as secretary of the Associated Student Government from the start of the 1988-89 year and signed the minutes into November 1988. She resigned before the year was out; her letter of resignation was read to Congress by the administrative vice president on 24 January 1989, and the president told Congress applications would be taken for a replacement. Robin Kinman was elected to the seat two weeks later.

Robin Kinman joined the Associated Student Government Congress as the Business College alternate on 24 January 1989, the same meeting at which Mickie Hennig's resignation letter as secretary was read into the record. On 7 February 1989, after hearing from the candidates for the vacant office, Congress elected Kinman secretary; she had already signed the minutes of that same meeting in the role.

Adrian Smoot served as administrative vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1988-89, calling the committee chairs together through the year. He walked Congress through the by-law amendments it passed on 20 September 1988, ran an evaluation of every ASG committee across November and December 1988, and read the secretary's letter of resignation to Congress on 24 January 1989.
holdings.source: ASG minutes, 20 September and 22 November 1988, 24 January 1989

holdings.what_they_did: Dan Knowles was named the Associated Student Government's lobby coordinator by the president on 22 November 1988. Knowles ran for the ASG presidency in the April 1991 election, one of four candidates named in the Herald's "Meet the Candidates" coverage. On 9 April 1991 the Herald reported that he had been accused of running a smear campaign; no source found reports how the accusation was resolved. Heather Falmlen won the election two days later, amid protests that included a call for students to boycott the vote and an editorial condemning the campaign's conduct.
holdings.source: ASG minutes, 15 and 22 November and 6 December 1988

holdings.what_they_did: Amos Gott served as public relations vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1988-89. He announced the Vote America registration drive for Downing University Center on 4, 5 and 6 October 1988, and an ASG hotline running every Wednesday afternoon from 1 to 4, which he told Congress on 25 October would open the next day. He also wrote pieces for the Herald that year explaining the organization to students, including "Understand Associated Student Government" that November. He ran for the ASG presidency the following spring and won, taking office for 1989-90.
Bill Parsons was named the Associated Student Government's SAFE coordinator by the president on 22 November 1988. He also served that year as Congress's parliamentarian.
Named SAFE coordinator by the President on 22 November 1988.

Dan Townshend was sworn in as the Associated Student Government's parliamentarian by the president on 1 November 1988, the same meeting at which Congress swore in a new Potter College alternate and a new off-campus representative. Bill Parsons had held the parliamentarian post since the start of the year and was named SAFE coordinator three weeks later, on 22 November 1988 — consistent with, though the minutes do not explicitly state, a handover of the parliamentarian role to Townshend.
Accepted as Chair of the Judicial Council by Congress at the first meeting of the year, 6 September 1988, and sworn in the same evening.

Chris Gaddis was accepted by Congress as vice-chair of the Associated Student Government's Judicial Council on 6 September 1988, the first meeting of the year, alongside chair Jeff Key, and sworn in the same evening.

Dana Baith was accepted as chair of the Associated Student Government's Rules and Elections Committee on 6 September 1988, Congress's first meeting of the year, with Kim Summers — who had served as public relations vice president the year before — as co-chair. Baith drew up revised campaign regulations, which Congress adopted a week later on 13 September 1988, then ran the freshman-class primary held 27 September 1988 and organized the general congressional election set for 11 October 1988.
Accepted as co-chair of Rules and Elections on 6 September 1988, the year after she served as Public Relations Vice-President.

Kevin Hargrave was one of four correspondents whose letters the Herald printed on 10 December 1987, amid the Bill Schilling watchdog-committee controversy in Associated Student Government. The surviving index line for that issue runs the titles and the writers together, so which of the four letters was his is not established here. Congress accepted Hargrave as chair of the Legislative Research Committee on 13 September 1988. The committee reported to Congress that he had to resign the chair — the minutes do not give a reason — but he continued sitting in Congress afterward and reported for Ogden College on the Academic Council's General Education study.

Brad Cooper chaired the Associated Student Government's Student Affairs Committee for 1988-89, accepted into the post by Congress on 13 September 1988 with Victor Click as co-chair. His committee produced ASG's student discount card and went on to take over the Book Exchanger textbook-listing service for the spring semester.

Victor Click co-signed the same 2 April 1987 Herald letter with Hollie Hale endorsing Tim Todd for the Associated Student Government presidency. Todd won the race, in a re-run of the election the Herald reported on 16 April 1987. By the fall of 1987 Click chaired the Associated Student Government's Student Affairs Committee, which ran the Book Exchanger — a free listing service through which students advertised used textbooks to each other instead of selling them back to the bookstore. Click told the Herald in November 1987 that the exchange had raised about $60 the previous fall and nothing that spring against roughly $653 in printing costs, against a $750 budget for the service, and said he would recommend dropping the project if that semester's run failed too. Click continued in student government the following year as co-chair of the Student Affairs Committee, accepted by Congress on 13 September 1988 alongside chair Brad Cooper.

In the spring 1987 Associated Student Government election season, Hollie Hale and Victor Click co-signed a Herald letter endorsing Tim Todd for the presidency, printed in the paper's 2 April 1987 issue. The Herald's own editorial that month endorsed his opponent Greg Elder, but Todd won: the paper reported the result on 16 April 1987 under the headline "Tim Todd Beats Greg Elder in Election Re-Run," and Todd served as president through 1987-88. That December, amid a controversy inside student government over member Bill Schilling — placed under a Congress watchdog committee after an earlier impeachment attempt against him — the Herald of 10 December 1987 carried a cluster of letters on the affair, among them one from Hale. The surviving index line for that issue runs the titles and the writers together, so which letter belongs to which correspondent is not established here; the titles indexed are an explanation of student government's actions, a letter calling an editorial an attack, a defence of the rescission and a piece on expanding to Glasgow, and the names indexed beside them are Hale, Kevin Hargrave, Van C. Hodge Jr. and Phillip Sellers. The following year Congress accepted Hale as chair of the Student Rights Committee on 13 September 1988, with Elaine Burge joining as co-chair a week later. Her committee worked that autumn on handicapped-accessibility facilities and a dispute over the campus ticket outlet, and Hale also served as the college representatives' contact for the Academic Council committees.
Elaine Burge was accepted as co-chair of the Associated Student Government's Student Rights Committee on 20 September 1988, alongside chair Hollie Hale.
Accepted as Public Relations co-chair on 20 September 1988, having been sworn in as a Representative At-Large a fortnight earlier.
