Gott was a visible member before he was president, signing Herald letters on ASG's behalf, including a January 1989 piece promoting Campus Pride '89 and an earlier letter urging readers to understand the organization. He won the presidency in April 1989, edging Lynn Groemling in a race that had drawn candidate complaints about the brief primary. His presidency ran on correspondence: resolutions went out over his signature as memoranda to named administrators and answers came back. In spring 1990 he wrote to six administrators under Resolution 90-6-S seeking changes to the final exam schedule, part of a surviving file that also covers extended library hours, the Downing University Center flagpole, mace sales at the bookstore, AIDS education and larger diplomas. Gott was already writing on Associated Student Government's behalf before he led it, signing a January 1989 Herald piece promoting Campus Pride '89. That spring he ran for president, survived a primary that several candidates complained had been too brief, and then edged Lynn Groemling in the runoff to take the office for 1989-90. He started early. The Herald's second issue of the fall reported that Gott had gotten a jump on the ASG semester, running alongside a piece urging students to participate. The fall that followed was busy and money was tight: the paper reported ASG's budget was tiny compared with other schools, the congress approved a new statewide board before admitting it could not afford the dues, and it spent the semester picking up and putting down a proposed Public Interest Research Group. Gott opened the spring with a Herald letter asking students to become involved, and by February he was defending an Anti-Apathy Week in print after it drew criticism. The rest of his spring ran through the congress: opening Pearce-Ford Tower's windows, more parking on the lower end of campus, a revised WKU Glasgow constitution, and a vote to expand the congress so classes and student groups had more voice. He handed off to Michael Colvin in April 1990.

Eddie Smith served as treasurer of the Associated Student Government for 1989-90. At the first meeting of the year, 29 August 1989, he presented the budget summary and told Congress it was an operational budget; Congress accepted the 1989-90 budget that same night.

Julie Fleming served as secretary of the Associated Student Government for 1989-90 and signed the minutes all year. She kept and read out, week by week, the standing list of unfilled Congress seats, and required proposed resolutions to reach her by Thursday or Friday of each week.

Michael Colvin served as administrative vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1989-90, under president Amos Gott. At the first Congress meeting of the year, 29 August 1989, he walked members through the congressional notebook and how to write a resolution, set out the attendance policy, and raised a resolution for a stop light at the corner of Regents Avenue and Normal Drive. He was elected president for 1990-91, succeeding Gott.

Van Hodge served as public relations vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1989-90, the first of two consecutive terms in the office. In his first officer report he described correspondence made with other universities at a NACA conference and a meeting held with the Herald, and he ran a Promote ASG Night at South Hall that evening. By February 1990 he was working with President Amos Gott on a minority handbook. His second term, and his resignation from it, are recorded under 1990-91.

Dwight Adkins was sworn in as an Associated Student Government representative at-large on 6 September 1988, alongside Ron Hennig, and was accepted as co-chair of the Public Relations Committee two weeks later, on 20 September 1988. The following year Congress approved Adkins as Student Rights chairman on 29 August 1989, the same meeting at which it accepted him as junior class vice president. His committee reported to Congress on 10 October 1989 that it had reviewed the university's alcohol policy with the campus lawyer and discussed expanding co-ed housing and 24-hour visitation; Adkins himself was recorded absent from that meeting. He resigned from the organization altogether at the 5 December 1989 meeting, citing schedule conflicts, and Congress replaced him as Student Rights chairman with Heather Falmlen. Adkins ran for the Associated Student Government presidency the following spring: the Herald's coverage on 5 April 1990 named him and Michael Colvin as the field, and the paper ran further pieces backing his campaign over the following week. Colvin won the 19 April 1990 election and took office for 1990-91, not Adkins.

holdings.what_they_did: Michael Colvin won the Associated Student Government presidential election in results the Herald reported on 19 April 1990 under the headline "Michael Colvin Aces Associated Student Government Election." The 1991 Talisman independently lists him as Associated Student Government President for 1990-91. In office, the Herald reported ASG considering a four-day class week (7 February 1991) and covered concern inside the organization over a change affecting student insurance (15 January 1991). The archive does not preserve further detail of how the term ended or what Colvin did afterward. Colvin took office in August 1990, introduced by the Herald as a new leader who wanted to make ideas reality. He had been active in the organization at least since September 1989, when he signed a Herald piece soliciting help for ASG. His spring 1991 agenda was the widest of the era: in a single February week ASG moved to cap tuition boosts, proposed overhauling the Detrex registration system, and planned lobbying to protect student financial aid. Letters he signed under Resolution 91-7-S survive in the SGA records, pressing administrators Kemble Johnson and Debby Cherwak for improvements to Detrex Field. Legislative records fill out the year beyond what the Herald's brief items captured. In fall 1990 the body introduced bills for a roundtable of student organization presidents (Bill #90-2-F) and for microwaves in the cafeterias (Bill #90-4-F). On 29 November 1990 it passed Resolution 90-10-F asking for a left-handed desk in every classroom, and killed Resolution 90-12-F, which had asked that absences tied to Iben Browning's widely publicized New Madrid Fault earthquake prediction be excused; no earthquake came. In the spring the Senate suspended and amended its own by-laws in a short cluster of bills, including Bill #91-6-S changing the procedure for overriding a presidential veto - a procedure tested weeks later when the emergency-kit resolution survived a veto on 14 March 1991. The spring term also produced a resolution asking the university to improve Detrex Field, the intramural field, and bills on joining the Hilltopper Athletic Foundation, recognizing presidential scholars in the Herald, and a book exchange board for Grise Hall.

holdings.source: Herald 65:55, 19 Apr 1990, "Michael Colvin Aces Associated Student Government Election"

holdings.what_they_did: The Associated Student Government's treasurer's seat stood vacant when the 1990-91 year opened. Candidates spoke to Congress on 11 September 1990 and Rob Evans won the floor election. The following February he asked Congress for ideas on how to appropriate money left over in the ASG budget. Evans was one of four candidates named in the Herald's "Meet the Candidates" coverage ahead of the April 1991 ASG presidential election, alongside Heather Falmlen, Van Hodge and Dan Knowles. Falmlen won.

Shannon Montgomery served as secretary of the Associated Student Government for 1990-91, reading the list of vacant Congress seats at every meeting and chasing committees and organizations for their written reports. She had earlier worked, through the Academic Affairs committee, on getting more evening classes offered.

Falmlen served as Administrative Vice-President in 1990-91, the year before she was elected president. She met individually with that year's committee heads, drove a campus recycling programme she reported should be solidly under way by the end of November 1990, and discussed the possibility of adding one or two more co-educational dormitories with Dave Parrott. She was elected Associated Student Government president for 1991-92 the following spring.

After his term as ASG president ended in 1990, Amos Gott returned to Congress as chairman of the Judicial Council. He resigned in January 1991, when a new part-time university staff job made him ineligible for office under the ASG constitution. The Herald reported his departure, alongside that of public relations vice president Van Hodge, on 17 January 1991 under the headline "Two Associated Student Government Officers Step Down."
holdings.source: Herald 66:33, 17 Jan 1991, "Two Associated Student Government Officers Step Down"

Paul Sagun was one of five people Congress accepted to the Judicial Council on 28 August 1990, alongside Amos Gott, Eddie Smith, Julie Fleming and Jeff Welch. The minutes of 5 February 1991 record him swearing in a slate of new officers: Karl Miller as public relations vice president, with Nancy Rascoe, Deanna Mills, Gretchen Ploch and Eric McWilliams taking representative seats. That page of the minutes gives his surname as Sagan; the August roster and the Herald both give Sagun. Falmlen won the Associated Student Government presidency in results the Herald reported on 11 April 1991 under the headline "Heather Falmlen Wins Amid Associated Student Government Election Protests." A Herald "Meet the Candidates" feature on 2 April had previewed four contenders for the race: Falmlen, Rob Evans, Van Hodge, and Dan Knowles. The same 11 April issue reported a rival group urging students to boycott the vote, an editorial calling the contest's "immature antics" a disappointment, and a published complaint that the Herald's own election coverage had been biased. In office, her administration fought a running battle over the makeup of the Board of Regents. On 29 October 1991 the Associated Student Government passed Resolution 91-6-F asking that Joe Iracane not be re-elected chair of the board; the Herald covered the vote the same day under "Associated Student Government Opposes Joseph Iracane." The board went ahead and re-elected him a week later, the university's own "On Campus" newsletter reported on 6 November. On 30 January 1992 the Herald reported the Associated Student Government was separately planning a committee aimed at student access to the regent, in the same issue that carried an editorial cartoon, "Ventriloquist's Dummy," targeting Falmlen. On 4 February 1992 the body passed Resolution 92-7-S, declaring its support for the WKU football program in spite of budget cuts; the Board of Regents voted that May to keep the program. That fall the body passed Resolution 91-2-F, asking for a change to Big Red Shuttle bus fares, and held its regular fall senate elections in October, including a separate freshman senator election on 15 October. The signature action of her term was procedural: on 7 April 1992 the Associated Students voted to rename itself the Student Government Association, a change students ratified in a referendum a week later, effective that autumn. WKU's own "On Campus" newsletter had confirmed on 22 May 1991, at the start of her term, that Falmlen held both the presidency and the student regent seat - the same dual role held by the presidents before and after her in this period. The archive does not preserve further detail of her regency or of what she did after her term. Other legislative business that fall included Resolution 91-7-F, backing the renewal of President Thomas Meredith's contract by the Board of Regents; a bill funding a "President for a Day" fundraiser (Bill #91-09-F); a bill funding renovation of the ASG chambers (Bill #91-03-F); and a bill proposing a new organizational slogan (Bill #91-11-F), introduced the same season the body renamed itself from the Associated Students to the Student Government Association.
holdings.source: Herald 66:54, 11 Apr 1991, "Heather Falmlen Wins Amid Associated Student Government Election Protests"

holdings.what_they_did: Joe Rains was elected Associated Student Government president on 14 April 1992, a contested race the Herald's election-day issue covered with dueling opinion pieces: an editorial headlined "Associated Student Government Needs Joe Rains" ran alongside a cartoon depicting him as Darth Vader, and the paper carried separate profile pieces on candidates Mark Miller, Mistianna Holcomb and Melony Jones. The same ballot carried the referendum that renamed Associated Students as the Student Government Association; Rains took office that autumn as the first president to serve under the new name. In office, Rains argued that SGA should support a campus student escort service (Herald, 10 December 1992) and took part in a rally at the state capitol in Frankfort urging the legislature to stop cuts to higher-education funding, for which the WKU University Senate commended him in Resolution R92.11. The archive does not preserve further detail of how the term ended. Rains ran for the presidency in April 1992 against Mistianna Holcomb, in the same election week that students voted on a referendum to rename the Associated Student Government as the Student Government Association. The Herald covered both races in a single issue, so his campaign and the rename were decided together. On election day the Herald's opinion pages carried a letter headlined "Associated Student Government Needs Joe Rains" alongside a Patrick Richardson editorial cartoon depicting Rains as Darth Vader, a sign of how visible the race had become on campus. The SGA's own list of presidents, published on its website in 2001, records Joe Rains of Nashville, Tennessee as the organization's 26th president, serving 1992-93, and marks him as having also served as student regent. The digitised record of his year does not name him directly in any indexed description, but it carries one distinctive trace: the minutes for December 1, 1992 record plans for a call-in radio show the association titled 'Just Ask Joe,' alongside Project Western and President for a Day. The same year's minutes show a congress preoccupied with state budget cuts, tuition increases, student health insurance and repeated plans for a rally in Frankfort.

Susan Mitchell served as SGA Administrative Vice President for 1992-93, the first year under the association's renaming from ASG to SGA. She chaired the ad hoc Vote America committee and ran a voter registration drive under the slogan "VOTE ABOUT IT," took applications for open Congress seats, and organized the September 1992 freshman elections. In February 1993 she reported to Congress that the President for a Day fundraiser, for which tickets had gone on sale that January, had gone well.

Jeremy Sublett served as SGA Treasurer for 1992-93. He instituted a fortnightly expense report and held organizational aid back while the loss of SGA's agency account was resolved. By February 1993 he reported that seventeen student groups had signed up for Project Western.

Ashley Rose served as SGA Secretary for 1992-93. She enforced the association's attendance rule, under which more than ten minutes' lateness counted as an absence and five absences was the limit for the year. She reported that Executive Council had vetoed Bill 93-2-S, which would have bought a fax machine for the SGA office.

Patrick Monahan served as SGA Public Relations Vice President for 1992-93; the minutes spell his surname both Monahan and Monohan. He distributed 16,000 student discount cards and announced that the state SGA conference would be held at Western the weekend of 31 October 1992. He reported the kick-off of Project Western and told Congress that every committee needed to produce one piece of legislation a week.

The Executive Council slate approved on 25 August 1992 named Donald Smith chair of the Legislative Research Committee, a post he still held that February, ahead of the spring election in which he won the SGA presidency for 1993-94.

Eric McWilliams was named chair of the Senate's Campus Improvements Committee on 25 August 1992, in the first Congress meeting of Joe Rains's administration. By February 1993 he had moved to chair Student Affairs instead, whose resolution proposing a study day before exam week passed unanimously on 9 February. He was one of two authors of Resolution 91-6-F, which opposed Joe Iracane's re-election as chairman of the Board of Regents. McWilliams ran for the Student Government Association presidency himself that spring, one of two juniors in the 1993 race against fellow committee chair Donald Smith. Smith won the 22 April 1993 election, which the Herald reported under the headline "Donald Smith Rolls to Victory."

Mark Miller was named chair of the Senate's Public Relations Committee on 25 August 1992, at the start of Joe Rains's administration, and co-authored Resolution 91-6-F with Eric McWilliams, opposing Joe Iracane's re-election as chairman of the Board of Regents. An opinion piece in the Herald's 14 April 1992 special election issue, printed alongside endorsements for presidential candidates Joe Rains, Melony Jones and Mistianna Holcomb, argued that Miller's campus involvement made him a leader; it did not name which office he sought. Rains won that spring's presidency. Two years later the Herald printed an opinion piece by Donald Smith and a Mark Miller urging the Class of 1994 to give back to Western; the shared name and Smith's own service in the same Congress make it likely, but not certain, that this is the same Miller.
Andrea Cailles was named chair of Student Affairs at Congress's meeting of 25 August 1992. No further record of her committee's work survives in this archive.

Smith won the April 1993 election decisively. The Herald's headline was "Student Government Association Election: Donald Smith Rolls to Victory." That September the Herald profiled the new president under the headline "Donald Smith Followed Grandfather's Lead All the Way to President's Office," tracing a family connection to the role he had just taken up. Smith, from Elizabethtown, went on to become president of the College Heights Foundation. Interviewed by the Herald in 2022, he said that while the structure had changed over the years, "the fundamental principle for SGA to be a voice for the students has remained unphased," and that if SGA improves over time the WKU experience improves with it.

holdings.what_they_did: Jason Embry served as SGA Treasurer for 1993-94. He required his own approval on all payments and reported expenditures and account balances to Congress: $308.06 in July 1993 and $5,467.56 in August, with the account standing at $38,977.50 on 12 October 1993, $16,839.28 on 22 March 1994 and $13,672.20 on 19 April 1994. He ran the organizational aid interviews of 12 and 13 October 1993.

Andrea Wilson served as SGA Secretary for 1993-94. She rewrote how legislation was filed, requiring it in by noon on Mondays on official forms or it would not be accepted, and she administered the constitutional rule sending members with five absences to Judicial Council. She ran the end-of-year awards nominations and organized the 26 April 1994 banquet at the Kentucky Museum.

Scott Sivley served as SGA Administrative Vice-President for 1993-94. He announced the first reading of a constitutional revision for 7 September 1993, required every Congress member to serve on two committees, and ran the committee behind the 3 November 1993 rally against tuition increases. He ran the April 1994 primary and called the 19 April 1994 meeting to order. He was himself a candidate in that primary, and the Herald reported in its 14 April issue that he had not followed SGA and university procedures during the election; the paper closed the season a week later with "Rob Evans & Tara Higdon Ready to Lead Students."
holdings.source: SGA Minutes, 31 Aug 1993, 29 Mar 1994 and 19 Apr 1994

As sole author of Bill 92-10-F, sponsored by the Campus Improvements Committee, introduced 27 October 1992 and passed unanimously, she created the office of Community Affairs Spokesperson, one delegate and two alternates appointed by the president to attend Bowling Green city council meetings and report city and community business back to SGA. In February 1993 she was one of six co-authors, with Matt Anderson, Trent Lyda, Eddie Myers, Molly Schreiner and Pamela Wells, of Resolution 93-2-S, sponsored by the Student Affairs Committee and passed unanimously, asking the university to set aside the Friday before exam week as a day of study rather than a class day. SGA's minutes of 31 August 1993 record Ahsan among the members seated that year on the Judicial Council.

The minutes spell the surname both Raffaelli and Rafaelli.

In that role he authored Bill 94-06-S, introduced 29 March 1994, recommending the Student Athletic Committee compile and publish a WKU athletics calendar with team schedules and photos, funded by advertising sold to local businesses.

Running for president in April 1994, Evans was profiled by the Herald as the candidate who urged discussion of the issues. He faced Scott Sivley in a contested race; on election day, 19 April, the Herald reported Sivley had been warned by SGA for violating the organization's campaign policies, alongside an opinion piece urging a vote for "Rob Evans, Tara Higdon" and another arguing that "Sacrificing Student Government Association Means Saving Needed Programs." The same issue's editorial pages told students "The Choice Is Yours" in the SGA vote. He won, and the Herald introduced the incoming leadership with "Rob Evans & Tara Higdon Ready to Lead Students." Higdon, elected alongside him, would succeed him as president a year later. The SGA's 2001 list of presidents records Robert Evans of Owensboro as the 28th president, serving 1994-95, and marks him as having also served as student regent. The Board of Regents' quarterly meeting of 15 August 1994 swore him in alongside Joy Gramling and Cornelius Martin, and carried resolutions of appreciation for outgoing officers Donald Smith - his predecessor as SGA president and student regent - and Monnie Hankins. The Board's quarterly meeting of 22 September 1995 - the start of the following academic year - swore in Tara Higdon as his successor on the board, marking the end of his regency. After his year leading the WKU student body, Rob Evans kept a statewide role: in April 1996 the Herald profiled him under the headline 'Rob Evans Representing Students from Across State,' describing his seat on the Kentucky Council on Higher Education, the body that then oversaw the state's public universities.

holdings.source: Herald 69:52, 21 Apr 1994, "Rob Evans & Tara Higdon Ready to Lead Students"

holdings.what_they_did: Tara Higdon was elected Administrative Vice President in April 1994, running alongside presidential candidate Rob Evans against Scott Sivley, and served in that office through 1994-95. A year later she was elected to succeed Evans as president and student regent for 1995-96. The Herald reported that result on 11 April 1995 under "Tara Higdon Moves Up; Voting Down," and SGA's own 2001 roster of former presidents records Tara D. Higdon of Slaughters as the 29th president. Her term is recorded on this site under the plaque's form of her name, Tara (Higdon) Howard.
holdings.source: Herald 69:52, 21 Apr 1994, "Rob Evans & Tara Higdon Ready to Lead Students"

No source directly identifies this Angelo Rodriguez with the Judicial Council member six months later; the connection rests on the matching full name and the short interval between the two records, not on independent corroboration.

The spelling is close enough to Derrek Duncan, who chaired the Legislative Research Committee the year before, that they may be the same person, but nothing in the archive confirms it, and the two are recorded separately here rather than merged.

Reporting to Congress on 8 November 1994, he said the committee had reviewed Resolutions 94-10-F, 94-11-F and 94-12-F and recommended all three for passage, and had tabled Bills 94-6-F and 94-7-F pending cost estimates.

Jason Young was named chair of the Senate's Public Relations Committee at Congress's first meeting of 1994-95, on 30 August 1994. The following spring, Young ran for the Student Government Association presidency. The Herald of 6 April 1995 covered him together with Jason Hays under the heading "Jason Young, Jason Hays Back New Level"; what office Hays sought, and whether the two ran as a ticket, the archive has not established. Young lost to Tara Higdon, the paper's issue of 18 April 1995 carrying the two candidates' closing statements on the day of the vote.

In that role he authored Bill 94-06-S, introduced 29 March 1994, recommending the Student Athletic Committee compile and publish a WKU athletics calendar with team schedules and photos, funded by advertising sold to local businesses.

Almost certainly the Jeff Yan (also written Jeffery Yan in the minutes) elected SGA Vice President on 18 April 1995 for 1995-96.

Higdon's path to the presidency ran through the campus security debates of 1995. During the spring campaign the Herald reported that her experience of being stalked had influenced her, under the headline "Campus Security: Stalking Influenced Tara Higdon." After a year as part of the elected leadership alongside Robert Evans, she won the presidency, and the Herald marked the transition with "Tara Higdon Sees New Beginning." Her term brought new emergency phones, a skywalk proposal, a campus store proposal and a push for longer visitation hours. The SGA's 2001 list of presidents records Tara D. Higdon of Slaughters as the 29th president, serving 1995-96, and marks her as having also served as student regent. Higdon won the presidency in April 1995, with the Herald reporting the result under the headline 'Tara Higdon Moves Up; Voting Down' - she moved up to the top office even as voter turnout fell. The paper's year-end editorial the following week argued that visibility would be the key to the association's success. Her year ended in a contested, four-way race to succeed her, and Higdon took a public side: her letter 'Vote for Kristin Miller' ran in the Herald's April 16, 1996 issue, in the same election-week pages as the candidates' debate coverage and the campaign for SGA's constitutional amendments. The spring of her term was the stormiest stretch in the association's decade of Herald coverage: within a single week in February 1996 the paper carried both SGA's skywalk proposal for the bottom of the Hill and a letter dismissing the association as a 'puppet' group, and by late April a columnist was asking whether students cared about student government at all.
A Slaughters junior; had served as Administrative Vice President and student regent in 1994-95 before moving up to the presidency.
holdings.source: Herald 70:51, 11 Apr 1995, "Tara Higdon Moves Up; Voting Down"

holdings.what_they_did: Elected 18 April 1995. The minutes record him as vice-president through the year: he called the regular meeting to order on 29 August 1995 and at nearly every meeting thereafter, and gave the vice-president's officer report. He designed the winning entry in SGA's Western flag contest, chosen by Congress on 14 November 1995. SGA's own minutes write the name Jeffery L. Yan, Jeffery Yan and Jeff Yan, and the Herald Jeffrey Yan; the variants are flagged rather than settled. A later pass filed him under the compound surname Adelson-Yan, which no cited source of the period carries.

Brandon Rucker served two consecutive years as SGA treasurer, 1994-95 (recorded in the minutes as Brandon T. Rucker) and 1995-96. In his first year he ran Organizational Aid, the child care grants and the Points of Light programme, all of them business of the opening meeting of 30 August 1994, and explained to new members the difference between a bill and a resolution. In his second year he reported summer expenditures of $4,497.08 and a balance of $37,256.92, and told Congress in January 1996 that about 60 per cent of the year's budget remained.

Erin Schepman was elected secretary of Congress on 18 April 1995. In that post she set out the attendance rule under which three unexcused absences from a Congress meeting sent a member before the Judicial Council, and she wrote to every campus organization about the Points of Light programme. Congress approved her, on a motion from David Apple, as Coordinator of Committees at the first meeting of 1996-97, on 27 August 1996, moving up after her year as secretary.

Stephanie McCarty chaired SGA's Academic Affairs Committee in 1994-95 and wrote Resolution 94-11-F, asking the university to require some form of examination before the end of the withdrawal period; it passed on second reading 8 November 1994, the same night she was voted Congress Member of the Month. She sat on Academic Council for Potter College that year and the next. In 1995-96 she moved to Coordinator of Committees, convening the committee heads after each Congress meeting and organising a phone-a-thon in September 1995.

holdings.what_they_did: Horace Johnson held an SGA office in 1995-96 whose title the archive does not record. He surfaces in the row that followed SGA's proposal of a campus skywalk that February: in the Herald of 13 February 1996, a letter from Tracie Webb defended Johnson and fellow officer Kristen Miller against the charge that the pair had been "hair-brained" over it.

Kristen Miller served as director of public relations for the Student Government Association in 1995-96. She explained the new place cards for the Congress chamber at the first meeting of the year on 29 August 1995 and proposed a dress code for Congress members, which the body discussed and voted down the following week. Through the winter she pushed the Western flag campaign her committee had launched that October, and on 5 March 1996 reported that Fred Hensley had taken SGA's flag designs to President Thomas Meredith. She ran for the SGA presidency that spring, with outgoing president Tara Higdon endorsing her in the Herald on 16 April, won, and took office for 1996-97. Some minutes and one Herald headline spell the forename Kristin; the spelling here follows the archive's other records and is not settled.

Swanson was announced as chair of the Academic Affairs Committee for the year at the SGA meeting of 29 August 1995. By the committee's report to Congress on 14 November 1995, David Apple was chairing it instead; the record does not show when or why the chairmanship changed hands.

David Apple chaired the Academic Affairs Committee for two consecutive years, 1995-96 and 1996-97. In November 1995 he reported the committee had legislation up for first reading and was working on a measure about available internet hours for students. By 1997-98 he sat on the Judicial Council. At the 21 April 1998 Congress meeting he announced the results of that spring's primary election from the floor: Brad Sweatt with 140 votes and Amy France with 95 advanced to the general election for Public Relations Director, ahead of Christoph Miller's 72.

Darlene Lodmell and her sister Carlene were accepted onto Congress together as sophomore off-campus representatives in August 1995. Darlene chaired the Student Affairs Committee that year, planning a Career Services forum for January 1996, and Congress voted her Committee Member of the Month on 14 November 1995. She served as secretary of Congress in 1996-97, signing that year's minutes and introducing a bulletin she called the Seconds, circulating important dates and the highlights of the previous meeting; she also set herself the goal of tracking legislation after Congress passed it. By 21 April 1998 she was serving on the Judicial Council.

Carlene Lodmell and her sister Darlene were accepted onto Congress together as sophomore off-campus representatives in August 1995. Carlene chaired the Legislative Research Committee that year, taking it through a review of the SGA constitution in the spring of 1996. The resulting amendments went to Congress as Bill 96-2-S and passed second reading on 5 March 1996, except for a proposed 2.5 GPA requirement for Congress members, which failed. Those amendments went before the student body that April; Shawna Whartenby, another Congress officer, urged a yes vote on them in a College Heights Herald piece printed 16 April 1996. Lodmell was elected vice president for 1996-97, calling every Congress meeting of the year to order, running the residence hall elections and serving as the student member of the OAR board. She stood for president in the spring 1997 election and lost to Keith Coffman, who thanked her from the floor of Congress for running a good campaign.

Steve Roadcap chaired the Campus Improvements Committee in 1995-96, working on campus lighting through the autumn and writing legislation in March 1996 about removing pay phones from campus. He was elected treasurer for 1996-97 and drew up that year's budget, cutting administrative costs while increasing organizational aid, the Glasgow campus budget, program funding and campus improvements; Congress rejected a motion to table the budget and approved it on 27 August 1996. President Keith Coffman swore him in as Judicial Foreman on 9 September 1997, and Roadcap in turn swore in the new members of Congress, telling them the Judicial Council would be more involved than in previous years.

Cindy Chiapetta was named chair of the Public Relations Committee on 29 August 1995. By that November the committee was reporting under co-chair Shawna Whartenby instead. Her surname appears as Chiappetta on 1998 legislation.

Shawna Whartenby co-chaired the Public Relations Committee in 1995-96. She gathered more than 175 signatures on a petition for a bandstand on the south lawn of the Downing University Center, and Congress voted her Member of the Month for February 1996. That April she wrote in the College Heights Herald urging students to vote yes on the SGA constitutional amendments then on the ballot, a package the Legislative Research Committee under Carlene Lodmell had brought to Congress as Bill 96-2-S that March. As Public Relations Director in 1996-97 she set the year's theme, recorded in the minutes as "SGA - Changing the Course of History At WKU!", ran publicity for the Provide-A-Ride service, and organized an AIDS Day banner with Student Health Services in December 1996.

Jason Loehr chaired the Programming Committee, created in autumn 1995 to plan SGA's events alongside the Public Relations Committee. He arranged SGA's halftime activities for the home game against Southwestern Louisiana on 18 February 1996.
Hadnot chaired the Cultural Diversity Committee, new that autumn, and reported to Congress on 14 November 1995 that it was drafting legislation for Black History Month.
Carter was chairing the Cultural Diversity Committee by 5 March 1996, when she reported to Congress that she was working on a forum about conflict between black women and white women.

Miller had been a Herald columnist and an SGA officer before winning the presidency; her letters in the paper defending the organization date to 1994. In her first weeks as president in August 1996 she made a plan to drive party-goers home, the beginning of what became the Provide-A-Ride service. As student body president she was the student representative on the committee searching for WKU's ninth president. Interviewed in 2016, she recalled serious talk of cutting football or academic programs, saying "there was one pot of money everyone was fighting over," and described how a late-arriving alumnus candidate named Gary Ransdell impressed the committee by pulling out a binder full of plans after his interview. In March 1997 the Herald ran "Kristen Miller Reflects on Year as Student Government Association President" as her term wound down. The SGA's 2001 list of presidents records Kristen L. Miller of Louisville as the 30th president and marks her as having also served as student regent. Miller won the SGA presidency in April 1996 at the end of a four-way race, with the Herald's news coverage declaring 'It's Kristen Miller's Time.' A week earlier the paper had profiled her campaign under the headline 'Kristen Miller Focuses on Experience in Student Government Association.' Days into the fall semester, the Herald reported 'Kristen Miller Makes Plan to Drive Party-Goers Home.' The idea became Provide-a-Ride, the safe-ride program that appears in SGA's minutes throughout 1996-97 and was still being funded by the congress years later. Near the end of her term, the Herald ran 'Kristen Miller Reflects on Year as Student Government Association President,' looking back on a year that included the creation of a Technology Committee, the Provide-a-Ride launch and SGA's narrow vote to back adding sexual orientation to Western's anti-discrimination policy.

Carlene Lodmell and her sister Darlene were accepted onto Congress together as sophomore off-campus representatives in August 1995; that spring they had already co-authored Resolution 95-6-S, asking for an annual Sibling's Day so that siblings under 18 could visit campus outside of the autumn Parents' Day. In 1995-96 Carlene chaired the Legislative Research Committee, taking it through a review of the constitution and bringing the resulting amendments to Congress as Bill 96-2-S, which passed on second reading on 5 March 1996 — all but a proposed 2.5 GPA requirement for Congress members, which failed. The amendments went to a student ballot in April 1996; fellow officer Shawna Whartenby urged students in a Herald letter to vote yes on them. Lodmell was elected vice president for 1996-97, calling every Congress meeting of the year to order, running the residence hall elections and serving as the student member of the OAR board. She stood for president in spring 1997 and lost to Keith Coffman, who thanked her from the floor for running a good campaign.

Steve Roadcap chaired SGA's Campus Improvements Committee in 1995-96, working on campus lighting through the autumn and writing legislation in March 1996 about pay phones being removed from campus. He was elected treasurer for 1996-97 and drew up that year's budget, cutting administrative costs and increasing funding for organizational aid, the Glasgow campus, programmes and campus improvements; Congress rejected a motion to table it and approved it on 27 August 1996. In 1997-98 he served as Judicial Foreman, sworn in by President Keith Coffman on 9 September 1997 and then swearing in all new members of Congress himself.

Darlene Lodmell and her sister Carlene were accepted onto Congress together as sophomore off-campus representatives in August 1995, after co-authoring Resolution 95-6-S that spring asking for an annual Sibling's Day. She chaired SGA's Student Affairs Committee in 1995-96, planning a Career Services forum for January 1996 and was voted Committee Member of the Month on 14 November 1995. As secretary in 1996-97 she signed the year's minutes and introduced a bulletin she called the Seconds, circulating important dates and highlights from the previous meeting, and set herself the goal of tracking legislation after Congress passed it. She was still active on the Judicial Council in 1997-98, present at the meeting of 21 April 1998.

Erin Schepman was elected SGA secretary on 18 April 1995 and served through 1995-96. She set out the attendance rule under which three unexcused absences sent a Congress member before the Judicial Council, and wrote to every campus organisation about the Points of Light programme. Congress approved her as Coordinator of Committees on a motion of David Apple at the first meeting of 1996-97, 27 August 1996, moving up after her year as secretary.

Ryan Faught chaired the Legislative Research Committee in the autumn of 1996. Giving his last remarks as chair on 21 January 1997, he told the bylaws committee that legislation could not be reviewed without its author present. Congress accepted him as Coordinator of Committees the same day, 21 January 1997, moving him across from the Legislative Research chair.

Shawna Whartenby co-chaired SGA's Public Relations Committee in 1995-96, gathering more than 175 signatures on a petition for a bandstand on the DUC south lawn and was voted Congress Member of the Month for February 1996. That April she wrote a Herald letter urging students to "Vote Yes on Student Government Association Ballot for Amendments," the constitutional amendments Carlene Lodmell's Legislative Research Committee had brought to a second reading the previous month. She was named public relations director for 1996-97, setting the year's theme - recorded in the minutes as "SGA- Changing the Course of History At WKU!" - and announcing it at the first meeting. She ran the Provide-A-Ride publicity and organised an AIDS Day banner with Student Health Services in December 1996.

Jeff Yan (also written Jeffery Yan in the minutes) was elected SGA vice president on 18 April 1995 and called every Congress meeting of 1995-96 to order. He designed the winning entry in SGA's Western flag contest, chosen by Congress on 14 November 1995. In 1996-97 he moved to Judicial Council Foreman, swearing in the Congress members elected the previous spring at the opening meeting of 27 August 1996 and then swearing in newly approved members.
Josh Detre served as parliamentarian in 1996-97 and received one of the Senate's Public Relations awards at the 19 November 1996 meeting.

Chad Lewis was elected to Congress as a freshman council member in the fall of 1995. He served as Sergeant of Arms in 1996-97, and Congress named him, alongside the parliamentarian, a Public Relations award winner on 19 November 1996. As treasurer in 1997-98 he presented a budget of $41,756 for approval in September 1997 and reported that November that expenditures to date stood at $11,150.68 against a balance of $30,605.32. In April 1998 the Herald covered his campaign for vice president as a contested race against Laura Hancock, under the headline "Race for Student Government Association Vice Presidency Heats Up." He was elected executive vice president for 1998-99. As executive vice president he called Congress to order through the year in place of the president, and set goals of a spring turnout of 1,400 voters, every Congress seat filled, and a doubling of Provide-A-Ride use. By January 1999 he reported more than 100 people had used the ride service in the last week of the fall semester.

Apple chaired the Academic Affairs Committee across two years running. By November 1995 he was reporting for the committee, which by then had passed from Terra Swanson's initial August appointment to him; on 14 November 1995 he reported legislation on internet hours. He continued as Academic Affairs chair into the following year, named again to the post at the SGA meeting of 27 August 1996. In 1997-98 Apple sat on the Judicial Council instead. At the SGA meeting of 21 April 1998 he announced from the floor the results of that spring's primary election for Public Relations Director, reporting vote totals of Brad Sweatt 140, Amy France 95 and Christoph Miller 72, which sent Sweatt and France to the general election.

Met Charlie Wolfram of Facilities Management about campus lighting and recommended three pieces of legislation on it; Resolutions 96-5-F, 96-9-F and 96-10-F on lights near Gilbert, East and West Halls and the Diddle parking lot went to first reading on 19 November 1996. She was president two years later.

Ryan Faught chaired SGA's Legislative Research Committee in the autumn of 1996-97 and gave his last remarks as chair on 21 January 1997, telling the bylaws committee that legislation could not be reviewed without an author present. Congress accepted him as Coordinator of Committees the same day, moving him from the committee chairmanship into the cabinet.

Congress accepted Gailor as chair of the Legislative Research Committee on 21 January 1997; he also served as SGA's City Commission representative that year. He continued as Legislative Research chair into 1997-98, and on 18 November 1997 reported that the committee had reviewed eleven pieces of legislation that session, voting down Resolution 97-17-F for insufficient research and untabling Resolution 97-10-F.

Leigh Ann Sears chaired the Campus Improvements Committee in 1996-97, running the Designated Driver card scheme and the spring campus clean-up, and working with treasurer Steve Roadcap on a gazebo project. She was elected vice president for the following year. As vice president in 1997-98 she presided over Congress all year, ran the Weekend in the Woods retreat, and reported Provide-A-Ride ridership week by week, telling Congress on 18 November 1997 that 52 people had ridden the service the previous Thursday night. In April 1998 she announced that year's presidential debate and the dates of the general election.

Heather Rogers chaired the Public Relations Committee in 1996-97, and became Director of Public Relations the following year. In that post she revived SGA's old newsletter, The Gavel, set up a monthly SGA and University Center Board calendar in the College Heights Herald, and organized a blood drive in West Hall Cellar in December 1997; she asked every committee to file three goals for the spring. She was named to the Judicial Council at the executive retreat in July 1998, moving into that role after her year running public relations.

Kip Carr chaired both the newly created Technology Committee and the Bylaws Committee in 1996-97. He built SGA's website, surveyed peak usage of the campus computer labs, and was voted Congress Member of the Month for November 1996; the week before, he had filled in as acting secretary and typed the minutes himself.

Coffman presided over one of the busiest legislative years in the surviving 1990s record. The SGA's own legislation archive for 1997 preserves at least 24 numbered bills and resolutions from his fall semester alone, from the Dogwood Drive crosswalk to the ten-point grade scale, student e-mail addresses in the directory and ice machines in every residence hall. The SGA's 2001 list of presidents records Keith Coffman of Russellville as the 31st president, serving 1997-98, and marks him as having also served as student regent. His term coincided with Gary Ransdell's first year as university president. Coffman's presidency opened with the Herald's April 24, 1997 headline 'Keith Coffman Takes Charge,' paired with a story in the same issue in which the new Student Government Association president mapped out his upcoming term.

Leigh Ann Sears was elected vice president on 22 April 1997 and presided over Congress meetings throughout Keith Coffman's term. She organized the Weekend in the Woods retreat and gave Congress weekly ridership counts for the Provide-A-Ride van service, reporting on 18 November 1997 that 52 students had used it the previous Thursday night. In April 1998 she announced the SGA presidential debate and set the dates of that spring's general election.

Chad Lewis served as treasurer under Keith Coffman, presenting a 1997-98 budget of $41,756 for Congress's approval in September 1997. By November he reported expenditures of $11,150.68 against a remaining balance of $30,605.32. He was elected executive vice president for the following year.

Jamie Fite served as secretary under Keith Coffman and signed SGA's outgoing correspondence to the university administration throughout the year, including letters pushing for more student seating at athletic events, housing stipends for off-campus students, and action on legislation that had stalled with the administration.

Stephanie Cosby served as coordinator of committees under Keith Coffman. She convened the committee heads after each Congress meeting, organized a secret Santa exchange for Congress in December 1997, and authored Resolution 97-20-F recognizing honors graduates, which passed unanimously on 18 November 1997.

Heather Rogers served as director of public relations under Keith Coffman. She revived SGA's newsletter, The Gavel, and arranged a monthly SGA and University Center Board calendar printed in the College Heights Herald. She organized a blood drive in West Hall Cellar in December 1997 and asked every Congress committee to file three goals for the spring semester.
Sworn in by President Coffman on 9 September 1997 and then swore in all new members of Congress, telling them the Judicial Council would be more involved than in previous years.
Boyer is recorded as a guest of Congress alongside the other Judicial Council members at the meeting of 21 April 1998.

Apple chaired the Academic Affairs Committee across two years running. By November 1995 he was reporting for the committee, which by then had passed from Terra Swanson's initial August appointment to him; on 14 November 1995 he reported legislation on internet hours. He continued as Academic Affairs chair into the following year, named again to the post at the SGA meeting of 27 August 1996. In 1997-98 Apple sat on the Judicial Council instead. At the SGA meeting of 21 April 1998 he announced from the floor the results of that spring's primary election for Public Relations Director, reporting vote totals of Brad Sweatt 140, Amy France 95 and Christoph Miller 72, which sent Sweatt and France to the general election.
Present as a Judicial Council member on 21 April 1998, after serving as secretary in 1996-97.

Detre continued as parliamentarian in 1997-98, moving at the 9 September 1997 meeting that all candidates running unopposed be accepted by acclamation. He ran for the presidency himself in spring 1998, and the Herald profiled him on election day under the headline "Josh Detre Doesn't Fit Traditional Mold." Stephanie Cosby won the election.
Took the dead week proposal to Academic Council and authored Resolution 97-15-F on announcing syllabi in the schedule bulletin, passed unanimously on 18 November 1997.

Jason Cole chaired the Student Affairs Committee in 1997-98 and researched a proposed career and job fair for the university. He authored Resolution 97-12-F to extend campus parking spaces limited to ten minutes up to fifteen minutes; Congress defeated it 20-28 on 18 November 1997.

Congress accepted Gailor as chair of the Legislative Research Committee on 21 January 1997; he also served as SGA's City Commission representative that year. He continued as Legislative Research chair into 1997-98, and on 18 November 1997 reported that the committee had reviewed eleven pieces of legislation that session, voting down Resolution 97-17-F for insufficient research and untabling Resolution 97-10-F.

Anne Guillory chaired the Constitutional Review Committee, which spent 1997-98 revising SGA's constitution, and was chairing the Legislative Research Committee by April 1998. She authored Resolution 98-16-S, establishing a student mentor program, and argued for it on the ground that students find it easier to talk to their peers; Congress passed it unanimously on 21 April 1998.

Chaired the Legislative Research subcommittee set up to prepare a revised constitution for a student vote at the spring 1998 election. She reported on 18 November 1997 that the committee had reworked the draft with the Executive Council.

Callie Varner chaired the Campus Improvements Committee in 1997-98, setting the committee's goals as a more accessible campus for disabled students, finishing the Designated Driver card scheme, and continuing work on the gazebo project.

Vice-chair in November 1997 and chair by April 1998. He authored Resolutions 98-13-S on on-campus phones in Grise Hall and 98-18-S on maintaining lights on the sidewalk between DUC and Preston, both passed unanimously on 21 April 1998.

Jenny Stith chaired the Public Relations Committee in 1997-98 and authored Resolution 97-10-F, extending housing scholarships to off-campus housing. The minutes record it as heavily discussed, with several voices in favour and several against, before Congress passed it 35-15 on 18 November 1997; she had spoken in its favour and taken questions from the floor.

Cosby is documented in office from the start of the 1998 fall semester, when the Kentucky Board of Student Body Presidents billed its dues in a memo addressed to "SGA president Stephanie Cosby." Her congress passed at least thirteen numbered bills that fall, from Murray State fire relief to Bookswap.com, and her officers answered public charges of unproductiveness with a written record of what had passed. The SGA's 2001 list of presidents records Stephanie Cosby of Greenville as the 32nd president, serving 1998-99, and marks her as having also served as student regent. Cosby campaigned on financial aid, with the Herald's election-week coverage reporting that she wanted more scholarships. She won the presidency in a rout: the paper's April 30, 1998 election story ran under the headline 'Stephanie Cosby Rolls to Huge Victory,' next to a report on how taxing election day had been for the officer candidates. Midway through her term she picked up a second title, with the Herald reporting 'Stephanie Cosby Named Queen of Hill' at homecoming in October 1998. Her year in office produced a steady advising-reform push, the failed University Boulevard widening request, the Kappa Alpha aid fight, and ended with the Judicial Council overturning the election to choose her successor.
Of Greenville; also served as student regent.
holdings.source: Herald 73:53, 30 Apr 1998, "Stephanie Cosby Rolls to Huge Victory"

holdings.what_they_did: As executive vice president under Stephanie Cosby in 1998-99, Chad Lewis called Congress to order in the president's absence throughout the year. He set goals of turning out 1,400 voters in the spring election, filling every Congress seat, and doubling use of the Provide-A-Ride service, and reported in January 1999 that more than 100 students had used the ride service in the final week of the fall semester.

Signed the minutes all year as vice president of administration, called the roll, read Resolution 98-1-F on a Normal Drive crosswalk for first reading, and set the spring 1999 election calendar. He co-authored Bill 98-10-F, the failed grant to Kappa Alpha after its house fire, circulated the fall 1998 legislative record to answer charges of unproductiveness, and wrote to president Gary Ransdell on student health services in April 1999. This archive recorded him for a time only as Vice President; the minutes give the fuller title.

Carleton Ruminer served as vice president of finance under Stephanie Cosby, presenting the 1998-99 budget to Congress on 1 September 1998 against a balance of $41,783 and reporting on it weekly through the fall semester. His stated goals for the year included extending library hours and creating a book exchange. His surname appears as Rumenier and Rumienier in SGA's 1997 minutes.

Ryan Morrison began 1998-99 as chief justice of the Judicial Council. By 13 April 1999 he was serving as vice president of finance, reporting a balance of $15,276.24 to Congress that week. A fortnight later he won a 26 April 1999 re-run election for vice president of finance for 1999-2000, after the initial 15 April result was voided.
Christoph Miller was appointed coordinator of committees at the executive retreat in July 1998 and introduced himself to Congress at its first meeting of the year, on 1 September 1998.

Amanda Cole was appointed historian at the executive retreat in July 1998. She also chaired the Public Relations Committee from the start of the year and set the theme for the 1999 Coming Home celebration, "Mardi Gras on the Hill."

holdings.office: Officer (title not specified in the archive)
holdings.what_they_did: Issued the Executive Council's written response to an anonymous congress member's complaint about the tone of SGA meetings, November 1998.

Brad Sweatt was elected vice president of public relations in the spring 1998 general election, after leading the primary with 140 votes. He launched SGA's new web page, crediting Jeff Baynham as its designer, and read Congress's theme for the year at its first meeting of 1998-99.

Cassie Martin introduced herself to Congress as the new vice president of public relations on 19 January 1999. She took over the Coming Home and Bowl for Kid's Sake events and handled SGA's advertising in the College Heights Herald.

Sworn in by President Cosby at the first meeting of 1 September 1998, then swore in all committee chairs, appointed officers and class and dorm representatives. He was still swearing in new members on 19 January 1999.
Drew Harrell was appointed to SGA's Judicial Council at the executive retreat of July 1998.
Named to the Judicial Council at the July 1998 executive retreat, having been director of public relations the previous year.

Jeff Baynham was appointed parliamentarian at SGA's executive retreat in July 1998. He designed the organization's new web page, for which the vice president of public relations thanked him at Congress's first meeting of the year.
Called the Congress meeting of 13 April 1999 to order while the president and executive vice president were counting election ballots.

Joe Murrell was appointed sergeant of arms at SGA's executive retreat in July 1998. The Congress minutes of January and April 1999 record a "Joe Morel" moving to adjourn the meeting; the spelling is not reconciled with his in the record.

Mitchell Bailey represented Pearce-Ford Tower in SGA's Congress for 1998-99. The archive's two sources on him disagree on his role: one credits him with issuing the Executive Council's written response to an anonymous Congress member's complaint about the tone of SGA meetings in November 1998, while the Congress minutes of 17 November 1998 record him only as the Pearce-Ford Tower representative, addressing Congress with remarks attached to the minutes, and note he held no executive office. Both describe the same November 1998 episode over the complaint about meeting tone.

Larry Murphy chaired SGA's Academic Affairs Committee in 1998-99. He co-authored Bill 98-10-F, which would have allocated $250 to the Kappa Alpha Order fraternity after its house burned on 17 November 1998; the bill failed on its second reading on 1 December. He also reported to Congress that a proposed teacher block-scheduling resolution had been shelved because Dr Barbara Burch had already put the change in place.

Recommended Resolution 98-15-F on publishing the SGA advisor checklist in the schedule bulletins, and postponed Resolution 98-11-F on teacher education indefinitely. He co-authored Resolution 98-7-F with President Cosby on widening University Boulevard, which failed on 13 October 1998, and authored Resolution 99-3-S releasing the Student Health Service reserve fund, which passed on 13 April 1999.

Tim Hatton chaired SGA's Student Affairs Committee in 1998-99. He ran the spring 1999 camp fair, worked on a weekend student survey and a proposed SGA scholarship, and authored Bill 99-20-S to extend library hours during finals week; Congress postponed the bill on 13 April 1999 over the cost of paying student workers overtime.

Laura Hancock ran for Student Government Association vice president in spring 1998, in a race the Herald covered on 16 April under the headline "Race for Student Government Association Vice Presidency Heats Up." Her opponent, Chad Lewis, won the office. Congress appointed Hancock chair of the Senate's Campus Improvements Committee at the July 1998 executive retreat instead; her committee worked on campus lighting, ashtrays, a Habitat for Humanity project and adding copy machines on campus. She was nominated in April 1999 for both the Dero Downing and Mary Angela Norcia awards.
Matt Bogard introduced himself to Congress as the new chair of the Campus Improvements Committee at the meeting of 19 January 1999.

Amy France ran for Student Government Association public relations director in the spring 1998 election, one of three candidates the Herald named on 9 April in a story headlined "Race for Public Relations Post Heating Up," alongside Christoph Miller and Brad Sweatt. Sweatt won the office. Congress appointed France chair of the Senate's Public Relations Committee at the July 1998 executive retreat instead, but by the first Congress meeting that September the committee was already reporting under a successor, Amanda Cole.
Reported for the committee from the first meeting of 1 September 1998; her committee drafted the measure to help the Kappa Alpha members after the fire and set the 1999 Coming Home theme.

Sally Eilerman co-chaired SGA's Hillraisers committee in 1998-99, running it through the basketball season and arranging a meeting with Coach Felton in November 1998. Congress nominated her that April for both the outstanding Congress member award and the Charles A. Keown award.
After losing the presidency, Detre stayed active in the Senate, co-chairing the Hillraisers Committee in 1998-99 under president Stephanie Cosby.

Contemporaneous records give her name as Amanda J. Coates. The SGA's own 2001 list of presidents records Amanda J. Coates of Brownsville as the 33rd president, serving 1999-2000, and marks her as having also served as student regent. The organization's website during and just after her term consistently refers to "President Amanda Coates." She won the presidency in a contested April 1999 race against Will Jones, in results so close the Coates-Martin ticket demanded a recount: the initial 616-611 tally over Jones and running mate Kara Yeckering narrowed to 614-611 on the recount. A write-in ticket, Dwight Campbell and Kerri Richardson, took 145 votes. The same election saw a bitter down-ballot fight for vice president of finance, where Joe Matheis beat Ryan Morrison 700-688 only after SGA's judicial council reviewed - and let stand - his victory over a campaign-flier violation, and a Herald letter to the editor questioned SGA's handling of an investigation into racially charged fliers that had targeted Jones, the first Black SGA presidential candidate in years. The Herald's pre-election issue had separately reported SGA questioning an election-eve pizza party Jones held, and a debate over dropping the rule requiring a year of SGA service before running for office. Her signature project was publishing faculty evaluations. From February 2000 she led meetings with the university president, the Faculty Senate chair and the senate's executive committee, and in April she co-authored Resolution 00-2-S with Adam Howard asking the Faculty Senate to approve a mandatory published evaluation beginning that fall. At the end of her term the SGA website opened with the words "What SGA has done for you," showcasing three things: the faculty evaluations project, the fight over the Vice President of Student Affairs position and the Provide-A-Ride service. It is as close to a self-written record of her administration's priorities as survives. As her term closed, the Herald ran an exit interview, "Amanda Coates Reflects on Year as President," in its April 25, 2000 issue. The election to succeed her, held in late March 2000, was contested between Cassie Martin and Duan Wright; Martin won, and by the following issue the Herald was asking the incoming president to "stand up on tough issues" while confirming that the faculty evaluations Coates had championed would be conducted and published starting that fall. The Herald introduced the incoming 1999-2000 president on April 22, 1999 under the headline 'New Student Government Association Leader Workaholic.' The paper's index records the new leader's name as Amanda Coates, and she took office in the aftermath of a spring election that SGA's Judicial Council had overturned two days earlier. Her congress spent the fall of 1999 building institutions: it created an Information Technology Director and website guidelines, established a senior awards banquet and hall of distinguished seniors, launched the toll-free Topline activity line, and publicly opposed an administrative move in Student Affairs while asking that Vice President Jerry Wilder be retained. Her public service continued past her SGA year at the state level. Kentucky's Council on Postsecondary Education carries a statewide student member, and the council's minutes of 13 November 2000 record a district judge swearing her in, introducing her as Amanda Coates, a graduate of Western Kentucky University then studying public policy at the University of Kentucky. The council's minutes of 30 July 2001 record Governor Paul Patton appointing Christopher J. Pace to replace the outgoing student member, named there as "Amanda Coates Lich." Those two records together are what tie the Coates who led WKU's SGA in 1999-2000 to the surname the SGA Chambers plaque uses for the same year.
Won a recount, 614-611, over Will Jones and running mate Kara Yeckering.
Coates's running mate; elected SGA president the following year, 2000-01.

Cassie Martin, a junior from Glasgow, was elected SGA president in April 2000 to lead the association for 2000-2001. With running mate Leslie Bedo, she defeated the ticket of Duan Wright and Dwight Campbell by 654 votes to 541, and the win also made her the student representative on Western's Board of Regents. The race followed weeks of Herald coverage of proposed SGA election-code reforms meant to close loopholes and set spending limits, and the Martin-Wright contest itself was covered from the candidacy announcement in late March through a pre-election issues debate. Her most visible stand of the year came at the Board of Regents meeting on October 27, 2000, when the board voted 8-2 to raise the student athletic fee by $80 in two installments. Martin was one of only two dissenters, alongside Faculty Regent Mary Ellen Miller. She said she understood the need for the additional funding but questioned the timing and the amount, and disagreed with raising student fees in the middle of an academic year. SGA's congress in 2001 passed legislation putting $13,000 toward a campus gazebo that was never built. In October 2002 the Herald reported that the money had mistakenly gone back into SGA's general fund and been spent on other things, including computers, and SGA's finance vice president said leaders from the past two years, including former presidents Martin and Leslie Bedo, were all partly responsible for not properly earmarking it. Leslie Bedo, a senior corporate communications major from Bowling Green, served as SGA president for 2001-02 after three years in the organization, having previously been parliamentarian, public relations committee chair and executive vice president. Her stated priorities for the year were tuition, student health and online course syllabi, and she described SGA as run "by the students, for the students." As student regent, Bedo pushed back in August 2001 when the Board of Regents raised tuition 9 percent at a meeting held before fall classes officially began. She said the timing sent "a message to students" that the increase would pass before they could weigh in, though she ultimately joined the board's unanimous vote approving it. That November, Bedo wrote a Herald op-ed titled "Meeting Goals of Student Government Association, But Not Students'", questioning the organization's effectiveness; fellow member Troy Ransdell responded in the same issue with a piece headlined "Action, Not Complaints." The same paper reported SGA was buying Christmas presents for children at Potter Children's Home that season. In March 2002, near the end of her term, Bedo publicly challenged the university after a land deal meant to add 400 to 500 parking spaces fell through while the Diddle Arena renovation was removing about 200 spaces. She noted regents had raised the student athletics fee on the expectation of more parking, said "the parking has been put on hold," and called added parking imperative because more students parked on campus than attended basketball games. As her term wound down, an April 30, 2002 Herald profile by Molly O'Connor reported renewed interest in SGA under Bedo's leadership. Jamie Sears was elected to succeed her that April; Bedo's own former rival for vice president of administration, Patti Johnson, went on to become SGA president herself in a September 2004 special election.
Already recorded as president/regent for this year from other sources; corroborated here as the officer presiding over the President's report at Congress's first meeting of the year.

Sears, a junior public relations major from Melber, won the presidency in a landslide, defeating senior Sam Stinson 1,284 votes to 594 in the April 2002 general election that also seated her incoming executive team: John Bradley as executive vice president, Ross Pruitt as vice president of finance, Anna Coats as vice president of public relations, and Brandon Copeland as vice president of administration. Sears opened her 2002-03 term as SGA president under immediate scrutiny. Seventeen months after congress passed a bill putting about $5,000 of leftover budget money toward an on-campus gazebo, members discovered the gazebo was never built and the money was gone. When three members petitioned congress in September over $28,000 they said was unaccounted for, Sears told the Herald, "I have absolutely no idea where that money went." The petition was withdrawn only after her executive council created an ad hoc financial review committee. By October the money had been traced: it had slipped back into SGA's general fund and been spent on other things, including computers for the SGA office. Sears acknowledged that she and former student activities director Scott Taylor had decided during the summer where the leftover money, which included the gazebo funds, would be allocated, saying other executive council members were consulted through email. She said the financial review committee would explain the budget findings to congress, and no move was made to set aside new gazebo money. Sears finished the year on stronger footing. She traveled with about 20 Western students to Frankfort to oppose state budget cuts to higher education, calling the trip one of SGA's greatest accomplishments: "That was a great feeling seeing students from everywhere rallying for the same cause." Under her leadership congress debated more than 55 pieces of legislation and passed the first student referendum in SGA history, a $3 fee for radio station Revolution 91.7 that students approved in the spring election. Her final meeting as president came on April 22, 2003.
holdings.source: College Heights Herald 77:51, 11 Apr 2002 - "Jamie Sears Wins Election in Landslide" (O'Connor, Molly)

Ross Pruitt took office as vice president of finance for 2002-03, his candidacy covered in the Herald's election issue of 28 March 2002. Reporting the finding to the Herald on 1 October 2002, Pruitt said past leaders had not properly earmarked the money and that year's executive council had spent it without knowing what it was, and that responsibility ran across his own council and those of the previous two years, including former presidents Leslie Bedo and Cassie Martin. Robert Watkins, a Bowling Green sophomore, was serving on Congress in October 2003 when he authored a resolution recommending students vote in the 4 November election, moving to suspend the by-laws so it could pass without the usual delay; it passed unanimously. The following spring Watkins wrote the new three-branch constitution as chair of the Legislative Research Committee, and Congress elected him the senate's first speaker on 13 April 2004, defeating Brittany Fausey 9 votes to 8 with 17 of 20 members present. The result was disputed immediately because the new constitution did not make clear whether two-thirds of eligible voters or of the full membership was required, and three members present had been barred from voting by a judicial council ruling; one member warned of a “semester of frustration” if the dispute went unresolved. Abby Lovan had withdrawn from the race before the ballot, and Fausey declined to challenge the result. Watkins went on to win the SGA presidency in April 2006 and served until his resignation that November; his full term is recorded under his leader entry for 2006-07.

Nick Todd, a Henderson senior and SGA's outgoing vice president of finance, won the presidency in March 2004 with 772 of the 1,232 votes cast. Days before the new officers were sworn in on 27 April, the judicial council found $611 missing from the SGA Aramark Dining Dollars account, which had opened the year with $5,000. A senator drafted articles of impeachment against the finance post Todd was about to leave, and the council ruled a two-week process could not finish before he left it anyway. Only Todd, outgoing president John Bradley and the adviser held cards to the account. He submitted his resignation in July, citing personal conflicts within the association. In May the university's internal auditor had reported more than $800 of questionable purchases from the account between August 2003 and May 2004, mostly small buys at campus restaurants with no receipts, and recommended he reimburse the money along with $71 charged on the SGA purchasing card after a spring break car rental. Campus police determined no police action was necessary. In September the dean of Student Life said Todd had been sanctioned by judicial affairs in July, disputing Todd's public account that losing the card was the only action taken against him. Executive vice president Katie Dawson acted as president until the special election of 14 and 15 September. Patti Johnson, the previous year's executive vice president, was the only student to come forward for the office, saying she ran because of the turmoil within the organization, and was sworn in on 23 September. The Herald noted at the time that a re-election for SGA president is rare.
holdings.source: Herald, 24 Aug 2004 - Todd cites personal conflicts in resignation

holdings.what_they_did: Katie Dawson held the SGA presidency for about two months in the summer of 2004 without having been elected to it. She had come up through the cabinet as Nick Todd's running mate in the March election and was his executive vice president when he resigned in July amid the Dining Dollars investigation. She acted in the office until students voted in a special election that September. Hers is the only one of the archive's four mid-year vacancies filled this way. In 2004 the presidency was treated as vacant and put back to the students, with the executive vice president acting until they had voted. When Rob Watkins resigned in November 2006 and when Johnathon Boles resigned in January 2009, the executive vice president succeeded to the office instead, Jeanne Johnson being sworn in as president at that year's Winter Banquet. The same organisation met the same kind of vacancy in two different ways within five years. She was elected president in her own right for 2005-06, and the Chambers wall carries her for that year alone.
holdings.source: Herald, 24 Aug 2004 - Todd cites personal conflicts in resignation

holdings.what_they_did: Patti Johnson, a senior from Marion, had been active in SGA for over three years and served on committees including public relations and athletics before becoming executive vice president in 2003-04. Nick Todd, the vice president of finance, was elected president for 2004-05 in March 2004, but before the new officers were sworn in on April 27, SGA's judicial council fielded an allegation that $611 was missing from the SGA Dining Dollars account, an account that had started the year with $5,000. Senator Josh Collins drafted articles of impeachment against Todd's vice presidency, but the judicial council ruled a two-week impeachment process could not finish before he left that office anyway. Johnson had not planned to run for president herself, but after Todd's resignation that July she entered the September 2004 special election as the only candidate to show interest, saying she stayed on because of "the turmoil within the organization" and that she knew "what it takes to get the job done." Johnson ran unopposed for president and student regent in the Sept. 14-15 online election, the group having been without an elected president since July. She said she was disappointed that students would not "really get to make a decision," but still planned light campaigning, and she wanted to continue reviewing the plus/minus grading proposal and to make faculty evaluations available to students. Johnson received 1,291 votes in the two-day uncontested election and was sworn in as president at SGA's fall reception on Sept. 23, 2004, one week after her election. She said committees had been formed and members had begun proposing legislation, and she looked forward to being sworn in as student regent at the Oct. 29 Board of Regents meeting, declaring it was "back to business." She served through the year until Katie Dawson was elected to succeed her in the March 2005 spring election. Johnson served as the Board of Regents' student member from August 2004 to July 2005, a term confirmed by the resolution of appreciation the board read into its July 22, 2005 minutes when Katie Dawson, the executive vice president who had served alongside her all year, was sworn in to replace her. Dawson had come up through the cabinet as Todd's running mate in the original March 2004 election and had acted as interim president during the summer vacancy before Johnson's win.
Also held the Board of Regents' student seat from August 2004 to July 2005.
holdings.source: WKU Board of Regents minutes, 22 Jul 2005 (TopSCHOLAR)

Evelina Petkova, a junior from Sofia, Bulgaria, ran for administrative vice president in March 2004 after three years in SGA, beginning as secretary of the public relations committee and chairing it in 2003-04. Other candidates that spring pledged continued opposition to plus/minus grading, but Petkova's own remarks focused on making the grading pilot the academic quality committee had proposed work well for students, and on improving communication between SGA's officers and its new legislative branch, telling the Herald “the administrators don’t listen to the students’ opinions, which is very disappointing.” Petkova defeated Josh Collins 692 votes to 481 in the March 2004 election, alongside Nick Todd's win for president. In office for 2004-05, she sat on SGA's Executive Board and the WKU Budget Council, and was recorded as the first international student to serve on the SGA executive board.
