holdings.what_they_did: Dawson served as both SGA president and student regent during Western's centennial year. When the university launched its 14-month centennial celebration on Nov. 19, 2005, she spoke at the dedication of Centennial Plaza, offering her own meaning for the school slogan: "Find what you love and carry it with you your whole life through." Her spring semester was dominated by a proposed $46-per-semester fee for three campus construction projects. At a student forum with President Gary Ransdell she suggested exempting the next year's seniors, who would graduate before any project was finished; the Board of Regents rejected the exemption 10-1 at its April 7 meeting and approved the fee 9-1. Dawson cast the lone abstention, saying that although she supported the fee, she could not vote for it with so many seniors counting on the exemption. Her term ended at Western's 159th commencement on May 13, 2006, where the Radcliff native graduated with a degree in corporate and organizational communication and addressed her 1,797 fellow undergraduates as SGA president. She charged the graduates to have courage, endurance, strength, patience and character, saying success was knowing "when to throw in the towel and when to wave it around and cheer."
holdings.source: College Heights Herald 80:38, 24 Feb 2005 - "Two Announce Plans to Run for Student Government Association President - Katie Dawson, Josh Collins" (Coulter, Amber)

holdings.what_they_did: Mason Stevenson, a Princeton junior double-majoring in broadcasting and political science, joined SGA as parliamentarian in fall 2003, a non-voting post he said taught him parliamentary procedure; he had previously served as treasurer of the Southwest Hall Council and was a resident assistant at Bemis Lawrence Hall, and had earlier helped start a College Republicans chapter at Paducah Community College. He ran for one of the new senate's elected seats that March, saying he wanted a vote in decisions rather than the parliamentarian's advisory role, and won; that fall he chaired the senate's Legislative Research Committee. In March 2005 Stevenson and Melissa Paris were elected to SGA's two vice presidencies unopposed, alongside Katie Dawson's contested win for president. As executive vice president in 2005-06, he read a letter to the 2 March 2006 SGA meeting airing a rift between the executive and legislative branches, saying some members protecting their own political interests had “thwarted” the organization's mission to improve Western; the Herald headlined its report “We’ve Got Problems.”

She said raising student awareness was her biggest issue, and that the plus/minus grading pilot mattered to her because she believed the administration meant to fold it into GPAs within two years; she was elected. In March 2005 Paris was elected, alongside Mason Stevenson, to SGA's two vice presidencies unopposed. The senate's own minutes give her title as administrative vice president from the first meeting of 2005-06; she distributed the SGA budget to senators, ran the Organizational Aid interest meeting and application process, and sat on the WKU Budget Council.

Robert "Rob" Watkins, a Bowling Green student, wrote the SGA constitution adopted in 2004 and was elected the first speaker of the senate under it on 15 April 2004, defeating Brittany Fausey 9 votes to 8 in a result immediately contested over what quorum the new constitution required; the vote was upheld later that month. Watkins won the SGA presidency in the 13 April 2006 online election, defeating Berea junior Kara Ratliff after more than a week courting TopNet voters, with results announced at a crowded Revolution 91.7. He took office for 2006-07 alongside Administrative Vice President Amanda Allen, who by October was tightening the budget after the prior administration left roughly $24,000 unspent. Watkins resigned as SGA president and student regent on 28 November 2006, with the resignation read into the senate's own minutes at that day's regularly scheduled Tuesday meeting, after senators had aired concerns about him at an unannounced 10 p.m. meeting the evening before. (A Herald account this site had followed gave the date as 30 November; the primary senate minutes are treated as authoritative here.) A Herald editorial the same week was headlined "SGA actions an embarrassment to Western." The resignation left students without a voting voice on the Board of Regents for at least a month and put junior Jeanne Johnson, already serving as his executive vice president since the 5 September season-opening meeting, in as a fill-in leader for the rest of the term, formally sworn in as president at the 5 December Winter Banquet.

Jeanne Johnson was executive vice president when Rob Watkins resigned the presidency and the student regent seat in November 2006. The senate minutes for 28 November record his resignation being read to the chamber and senators being told she would be sworn in at the Winter Banquet on 5 December; the minutes of that meeting list the executive vice presidency as vacant because she had moved up. The regent seat did not pass with the presidency, and Western went about two months without a student on its governing board. At the Board of Regents meeting of 26 January 2007 she spoke against the size of a 7.8 per cent tuition increase for online and distance learners without holding a vote, saying tuition increases were inevitable but that distance learners should not carry the burden. She won the special election for the seat the following week with 688 votes, 41 per cent of those cast. She was elected to a full term in her own right and sworn in as president and student regent at the SGA banquet on 1 May 2007, where she also received the Dero Downing Award.

Jeanne Lynn Johnson, a Marion senior and Kappa Delta member, had served as SGA's president pro tempore after Rob Watkins's November 2006 resignation and won the February 2007 special election for the vacant student regent seat with 688 votes. She became SGA president and student regent for 2007-08 in her own right, sworn onto the Board of Regents on April 27, 2007, and installed as president at SGA's May 2007 banquet. That fall her administration reported record interest in the senate election, 25 candidates for 20 seats, and she and Executive Vice President Johnathon Boles helped organize a mock gubernatorial election that drew 127 student voters. She pushed a senate resolution asking the state for more funding after Western received only 54 percent of its recommended budget increase, and organized Walk Out Western, an Oct. 25 class walkout protesting state budget cuts that President Gary Ransdell said he could not condone. As student regent, Johnson voted against the scale of the board's 9 percent tuition increase at the April 24, 2008 quarterly meeting, seconding Louisville regent Larry Zielke's motion to cap the increase at 6 percent and push the General Assembly for more funding instead; the motion died with only two votes. At the same meeting she argued the $370,000 budgeted for the Honors College should be cut, saying the college "only benefits 900 students" and other students should not have to pay for it; Ransdell defended it as part of the university's strategic plan. In the spring, as her administration ran the election to choose her successor, Johnson defended the one-week campaign window written into election codes she said were inherited from past administrations, warning that longer campaigns could hurt candidates' schoolwork and that "too much PR hurts." She pointed to new turnout efforts her administration tried, including holding the debate during SGA week and adding candidate profiles and questionnaires to the SGA website. Johnathon Boles won the March 2008 election and was installed as SGA president at the spring banquet, but Johnson kept the Board of Regents seat until the board's next quarterly meeting; a resolution read there on July 18, 2008 thanked her for "able leadership, faithful service, and dedication" and Boles took the oath as student regent the same day. Johnathon Boles ran for SGA president in spring 2008 on the "Red Towel Party" ticket, a slate that also carried Theodore Harden, Reagan Gilley, Skylar Johnson, Kayla Shelton and Kevin Smiley as candidates for other executive and senate offices. After Boles's ticket won, Skylar Jordan filed a complaint against the Red Towel Party; the SGA council took no action on it on 22 April 2008, and the result stood. Boles, a junior from Elizabethtown, served as SGA president and student regent for 2008-09. In November 2008, Gov. Steve Beshear appointed him and fellow SGA member Kevin Smiley to the student committee of the governor's College Access Work Group on college affordability, and Boles traveled to Frankfort for its first meeting, where he raised the burden of textbook costs. "I'm honored the governor chose me to represent WKU," he said. In December 2008, Boles led SGA through its first mid-year budget cut, after a state shortfall required the university to trim about 4 percent. He and Administrative Vice President Reagan Gilley cut $4,100 from SGA's $110,000 budget while protecting scholarships and Provide-A-Ride, and Boles addressed the senate about the cuts, saying he would keep fighting for the affordability of higher education. He also worked to arrange charter buses to a Feb. 3 rally in Frankfort against cuts to higher education. Boles resigned on Jan. 30, 2009, for health reasons, midway through his term. Executive Vice President Kayla Shelton took his place as president but not as student regent, and the student body went 26 days without a regent until Reagan Gilley won a special election on Feb. 25. Gilley said he planned to contact Boles the day after his win to get up to date on Board of Regents business.

Kayla Shelton ran on Johnathon Boles's "Red Towel Party" ticket in the spring 2008 SGA election and served as executive vice president for 2008-09. When Boles resigned as president and student regent on 30 Jan. 2009 for health reasons, Shelton succeeded him as president but not as student regent, leaving the regent seat vacant. As president, Shelton backed the SGA Judicial Council's 2-1 decision to hold a special student regent election rather than leave the seat vacant, over the dissent of Executive Vice President Skylar Jordan, saying "That's what they decided, so I support it" and that her main focus remained serving the student body. She also accepted Chief Justice Lisa Kappler's resignation in mid-February, which came with the regent election two weeks away. Administrative Vice President Reagan Gilley won that special election on 25 Feb. 2009, taking over the regent's seat while Shelton continued as president through the rest of the term. Shelton presided over the senate through the spring, including a Feb. 24 meeting where senators debated and rejected, 13 votes to 9, a bill to cover an extra $82.27 for water bottles SGA had earlier agreed to fund as prizes for a Housing and Residence Life energy-saving contest. Shelton said she thought it was great that the senate debated something it felt passionate about rather than casting "just a general yes or no." Shelton did not continue as president into 2009-10; Kevin Smiley won the regular spring election for that term on 16 April 2009. Kayla Shelton, who had been executive vice president, became SGA president after Johnathon Boles resigned, serving out the rest of the 2008-09 year. She inherited a dispute over whether to hold a special election for the vacant student regent seat, and when the Judicial Council voted 2-1 in February to hold one despite objections from other executives, she backed the decision. "That's what they decided, so I support it," Shelton said, adding that her main focus remained serving the student body.

Reagan Gilley was a Pineville senior and the Student Government Association's administrative vice president when he won the special election for student regent held 25-26 February 2009, filling the seat left empty for 26 days after President Johnathon Boles resigned on 30 January for health reasons. He beat Fairdale senior Nate Eaton, the speaker of the senate, 477 votes to 224 of the 701 cast, and Chief Justice Corey Bewley announced the verified result at 12:17 a.m. Thursday in the SGA office. Gilley had campaigned on short notice through a Facebook group, announcements in classes and a YouTube video built around the Rick Astley song "Never Gonna Give You Up," and after the count he handed Eaton a plaque he had bought at Kroger that day. He said he planned to contact Boles the next day to catch up on Board of Regents business and then to contact Faculty Regent Patricia Minter, and that he wished more students had voted. "I am very relieved but excited for things to come," he said. Gilley took the constitutional oath of office from Board Chair Lois Gray at the second quarterly meeting on 24 April 2009, where President Gary Ransdell presented him with the regent's pin, and he answered the roll call as student regent. He seconded Larry Zielke's motion to approve the naming of designated facilities and rooms, and seconded Yevette Haskins's motion to accept the 2008-09 second quarter statement of revenues and expenditures for filing. On the 2009-10 tuition and fees schedule, which carried a 4 percent increase, Gilley asked to amend the motion to strike the proposed per credit hour fee on course loads above 15 hours; the amended motion was seconded by Zielke and carried unanimously. He then moved to add a drop/add fee of $50 per transaction to the schedule, which Zielke seconded and which also carried unanimously, and afterwards told the Board that tuition increases were a major concern of the student body and that "for the record, I meant to vote in opposition to the tuition increase." During a long exchange over personnel actions and campus morale, in which the faculty and staff regents described resignations and low morale, Gilley said that on behalf of the student body there was concern about fewer staff being available for classes. The minutes list the Board's next meetings as a special budget meeting on 19 June 2009 and the third quarterly meeting on 31 July 2009. His time on the Board was over by the summer. The minutes of the special budget meeting of 19 June 2009 record the constitutional oath of office being administered to Kevin Smiley as student regent, again by Chair Lois Gray and with the regent's pin presented by President Ransdell, and the roll call for that meeting lists Smiley rather than Gilley. Gilley's name does not appear in those minutes at all, so the quarterly meeting of 24 April 2009 was the only Board meeting that fell within his tenure, and the record of his service as student regent runs to that single day of votes. Gilley's name does not appear in those minutes, so the handover had happened by 19 June 2009, earlier than the 31 July roll call previously recorded here.
holdings.source: Herald 84:35, 26 Feb 2009 - Gilley elected student regent

He held the same post in 2006-07, reporting in February 2007 that he had met with the university about textbook ordering at the bookstore, was looking into space for a Gay and Lesbian Resource Center, and was researching SGA's own history in the Kentucky Building archives. Jordan moved to chief of staff for 2007-08, laying groundwork that fall for the "Listen Up Legislators" spring lobbying campaign after a February Frankfort rally alone had failed to move the legislature. That April, after Johnathon Boles's "Red Towel Party" ticket won the SGA election, Jordan filed a complaint against the party; the SGA council took no action on it on 22 April 2008, and the result stood. He returned to serve as Boles's chief of staff again in 2008-09, nominated on 26 August 2008 after serving in the role pro tem, and built a master schedule of every SGA committee's meeting time for senators to consult. In September 2009, after Boles had resigned and been succeeded by Kevin Smiley, Jordan publicly criticized Smiley's decision to nominate his own brother, Eric Smiley, as chief of staff. The Herald identified him in that report as "former executive vice president Skylar Baker-Jordan" — a title and surname variant not otherwise recorded for him in SGA's own minutes, which consistently give his office as director of academic and student affairs and then chief of staff, never executive vice president.

Kevin T. Smiley, a senior from Danville, served as SGA president and student regent for 2009-10. His executive branch included Executive Vice President Kendrick Bryan, Administrative Vice President Justin Thurman, and four appointed officials, among them his brother Eric Smiley as chief of staff. Smiley opened his term with controversy in September 2009 when he nominated his brother, Danville sophomore Eric Smiley, for the paid chief of staff position, saying he chose him because he had no previous political agenda and was "somebody I truly trust." Former executive vice president Skylar Baker-Jordan called the move "completely unethical," though Thurman defended the president's right to pick a qualified adviser. In October 2009 three senators resigned after Smiley nominated Greg Capillo to the Student Publications Committee, with Michel Stephens charging the pick was not based on merit. Smiley called the accusations of favoritism and corruption unfounded, described the resignations as a misunderstanding, and said he would begin contacting fall election candidates to fill the vacant seats. His term ran through the April 2010 election of his successor.
Also held the student regent seat, per the roles having merged by this period.
Bryan was a candidate for Executive Vice President in the March 2010 election, facing Currie Martin, and a Herald editorial of 30 March 2010 endorsed Jessie and Bryan for the two offices.

Justin Thurman served as administrative vice president for 2009-10 under President Kevin Smiley. In September 2009, when a former officer publicly criticized Smiley's decision to nominate his own brother, Eric Smiley, as chief of staff, Thurman defended the president's right to choose a qualified adviser for the position. Thurman ran for SGA president in the March 2010 election against Colton Jessie and lost; Jessie went on to serve as SGA president for 2010-11.

Eric Smiley's September 2009 nomination as SGA's paid, voting Chief of Staff, put forward by his brother, President Kevin Smiley, drew immediate public criticism as nepotism. The Herald covered it across its 4 and 11 September 2009 issues with a news report, an editorial cartoon and two opinion columns, including one headlined "Nepotism Has No Place in Student Government Association" and another, "Wrong Message: For Student Government Association, It's Same Old, Same Old." A former executive vice president publicly called the nomination "completely unethical."

Jessie opened the 2010-11 year having spent the summer preparing with his executive board, which attended the Kentucky Leadership Academy at Barren River State Park alongside SGAs from Kentucky's other public universities. His early priorities included building a closer relationship with international students, whom SGA hosted at a dinner during orientation, planning a study away program for students to study elsewhere in the country, and setting up a forum for South Campus concerns. "We are trying to reach out to South Campus," he said, and he and Executive Vice President Kendrick Bryan reallocated the budget to fund scholarship and study abroad programs. By the end of his term, SGA had given out more scholarship money than ever, with the scholarship fund raised by $8,000 and organizational aid increased to $40,000, and the senate had passed first-of-their-kind bills reimbursing CLEP exam fees and buying test prep books for libraries. Jessie called the DUC renovation "one of the biggest things SGA has done in a while," and Ransdell credited him with taking the initiative to start the renovation talks. A senior, Jessie handed the office to Billy Stephens and left for Chicago after graduation to work for Teach for America.

Colton Jessie served as SGA president for 2010-11, the year after he was clerk of the Judicial Council. His full term — the Kentucky Leadership Academy retreat, the DUC renovation talks, and the increases to scholarship and study-abroad funding — is recorded under his leader entry for this year.
Re-elected unopposed to a second term as EVP for 2011-12.

Wade Pierce was elected speaker of the senate for 2009-10, then ran unopposed for administrative vice president in the March 2010 election and served in that post for 2010-11, chairing the organizational aid committee. During his term, Pierce adopted a fellow Lambda Chi Alpha fraternity member, Devon Hilderbrandt, as his fraternity little brother. Pierce encouraged Hilderbrandt, who wanted to get more involved on campus, to join SGA at the start of fall 2010, brought him onto the organizational aid committee as his co-chair, and mentored him in running it. Hilderbrandt ran unopposed to succeed Pierce as administrative vice president for 2011-12.

Charlie Harris served as SGA's director of information technology in 2007-08 and 2008-09, building a new SGA website and blog; the office was recorded as unassigned by the Senate's 28 October 2008 meeting. A Morganfield senior, Harris told the Herald in May 2011 that he had been an SGA senator his freshman year, resigned during his sophomore year, and was persuaded by President Colton Jessie to return for his senior year as chief of staff. Outside SGA, he co-founded WKU Americans for Informed Democracy with fellow student Matt Vaughan during their freshman year and did extensive work on the ONE Campaign and Earth Day activities. Jessie praised him publicly as an outstanding WKU student with "a work ethic like I've never seen." As chief of staff, Harris helped run SGA's awareness campaign for the Downing University Center renovation; at the meeting reported on 2 February 2011 he said SGA would begin holding sessions in DUC the following week, with open forums where students could discuss the renovation plans with officers in more depth.

holdings.what_they_did: Billy Stephens joined SGA in the spring of 2009 and worked on organizational aid before being appointed director of academic and student affairs in the fall of 2010. He ran for SGA president in the spring 2011 election while holding the post, one of the candidates who presented platforms at a public debate in Downing University Center on 23 March 2011. His central proposal was a pre-finals "Dead Day" with classes canceled, which he called unfair to students left short of study time, noting other schools already did it. He also pledged to fix SGA's Provide-a-Ride service, which he said had been less dependable that year, by negotiating a better contract for a fixed route or more buses, and to improve SGA's public relations to raise awareness of the organization. He won the presidency the following month, detailed in his profile for 2011-12.

Cory Dodds, then a sophomore, was SGA's director of information technology in 2010-11. In February 2011 the Herald reported he would build and maintain an off-campus housing listings website in-house using open-source software, after Executive Vice President Kendrick Bryan said SGA lacked a "one-stop shop" for such listings. An earlier attempt to build the site through an outside vendor, considering options including a company called Off Campus Partners, had stalled over cost and fit for the Bowling Green market, Dodds said. He aimed to have the site functional by the end of April 2011 and said he planned to maintain it himself until he graduated. He went on to be elected SGA president for 2012-13, detailed in his own presidential profile.

Austin Wingate served as Speaker of the Student Senate under President Colton Jessie in 2010-11. At the SGA meeting of 14 September 2010 he reported that the fall retreat would be held on 2 October, hosted by the WKU Institute for Citizenship and Social Responsibility, and made appointments of a secretary and a parliamentarian that the Senate then approved. Wingate later ran for SGA president in the spring 2013 election. He finished third with 300 votes, behind administrative vice president Cain Alvey, who had 419, and the election's winner; asked about the result he said the students had voted the way they wanted and that he stood behind that.

Executive Vice President Kendrick Bryan called her a "wonderful branch member", said she had emphasised accountability and transparency in the branch, and described her departure as an unfortunate circumstance. President Colton Jessie said he would look both inside and outside the judicial branch for a replacement; the senate approved Art Scisney to succeed her at its next meeting.

Billy Stephens, a junior from Hawesville, was elected SGA president in the spring 2011 election, announced just after midnight on April 7. He defeated Diego Leal Ambriz, a senior from Monterrey, Mexico, with 56 percent of the 1,066 total votes. Outgoing president Colton Jessie called him "a fantastic candidate for the job," and Kendrick Bryan and Devon Hilderbrandt were elected unopposed as his executive and administrative vice presidents. Stephens opened his term in August 2011 with a revamped public relations campaign built around asking students what SGA could do for them. "I want PR to be visible on campus," he said, complaining that new students often did not hear about SGA until the second semester. The campaign aimed to raise turnout in the fall senate elections, produce contested races and fill all 36 senate seats. The fall brought open conflict: the senate voted down, 19-8, a resolution to rename Downing University Center that campus improvements chair Keyana Boka had written, the Herald editorial board told Stephens to focus on his own platform promises instead, two senators were dismissed for absences, and SGA was surprised by a $15,000 bill for the prior administration's unpaid Provide-A-Ride service. Chief of Staff Katie Stillwell resigned before the spring semester was out; Stephens replaced her with Eric Smiley, who had held the same post two years earlier under his brother's administration. The senate passed a spring budget of $50,026 in February 2012, down from $54,000 in fall spending.

The full account of Stephens's year - the public relations relaunch he opened it with, the resolution to rename Downing University Center that the senate voted down, the unpaid Provide-A-Ride bill left behind by the previous administration, the resignation of his chief of staff and the spring budget - is under his leader entry for this year.

Kendrick Bryan was elected executive vice president for 2009-10 under President Kevin Smiley, and won re-election to the post twice more: in the March 2010 election over Currie Martin, campaigning in a Herald commentary for students to "vote for an organization you can stand up and cheer for," and again in March 2011, unopposed after his only declared challenger, Secretary of the Senate Katie Stillwell, dropped out of the race. He served three consecutive years as executive vice president, under presidents Smiley, Colton Jessie and Billy Stephens. As EVP under Jessie in 2010-11, Bryan helped reallocate the SGA budget toward scholarship and study-abroad funding. He was also hired to teach a section of University Experience, WKU's freshman orientation course, in the autumn after his final term ended. Keyana Boka, who ran to succeed him as EVP that spring, said she had worked closely with Bryan on SGA projects and that he had helped her learn the office; Bryan said he had not recruited a successor himself but backed her decision to run. After leaving SGA, Bryan ran as a Democrat for the Kentucky House's 25th District against incumbent Jimmie Lee, in an election the Herald reported on 24 May 2012. He took 18.62 percent of the vote to Lee's 77.63 percent and third-place candidate Glenn Fonda's 3.75 percent, campaigning on government transparency and university funding without accepting outside campaign contributions, spending roughly $1,000 of his own money. He said afterward he could see himself running again. In July 2013, identified by the Herald as a former SGA officer, he wrote a commentary defending President Cory Dodds's decision to keep the Downing University Center's name against a later administration-driven change to Downing Student Union, arguing the Student Senate had already voted against renaming it and student opinion had not shifted.
holdings.source: Herald, Apr 2011, "Uncontested elections don't concern SGA"

holdings.what_they_did: Devon Hilderbrandt joined SGA in fall 2010 after his fraternity big brother, administrative vice president Wade Pierce, encouraged him to get more involved on campus. He joined the organizational aid committee under Pierce, became his co-chair, and ran unopposed to succeed him as administrative vice president for 2011-12. As administrative vice president, Hilderbrandt oversaw SGA's organizational aid program, which gave out roughly $34,000 to about 50 student organizations that year. Students applied online, and Hilderbrandt read every application himself before an organization could meet with the organizational aid committee; the maximum award to any one organization was $500.

Katie Stillwell served as secretary of the student senate for 2010-11. In March 2011 she ran against Kendrick Bryan for executive vice president, saying she had worked hard in the legislative branch and felt she could help on the executive side; she later dropped out, and Bryan was re-elected unopposed. Named chief of staff for 2011-12, Stillwell announced her resignation at the Senate meeting of 20 March 2012, telling it she had always taken the position seriously but that her grades had slipped over the year under the combined load of a part-time job and roughly 10 hours a week of SGA work, and that continuing without doing the work properly would not have been ethical. President Billy Stephens thanked her for her service, and named former chief of staff Eric Smiley — who had held the post two years earlier under President Kevin Smiley, his brother — to finish out the term.

Kaylee Egerer was Speaker of the Senate in 2011-12, under President Billy Stephens. At the semester's first meeting on 6 September 2011 senators postponed a vote on the tobacco-free campus resolution so new members could review it, and Stephens's executive, judicial and committee-chair appointments were confirmed in a single unanimous vote. Egerer became a leading voice for SGA's position on the proposed tobacco ban. When the Senate passed its resolution on 13 September 2011 she said SGA supported a campus ban "if and only if" the requirement that students live on campus for two years was ended. She later said she never expected the Board of Regents to adopt SGA's version because the housing link was so central, and called the ban as proposed unfair and unrealistic. At SGA's end-of-year banquet on the night of 8 May 2012 she handed the speaker's gavel to her successor, Christopher Costa, as the incoming 2012-13 officers were sworn in.
holdings.source: Herald, 7 Sep 2011 - SGA holds talks about tobacco-free campus resolution

holdings.what_they_did: Rachel Calhoun served as secretary of the student senate in 2011-12 and worked on SGA's organizational aid committee, which distributed roughly $34,000 to about fifty student groups that year in grants capped at $500 each. She said one of the criteria for funding was that a grant should not simply pay for a party unless the event was open to a large number of students: "It had to affect a lot of students and be legitimate." She recalled a trip by a group of Chinese students touring Kentucky's sites and culture as one of the more memorable requests the committee funded. In May 2012 she spoke in the senate's debate over a resolution backing gender-neutral and transgender-inclusive campus housing, arguing that student government was there to listen to students and that SGA should support a group of them who said they didn't feel safe; the resolution passed.

David Spalding was SGA's chief justice in 2011-12. That November he ran the semester's judicial reviews after nearly a third of the senate's 36 members were called up for excessive absences; two senators, Kevin Adams and Kevin Preston, were dismissed after failing to attend their own review hearings, which he said the judicial council read as an intention to resign. Spalding said the rest were given the sternest of warnings and that the branch would administer oaths to their replacements, calling the episode a "very minor speed bump" and noting some senators flagged for review had simply had trouble submitting absence excuses to the right place on SGA's website. In February 2012, after President Billy Stephens moved to reappoint Adams to the senate, Spalding said Stephens had not needed the judicial branch's sign-off but the two had discussed the situation; he noted SGA's constitution has no rule barring a removed senator's return, so long as they affirm they again have the time for it.

Chris Jankowski was appointed an associate justice of SGA's Judicial Council on 29 March 2011, alongside Aaron Pawley, when Art Scisney was elevated to chief justice. He continued on the council into 2011-12, when nearly a third of the senate's 36 members were called before judicial review for excessive absences; Jankowski said the two dismissed senators, Kevin Adams and Kevin Preston, had racked up eight to ten absences across senate and committee meetings, while Chief Justice David Spalding said the council read a failure to appear at a review hearing as intent to resign. Jankowski told the Herald the council would soon issue a judicial opinion reinterpreting the constitution to give senators "a little more leeway" on absences. In February 2012 he was one of four WKU SGA members who traveled to Frankfort for the Rally for Higher Education, held to protest a proposed 6.4 percent cut to Kentucky's post-secondary education budget, telling the Herald that students needed to get their voice out and make themselves heard on the need for funding.

Cory Dodds, a junior political science major from Smithland, Kentucky, was elected SGA president for 2012-13 in spring 2012 over Austin Wingate and Corey Johnson, after two years as SGA's director of information technology, during which he built a legislation and minutes archive for the SGA website that he said promoted transparency and accountability. Under the merged offices, Dodds also served as the student regent representing students on WKU's Board of Regents. In office, Dodds led SGA in unanimously opposing an administration proposal to shift tuition to a per-credit-hour, bi-term model, which Provost Gordon Emslie dropped in February 2013 after student and faculty pushback. His administration also drafted a teaching assistant evaluation program the senate passed in February 2013, worked to restart a dormant student government at WKU's Glasgow campus, donated cameras to the Teaching and Learning Resource Center, and passed a resolution opposing a new $150 Study Abroad application fee; a Dodds amendment to bar SGA members from receiving SGA-awarded study-abroad scholarships, after 11 of 125 such awards had gone to SGA members that year, failed. Dodds's term ended amid a contested succession: his successor, Keyana Boka, was elected in April 2013 but disqualified five days later by the Judicial Council 3-2 over a campaign email, then reinstated after appealing to Vice President for Student Affairs Howard Bailey. Later in 2012 Dodds was named a finalist for the Harry S. Truman Scholarship and, that November, WKU's first finalist for the George J. Mitchell Scholarship, the only Kentuckian among 20 national finalists. He went on to earn a law degree from Georgetown University, worked as directing attorney of the Children's Law Center and as a legal services staff attorney representing low-income clients in public benefits, housing and family law matters, and by the mid-2020s was a visiting professor at the University of Kentucky's J. David Rosenberg College of Law teaching Civil Procedure and Children and the Law, with research on rural "legal deserts" and the attorney shortage.
Also served as student regent under the merged offices.

Keyana Boka, a Bowling Green sophomore, was elected executive vice president uncontested alongside presidential candidate Cory Dodds in the March 2012 SGA election. She was sworn into office at SGA's end-of-year banquet on 8 May 2012, succeeding executive vice president Kendrick Bryan. She said she had big shoes to fill after Bryan's two years in the office. She went on to be elected SGA president for 2013-14, where her name appeared in that year's coverage spelled "Keyanna"; the spelling is unverified between the two forms.

Cain Alvey served as administrative vice president for 2012-13 under President Cory Dodds. He ran for president in the April 2013 election, finishing second with 419 votes (31 percent) to winner Keyana Boka's 626 (47 percent) and third-place candidate Austin Wingate's 300 (22 percent). A later SGA president, Nicki Taylor, recalled in 2015 that Alvey had spent his full $350 campaign-spending limit on posters and handbills, paying a photojournalism student to photograph him and a design student to produce his materials. Alvey continued serving as a senator into 2013-14 under Boka's administration. In October 2013 he amended a Campus Improvements bill funding phone-charging stations, moving one planned location from a library periodicals room to the Commons at Cravens Library, though the executive council vetoed the whole bill later that same night. In February 2014, when a senator questioned whether members understood a constitutional amendment increasing the Judicial Council to seven justices and shifting justice appointments to the executive branch, Alvey argued in the amendment's defense that senators had had two weeks to read and study it before the vote.

Travis Taylor was SGA's director of academic and student affairs in 2011-12. The senate funded a transcript-voucher program that February, providing 175 vouchers, and when the Herald followed up in March, Taylor said SGA had held the program back a semester over budget problems, scheduling difficulties and planning, rather than launch one that would fail. He moved up to chief of staff for 2012-13 under President Cory Dodds. In March 2013 he joined Dodds, Brittany Crowley and Drew Mitchell in a Herald commentary accusing the senate of rejecting a constitutional amendment that would have barred sitting SGA members from receiving SGA-administered scholarships and grants, writing that eleven members had received such awards since spring 2011 and calling it a conflict of interest. The following month he gave the cabinet's report to the senate at the meeting that elected Paige Settles to succeed Christopher Costa as speaker.

holdings.what_they_did: Brittany Crowley served as SGA's director of academic and student affairs in 2012-13. She signed the cabinet's December 2012 statement backing the provost's proposed "value-added" grading scale, which the Senate went on to reject in February 2013. In March 2013 Crowley joined President Cory Dodds, Travis Taylor and Drew Mitchell in a Herald commentary attacking the Senate for rejecting an amendment that would have barred sitting SGA members from receiving SGA-sponsored scholarships and grants; the four wrote that 11 SGA members had received such scholarships or grants since spring 2011 and called it a breach of student trust and a conflict of interest.

Sarah Hazelip held SGA's director of information technology post from 2012-13 through 2014-15, one of the four appointed executive offices listed on SGA's own site, and stayed in the role as Keyana Boka's administration took over for 2013-14. In October 2013 she told the senate she was working to put SGA's newly finalized $125,000 budget online. By September 2014, at an executive cabinet meeting with only four officers present, she moved approval of Senate Bill 3-14-F and then moved to adjourn; both motions passed unanimously.

holdings.what_they_did: Drew Mitchell, a Bowling Green senior, served as SGA's director of public relations in 2012-13. He signed the cabinet's December 2012 statement backing the provost's proposed "value-added" grading scale. In March 2013 Mitchell joined President Cory Dodds, Travis Taylor and Brittany Crowley in a Herald commentary accusing the Senate of rejecting accountability after it voted down an amendment barring sitting SGA members from SGA-sponsored scholarships and grants. He received the Dero Downing Award at SGA's May 2013 banquet.

Christopher Costa was elected to the senate in the fall 2011 election with 977 students voting. By spring 2012 he had joined the four SGA members who traveled to the Rally for Higher Education in Frankfort to protest a proposed 6.4 percent cut to the state's postsecondary education budget. On 18 April 2012 the senate elected him speaker of the student senate for 2012-13, over fellow senator Poorvie Patel and public relations committee head Mallory Treece; he told senators his time in the Army had taught him to follow before he learned to lead, and he was sworn in at SGA's end-of-year banquet on 9 May 2012, receiving the gavel from outgoing speaker Kaylee Egerer. As speaker, Costa presided over a year in which SGA rewrote its own constitution, restructuring senate seats by college rather than class year and adding representation for the Glasgow and Owensboro regional campuses. During floor debate in September 2013 he spoke against a separate proposal, opposing a dedicated Navitas/ESL international senate seat even though he supported the broader goal of international student involvement, arguing the seat would function as a band-aid; the amendment passed anyway. Throughout his term Costa said his hardest task was remaining impartial as speaker, saying it was hardest "when there were issues present which I had a strong position or opinion on." Costa chose not to seek a second term, and the senate elected Paige Settles to succeed him as speaker on 16 April 2013. He said at the time that the responsibilities of the office had grown difficult to balance with his coursework as he entered his senior year, and that he intended to return to an ordinary senate seat after the spring semester ended.

Mallory Treece, a Smiths Grove freshman, was elected to the SGA senate in the fall 2011 election. By February 2012 she had been named public relations committee head, and the same semester she was one of four SGA members who traveled to the Rally for Higher Education in Frankfort, telling the Herald she wanted to "come to the state capitol and rally for something I really care about." In April 2012 Treece ran for speaker of the student senate against Christopher Costa and Poorvie Patel, telling senators she had fallen in love with SGA at her first meeting and believed her passion for the organization qualified her for the role; she lost to Costa. As public relations committee head that spring she co-authored the bill funding SGA's sponsorship of International Night, and she was a guest at the SGA delegation's picnic with WKU President Gary Ransdell in October 2012, by then serving as secretary of the senate, a post SGA's own leadership roster credited to her for 2012-13. She moved from secretary to public relations committee chair the following year.

holdings.what_they_did: Christopher Jankowski was appointed an associate justice of SGA's Judicial Council on 29 March 2011 by President Colton Jessie, filling out the council alongside Aaron Pawley after Chief Justice Dajana Crockett's resignation. In that role during the 2011-12 year he explained the council's meeting-absence rules to the Herald after ten of the senate's 36 members were called in for excessive absences, two of whom were dismissed; he said committees, not the full senate, were where senators actually shaped legislation. He also said the council was preparing a judicial opinion that would give senators more leeway on absences, and in February 2012 he was one of four SGA members who traveled to the Rally for Higher Education in Frankfort, telling the crowd it was important that students "make ourselves heard." SGA's own roster, published 29 August 2012, named Jankowski chief justice of the Judicial Council for 2012-13 after his two years as an associate justice. By the time of the disputed April 2013 presidential election, however, the chief justiceship had passed to Seth Church, and the archive has found no further record of Jankowski's SGA service after that transition.

holdings.what_they_did: Seth Church served on SGA's Judicial Council, becoming chief justice by April 2013 after having been an ordinary justice as of the previous August. As chief justice he announced the council's 3-2 vote disqualifying president-elect Keyana Boka after runner-up Cain Alvey complained that a self-promotional campaign email had gone to Honors College students at Boka's request. When Howard Bailey overruled the disqualification and reinstated Boka, the council voted unanimously not to challenge his decision but registered its disapproval; Church called Bailey's intervention "a serious infringement on our autonomy" and said it set a bad precedent. Church remained chief justice for 2013-14. In April 2014 he delivered the council's Opinion 2014SP-002, holding that senators who abstain neither vote yes nor no but concur with the majority of those voting, and that they still count toward quorum; Julia Payne and Jackie Stewart joined the opinion, and Megan Lemmons took no part. He moved into the executive branch as chief of staff for 2014-15 under President Nicki Taylor. Church wrote the resolution supporting private spaces on campus for expressing breast milk, prompted by a non-traditional student who had just had her third child and found the existing unlocked room uncomfortable; it passed unanimously without debate. He proposed and chaired a new Cultural and Diversity Affairs Committee developed in collaboration with Taylor, and wrote the resolution rewriting the Glasgow regional campus's constitution after Glasgow struggled to keep members. He also argued against a smoke-free campus resolution that the senate passed and the Executive Cabinet then vetoed, saying a ban was unfair to students required to live on campus for two years, and objected that a proposed $10 million parking garage had moved too fast and left out the regional campuses.

Boka, the outgoing executive vice president, was elected 2013-14 SGA president on 4 April 2013 with 626 votes (47 percent), beating administrative vice president Cain Alvey (419 votes) and Austin Wingate (300). Five days later the Judicial Council voted 3-2 to disqualify her after Alvey, the runner-up who stood to become president if she were removed, complained that a self-promotional email had gone to Honors College students at her request. Boka appealed to Howard Bailey, WKU's vice president for Student Affairs, who reinstated her; the Judicial Council declined to contest his ruling in an emergency meeting on 16 April, with Chief Justice Seth Church calling the intervention "a serious infringement on our autonomy" and Boka countering that the council itself had conflicts of interest. In office, Boka's fall 2013 senate created a new international student senate seat for Navitas/ESL students and finalized a $125,000 budget, part of which sent her and executive vice president Mark Reeves on a Washington, D.C. higher-education lobbying trip. She fielded student anger over new two-tier priority registration rules at a November open forum with Provost Gordon Emslie, and announced the permanent closure of Thompson Complex North Wing, long slated for demolition. A senate attempt to reverse SGA's support for the Talisman's student fee was struck down by the Judicial Council as unconstitutional, as was the underlying 2005 policy. In spring 2014 Boka organized a Frankfort rally against a $1.8 million state budget cut to WKU and opposed a senate amendment stripping the president's sole power to appoint Judicial Council justices, which was sent back to committee after the council found too few senators had been present to pass it. At the year's final meeting she announced a 4.8 percent tuition increase for the coming year, and the senate passed a resolution backing a Good Samaritan policy to protect students who called 911 during drug or alcohol overdoses.

Boka's year - the Judicial Council's attempt to disqualify her days after the election and her reinstatement by vice president for Student Affairs Howard Bailey, the new international student senate seat, the budget, the priority registration forum with Provost Emslie and the Frankfort rally against the state budget cut - is recorded under her leader entry for this year, filed there under the plaque spelling Keyanna Boka.

Mark Reeves, a Louisville graduate student, was sworn in as a graduate senator in September 2012 before running for executive vice president the following spring. He won the April 2013 general election with 632 votes, 57 percent, defeating Brad Cockrel's 485; asked how it felt, he said he was "really privileged and honored that the students chose this" and that he appreciated the chance to serve. As executive vice president in 2013-14, Reeves co-authored with President Keyana Boka a constitutional amendment creating a senate seat for Navitas and English-as-a-second-language international students; the Judicial Council initially struck the wording down as unconstitutional before the senate passed a revised version. He also introduced a resolution opposing WKU athletics' automatic annual fee increase ahead of the move to Conference USA, arguing that WKU paid $80,000 in Sun Belt Conference dues but received only $40,000 back in revenue sharing. A Herald editorial later criticized him for voting for a new priority-registration policy at the University Senate without first bringing it to SGA for debate. Reeves also spoke to senators about the state budget, warning in February 2014 that further cuts were likely, and joined Boka on a Washington, D.C. lobbying trip that year. At a South Campus forum that November he said WKU had made the same mistake it made when it closed the South Campus food court, again failing to consult South Campus students before closing the campus store there.

Nicki Seay was appointed SGA's parliamentarian in February 2012 and later served as legislative research chair in 2012-13 before she was elected administrative vice president for 2013-14, alongside presidential candidate Keyana Boka and executive vice president Mark Reeves, in the April 2013 election. By the time she ran unopposed for president in April 2014, the Herald reported she had been on SGA for three years and wanted to use Adobe Connect to broadcast SGA meetings to students who could not attend in person. Asked at an executive candidates' debate on 2 April 2014 whether she could balance the presidency with a double major, she said she planned to take 12 hours with no Friday classes that fall. She won the presidency in that election; the year opened under "Nicki Seay" before her name changed partway through to "Nicki Taylor," and the fuller account is in her presidential profile for 2014-15.

Brad Cockrel ran for executive vice president in the spring 2013 election, one of the candidates in the presidential and vice-presidential debate that March. He lost the April 2013 general election to Mark Reeves, taking 485 votes, 43 percent, to Reeves's 632. Cockrel was nonetheless named chief of staff for 2013-14, and that November he and President Keyana Boka met with Talisman staff to discuss long-term funding options for the yearbook after it reported a funding shortfall, with its budget at $127,000.

Laura Harper served as SGA's director of public relations for 2013-14. That October she introduced a resolution supporting changes to WKU's internet-usage policies after the Foundation for Individual Rights in Education gave the university a red-light rating over Computing Policy 12-13, which covered email content deemed likely to be perceived as offensive or disparaging; the resolution passed later that month at a lightly attended meeting held during a home football game. When SGA finalized its $125,000 budget that October, Harper explained the figure to students as the equivalent of about $6.25 a head.

As student affairs chair Greenwell reported to the senate in February 2014 that the library would soon carry hard-copy study materials for the MCAT, LSAT and CLEP. He also worked with Kelly Cannon of WKU's Students for Sensible Drug Policy chapter on a resolution asking the university to extend its medical amnesty policy to drug emergencies as well as alcohol; the senate passed it at the last meeting of the spring, and Judicial Affairs rewrote the published policy that October.

Paige Settles, a Floyds Knobs, Indiana freshman, was elected speaker of the student senate in April 2013, succeeding Christopher Costa, and was sworn in by outgoing president Cory Dodds at SGA's awards banquet that May. She said she felt qualified for the job because she had already spoken with Costa about its responsibilities, and that her priority was fostering senators working well together; Costa in turn said she had "a lot of talents that will be very useful for the position." In 2014-15 Settles moved from the speakership to chair the Legislative Research Committee, a post SGA's own records rendered inconsistently as "Paige Settle." She returned to the speaker's chair for 2015-16, calling the first meeting of the Fourteenth Senate to order on 1 September 2015, and in February 2016 she reported that she was updating the senate's records and procedures.

Nicki Seay had been SGA's Legislative Research Chair in 2012-13 and ran successfully for administrative vice president in the spring 2013 election. She took office as SGA president in August 2014, a Crofton senior, alongside Administrative Vice President Liz Koehler and Executive Vice President Nolan Miles, and named student involvement, retention and graduation her priorities. Her administration opened the year by expanding SGA's summer and winter need-based scholarship program from $6,000 to $21,000. By the middle of October 2014 the Herald was referring to the same sitting president as Nicki Taylor; no election or resignation separates the two names in the paper's coverage. As Taylor, she presided over a fall senate that voted down a nonsectarian prayer resolution, saw its smoke-free campus resolution vetoed by the Executive Cabinet and sustained on a failed override vote, and passed a resolution backing changes to the campus alcohol policy. She addressed WKU's December 2014 commencement as SGA president, telling graduates, "You have the rest of your life to look forward to." In the spring semester the senate under Taylor passed a limited-smoking-campus resolution and a resolution backing a $10 million parking garage funded by a new student fee; President Gary Ransdell responded formally to both. She also sat, by virtue of the office, on the WKU Board of Regents, and abstained from an Executive Council vote on the smoking measure because of that seat. Her term ended with the 2 April 2015 election of Jay Todd Richey as her successor.
Took office in August 2014 as Nicki Seay; called Nicki Taylor in coverage from mid-October 2014 on.

Nolan Miles won a senate seat in the fall 2011 election, one of eleven senators elected from a field of twenty with 977 students voting. He served as executive vice president for 2014-15 alongside President Nicki Seay — who was going by the surname Taylor in Herald coverage by mid-October that year — and Administrative Vice President Liz Koehler. Miles ran unopposed for a second term as EVP in the spring 2015 election that made Jay Todd Richey president, and that August, opening the new term, said he would push senators to sit on university committees and revive the Dine with Decision Makers event.

Liz Koehler served as SGA's administrative vice president for 2014-15, taking office that August alongside President Nicki Seay and Executive Vice President Nolan Miles. Koehler won a second term in the spring 2015 election, taking 66 percent of the vote over J. William Berry, in the same election that made Jay Todd Richey president and returned Miles unopposed for a second term as executive vice president. That September, after SGA's budget fell $19,500 — largely because a one-time $15,000 private donation was not repeated and the university cut a further $4,500 — she reallocated $4,000 from organizational aid back into scholarships to soften the loss. The following February she reported an expected 4.5 percent cut to SGA's own budget, a loss of $1,301.27, amid the senate's debate over a state tuition-freeze bill.

Church proposed the Cultural and Diversity Affairs Committee with President Nicki Taylor and chaired it in its first term, taking it into the Campus Pride Index and into work with Housing and Residence Life on gender-neutral housing and on letting applicants identify as transgender. He opposed the smoke-free campus resolution, arguing it was unfair to students required to live on campus for two years, and signed the executive cabinet's veto of it in November 2014; he then wrote with senator J. William Berry the limited-smoking resolution that passed 13-11 in February 2015. He authored the resolution on private space for breastfeeding students, brought to him by a non-traditional student, which passed unanimously in March 2015; co-authored with senator Zach Jones a resolution to publish SGA's attendance and voting records; and argued against the $10 million parking structure resolution on the ground that regional campus students would pay the $30 fee without using it. In April 2015 he wrote to the Judicial Council opposing the disqualification of president-elect Jay Todd Richey over misplaced campaign posters.

holdings.what_they_did: Megan Skaggs was head of the Academic Affairs committee in the Student Government Association senate in fall 2013, when she authored a bill re-funding SGA's Transcript Voucher Program, which let students get a transcript free with a voucher instead of paying the $7 fee, limited to two per student under this funding round. The bill passed unanimously at the senate meeting the Herald reported in its 26 September 2013 issue. Skaggs told the Herald, "students pay quite a bit as it is for tuition and other fees." By the start of the spring 2015 semester SGA had appointed her director of Academic and Student Affairs; the appointment was reported at the senate's first meeting back from winter break, alongside President Nicki Taylor announcing several other new positions. Skaggs ran for senate in the April 2015 elections and won one of the 20 seats filled out of 34 candidates. By the fall 2015 semester the Herald identified her with legislative research in its coverage of a late-September SGA meeting, where senators also voted her the organization's Homecoming queen candidate.
With only four officers present on 16 September 2014 she moved approval of Senate Bill 3-14-F and then moved to adjourn; both passed unanimously.

She was absent from the cabinet's 28 October 2014 meeting, and by February 2015 Sawyer Coffey held the office in her place; the archive has found no record explaining the change.

holdings.what_they_did: Sawyer Coffey was in office as SGA's director of public relations by the cabinet's 10 February 2015 meeting, succeeding KJ Hall, and on 14 April 2015 she seconded and voted for Senate Resolution 7-15-S. After a competitive and closely watched 2015 executive and senate election, SGA published an open letter thanking the Herald for its election coverage and announcing a coming "rebranding period," listing Coffey as the contact for questions. Coffey continued as public relations director in 2015-16. That November she said SGA removed "Spirit Masters" from its "Dub the Pub" naming contest for the new Garrett Conference Center pub "out of respect for the organization," after WKU administrators objected that it demeaned the university's student ambassador group. In spring 2016 she reported to the senate that a promotional video for SGA and WKU had reached 28,000 views and 27 shares.

holdings.what_they_did: Cole McDowell was sworn in as a freshman senator in September 2012, representing the incoming class alongside Barrett Greenwell, Paige Settles and Gatton Academy senator Linda Cruz. As a senator in 2014-15 he authored a resolution objecting that SGA had not been consulted before Housing and Residence Life decided to move Gatton Academy students into Bates-Runner Hall, introduced and reported to the senate on 11 November 2014, where it was postponed to await a joint SGA, Gatton and Housing meeting; he said the resolution was not a judgment on the decision itself, but a statement that senators could not represent student views on decisions they were never told about. SGA's cabinet minutes also name him secretary of the student senate that year, though the senate's own leadership page rendered the name "Patrick Mcdowell" for the same office — a discrepancy the archive has left unresolved rather than guessed at. The Senate reappointed McDowell secretary for 2015-16, this time named by Speaker Paige Settles and approved at the senate's first meeting on 1 September 2015; he asked fellow senators that December to tell him if they did not plan to return in the spring. In that capacity he argued in February 2016 for lowering SGA's own senator GPA requirement from 2.5 to 2.0, saying "if a 2.0 is good enough for the university, then it's good enough for me" — the amendment failed. The same spring he brought a resolution asking WKU to include a faculty and staff salary increase in the 2016-17 budget and to guarantee raises in future years, citing a Herald report that administrators were considering the idea; President Gary Ransdell had already expressed support for a raise, though the archive has found no record of the resolution's ultimate fate.
Attended the 26 August 2014 cabinet meeting held as a committee chair orientation, at which the Executive Vice President asked each chair to set out goals for the year.

holdings.what_they_did: Richey opened his first term in fall 2015 "leaving behind the Postergate controversy" of the spring election, saying he had "about a hundred things" he wanted to do. His priorities included MyCampusToo, a campaign initiative to bring underrepresented students into SGA, more outreach to international students and the regional campuses, and stronger communication between the executive cabinet and senate. He also oversaw a student competition to name the new pub coming to the Garrett Conference Center, a product of the alcohol-policy change SGA had supported the previous year. In September he championed the senate's resolution disapproving of how the Confucius Institute building was approved, writing in a letter to the Herald that the contract was signed in China before the Board of Regents voted and that many controversial details were never disclosed. He rejected warnings that the vote made "powerful enemies," saying he hoped it sent a message that "accountability and transparency should always be top priorities" at WKU, while noting he respected Ransdell and would keep working with him. In April 2016 Richey won reelection with 1,497 of 2,341 presidential votes, becoming a two-term president in a high-turnout election announced after midnight in the Downing Student Union senate chambers. "It's a tremendous honor to be elected the first time," he said, "but a second time is verification of promises kept." His running mate Kate Hart won executive vice president and MyCampusToo chairwoman Hannah Neeper won administrative vice president, keeping his allies in the executive branch for 2016-17. A March 2017 Herald profile noted the win made him WKU SGA's first two-term president since 1988 and one of only three since 1974.
Also served as student regent under the merged offices.

Miles was returned unopposed to a second term as executive vice president in April 2015. He opened the year telling senators that sitting on university committees mattered and promising to revive Dine with Decision Makers, and reported through the autumn on the housing shortage and the Student Life Foundation's building and wiring work. He organised SGA's lobbying trip to Frankfort on 23 February 2016 against Governor Bevin's proposed cuts, setting up meetings with three state representatives and one state senator, and in March 2016 announced the open forum at which the presidential search committee would hear students.

Koehler was elected administrative vice president in April 2015 with 66 percent of the vote against J. William Berry, and kept the budget through a year in which SGA's money fell by $19,500 after a $15,000 private donation was not repeated. She moved $4,000 out of organizational aid back into scholarships and warned that fewer organisations would be funded; in February 2016 she reported a further 4.5 percent cut worth $1,301.27. At the executive cabinet on 1 December 2015 she moved the $600 that kept the library open longer through finals week, argued against a separate Judicial Council adviser and a code of conduct, and proposed that SGA take up suicide awareness after a student's death.

Line was appointed chief of staff by Jay Todd Richey and sworn in at the first meeting of September 2015, saying the MyCampusToo initiative to widen SGA's membership would be the centrepiece of the year. He worked through the spring on a policy for student parents, telling the senate SGA had nothing on its books about student mothers, and met the Counseling and Testing Center about Sexual Assault Awareness Month. He was one of the authors of the resolution setting out what SGA wanted from WKU's tenth president.

His re-election made him WKU SGA's first two-term president since 1988 and one of only three since 1974. Over his two terms he led the creation of three new committees, Sustainability, MyCampusToo and SAVES (Standing Against Violence and Ending Self-harm), revamped SGA's website, authored nine bills and resolutions, and represented students on the Board of Regents, the University Senate and the presidential search committee that chose WKU's 10th president. A Herald profile in March 2017 described a president who arrived late to office hours from overrun meetings, fielded budget questions and calls from the chief of police, and admitted he still struggled with low self-esteem. In a farewell letter published as his term ended, Richey wrote that fighting for college affordability had been a personal priority: SGA rallied at the Kentucky Capitol and lobbied the General Assembly against university budget cuts, and he chaired the Board of Student Body Presidents of Kentucky. He cited expanded services for military and veteran students, the Rave Guardian safety app, WKU's first eSports program, an SGA Voter Empowerment Initiative that registered hundreds of voters, new SGA scholarships including one for students with disabilities, and helping select president Tim Caboni. His successor Andi Dahmer took the oath of office on May 2, 2017.
holdings.source: Bowling Green Daily News, Apr 2017 (archived copy)

holdings.what_they_did: Also served as student regent under the merged offices.

Hart had chaired SGA's Academic Affairs committee before running as Jay Todd Richey's running mate for executive vice president in the April 2016 election. Richey was re-elected president with 1,497 of 2,341 votes cast, and Hart was elected executive vice president over senator Zach Jones the same night. The Senate's 13 September 2016 minutes show Hart's office coordinating correspondence between senators and their assigned university-committee contacts and running that year's homecoming queen nomination, which put forward Hannah Neeper alongside Hart's own name and Andi Dahmer's. She co-authored, with President Richey, Bill 1-17-S, a constitutional amendment reforming how WKU's regional campuses at Elizabethtown-Fort Knox, Glasgow and Owensboro were represented in SGA, replacing the old "Regional Affiliates" structure with elected "Regional Ambassadors"; the Senate passed it 30-0 in February 2017. She also co-authored Bill 27-17-S with Hizareth Linares, making the SGA SAVES committee, which addressed mental health and sexual assault awareness, a permanent standing committee under the Constitution; it passed 27-0-1 that April.

Neeper chaired SGA's MyCampusToo committee in 2015-16, closing that year by announcing the committee's World Festival at the Senate's final spring meeting. She then ran as administrative vice president on Jay Todd Richey's ticket and was elected in April 2016, telling the Herald afterward, "I feel wonderful." As administrative vice president that year, bills before the Senate repeatedly name her chair of the Organizational Aid committee, sponsoring or authoring appropriations to student organizations including the WKU Horticulture Club, the Indian Student Association, Women in Science and Engineering, Young Life, Sigma Tau Delta, Kappa Sigma and the Nonprofit Student Association, among others. In April 2017 she and Chief of Staff James Line proposed a Senate resolution supporting future faculty pay raises, after the Faculty Senate had unanimously approved a concurrent resolution of its own. The SGA resolution passed. Neeper said it was meant to show that students and not only faculty wanted the raises, arguing that classroom morale "affects [students] as much as it affects [faculty]."

In his second year as chief of staff Line ran SGA's voter work: Richey gave him the job of registering students and getting them to the polls, and on 8 November 2016 he ran the Ride To Vote shuttle from three campus pick-up points. He authored the bill co-sponsoring the 2016 Presidential Debate Fest, the constitutional amendment lowering SGA's membership requirement from a 2.5 to a 2.0 grade point average, which passed 24-7, the organizational aid inclusivity pledge, and, with administrative vice president Hannah Neeper, the resolution asking WKU to put faculty salaries ahead of new construction.

holdings.what_they_did: Knight served as SGA's Director of Academic and Student Affairs in 2016-17. The Senate's 13 September 2016 minutes record him reporting 13 applications already in for the Earn-a-Computer program, and a week later he told the Senate he planned to work with WKU Athletics on a partnership to raise student attendance at games. That November he was a co-author, with senators Chase Coffey, Jody Dahmer, Francisco Serrano and Andi Dahmer, of Bill 14-16-F, which created the Jonesville Memorial Scholarship: $750 for incoming Black students who graduated from the Warren County or Bowling Green school systems, named for the historically Black Jonesville neighborhood WKU's 1963 campus expansion displaced. It passed 27-4-1. He also authored or sponsored several of the year's other scholarship bills, including funding for study-abroad awards and SGA's general scholarship recipients.

Bose served as SGA's Director of Information Technology in 2016-17; the Senate's 13 September 2016 minutes record his report as simply that the SGA website was being updated regularly. That spring the Herald named him the newly elected chair of the Indian Student Association, ahead of its April 2017 Holi festival on the Honors College lawn.

Burke served as SGA's Director of Public Relations in 2016-17, reporting to the Senate that September on tabling and voting-booth outreach in Centennial Mall during senate elections. In November 2016 he was the public face of SGA's new SafeWalk initiative, a phone line students could call to get a walking companion on campus at night. He told the Herald the idea came directly from students who "didn't feel safe on campus" but did not want to call police over something that was not an emergency. That February he authored Bill 6-17-S, allocating $100 in SGA funds toward "Love Has No Borders," a Feb. 10, 2017 event co-sponsored with the International Diplomats supporting WKU's international students after a federal executive order restricted travel from seven countries; the bill noted 22 WKU students came from the affected countries.

Nathan Cherry was Speaker of the Senate in 2016-17, the year of Jay Todd Richey's presidency. On 20 September 2016 he told the Senate that eleven at-large seats should have been filled the previous spring but only ten were, leaving SGA a senator short through the summer, and took responsibility, saying "I failed to catch that"; Lucas Knight was appointed to the open seat. In February 2017 Cherry backed the bill requiring every senator to keep one office hour a week, which passed alongside a measure creating non-voting regional ambassador positions; he said the office-hour requirement would make senators feel more connected and more willing to write legislation.

Lowry kept the senate's records and sat on the organizational aid committee, appearing as a contact on its funding bills. She co-authored the constitutional amendment of April 2017 that wrote a report on executive discretionary spending into the administrative vice president's duties, passed 29-0-1, and the resolution asking WKU to waive a $10 parking late fee in exchange for a donation to the campus food pantry, passed 31-0-0. She was elected administrative vice president for the following year.

Cox was elected an associate justice of the SGA Judicial Council alongside Amber Daniel's election as chief justice, a Judicial Council meeting reported to the Senate on 2 February 2016, and moved up to chief justice himself for 2016-17. As chief justice he reviewed that fall's election codes with the Senate on 6 September 2016 and told senators to report any justice seen campaigning for a candidate. On 11 October 2016 he told the Senate the council had received a complaint that several SGA members had made racist remarks, and that the council would meet the next day to decide whether to investigate. Cox told senators such conduct "is not tolerated in the Student Government Association ... whatsoever." The investigation was dropped when the members concerned resigned that morning; because no investigation was held, SGA did not release their names or the nature of the remarks. In November Cox reported that justice Amarah Reed had stepped down and that the council was looking for a replacement. In March 2017 Cox announced the council had chosen Annalicia Carlson to succeed him as chief justice and Lane Hedrick as associate chief justice, both pending Senate confirmation. That spring he ruled on eligibility questions in a crowded presidential race, and in April the council split 5-2 on granting freshman candidate Kenan Mujkanovic a late exemption to run without a full year of Senate service, with Cox and Carlson in the minority against allowing it.
holdings.source: SGA Judicial Council page, archived 1 Nov 2016 (last modified 29 Aug 2016)

holdings.what_they_did: John "Jack" McKinney served as an Associate Justice on WKU SGA's Judicial Council beginning in fall 2016. At the SGA meeting of 11 October 2016, Chief Justice Cody Cox said he had received a complaint that several SGA members had allegedly made racist remarks, and the Judicial Council met the next day to decide whether to open an investigation. McKinney and senator Braxton Powell both resigned from SGA that Wednesday morning, 12 October 2016; Powell's resignation letter cited scheduling conflicts, and Associate Chief Justice Annalicia Carlson said McKinney resigned for "personal reasons." The Herald reported that neither man confirmed or denied the allegations, or said their resignations were connected to them, and that SGA did not release the names of those accused or describe the alleged remarks. The Herald also reported that the Judicial Council did not go forward with an investigation because the students it would have examined had already left SGA, without identifying those students as McKinney and Powell. The record does not show the allegation being confirmed, denied or otherwise resolved.

The committee had been created the previous October with Senator Francisco Serrano as its first chair; the record does not show when or why the chair changed to Linares. She co-authored Bill 17-17-S with MyCampusToo chair Andi Dahmer, allocating $550 for the Miss World Fest WKU Pageant, which passed 25-4-0 on 28 March 2017. A week later she authored Bill 23-17-S, allocating $250 to the WKU Counseling and Testing Center to co-sponsor Take Back the Night, tying the sponsorship explicitly to SAVES's creation; it passed 27-3-0 on 4 April. That same night, 4 April 2017, she co-authored Bill 27-17-S with Executive Vice President Kate Hart, amending the constitution to make SGA SAVES a permanent standing committee; it passed 27-0-1.

Vickrey chaired SGA's MyCampusToo committee by the autumn of 2016. The senate's 13 September 2016 minutes still show Michael Shelton reporting as MyCampusToo chair, sworn in to the post that night; the record does not show when the chair changed, but the Herald was calling Vickrey the committee's chair by 17 October and she was authoring committee legislation as chair from 1 November. She authored Bill 18-16-F, allocating $100 for Project Pengyou Day, an event bridging U.S. and Chinese students, co-authored with Senator Andi Dahmer and passed 15 November 2016. The same day, the senate passed Bill 17-16-F, which Vickrey co-authored with Andi and Jody Dahmer, amending the constitution to make MyCampusToo a permanent standing committee under the name Committee for Diversity and Inclusion. After Chief Justice Cody Cox told the 11 October 2016 senate meeting he had received a complaint that several SGA members made racist remarks, two members resigned the next morning citing unrelated reasons — neither confirmed, denied, nor acknowledged any link to the complaint — and the Judicial Council's planned investigation was dropped because they had already left the organization. President Richey and Vickrey, as MyCampusToo chair, released a joint statement the following day, Thursday 13 October, condemning the alleged acts and undertaking to continue SGA's work with underrepresented students.
Chaired MyCampusToo through the spring of 2017, authoring or co-authoring at least seven bills and resolutions out of it, before being elected student body president in April 2017.

Chase Coffey served as a WKU Student/SGA senator during the 2016-17 year. He was one of five authors, with Jody Dahmer, Josh Knight, Francisco Serrano and Andi Dahmer, of Bill 14-16-F, which the Senate passed 27-4-1 on Nov. 29, 2016 to create the $750 Jonesville Memorial Scholarship for incoming African American students from the Warren County or Bowling Green school systems, memorializing the historically Black Jonesville neighborhood WKU displaced during its 1960s campus expansion. At the Feb. 21, 2017 meeting Coffey introduced a resolution to let former senators who had resigned in good standing attend SGA's year-end banquet; the Senate passed it unanimously, but the Executive Council vetoed it as unconstitutional. Coffey then announced his own resignation, citing a scheduling conflict with a night class, and thanked the Senate "for getting to serve beside you all through the Fall." A freshman, Olga Shoyat, was appointed to fill his seat.
