holdings.what_they_did: Jody Dahmer served as an SGA senator during the 2016-17 year. At the Nov. 29, 2016 meeting she spoke in the debate over the Jonesville Memorial Scholarship bill, arguing the scholarship should stay limited to African American students because their ancestors had been displaced to build sports stadiums on the site; the Senate agreed and passed the bill in its original, race-restricted form. Dahmer went on to co-author Bill 19-17-S with Andi Dahmer and Luke Edmunds, which the Senate passed 27-3-0 on April 4, 2017 to allocate $650 in discretionary funds toward new equipment for the WKU Makerspace, and Bill 12-17-S with Andi Dahmer and Savannah Molyneaux, passed 27-0-0 on March 7, 2017, funding a $20 sustainability and social-justice panel discussion. She was also a named senator on a passed resolution asking WKU to add elevator access to Gordon Wilson Hall for students with disabilities.

holdings.what_they_did: William "Will" Hurst was already sitting as a senator at large in 2016-17. He co-authored Bill 13-17-S, which the Senate passed 19-11-1 on March 21, 2017 (after being tabled two weeks) to buy a $225 portable whiteboard for SGA committees and events, and he authored Bill 26-17-S, a constitutional amendment to strip the Executive Branch of its power to propose legislation to the Senate; it failed 7-22-1 on April 4, 2017. Later that month he was returned as one of twelve at-large student senators in the April 2017 election, serving through the 2017-18 year and chairing the Public Relations Committee. As a senator at large in 2017-18 he co-authored a bylaws amendment fixing set election windows for constitutional amendments (with Lucas Knight, passed) and a resolution asking WKU to add a required sexual-assault-education course (with Ashlyn Jones, Annabelle Ford, Garrett Edmonds and Alex Sergent). At the Sept. 12, 2017 meeting, as Public Relations Committee Chair, he said LGBTQ rights were "fundamental rights as Americans" in supporting funding for Bowling Green's inaugural Pride Festival. On Jan. 23, 2018 he voted against, and spoke against, the reappointment of former senator Stephen Mayer, calling it "hypocritical" for the executive board to nominate a second fraternity member after criticizing SGA's Greek overrepresentation. Hurst walked out of an emergency Judicial Council meeting on Jan. 29, 2018 amid a tense stretch in the Senate. He did not attend the March 20, 2018 meeting, where fellow senator Alex Sergent, the Public Relations Committee's vice chair, sat in his usual seat at the front of the chamber as interim chair; SGA President Andi Dahmer said at the time that "nothing is official" about Hurst's status. By the following week's Herald coverage of Senate tensions, he was being described as "former Public Relations Committee Chair."
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Bill 13-17-S, Funding for a Portable Whiteboard for SGA

holdings.what_they_did: Luke Edmunds served as an SGA senator during the 2016-17 year. At the Nov. 29, 2016 meeting he argued in the Jonesville Memorial Scholarship debate that the scholarship should be open to all students, saying every WKU student was, in his words, "using the land that Jonesville once was;" the Senate did not adopt his broader version and passed the bill limited to African American applicants. Edmunds went on to co-author Bill 19-17-S with Jody Dahmer and Andi Dahmer, which the Senate passed 27-3-0 on April 4, 2017 to put $650 in discretionary funds toward new WKU Makerspace equipment. Edmunds was re-elected in the April 2017 SGA election as one of three junior student senators for the 2017-18 year.

holdings.what_they_did: Andrea Ambam was a senator in WKU SGA's 2016-17 session. With fellow senator Brian Anderson, she authored Resolution 6-17-S, "Resolution to Support Reparations," which called on the university to acknowledge slavery as "a debt that will never be paid," asked for a task force to study test-optional and geographically weighted admissions, and called for full and free access to WKU for Black students. It passed the Senate 19-10-1 on second reading, 18 April 2017, and was modeled on legislation passed earlier that year at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, whose petition Tyriek Mack, a student activist there, helped write. The resolution drew national attention: Herald news coverage reported it reached the Associated Press, the Rush Limbaugh Show and the New York Post, and that Ambam was interviewed by Tucker Carlson on Fox News. The Herald's editorial board separately wrote that coverage also reached commentator Milo Yiannopoulos and The Blaze, and called the resolution a symbolic gesture that risked SGA's credibility. WKU President Gary Ransdell issued a statement saying the university would not adopt a free-tuition reparations policy. In Herald news coverage and in a letter to the editor written by Anderson, the authors said the resolution's language was largely symbolic, that they did not expect free tuition for Black students to result, and that their goal was to start a conversation about barriers facing Black students at WKU.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Resolution 6-17-S, Resolution to Support Reparations

holdings.what_they_did: Anderson chaired SGA's Legislative Research Committee in 2016-17, the committee senators sent bill ideas to for drafting help, as the senate's own 13 September 2016 minutes and later legislation both record. In April 2017 he co-authored two resolutions in the senate's final weeks. Resolution 6-17-S, written with Senator Andrea Ambam and sponsored through MyCampusToo, called for a university task force on test-optional and geographically weighted admissions and for reparations for Black students; it passed 19-10-1 on 18 April and drew national wire coverage after President Ransdell said within days it was not a university position. A week later, Resolution 10-17-S, co-authored with Francisco Serrano and Serenda Lobue of Hope Harbor, asked that WKU police receive mandatory diversity, hate-crime and sexual-assault training; it passed unanimously, 23-0-0, on 25 April. He was first-named author of Bill 20-17-S, requiring student organizations to sign a nondiscrimination pledge before receiving SGA Organizational Aid, written with Murphy Burke, James Line, Lily Nellans and President Jay Todd Richey after Kentucky Senate Bill 17, signed on 20 March 2017, permitted campus organizations to discriminate against students where doing so aligned with the organization's beliefs; it passed 17-9-1 at the senate's 28 March 2017 meeting.

Wysong chaired SGA's Public Relations Committee in early 2017. She co-authored Bill 13-17-S with Senator William Hurst, allocating $175 from Senate Discretionary funding and $50 from the Public Relations budget for a portable whiteboard for SGA committees and councils to use for tabling; it passed 19-11-1 on 21 March 2017 after being tabled for two weeks. The following fall, in November 2017, by then a senator at large, she co-authored Resolution 10-17-F with William Hurst and College Heights Herald editor-in-chief Andrew Henderson, standing with the paper in the lawsuit WKU had brought against it over its request for the university's Title IX records; it was sponsored through the Campus Improvements committee. The copy on file does not record whether it passed.
holdings.source: SGA Bill 13-17-S, Funding for a Portable Whiteboard for SGA

She was elected executive vice president for 2017-18.

McCormick served on the organizational aid committee and is recorded among its members on Bill 22-16-F, the November 2016 bill that split $1,500 between three student organisations.
Sworn in with eight others in one batch, 31 Jan 2017. Also spelled "Mujcanovic" in the Senate's own 21 Feb 2017 minutes; not resolved, only flagged.

Nellans was one of the five authors of Bill 20-17-S, the bill requiring student organisations to sign a nondiscrimination pledge before receiving organizational aid, passed 17-9-1 on 28 March 2017. Her wider part in the year is under her senate officer entry.

Pettway authored Bill 18-17-S, $100 for refreshments at 'Hidden Hacks of the Hill', an event to explain SGA's resources to minority students, passed 27-2-0, and Resolution 3-17-S, which asked that the first three rows of section 127 beside the marching band be restored to the Major Redz, passed 28-0-1. Both were read on 21 March and passed on 28 March 2017. At the meeting of 18 April she asked senators interested in mentoring minority students to speak to her.

Richardson authored Bill 28-17-S, the constitutional amendment merging the academic affairs and student affairs committees, passed 28-0-0 on 25 April 2017. His later offices are under his senate officer entry.

Saeed was approved as a senator on 7 February 2017 to fill the Gatton Academy seat, which had not been elected the previous autumn. She was the only senator directly representing Gatton students and said she took the seat to bridge that gap and advocate for the Academy.
Sworn in 27 Sep 2016. Spelled "Francisco" elsewhere in this year's own minutes and in the archive's existing profile text; not resolved, only flagged.

Appointed by Executive Vice President Kate Hart and sworn in as a senator at large, 21 February 2017. The minutes record the appointment but do not say which seat; the Herald's report of the same meeting says she was appointed in place of Chase Coffey, who resigned that night.
Sworn in with eight others in one batch, 31 Jan 2017.
Appointed by President Richey and confirmed by the senate 13 Sep 2016.

Jones's committee ran the campus safety walk each semester, starting from Centennial Mall on 15 September 2016, and polled students on where they felt unsafe; he told the senate some places were thought unsafe that were not. In March 2017 he sat on the university's food service bid and said he had tried to represent the whole student body in the vote that gave Aramark a new letter of intent.
By mid-October 2016 Helen Vickrey was reported as MyCampusToo committee chair; the record does not show when or why the chair changed.

Under Molyneaux the sustainability committee went from a body renewed each year to a permanent one written into the constitution. It brought reusable takeout containers to Fresh in September 2016, ran a panel on social justice and sustainability in April 2017 for $20, staged the Earth Day festival in Centennial Mall, and funded the Double Dollars matching programme at the Community Farmers Market and the Big Red Bikes scheme.

Anderson's committee researched legislation before it reached the floor, and he asked senators to bring him their bill ideas. He co-authored the organizational aid nondiscrimination pledge, passed 17-9-1; the Resolution to Support Reparations, which asked WKU to set up a task force on test-optional and geographically weighted admissions and passed 19-10-1 on 18 April 2017; and the resolution asking WKU police to take diversity, hate crime and sexual assault training, passed unanimously, 23-0-0, a week later. He stood for executive vice president in April 2017.

Andi Dahmer, a Louisville sophomore who had served as a senator and chair of the MyCampusToo committee, was announced as the next student body president shortly after midnight on April 19, 2017, winning 930 of the 1,579 votes cast against Kenan Mujkanovic's 305 and Lily Nellans' 212. Her running mates Savannah Molyneaux and Kara Lowry were elected executive vice president and administrative vice president, and Dahmer entered office already drafting legislation aimed at improving retention, making study abroad more affordable and supporting sensitivity training. Her year in office was marked by internal division. The senate saw longer debates, more than 15 proposed constitutional amendments compared with about 10 the year before, and an emergency Judicial Council meeting on Jan. 29, with contention peaking around the DACA debates of October and November 2017, when the senate failed a clean DREAM Act resolution before passing a resolution supporting DACA students. Dahmer said the year had become "almost toxic in nature" and blamed partisan ideologies brought into what was supposed to be a nonpartisan organization. In April 2018 Dahmer told the Herald she had endured months of harassment as president and student regent, including senators cursing at her in the SGA office, a group message thread of eight people called the "Justice Friends" that wished her physical harm, and a profane note left on her car on Feb. 9 that prompted a police report. Of the note she said, "That's when I really started fearing for my life on this campus." Her residence hall director reported her case to the Title IX office, which found it did not meet the legal standard for harassment; it was processed instead through the Office of Student Conduct, which issued no-contact orders against two senators, and she did not seek reelection. In 2018 Dahmer, whose full name is Loandria "Andi" Dahmer, sued WKU, university president Timothy Caboni, director of student activities Charley Pride and assistant general counsel and Title IX coordinator Andrea Anderson, alleging sex-based discrimination and harassment by fellow SGA members, negligence by the university in responding to it, and that Caboni retaliated against her by declining to write a letter of recommendation for a Rhodes Scholarship application. U.S. District Judge David Hale granted the defendants summary judgment in March 2021, finding WKU had not been deliberately indifferent and that the incidents were not severe enough to constitute actionable harassment; the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals partially revived the case in 2022, directing the district court to consider whether student-on-student harassment had occurred before February 2018. The parties settled in January 2024, with WKU's insurance carrier paying Dahmer $10,000 and the university's attorney describing the payment as nominal and made without any admission of wrongdoing.
Also served as student regent under the merged offices.

Molyneaux chaired SGA's Sustainability committee in 2016-17 before running for re-election as executive vice president in April 2018 on a ticket with presidential candidate Conner Hounshell and Administrative Vice President Kara Lowry. Days before the vote, the Judicial Council disqualified, then suspended, the rival Mayer-Edmonds-Anderson ticket over a Pepe the Frog meme in its campaign chalking; Stephen Mayer's ticket was reinstated to run and won, with Hounshell's ticket placing second. Molyneaux, Lowry and Hounshell were all elected senators instead. In February 2018 she joined President Andi Dahmer, Lowry and Hounshell in writing Resolution 3-18-S opposing the scale of a renegotiated Aramark dining-fee increase, which would have raised a per-semester fee on students without meal plans from $75 toward $350 over ten years; the Senate passed it unanimously. At the Senate's final meeting of the year, Molyneaux spoke about what she called an "awful" year for the executive board, describing sexism and misogyny within the Senate and backing Dahmer's account, reported the same week, of harassment she said she had faced as president. Molyneaux cited the threatening note left on Dahmer's car and the derogatory names used in the SGA offices, and told senators who had taken part in it to think about what they had done.

Lowry served as SGA's administrative vice president in 2017-18 and ran for re-election that April on the Hounshell-Molyneaux-Lowry ticket, which placed second behind the Mayer-Edmonds-Anderson ticket after a Judicial Council fight over a campaign meme; Lowry was elected a senator instead. She went with President Andi Dahmer to the Title IX office in early 2018 as a witness supporting Dahmer's harassment complaint, and in February co-authored Resolution 3-18-S with Dahmer, Molyneaux and Chief of Staff Conner Hounshell opposing the scale of a renegotiated Aramark dining-fee increase. She authored the Senate's original "Go With the Flow" bill funding feminine hygiene products in campus restrooms; a Herald report on the program's 2020 renewal, after she had left office, still credited her by name as the bill's original author.

Hounshell served as SGA's Chief of Staff in 2017-18 and ran for president that April on a ticket with Executive Vice President Savannah Molyneaux and Administrative Vice President Kara Lowry, both seeking re-election. Days before the vote the Judicial Council disqualified, then suspended, the rival Mayer-Edmonds-Anderson ticket over a Pepe the Frog meme in its campaign chalking. Hounshell's ticket won 33 percent of the presidential vote to Mayer's 35 percent; all three were elected senators instead. In February 2018 he co-authored Resolution 3-18-S with President Andi Dahmer, Molyneaux and Lowry, opposing the scale of a renegotiated Aramark dining-fee increase on students without meal plans. He had recommended Garrett Edmonds, whom he met when Edmonds joined SGA in fall 2017, for the chair of the Campus Improvements committee, but by the following fall told the Herald his opinion of Edmonds had completely changed after the chalking controversy. The Herald's account of that criticism, and Edmonds's own answer to it, are in the article cited here; the archive does not restate one side of it in the other man's record.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Bill 1-17-F, A Bill to Amend the Constitution of the Student Government Association of Western Kentucky University

The bill was first read 7 November 2017; the copy on file does not record a second reading or a vote.

holdings.office: Chair of the Committee of Diversity and Inclusion
holdings.what_they_did: Clark was a senator in fall 2017, later confirmed as a senator at large by early 2018, co-authoring Resolution 7-17-F with Lily Nellans and student Francisco Serrano, backing a proposed Bowling Green Fairness Ordinance protecting LGBTQ residents from discrimination; it was sponsored through the Committee for Diversity and Inclusion and read 14-28 November 2017. He co-authored Bill 5-18-S with Administrative Vice President Kara Lowry in February 2018, proposing funding for a recycled computer for the Pride Center. He became chair of the Committee of Diversity and Inclusion in February 2018, replacing Corey Newsome, who had stepped down over scheduling conflicts. The same week, on 13 February, the senate unanimously passed Resolution 1-18-S, which Clark co-authored with Chief of Staff Conner Hounshell and Kara Lowry, supporting an integrated LGBTQ-health curriculum at WKU. As chair, he authored Bill 7-18-S, funding food for CDI's first spring meeting, and co-authored Bill 13-18-S with Hounshell and Jayden Thomas, funding $250 in stoles for the Lavender Recognition Ceremony honoring LGBTQ graduates; it passed 28-5 on 20 March 2018. After Senator Dallas McKinney cited his reading of the Bible as his reason for voting against the bill, LGBTQ students and SGA members addressed the senate on 3 April, and Clark, speaking as Diversity and Inclusion chair, told the meeting that people in the room had demonstrated discrimination towards the LGBTQ community while a harmless funding bill was being passed.
holdings.source: SGA Bill 7-18-S, Funding for the First Meeting of the Committee of Diversity and Inclusion

holdings.what_they_did: Peter served as SGA's Director of Information Technology in 2017-18, filing no report at the Senate's 12 September and 24 October meetings that fall. In March 2018 she led Bill 14-18-S with Administrative Vice President Kara Lowry and Chief of Staff Conner Hounshell, allocating $450 in Senate funds, matched by the executive board, toward the Indian Student Association's Holi Festival on South Lawn that month. At the Senate's final meeting that April, amid the year's disputes over sexism in the chamber, Peter told senators that "everyone on this campus is special and deserves respect" and that the Senate should never judge anyone based on gender.

holdings.office: Director of Academic and Student Affairs
holdings.what_they_did: Houston chaired SGA's Student Affairs committee in 2016-17, then became Director of Academic and Student Affairs in 2017-18 after the two committees merged. The Senate's 12 September 2017 minutes show her office already at work on study-abroad funding. In April 2018 she was one of the executive board members who spoke publicly about President Andi Dahmer's harassment experience, telling the Herald that derogatory language from senators was "only directed toward the female executive board members" in the SGA office. At the Senate's final meeting that April she told senators SGA had "never allowed" a toxic environment to take hold during her two previous years in the office, and said she was disheartened by what had unfolded that year and hoped SGA's culture would change.

Wyer chaired SGA's Academic Affairs committee in 2016-17 before serving as Director of Public Relations in 2017-18. Senate minutes that fall show her taking photos and video for SGA's social media and coordinating tabling at basketball games. At the Senate's final meeting in April 2018 Wyer used her officer report to answer claims circulating that SGA was taking money from Greek organisations, telling senators those organisations were funded by their own members and that SGA had no power over their money. She then spoke about the importance of intervening when a bystander sees something wrong, and disclosed something of her own experience that year; the archive leaves what she said in the Herald's account rather than repeating it here. She stayed in SGA after her term as an officer ended, taking the SGA SAVES chair in the spring of 2019 after the seat had stood vacant since January.

Ian Hamilton was a WKU SGA senator for 2016-17 and 2017-18. He authored a bill at the Senate's April 2017 meeting to move the power to appoint Senate committee heads from the SGA president to the speaker of the Senate; President Jay Todd Richey argued the change would compromise the speaker's meant-to-be-impartial role, and the bill failed 15-3. Hamilton was elected a senator-at-large for 2017-18 in that spring's election. As chair of the Sustainability Committee once it became a permanent SGA committee that fall, Hamilton co-authored Bill 10-17-F, funding a "No-Shave November" beard-growing contest; he amended its budget down from $250 to $100 at the September 2017 meeting, and it passed 25-3. He also co-authored Bill 16-17-F, funding an Interfaith Workshop on Sustainability and Social Justice, which passed unanimously, and, with Senator Garrett Edmonds, Bill 17-17-F, funding a chalk campaign for Mission: Thank You Veterans. The following February he authored Bill 10-18-S, funding the 2018 Earth Day Festival. At the Senate's 24 January 2018 meeting, called amid a dispute over a postponed appointment and a reported "irregularity" in that year's SGA election, Hamilton was one of four students who addressed the chamber; he read aloud a letter from former senate member Luke Edmonds, who could not attend, expressing condolences after the shooting at Marshall County High School.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Bill 10-18-S, Funding for the 2018 Earth Day Festival hosted by the SGA Sustainability Committee

holdings.what_they_did: Ryan Richardson was Speaker of the Senate in 2017-18, under President Andi Dahmer. He presided over the Senate's contentious spring 2018 business on funding Lavender Graduation stoles for LGBTQ students: the bill passed 28-5 on 20 March with Senator Dallas McKinney speaking against it without giving a reason, and at the following meeting on 27 March McKinney returned to explain that vote, citing his reading of the Bible, after which other senators spoke against deciding university business from scripture. Earlier that month, on 6 March 2018, the Judicial Council met online and dismissed Senator Annabelle Ford from the Senate for failing to notify the Judicial Council, President Dahmer or Speaker Richardson of the reasons for her unexcused absences.

McWilliams kept the senate's records and enforced the office hour rule, telling senators in September 2017 that each of them owed one hour a week and holding her own on Monday and Wednesday afternoons. She co-authored the resolution asking that the Major Redz's reserved section in Smith Stadium be restored.

Carlson served as associate chief justice of the Judicial Council for 2016-17, the year Cody Cox was chief justice, and was chosen by the council to succeed him as chief justice for 2017-18 in March 2017, pending Senate confirmation. As chief justice she swore in committee chairs, senators and cabinet members at the Senate's first meeting of the year on 29 August 2017, and in January 2018 chaired an emergency Judicial Council session on discrepancies in a fall referendum on constitutional amendments. In April 2018 she led the council through the most consequential ruling of her term: an emergency meeting disqualified the Mayer-Edmonds-Anderson presidential ticket, and separately senator candidate Anna McAvoy, for using a Pepe the Frog meme in campaign chalking that the council found violated the election code's ban on inappropriate depictions in sidewalk chalk and the constitution's anti-discrimination clause. Carlson told the Herald the whole ticket was held responsible because executive vice presidential candidate Garrett Edmonds had put the candidates' names on the chalking, and had been told the meme was used as a hate symbol but did not have it removed. After a senate meeting drew unusually large attendance from students objecting to the ruling, the Senate created a new appeal process, and the council itself voted 3-2 with one abstention to reduce the MEA ticket's penalty from disqualification to suspension with a required apology, later doing the same for McAvoy. The reinstated Mayer-Edmonds-Anderson ticket went on to win the election. Carlson's term ended in April 2018 when the Senate elected Associate Justice Jacob McAndrews to succeed her. Carlson returned to the council as an associate justice for 2018-19. In the spring of 2019 she argued against confirming President Stephen Mayer's nominee to a vacant council seat, saying the council itself preferred Erika Puhakka. In May 2019, in her final weeks as a graduating senior, an impeachment petition was brought against her alleging she had inconsistently listed spring 2019 candidates' preferred and legal names on the ballot and had overstepped her role during Wood Brown's confirmation hearing to advance Puhakka's candidacy instead. Carlson rebutted the naming allegation directly, saying names were checked for GPA eligibility, and more generally said that after four years in SGA she "would never intentionally jeopardize it." The Senate canceled the hearing for lack of attendance the day it was scheduled, and the archive found no record it was ever rescheduled.

Devan Richardson was sworn in as an Associate Justice on WKU SGA's Judicial Council by Chief Justice Carlson at the first meeting of the Sixteenth Senate, 29 August 2017, with the council still one justice short of a full bench. The archive has found no further record of the term.

holdings.office: Chair of the Organizational Aid Committee
holdings.what_they_did: Held alongside her office as Administrative Vice President; she told the Senate on 29 August 2017 that she was responsible for the budget and chaired the committee that awards funding to campus clubs, and she authored the year's organizational aid bills.

Sat as Potter College senator. Co-author with the Administrative Vice President and the Legislative Research chair of Bill 25-17-F, the Go With the Flow programme. Elected Executive Vice President for 2018-19.

Jones chaired SGA SAVES in 2017-18. In November 2017 she authored Resolution 5-17-F, formally backing the federal Campus Accountability and Safety Act (Senate Bill S.856), which would have required universities to standardize sexual-assault reporting and disciplinary procedures. The same month she co-authored Resolution 9-17-F with fellow SAVES members Olivia Simpson, Logan Hornback and Lauren Pedersen, supporting an online appointment system at the Counseling and Testing Center for students with social anxiety, and Bill 34-17-F with Savannah Molyneaux, funding $30 for posters advertising “Make Your Voice Heard,” an anonymous compilation of sexual-assault survivors' stories modeled on a Washington Post project. In March 2018 she led Bill 17-18-S, funding $500 for Take Back the Night t-shirts, co-authored with President Andi Dahmer, three senators (Olivia Simpson, Logan Hornback and Lauren Pederson) and WKU student Savannah Huffman; it was read 20-27 March 2018.

Cox chaired SGA's Student Affairs committee in autumn 2017, listed under that title in the committee reports of the senate's 12 September 2017 minutes. By November the committee's autumn legislation names her CASA chair — the Committee for Academic and Student Affairs — reflecting the prior year's merger of Academic Affairs and Student Affairs; both titles appear in SGA's own records for the same year. She was named as the contact on Bill 27-17-F, which proposed to allocate $18,700 for SGA scholarships out of CASA's work: 10 Scholar Development Grants at $250 each, 26 Winter Term Scholarships at $300 each, and 28 Study Abroad/Student Teach Abroad scholarships at $300 each. The bill was first read 7 November 2017; the copy on file does not record a second reading or a vote.

holdings.office: Vice President, Committee for Diversity and Inclusion
holdings.what_they_did: Corey Newsome served as Vice President of the Committee for Diversity and Inclusion in 2017-18, under chair Divya Gangavelli. In October 2017 the two co-authored Bill 20-17-F, allocating $200 from the Senate's discretionary fund for "Hidden Hacks of the Hill," an event held 14 November 2017 meant to connect minority students with campus resources including Student Support Services, Safe Spaces, the Counseling and Testing Center, the WKU Food Pantry and the Office of Student Conduct; the bill passed its second reading on 31 October 2017. The vice-presidential title is the one Bill 20-17-F itself gives him rather than the chair's; the archive's separate note that he later held the chair rests on other evidence.

Hurst chaired public relations and authored fourteen pieces of legislation, a total matched that year only by administrative vice president Kara Lowry. Most of it rewrote SGA's own rules: a constitutional and bylaw pair creating constitutional amendment elections at the end of each semester, a limit on the executive branch's power to propose legislation, a standing emergency committee to fill senate seats out of cycle, new senate debate procedure, and the office of parliamentarian. He also funded a $500 voucher scheme with the Counseling and Testing Center, a $230 camera for the public relations committee, a $250 SGA tailgate and $300 for a political forum run jointly by Young Americans for Freedom, the College Republicans and the Young Democrats, and wrote the resolution standing with the College Heights Herald in its lawsuit with the university. In January 2018 he alleged the executive board had failed to advertise the fall election; the Judicial Council found the board had complied and censured him, and censured him again on 4 February over his conduct at the emergency meeting, which he apologised for.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Bill 14-17-F, A Bill to Amend the Bylaws of the Student Government Association of Western Kentucky University

holdings.what_they_did: Jordan Tackett was elected one of twelve at-large student senators in the April 2017 SGA election and served through 2017-18. At the Sept. 12, 2017 meeting he questioned SGA's Bill 9-17-F funding the inaugural Bowling Green Pride Festival, calling it "somewhat controversial" and asking senators whether they were ready to face the backlash if something happened at the event; the bill passed 12-2 regardless. Tackett co-authored, with freshman senator Will Harris, Bill 12-17-F, a constitutional amendment creating a Senator Appointment Committee to vet vacant senate seats by a randomly chosen panel rather than leaving appointments solely to the president; it passed. He was also listed as a contact on Bill 32-17-F, which would have removed legislation's first reading to speed up the Senate's process; it failed on Nov. 28, 2017.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Bill 12-17-F, A Bill to Amend the Constitution of the Student Government Association of Western Kentucky University

holdings.what_they_did: Harris authored Bill 12-17-F, the constitutional amendment binding the president to a set process when appointing senators to vacant seats. He managed the Mayer-Edmonds-Anderson campaign in the April 2018 election and was one of those the Judicial Council called to speak about the Pepe the Frog image used in its chalking. He was elected SGA president in 2019.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Bill 12-17-F, A Bill to Amend the Constitution of the Student Government Association of Western Kentucky University

holdings.what_they_did: Clark authored or co-authored the year's LGBTQ legislation: the resolution backing a Bowling Green fairness ordinance, which he wrote with Lily Nellans and Francisco Serrano and which passed 34-2 at the meeting of 28 November 2017; the resolution for an integrated LGBTQ+ health curriculum in medical education; $150 for a recycled computer in the Pride Center; $250 for the stoles at WKU's first Lavender Graduation, passed 28-5 on 20 March 2018, a figure the Herald printed the morning after the vote and again a week later, though its recap of 4 April gave it as 26-5; and $150 for the first meeting of the new Committee of Diversity and Inclusion, which he chaired.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Bill 13-18-S, Funding for Lavender Graduation Stoles

holdings.what_they_did: Jayden Thomas was a senator in WKU SGA's 2017-18 session. With Chief of Staff Conner Hounshell and senator Mark Clark, Thomas co-authored Bill 13-18-S, allocating $250 from Senate Discretionary, matched by $250 from Executive Discretionary, to purchase stoles for graduates attending WKU's Lavender Graduation ceremony on 8 May 2018, honoring the university's LGBTQ and ally graduates. The bill passed on second reading, 20 March 2018. By 2018-19 Thomas chaired the Sustainability Committee. As chair, Thomas authored Bill 17-18-F, which passed 32-1 and put $100 toward a Sustainability Day gift basket for 14 November 2018, and presented Bill 33-19-S at the 23 April 2019 meeting, funding paid to Downing Student Union to cover the cost of an Earth Day festival, which passed 20-0.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Bill 13-18-S, Funding for Lavender Graduation Stoles

holdings.what_they_did: Lucas Knight was elected one of two senior student senators in the April 2017 SGA election and served through 2017-18, additionally holding the title Fairness Representative. At the Sept. 12, 2017 meeting he co-authored, with Chief of Staff Conner Hounshell, the bill funding SGA's support for Bowling Green's inaugural Pride Festival, and said he had "supported this concept for the past three years," a reference to Bowling Green's long-stalled Fairness Ordinance. In November 2017 he was a named senator on Resolution 7-17-F, asking Bowling Green to pass a Fairness Ordinance and voicing support for WKU's LGBTQ students. Knight co-authored, with William Hurst, a bylaws amendment fixing set election windows for constitutional amendments, and, with Chief of Staff Conner Hounshell, Matthew Barr and Dallas McKinney, a constitutional amendment restructuring several senator seats around transfer, non-traditional and Intercultural Student Engagement Center students. At the March 20, 2018 meeting he spoke in favor of funding stoles for the Lavender Recognition Ceremony honoring LGBTQ graduates, calling it "a very small way of giving back to the LGBTQ+ community"; the bill passed 28-5 after Senator Dallas McKinney spoke against it without giving his reasoning.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Resolution 7-17-F, Resolution to Support Our LGBTQ Students

holdings.what_they_did: Amanda Harder served as an SGA senator during the 2017-18 year. She co-authored, with senator Logan Hornback, Bill 15-18-S, which the Senate passed unanimously on March 20, 2018 to fund $300 for the newly formed WKU Students for Breast Cancer Awareness and its "#WhyIFight" fundraising campaign. Harder said her mother had been diagnosed with breast cancer and that the cause was "something I'm really passionate about." By the 2018-19 year Harder chaired the Academic and Student Affairs Committee. She was lead author, with students Mary Fyfe, Alec Zaffiro, Krystal Neal and Taylor Vowels, of Resolution 5-19-S, which the Senate passed 23-1 on April 23, 2019 to support installing a $5 student fee funding the College Heights Herald, citing SGA's past legislation backing the Herald in its public-records lawsuit against WKU.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Bill 15-18-S, Funding for the WKU Students for Breast Cancer Awareness

holdings.what_they_did: Logan Hornback was a senator-at-large in WKU SGA's 2017-18 session. With senator Amanda Harder, Hornback co-authored Bill 15-18-S, allocating $300 to the newly formed WKU Students for Breast Cancer Awareness for its #WhyIFight fundraising campaign, and was among six senators and officers named on Bill 17-18-S, which put $500 toward Take Back the Night event T-shirts during Sexual Assault Prevention Month. Both bills passed on second reading in March 2018. Student Body President Stephen Mayer nominated Hornback to fill a vacant at-large Senate seat at the meeting of 16 October 2018. A vote-counting software error initially reported that the confirmation vote had failed; the error was found and corrected later that night, and it was ruled Hornback had in fact been elected to the seat, the Herald reported two months later when a second contested nomination revived the story. Hornback continued serving into spring 2019 and spoke in favor of a $5 student fee to fund the Herald at the 23 April 2019 meeting, saying that although the fee would add to tuition, "at least we know it will benefit the rest of the students."
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Bill 15-18-S, Funding for the WKU Students for Breast Cancer Awareness

holdings.what_they_did: Hamilton chaired sustainability. He funded the committee's No-Shave November promotion ($100), the interfaith workshop on sustainability and social justice ($200), the 2018 spring movie series ($50) and the 2018 Earth Day festival ($50), and wrote the constitutional amendment changing how committee heads were appointed. His Bill 32-17-F took the first reading of legislation out of the bylaws so that bills could pass on a single reading.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Bill 16-17-F, Funding for the Interfaith Workshop on Sustainability and Social Justice

holdings.what_they_did: Deekshita Madas was elected one of twelve senators-at-large in WKU SGA's April 2017 election for the 2017-18 term. As senator, she co-authored Bill 16-17-F with fellow senator Ian Hamilton, allocating $200 from Senate Discretionary to support an Interfaith Workshop on Sustainability and Social Justice held 17 February 2018. The bill had its first reading 10 October 2017 and second reading a week later; the record does not show its final vote.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Bill 16-17-F, Funding for the Interfaith Workshop on Sustainability and Social Justice

holdings.what_they_did: Mujkanovic sat on the organizational aid committee and was among the senators listed as contacts on Bill 32-17-F, which removed the first reading of legislation. After a senator read Bible verses to explain his vote against funding the Lavender Recognition Ceremony in March 2018, he told the senate its members needed to learn to love one another. He ran for president that April and took 32 percent of 2,378 votes; his campaign was suspended by the Judicial Council for handing out perishable food inside the 48 hours before the election, and that suspension was not reversed.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Bill 32-17-F, To Support the Removal of the First Reading of Legislation

holdings.what_they_did: Townsend sat for the international students' organisation. She co-authored Bill 9-18-S, which replaced two at-large seats and a graduate seat with first-generation, transfer and international seats; Bill 22-18-S, which renamed the 'English as a Second Language international student senator' simply the international student senator; and the bill funding the first meeting of the Committee of Diversity and Inclusion.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Bill 9-18-S, A Bill to Amend the Constitution of the Student Government Association of Western Kentucky University

holdings.what_they_did: Alex Sergent chaired SGA's Public Relations Committee during the 2016-17 year. At the Nov. 29, 2016 meeting he argued the proposed Jonesville Memorial Scholarship should be open to all minority students rather than African American students alone, asking whether the goal was repaying Jonesville specifically or, in his words, "extending that same hand toward all minorities that are currently struggling on campus;" the Senate kept the scholarship limited to African American recipients. Sergent continued in the Senate as a senator at large through 2017-18, by his own account his third year in SGA. He was a named senator on two November 2017 resolutions, one asking WKU to add a required sexual-assault-education course and one supporting restoration of the Major Redz student organization's traditional reserved football-stadium section, and he made the motion, passed unanimously, to let student speakers address the Senate first at the April 17, 2018 meeting on the disqualification of the MEA executive ticket. As Public Relations Committee vice chair, he stepped in as interim chair when Will Hurst missed the March 20, 2018 meeting, telling the Herald, "I have not been given any details as to what is going on." Describing the Senate's fractious 2017-18 year, Sergent compared the tension to a storm, where "two major thoughts start to collide and they mix," and said the result was not inherently bad. He said the friction came from new senators challenging established norms, and that this was something worth celebrating.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Resolution 1-17-F, Resolution to require Western Kentucky University to add a Sexual Assault Education course for all first year students

holdings.what_they_did: Wysong co-authored Resolution 10-17-F, by which the senate stood with the College Heights Herald in the newspaper's lawsuit with WKU; it was read on 28 November and 5 December 2017. A senator of the same name had chaired the public relations committee the previous year.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Resolution 10-17-F, Resolution to Support the College Heights Herald

holdings.what_they_did: Lily Nellans was a senator in WKU SGA's 2016-17 session. With senators Brian Anderson, James Line and Jay Todd Richey, she co-authored Bill 20-17-S, "Bill to Encourage Inclusivity in Student Organizations," requiring student organizations to commit to inclusivity before receiving Organizational Aid funding, written in response to a Kentucky law signed 20 March 2017 that let campus organizations discriminate when it aligned with their beliefs. The bill passed 17-9-1 on second reading, 28 March 2017. In the April 2017 SGA election, Nellans ran for student body president and placed third, with 212 of 1,579 votes cast, behind winner Andi Dahmer (930 votes) and Kenan Mujkanovic (305 votes). In the same election she was elected one of twelve senators-at-large for 2017-18. That session, with senator Mark Clark and WKU student Francisco Serrano, she co-authored Resolution 7-17-F, "Resolution to Support Our LGBTQ Students," calling on the Bowling Green City Commission to pass a Fairness Ordinance protecting residents from discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity; it passed second reading 28 November 2017.
holdings.source: SGA legislation: Resolution 7-17-F, Resolution to Support Our LGBTQ Students

holdings.what_they_did: Barr wrote the campus safety legislation of his first year: the resolution asking WKU for more blue-light emergency phones, $300 for the campus safety seminar of 28 February 2018, and the constitutional amendment replacing the University College seat and one graduate seat with transfer and non-traditional student seats.

DeBord was elected a senator at large in April 2017 and served on the organizational aid committee, which reviewed student organisations' applications; he is recorded among its members on Bill 11-17-F of September 2017.

holdings.office: Gordon Ford College of Business Senator
holdings.what_they_did: Ford co-authored Resolution 1-17-F, which asked WKU to add a one-credit Colonnade course on sexual assault education and prevention for all first-year students; the senate passed it 29-1, with two abstentions, on 26 September 2017. On 6 March 2018 the Judicial Council dismissed her from the senate for not explaining a run of unexcused absences.
Harris authored Bill 12-17-F, the constitutional amendment setting a fixed process for appointing senators to vacant seats. His wider part in the year is under his senate officer entry.

Hornback sat on SGA SAVES. He authored the resolution asking the Counseling and Testing Center to take appointments online, $300 for the newly formed WKU Students for Breast Cancer Awareness, and $500 for T-shirts for Take Back the Night during Sexual Assault Prevention Month.

Huffman sat on the organizational aid committee. He wrote the bill supporting Big Red Rents, a scheme to lend students phone and computer chargers and headphones, and, with five other senators, the $100 for advertising and refreshments at the campus safety walk.

Luckett served on the organizational aid committee, which reviewed student organisations' funding applications; she is recorded among its members on Bill 11-17-F of September 2017, which split $1,000 between WKU's Habitat for Humanity chapter and the Financial Planning Association.
Madas co-authored Bill 16-17-F, $200 from senate discretionary funds for the interfaith workshop on sustainability and social justice held in February 2018.

McAvoy sat on the sustainability committee and worked on a reusable bag scheme; in August 2017 she explained the constitutional amendment that had made the committee permanent. She was among the senators listed as contacts on Bill 32-17-F, and in January 2018 spoke for confirming Stephen Mayer to a vacant senate seat. Her own campaign for a senate seat in April 2018 was disqualified and then suspended over a Pepe the Frog meme used in her chalking; she apologised to the senate and said she had meant no harm, and after the ruling was reduced she was elected a senator at large.

McCormick authored Bill 3-17-F, $200 for the legal observer training SGA ran with the Nashville chapter of the National Lawyers Guild in October 2017, and co-authored Bill 9-18-S on the new first-generation, transfer and international senate seats. He also sat on the organizational aid committee.

McKinney co-authored the No-Shave November funding bill, the resolution asking for more blue-light emergency phones, the campus safety walk funding bill and the amendment creating transfer and non-traditional senate seats. On 27 March 2018 he told the senate that his reading of the King James Bible was why he had voted against the $250 for stoles at the Lavender Recognition Ceremony, and read verses from Romans; the Queer Student Union president walked out and other senators spoke against him. The Judicial Council censured him unanimously on 10 April 2018.
Mujkanovic served on the organizational aid committee and is recorded among the contacts on Bill 32-17-F. His fuller record for the year is under his senate officer entry.
Also credited as an SGA SAVES member under the spelling "Lauren Pedersen" in Resolution 9-17-F, 2017-18.
Reynolds was elected a sophomore senator in April 2017 and is recorded among the senators consulted on Bill 32-17-F, the bylaw change that removed the first reading of legislation.

Sergent co-authored Resolution 1-17-F, for a required first-year Colonnade course on sexual assault prevention, and Resolution 8-17-F, asking that the Major Redz's reserved section in Smith Stadium be restored. In March 2018 he spoke against the bill creating a seat for the Intercultural Student Engagement Center, asking where reserving seats for particular organisations would end; it passed 25-2-1.

Simpson held the Gatton Academy seat and sat on SGA SAVES. She co-authored the resolution for online appointments at the Counseling and Testing Center and the $500 for Take Back the Night T-shirts. In March 2018, after a fellow senator read Bible verses to the senate to explain his vote against funding the Lavender Recognition Ceremony, she spoke against settling WKU's interests from scripture and told the senate that what benefited the student body was safety.

Townsend co-authored Bill 9-18-S, which replaced two at-large seats and one graduate seat with first-generation, transfer and international student seats. Her other legislation is under her senate officer entry.
Wysong co-authored Resolution 10-17-F, by which the senate stood with the College Heights Herald in its lawsuit with the university, read on 28 November and 5 December 2017.

Nellans's committee reviewed every bill and resolution before it reached the floor. She told the senate in October 2017 that at least one author of each piece in new business had to meet the committee about its research, and that everything being voted on that night had been cleared by it.
Censured by the Judicial Council in January 2018 over an election-discrepancy complaint.

Cox chaired student affairs, which merged during the year into academic and student affairs. She ran the autumn 2017 scholarship round, asking senators to help grade applications before the deadline of 31 October.

Chaired by Divya Gangavelli as of the September 2017 minutes; Corey Newsome later held the chair before stepping down over scheduling conflicts, and Mark Clark was approved to replace him in February 2018.

Hamilton's committee met weekly and, he told the Herald in August 2017, had about twenty members and wanted more. It ran No-Shave November, a spring film series and the 2018 Earth Day festival, each funded by a bill he wrote.

Mayer was elected SGA president and student regent in April 2018 on the MEA ticket with Garrett Edmonds and Harper Anderson, taking 35 percent of 2,378 presidential votes against Conner Hounshell's 33 percent and Kenan Mujkanovic's 32 percent; 2,447 students voted overall. His ticket won only after the Judicial Council reversed a disqualification it had imposed days before the election over the campaign's use of a Pepe the Frog meme chalked on campus sidewalks, downgrading the penalty to a campaign suspension. A biology and chemistry double major who had served three semesters as a senator and studied at Harlaxton College, Mayer opened his term in September 2018 promising greater transparency from both the Board of Regents and SGA, and required senators to log a weekly office hour. As student regent he was an outspoken critic of WKU's fee structure, especially the $450 online academic fee, and opposed that year's 4 percent tuition increase, saying he did not see the need to put the financial burden "on the students' backs."
Also served as student regent under the merged offices.

Edmonds had chaired campus improvements the year before, funding the Go With the Flow programme that put free menstrual products in Grise Hall, the campus safety seminar and Mission: Thank You Veterans. He was elected executive vice president with 54 percent against Savannah Molyneaux, after the Judicial Council disqualified and then suspended his ticket over a Pepe the Frog image used in its campaign chalking and reversed the disqualification the next day. In office he led the delegation of twenty-four SGA members to the 2019 Rally for Higher Education in Frankfort and co-authored Resolution 10-18-F denouncing the white nationalist group Identity Evropa's recruiting on campus, which passed 28-0 on 4 December 2018.

Harper Anderson was elected administrative vice president in April 2018 on the MEA ticket, with presidential candidate Stephen Mayer and executive vice president Garrett Edmonds, and served through 2018-19. The ticket had been disqualified two days before the results over a Pepe the Frog image in a campaign chalk drawing, a ruling the Judicial Council reduced to a suspension before the count was announced; Mayer won the presidency with 35 percent of the 2,378 votes cast. The archive's record of Anderson's year in office is limited to the roster and the election coverage.
Elected student body president for 2019-20 the following spring.

holdings.office: Director of Academic and Student Affairs
holdings.what_they_did: Third nominee for the seat; confirmed 24-3-4 on 25 September 2018. Ashley Cox, the first nominee, had her confirmation tabled 8-7 on 4 September and resigned before it was taken up again; Anna McAvoy's confirmation then failed 6-9-1 on 11 September, and the president reopened the position.
Brosky was one of the twenty-four SGA members who went to the Rally for Higher Education in Frankfort in February 2019, and said he hoped student opinion would reach the representatives there.

Noah Moore was SGA's director of public relations in 2018-19. As a senator the year before he had co-authored a resolution, passed 28-2 in April 2018, asking Housing and Residence Life to make the sexual-orientation and gender-identity question optional on housing applications, and had spoken against a colleague who cited scripture in voting down funding for LGBTQ graduation stoles. In April 2019 SGA and the Queer Student Union held the second Unite for Fairness night in Downing Student Union, where students wrote letters to Bowling Green city commissioners supporting a fairness ordinance. Moore, who had helped run the first event the previous semester, said a handwritten letter would reach a commissioner more than an email or a phone call.

Asha McWilliams was Speaker of the Senate in 2018-19, under President Stephen Mayer. On 12 February 2019 she presided as a bill that would have barred repeat recipients of SGA study-abroad scholarships from reapplying was pulled from the agenda after debate produced five competing motions. In the spring 2019 election McWilliams ran for student body president on a ticket with Jacob McAndrews and Symone Whalin. They were defeated by the WGK ticket of Will Harris, Garrett Edmonds and Kenan Mujkanovic, with results announced at SGA's election night, reported by the Herald on 17 April 2019.

Andrew Merritt was elected one of eleven at-large senators in WKU SGA's spring 2018 election, among the winners the Herald named on 18 April 2018. The new Seventeenth Senate confirmed him as Secretary of the Senate by a 14-2 vote at its first meeting on 4 September 2018; introducing himself, he said he "likes organization." In the role he circulated the Senate's constitution and bylaws to new members and coordinated senators' weekly office hours.

McAndrews was an associate justice on the Judicial Council in 2017-18 and took part in the council's January 2018 debate over whether the director of public relations had a constitutional duty to advertise a fall referendum. He argued it was "a little bit of a stretch" to read a referendum as one of the meetings, activities or programs a separate clause required the director to publicize, and separately that a clause on advertising filing dates read as written for senator and executive elections rather than referendums. In April 2018 the Senate elected him to succeed Annalicia Carlson as chief justice for 2018-19. As chief justice he ran orientation sessions on the council for incoming senators in September 2018, swore in the year's new senators and asked that any legislation touching the constitution or bylaws be routed through him first. In March 2019 he presented that spring's election codes to the Senate, then announced his resignation as chief justice in order to run for an elected office; the Senate confirmed Isaac Keller as his successor the following month. Days later, by then a former chief justice, he co-authored with senators Mark Clark, Kara Lowry and Connor Hounshell a resolution supporting administrative transparency after the sudden resignation of a Potter College dean.

Lane Hedrick, recorded on SGA's own site as "Katherine (Lane) Hedrick," served as an Associate Justice on the Judicial Council in 2016-17. SGA's judicial page listed her as Acting Chief Justice after its 17 April 2019 revision.

holdings.what_they_did: Carlson was chief justice in 2017-18 and an associate justice in 2018-19. In January 2018 she took the council into the dispute over whether the fall referendum had been properly advertised. In April 2018 the council she chaired disqualified the Mayer-Edmonds-Anderson ticket and a senate candidate over a Pepe the Frog image used in campaign chalking and suspended a third campaign under the election codes; she gave the Herald the minutes and rejected the suggestion that the meeting had been secret, and the council reversed the disqualification the following day. In April 2019 she opposed a presidential nomination to the council, saying another applicant was the better candidate, and the senate rejected it 17-11. In May 2019 an impeachment petition was brought against her over how candidates' names were listed on the spring ballot; she said the legal names had been used for a grade point check, and the hearing was cancelled for want of senators.

Townsend was elected a senator-at-large in the September 2016 fall elections and was re-elected to the Senate the following year. In April 2017 she authored a resolution, passed unanimously, calling for more centrally located and better-stocked vegetarian and vegan food options on WKU's dining campus, arguing existing options like Freshens and Burrito Bowl were poorly located or had limited hours. As SAVES chair she authored Bill 8-18-F, allocating $150 to SGA's student ID voucher program, which passed the same October 2018 meeting the Senate postponed a more contentious bill barring SGA funding to Greek organizations.

Harris won the student body presidency in April 2019 at the head of the WGK ticket with Garrett Edmonds and Kenan Mujkanovic, defeating Asha McWilliams. After the results were announced at SGA's election party, he said he looked forward to "making a positive impact for all students here at WKU" and to collaborating with the opposing ticket. He took office at SGA's annual banquet and presided over his first meeting the following Tuesday. The defining controversy of his fall semester was Resolution 4-19-F, the senate's push to punish Alpha Xi Delta after a video showed members singing a racial slur. Harris abstained when his executive board vetoed the resolution 4-0, explaining that the discrimination claim would have to come from the Student Code of Conduct and that no violation had been noted by the Office of Student Conduct. When senators suggested his position as a knight of Alpha Xi Delta motivated him, he rejected the charge and said he wanted to reach an amicable outcome with the resolution's authors.

holdings.what_they_did: Signed as J. Garrett Edmonds on legislation. Kenan Mujkanovic ran for student body president twice before winning executive office. In April 2017 the Judicial Council granted him a constitutional exemption to run despite less than a semester's service, and he finished second behind Andi Dahmer with 305 of the 1,579 votes cast, ahead of Lily Nellans's 212. In April 2018 his campaign was suspended for an election-code violation and he finished third, taking 32 percent of the vote in the three-way race Stephen Mayer won. In April 2019 he ran a third time, now for administrative vice president on the WGK ticket with Will Harris and Garrett Edmonds, and won, defeating Symone Whalin. As administrative vice president in 2019-20 he prepared and presented the year's budget, dropping the athletic-marketing sponsorship and reallocating the money, then joined the executive team in pulling the bill after the Senate amended it. He authored the year's organizational-aid bills and Bill 5-19-F, which continued a study-away scholarship partnership running since 2011 with $1,500 for 2019-20.

Aubrey Kelley served two years in the SGA executive branch, as director of academic and student affairs in 2018-19 and as chief of staff in 2019-20. She reached the first post in September 2018 only on the third attempt: the Senate confirmed her 24-3-4 after the initial nominee withdrew and a second nominee failed confirmation 6-9-1. As director she presented Bill 29-19-S in April 2019, which funded 53 SGA scholarships in a single bill — 27 summer-term awards, 18 study-abroad awards and eight first-generation awards. Confirmed chief of staff 16-1 at the first meeting of 2019-20, she sat on the university academic committee reviewing course fees and told the Senate that fees predating 2010 had to be resubmitted. The 2018-19 minutes spell her surname both ways — Kelly at her nomination and Kelley afterward — and the SGA website and the 2019-20 minutes give Kelley.

At the senator-confirmation meeting of 25 February 2020, when Senator Anthony Survance questioned nominee Parker Raybourne over his membership in WKU College Republicans, Terrell cut the line of questioning off, saying SGA was nonpartisan; five senators and two committee chairs were confirmed that night.

Mathews was confirmed to the Senate as parliamentarian on a 12-0-3 vote on 10 September 2019. The Speaker tried to move her to Secretary of the Senate on 1 October, but withdrew the attempt after a constitutional challenge from the floor; she was recorded as Secretary of the Senate from November 2019 onward regardless, a post she still held when the Senate moved its meetings onto Zoom in the spring 2020 COVID shutdown, and again for the opening weeks of 2020-21. As a senator, no longer secretary, she told the Senate in November 2020 that WKU's refusal to reinstate Pass/D/Fail grading left students choosing between attending an in-person semester or paying for an extra one out of pocket. She returned to the secretary's post in February 2021, and that March told the Senate the chamber would follow parliamentary procedure more strictly to clear its legislative agenda and budget by early April.

Herlick was one of four nominees Student Body President Will Harris brought before the Senate on 24 September 2019 to fill out the Judicial Council, alongside Derek Collins, Turner Reynolds and Holden Schroeder. A freshman with a background in the Kentucky Youth Association and the Kentucky United Nations Assembly, he told senators he formed his own opinion before being swayed by fellow justices and confirmed he had read SGA's constitution and rules; the Senate confirmed him unanimously. He remained on the council into 2021-22, when he was a listed author, with Chief Justice Holden Schroeder, of Bill 17-22-S adopting the Judicial Council's General Procedural Rules.

Reynolds was one of four nominees Student Body President Will Harris brought before the Senate on 24 September 2019 to fill out the Judicial Council, alongside Jason Herlick, Derek Collins and Holden Schroeder. A communications and media double major who was Panhellenic Delegate for Alpha Omicron Pi and said she planned to make the council her focus once she left that post, she was asked by Senator Symone Whalin how she would guard against bias toward Greek students; Reynolds cited her experience on the Honors Committee Board and Hall Council representing students outside Greek life. She was confirmed 10-2, the only one of the four nominees not seated unanimously.

Zaczek was confirmed as chair of SGA's Legislative Research Committee in the first meeting of the 2019-20 year, on 3 September 2019, and for the term's first month was the Senate's only confirmed committee chair, which led him to insist that his own sponsorship of a bill and his committee's approval of it be treated as separate steps and that all legislation clear his committee before a first reading. He was a persistent skeptic of executive spending plans that fall. During a September 2019 budget standoff over whether to fund scholarships or a special-projects fund for sand volleyball and hammock space in the new First Year Village, Zaczek argued the recreational spending did little more for student engagement than students already got from picnicking or playing frisbee, and the following week warned that halving campaign spending caps could shut low-income students out of running for office. When the hammock bill returned in March 2020, he pressed the executive board for a full accounting of how the money would be spent before he would vote for it, saying he wanted to know the funds were being used "in an all-inclusive way." On legislation, Zaczek proposed an amendment during February 2019 debate on a study-abroad-scholarship bill, and after it was pulled and rewritten by its authors he remained critical of the revised version, saying it was "detracting from a merit-based scholarship" and questioning how SGA could verify applicants' answers. In October 2019 the Senate struck "removal from campus" from the title of a resolution seeking penalties against a sorority chapter over members' use of a racial slur in a video; Zaczek's friendly amendment put "suspension from Greek affairs" in its place, and the resolution passed 24-7.

Seconded the President's first nomination of the year, co-authored Bill 3-20-S allocating the $5,000 special projects fund to hammock areas, and asked during the April 2020 emergency-clause debate what would happen to cabinet members who were graduating.

Stakelum was confirmed chair of the Public Relations committee at the 15 October 2019 meeting that also seated Matt Barr at Campus Improvements and Hope Wells at SAVES. She was one of seven senators who co-authored Bill 6-19-F, funding for WKU's WiSE, Jump Rope Club, HonorsToppers and Queer Student Union organizations, which had its first and second readings in mid-November 2019. During the Senate's 22 October 2019 debate over Resolution 4-19-F, which sought Alpha Xi Delta's suspension from Greek affairs after chapter members sang a racial slur in a song posted online, Stakelum said removing the sorority "would [not] solve the racial problems on campus"; the resolution passed 24-7 regardless. The executive board vetoed it 4-0 the following week, and the Senate confirmed the veto rather than overriding it. Defending that outcome, Stakelum argued that letting SGA strip an organization's funding on these grounds "could cause problems for us in the future," while saying she still believed those responsible for the video should be punished. She worked with Director of Public Relations Ashlynn Evans to keep SGA's social media running through the spring 2020 COVID shutdown and compiled a list of student resources for the website, and she spoke in favor of the Senate's emergency-clause bill that April.

As a senator in 2018-19, Whalin ran for administrative vice president on a ticket with presidential candidate Asha McWilliams and Jacob McAndrews in the spring 2019 election; the ticket lost, with Kenan Mujkanovic defeating her for the AVP seat. That February she co-authored, with Kara Lowry and Conner Hounshell, Resolution 1-19-S calling for the relocation of a campus marker identifying Bowling Green as the Confederate capital of Kentucky; it passed 29-1 and moved the marker into a Kentucky Museum display rather than removing it. In autumn 2019, by then Diversity and Inclusion committee chair, she and Senator Anthony Survance authored Resolution 4-19-F seeking Alpha Xi Delta's suspension from Greek affairs after chapter members sang a racial slur in a song posted online, and organized an October 2019 protest at Kappa Delta's Shenanigans philanthropy event to press the point after SGA voted to cancel that week's Senate meeting for the same event. "Their inaction just proved that students have to do action," she said of the university's response. On 22 October the Senate amended the resolution's title from "Removal from Campus" to "Suspension from Greek Affairs" and passed it 24-7; the executive board vetoed it 4-0 the following week, and the Senate confirmed the veto rather than overriding it, so Whalin and Survance had to draft a new resolution. She also secured a floor amendment raising the funding in a 2020 tampon-access bill from $1,176 to $1,300.

Edmonds, a senior from Island, Kentucky, spent his freshman year as chair of the Campus Improvements Committee, working with Vice President of Student Affairs Brian Kuster on projects including a campus safety walk, before winning election as executive vice president in April 2018 on a ticket with Harper Anderson and Stephen Mayer. He served two years as executive vice president under President Will Harris, pushing for a budget model geared toward campus amenities and recreational life and working to diversify Senate appointments with seats for underrepresented students. He ran for the presidency in fall 2020 on the Edmonds-Norvell ticket, after his original running mate for administrative vice president, Nathan Terrell, dropped out and was replaced by Abbey Norvell. The campaign centered on a pledge to create a Director of Outreach position to close the communication gap between campus organizations and SGA, and the Sept. 24 Herald town hall covered WKU's COVID-19 response and the summer's Black Lives Matter protests on campus. Voting ran Sept. 28-29 on TopNet; Edmonds defeated senator MJ Mayo, becoming SGA president and, since the two offices had merged by then, student regent on the WKU Board of Regents. Norvell was elected administrative vice president alongside him, with the Herald reporting no decision yet made on a separate executive vice president post. Taking office amid the pandemic, the senate confirmed Isaac Keller to a vice-president post 29-1 in October after Edmonds said he wanted a deputy willing to challenge him; the Herald's report on that vote first called the office executive vice president, then ran a correction changing it to administrative vice president -- the same title the Herald had given Norvell in September, a conflict the record does not resolve. Matt Barr, Ashlynn Evans, Kody Okert and Paul Brosky rounded out the executive and Shelby Robertson served as non-voting speaker of the senate. Early cabinet business set up officer office hours, an ad hoc outreach committee chaired by Me'Lon Craighead and a push toward inclusive pronoun language in Senate proceedings. That fall SGA petitioned WKU to restore Pass/D/Fail grading for COVID-disrupted students; Associate Provost Rob Hale initially rebuffed the request, calling the university's extended drop deadline sufficient, but by December the petition -- more than 3,500 signatures in three days -- had succeeded, and Edmonds thanked senators for the work behind it at the semester's final meeting alongside bills funding campus safe-driving signage and several student organizations. In the spring his senate passed the organization's largest-ever organizational aid bill and a resolution seeking a codified vetting process for campus dining vendors after a controversial social media post by a local pizzeria owner, alongside legislation backing WKU's Naming and Symbols Task Force in renaming buildings tied to racism, a community garden, and a diversity-event push by DEI chair Fatin Yaro. Near the end of his term he declined to fill the chief justice seat vacated by Erika Puhakka, saying the choice belonged to his successor: "I think that's the only thing that is right in this scenario." He also worried publicly that only 13 students were running for senate in the April election, and closed his term addressing the Class of 2021 at the delayed Fall 2020/Spring 2021 commencement, telling graduates their perseverance through "this past year" had brought them to their day of celebration.
Also student regent on the WKU Board of Regents.

Abbey Norvell served on the SGA executive branch for two years. Confirmed director of academic and student affairs in September 2019 — a former at-large senator who had sat on the Organizational Aid and Public Relations committees — she built the scholarship grading rubric and in November 2019 reported a record 398 scholarship applications. In 2020-21 she was elected on the Edmonds-Norvell ticket, which defeated MJ Mayo at a virtual election party in September 2020 after her running-mate slot opened when Nathan Terrell left the ticket. The Herald's election story called her administrative vice president and no decision had then been made on a separate executive vice president post; from October 2020 through March 2021 the Senate minutes headed her reports "Executive Vice President Abbey Norvell", with Isaac Keller confirmed administrative vice president that October. She sent out the Faculty Senate application form, tracked which senators sat on university committees, and appointed members to the Faculty Senate.

Isaac Keller came to the administrative vice presidency from the Judicial Council, where he had served two years and, as its longest-serving member, was confirmed chief justice 28-0 in April 2019. As chief justice in 2019-20 he ruled that a Senate majority is measured against those present rather than the full membership, told senators a resolution seeking to defund Alpha Xi Delta would be only symbolic because SGA cannot direct the university to defund an organization, and convened a cross-branch rewrite of the constitution. In 2020-21 President Garrett Edmonds nominated him administrative vice president, saying he wanted a deputy willing to challenge him, and the Senate confirmed Keller 29-1 in October 2020. The Herald first called the post executive vice president and ran a correction to administrative vice president — the same title given to Abbey Norvell in the election coverage — so the sources do not fully resolve the two vice-presidential titles for the year. He authored organizational-aid bills, among them one in February 2021 funding four student organizations and, in March 2021, what the Herald called the largest organizational aid bill SGA had passed.

Matt Barr chaired the Campus Improvements committee in 2018-19, where he authored the bill creating a recurring $2,000 scholarship for first-generation students, passed 31-1 in October 2018. In February 2020, as Campus Improvements chair, he defended a contested slate of senator nominees, saying committees exist to develop ideas together. He served as chief of staff in 2020-21, first on an interim basis under the outgoing cabinet in September 2020 and then confirmed that October. He ran the "Go With the Flow" programme, which put free menstrual-product dispensers across campus, reported the three hammock sites finished and new SGA signage and office computers installed over the winter break, and continued the programme into the spring semester.

Puhakka went on to become chief justice; she was in the post by March 2021, when she reported to the Senate that a constitutional review committee would meet in person and set the spring's constitutional-amendment and general election dates. Wininger ran for student body president in the April 2021 SGA election, with voting held on TopNet April 12-13. In the Herald's ballot guide he said he wanted to make SGA "the most active and vibrant organization on campus." Me'Lon Craighead, who would serve as his executive vice president, ran for that office in the same election. As president, Wininger opened the fall semester by welcoming new and returning senators to the second meeting of the 21st Senate. He presided over the unanimous confirmation of senators elected the previous semester and of his executive appointments, including Jamison Moorehead as IT director, Alexis Courtenay as public relations director and Parker Raybourne as chief of staff, and the senate adopted new election codes at the same meeting. In spring 2022 Wininger welcomed senators back from winter break and announced an initiative to create a student resource handbook aimed particularly at underclassmen, encouraging all SGA committees to pitch in on the project. At that same first meeting of 2022, the senate he led responded to the December tornado disaster by unanimously passing a $1,000 bill to restock the Office of Sustainability food pantry.

Me'Lon Craighead served as executive vice president of SGA for 2021-22, under President Matthew Wininger. At the meeting of 30 November 2021 she nominated Senator Nia Queen Douglas as an alternate restaurant-group committee representative, a nomination the Senate approved by unanimous consent. In February 2022 the Senate approved the creation of an iWKU app task force that Craighead had petitioned for, with Craighead to appoint its chair the following week. She was also the named contact officer on Bill 18-22-S, which funded the Diversity and Inclusion scholarship for the Mahurin Honors College membership fee.

Reed Breunig was administrative vice president of SGA for 2021-22. At the second meeting of the 21st Senate on 31 August 2021 he announced that the SGA budget would come up for a confirmation vote the following week. Holding the budget, he authored the year's organizational aid bills himself, Bill 2-22-S for $5,350 and Bill 10-22-S for $4,950, and reported the budget as updated at the last meeting of the 21st Senate on 19 April 2022.

Parker Raybourne was chief of staff of SGA for 2021-22. President Matthew Wininger appointed him at the second meeting of the 21st Senate on 31 August 2021, and the Senate confirmed him by unanimous consent, Chief Justice Holden Schroeder swearing him in with the rest of the cabinet nominees. He co-authored Bill 7-21-F, funding SGA polo shirts, with Speaker Tess Welch, and wrote Resolution 6-22-S asking for an SGA clause in course syllabi.
