Cole Bornefeld came to the presidency by an unusually fast route. He transferred to WKU from Volunteer State Community College as a junior, emailed then-President Matthew Wininger during his first week on campus, and was appointed a senator-at-large at their first meeting. He had not planned to run for president, but after senators urged him to, he formed a ticket the week of the filing deadline and won. He campaigned on programs he backed as a senator, including the Share-A-Swipe meal donation program and growing SGA's scholarship budget, which rose by $3,500 during his presidency. Adjusting to the office, he said it felt like "drinking out of a fire hose," and he sought advice from former student body presidents weekly. Bornefeld opened the 2022-23 year with an executive retreat on Aug. 29 at the Cliff Todd Center, where his team set three priorities: a one-stop resource guide for students, a push to represent WKU's five regional campuses, which he said was "an area that I really don't think SGA has ever touched," and financial assistance for students as the year's underlying goal. He had met with the director of regional campuses the week before to start that work. His spring semester was dominated by fallout from anti-LGBTQ Instagram posts he had liked. After the judicial council unanimously declined to censure him, the Queer Student Union removed SGA meetings from its list of campus safe spaces and said it would not associate with SGA until a public apology was released. Addressing the senate on Feb. 21, Bornefeld, who also served as student regent, said he "always commits to loving thy neighbor" but could not commit to always agreeing, tying his position to his Christian values and offering to meet any student over coffee or breakfast to discuss disagreements.

Garrison Reed was executive vice president of SGA for 2022-23, elected on Cole Bornefeld's ticket in the spring 2022 election alongside administrative vice president Sam Kurtz. He co-authored Bill 6-22-F amending the constitution and Bill 18-22-F funding the Gordon Ford and WKU career-fair scholarships. In September 2022 SGA announced that Reed had been appointed the student representative on Kentucky's Council on Postsecondary Education, a term set to end 30 June 2023.

Schroeder was one of four judiciary nominees Student Body President Will Harris brought before the Senate on 24 September 2019, along with Jason Herlick, Derek Collins and Turner Reynolds. He had been chief justice of Kentucky Boys State as a high school junior and was a prosecution attorney on WKU's mock trial B-team; the Senate confirmed him to the Judicial Council unanimously. By the start of the 2021-22 year he had become chief justice, swearing in senators and executive appointees at the Senate's first fall meeting on 31 August 2021 and bringing that semester's updated election codes to the floor. In April 2022 he read a statement from President Matthew Wininger during a Judicial Council hearing that cleared presidential candidate Cole Bornefeld of a self-promotion complaint over a student-wide email about the Swipe Out Hunger initiative. He wrote the council's General Procedural Rules and was lead author of Bill 17-22-S adopting them. He continued as chief justice into the 2022-23 year, walking new justices Isaac King and Garrett Baum through those rules at the council's 16 September 2022 meeting and swearing in that year's new senators and cabinet appointees on 30 August 2022. The Senate elected Justin Goins to succeed him as chief justice on 17 January 2023, and had filled his own vacated council seat by the 25th.

Sam Kurtz, then the outgoing administrative vice president, was elected student body president in results announced early on April 19, 2023 in the Downing Student Union senate chambers, after voting opened on TopNet on April 17. His KFL ticket, with Annalise Finch as executive vice president and Salvador León as administrative vice president, ran unopposed, and Chief Justice Justin Goins read the results. In a statement, Kurtz said the ticket would "listen to students' concerns, represent their voices, lead with integrity, and promote transparency." At the 23rd Senate's first fall meeting on Aug. 29, Kurtz nominated Ashley Ranger, Anna Kate Hardin, Ellen Henderson, Morgan Gammons and Garrison Reed to the Judicial Council from what he called a record number of applicants, and named seven committee heads, including Rush Robinson for Campus Improvements and Sustainability and Karley Solorzano for Diversity, Equity and Inclusion. The Senate's first bill of the year, passed unanimously that September, funded the SGA Pink Walk breast-cancer event. That November the senate backed moving DSU fire drills from 5 a.m. to 2 a.m. and funded a Boys and Girls Club toy drive. Speaker of the Senate Sydney Denney wrote or co-wrote several of the year's bills, including a resolution capping student parking fees at $50, a $700 fund to help students pay parking fines, and voucher funding for the Dental Hygiene Center and ID Center. In February 2024 Kurtz and Chief of Staff Donté Reed rolled out a 450-voucher Uber giveaway aimed at student safety and outreach, followed in March by a need-based scholarship awarding Uber vouchers and a Community Builder Excellence Scholarship for incoming Bowling Green-area freshmen; that month the senate also planned a Frankfort trip for the Rally for Higher Education. The year's fight was internal. In February 2024 the Judicial Council voted 6-0 to censure Administrative Vice President Salvador León after a hearing brought by Denney and the executive cabinet, which alleged León had spent SGA funds - including a $425.25 Preston Center deposit for Neurodiversity Acceptance Week - before the Senate passed the funding bill, in violation of the constitution's clause 2.5.3 requiring the administrative vice president to expend funds only as the Senate authorizes. Chief Justice Isaac King said the cabinet, excluding León, had asked for the censure after León spent the funds despite Kurtz's condition that he wait for Bill 22-23-F to pass, and after he pushed PR Director Preston Romanov to promote the week on SGA social media ahead of the vote, effectively forcing the Senate's hand. León countered that text messages showed Kurtz had signed off on the spending in advance; the council found the spending improper but recommended no discipline beyond the censure itself. In January 2024 Chief of Staff Lindsey Kelly and enrollment director Donte Reed both resigned, with Reed moving up to chief of staff. That April, Kurtz ran for a second term with Reed as his executive vice president candidate and junior senator Ethan Taylor for administrative vice president; the ticket again ran unopposed on a ballot of more than 60 legislative candidates, and the three were re-elected as the 24th Senate's 34 members were announced the night of April 16-17, 2024. Before that, SGA partnered with WKU Red Wave for a final Red Wave tailgate on April 9, with a student-DJ contest winner earning a $500 scholarship. The 23rd Senate held its last meeting on April 16 with no legislation on the agenda, and Kurtz thanked senators in his final report for what the group had accomplished that year.

Elected student body president in the spring 2023 election on an unopposed ticket with Salvador León as administrative vice president and Annalise Finch as executive vice president, the results being read out in the senate chambers in the early hours of 19 April 2023 by Chief Justice Justin Goins. Kurtz had been administrative vice president the year before.

Annalise Finch was executive vice president of SGA for 2023-24, elected on Sam Kurtz's ticket in the spring 2023 election, which ran unopposed, alongside administrative vice president Salvador Leon. In January 2024 she appointed two campus-committee heads, Jaden Marshall to the Graduate Advisory Council committee and Chloe Ralston to the Colonnade General Education committee, both approved by the Senate. She was elected a senior senator in the spring 2024 election, listed as Annie Finch.

Salvador Leon was administrative vice president of SGA for 2023-24, elected on Sam Kurtz's unopposed ticket in spring 2023. A "Salvador Leon Golib" had been elected international student senator in the fall 2022 election; the names appear to point to the same person, though the record does not confirm it. In February 2024 the executive cabinet filed a formal report to the Judicial Council seeking his censure, alleging that he had spent from the executive project and legislative discretionary budgets before Bill 22-23-S funding a Neurodiversity Acceptance Week had passed the Senate, that he had a promotional graphic posted before the bill passed, and that the premature spending forced the Senate's hand. The Judicial Council held a hearing on 7 February 2024 and unanimously voted to censure him, with no further disciplinary action.

She ran the ID and Preston Center voucher program and organized the SGA Christmas party held on 28 November 2023. President Sam Kurtz told the Senate on 23 January 2024 that she had stepped down.

holdings.what_they_did: Meghan Pierce served WKU SGA as a senior senator in 2021-22 and was elected the Potter College of Arts & Letters senator for 2022-23 in that April's election. That fall she authored or co-authored bills updating the SGA constitution and bylaws: correcting outdated references to the University Senate after it split into separate Faculty and Staff Senates, clarifying that the constitution provided only for impeachment and not for the Bylaws' separate expulsion process, and renaming the Committee of Enrollment and Student Experience. She also spoke in affirmation of Sophia Bryant's appointment as Student Mental Health and Well-Being Committee chair at the Senate's swearing-in meeting in January 2024.

holdings.what_they_did: Jaden Marshall served as a senator at large in SGA's 23rd Senate in 2023-24, co-authoring, with Administrative Vice President Salvador Leon and others, the bill funding Neurodiversity Acceptance Week. He returned to the Senate for 2024-25, reappointed to a senator-at-large seat and confirmed by unanimous voice vote on 11 February 2025, and again for 2025-26 as an ISEC senator (Intercultural Student Engagement Center), where he co-authored a bill funding the Go With the Flow menstrual-product program together with a WKU Food Pantry donation drive, a Black History Trivia Night held with Why Knot Us and Black Women of Western, graduation cords for transfer students, and resolutions supporting the installation of drinking-water dispensers, printers and computers in residence halls and an accessible 24-hour space on campus. In April 2026 Marshall ran for SGA president on a ticket with Kaden Blankenship and Miles VanRude, against Caden Lucas, Jakob Barker and Will Derryberry, taking questions at a town hall in the DSU auditorium. On 13 April 2026 the Judicial Council, acting on its own initiative rather than a complaint, found the Marshall ticket guilty 4-0 of breaching the election code's ban on distributing perishable food within 48 hours of an election, after Red Bull cans were handed out at their campaign table and photographed for their campaign's social media story; the council issued a formal censure but declined to remove the ticket from the ballot. Two days later, on 15 April 2026, the council found the same ticket guilty 5-0 on a separate, unrelated complaint of campaigning in the Commons while voting was open; it censured and disbanded the ticket's campaign team rather than issuing a second censure to the ticket itself. Lucas's ticket won the election, with turnout up 66 percent over the previous year's uncontested race. Marshall was sworn into a new role at the first meeting of the 26th Senate on 28 April 2026, alongside Gabby Pace, Cayden Bailey and Maggie Phelps.

Barton served as a Senior Senator in 2023-24 and continued as a Senator at Large in 2024-25. In February 2024 he was one of five co-authors — with Jaden Marshall, Joel Hornback, Kayla Distler and Salvador Leon — of Bill 4-24-S, funding a Neurodiversity Acceptance Week that ran 6 to 9 February. He and co-author Donte Reed then authored Bill 9-24-S, creating the Borrow-a-Calculator program letting students check out TI-84 calculators from the SGA office; they cited a survey finding 17 percent of students owned no calculator while 93 percent had taken a class requiring one, and the bill drew matching university funding for ten more calculators. In February 2025 he presented, alongside Alexandria Chumbley, the bill funding the Steven "Brent" Chumbley Student-Athlete Impact Scholarship, named for WKU's director of cross country and track and field, who had died weeks earlier; the Senate allocated $500 after Legislative Operations chair Caden Lucas resisted a motion to raise the figure to $1,000, calling it rash given what remained in the discretionary budget.

Bodemann served as a Senior Senator in the 23rd Senate, 2023-24. In November 2023 she was one of four co-authors — with Legislative Operations Committee chair Meghan Pierce, Hannah Evans and Joel Hornback — of two of the committee's bills correcting SGA's governing documents: Bill 8-23-F, rewriting the constitution's description of the Executive Vice President's power to make University Senate appointments, and Bill 9-23-F, reconciling the bylaws' language on committee-chair removal and senator expulsion with a constitution that provided only for impeachment. In March 2024 she was one of seven co-authors — with Ellen Henderson, Garrison Reed, Hannah Evans, Isaac King, Joel Hornback and Meghan Pierce — of the fourteen-bill constitutional amendment package, written after SGA anticipated university budget cuts. Thirteen of the fourteen bills passed the Senate and Executive Cabinet at the 28 March second reading, abolishing the directorships of information technology and enrollment and student experience, renaming the Executive Vice President and Administrative Vice President as Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, raising GPA floors for all three branches, requiring removal after a second censure in a year, and moving committee-head appointments to the Speaker.

holdings.what_they_did: Kurtz opened the 2024-25 year presiding over the 24th Senate, which passed SGA's $100,000 budget at its first meeting on Aug. 27. Sitting down with the Herald editorial board alongside his executive cabinet, he described SGA as "a vessel for good" and a group of 45 to 50 people advocating for students, and credited President Caboni with keeping the budget untouched for several years. Through the spring he presided over a run of student-welfare legislation, including the Gordon Wilson Hall elevator resolution and a resolution seeking 24/7 library hours during finals week. In February he announced a POLLapalooza push to raise election participation, telling the Senate, "My goal is that 3,000 students vote in our election." Kurtz closed his term at the 24th Senate's final meeting on April 15, having served as student body president for two years and holding executive branch positions for most of his college career, and prepared to graduate at the end of the semester. He received a standing ovation after his last report, and his parting words to senators were "Please be for the students."
Re-elected without opposition to a second term.

Donte Reed was executive vice president of SGA for 2024-25, elected on Sam Kurtz's ticket in the spring 2024 election announced just after midnight on 17 April 2024, alongside administrative vice president Ethan Taylor. In August 2024 he sat down with the Herald editorial board with the rest of the cabinet, saying SGA tried to use its roughly $100,000 budget in full to help as many students as possible.

Ethan Taylor co-authored Bill 17-22-F, funding the Midnight on the Hill student organization, as a sophomore senator; the Senate passed it 28-0 on 8 November 2022. He ran for administrative vice president in the spring 2024 general election on a ticket with Sam Kurtz for student body president and Donté Reed for executive vice president, and all three ran unopposed. At an Executive Town Hall on 11 April 2024, Chief Justice Isaac King questioned the unopposed candidates about their plans; Kurtz said the ticket intended to create more voucher programs and keep grilling at SGA events for food-insecure students. As chief financial officer for 2024-25, Taylor's $100,000 budget was approved unanimously by the 24th Senate at its first meeting on 27 August 2024; it raised legislative discretionary and office-worker spending and cut public relations spending. He, President Kurtz and Vice President Reed each received a standing ovation at the 24th Senate's final meeting on 15 April 2025.

As a junior senator, Anne-Marie Wright co-wrote Bill 1-23-F with Donté Reed and Rush Robinson, funding the SGA Pink Walk breast cancer awareness event; it was the 23rd Senate's first piece of legislation, passing 28-0 on 20 September 2023. She was appointed chief of staff at the 24th Senate's first meeting on 23 April 2024, sworn in by outgoing Chief Justice Isaac King alongside newly elected Speaker Sarah Vincent and Chief Justice Ellen Henderson. On 3 September 2024 Wright told the Senate the Borrow-a-Calculator programme had started, a partnership with the Center for Innovative Teaching and Learning, the Department of Mathematics and Ogden College letting students borrow a graphing calculator free for a week on presentation of a student ID.

Appointed over the summer of 2024 on what Chief of Staff Wright described to the Senate as President Kurtz's executive decision, and welcomed at the first meeting of the year on 27 August 2024. He handled the fall election and Uber voucher graphics and the senators' t-shirt orders. He was reappointed in April 2025 and served a second year.

Sarah Vincent, a College of Health and Human Services senator, was elected Speaker of the Senate over Sophia Bryant at the first meeting of the 24th Senate on 23 April 2024, when the newly elected senators were sworn in and Ellen Henderson was named chief justice. A year later, at the first meeting of the 25th Senate on 22 April 2025, Vincent, by then the outgoing speaker, swore in the new Senate after Hadley Whipple was elected to succeed her.

holdings.what_they_did: Chief Justice Isaac King nominated Henderson associate chief justice at the Senate's 5 September 2023 meeting; she told senators she was honored by the nomination and excited to be more involved in SGA, and was confirmed by unanimous voice vote. At the 24th Senate's first meeting on 23 April 2024, the outgoing King swore Henderson in as chief justice, alongside newly elected Speaker Sarah Vincent and Chief of Staff Anne-Marie Wright. She continued in the role into the fall, swearing in the winners of the October 2024 senate election at the 1 October meeting, where the Senate also passed a bill requiring school safety training for WKU professors. On 19 November 2024, ahead of her graduation, Henderson swore in Associate Chief Justice Morgan Gammons as her successor.

Morgan Gammons was one of five students — with Ashley Ranger, Anna Kate Hardin, Ellen Henderson and Garrison Reed — nominated by President Sam Kurtz to the 2023-24 Judicial Council out of what Kurtz called a record field of applicants. She was serving as chief justice by SGA's 4 February 2025 senate meeting, though Herald coverage does not pin the exact date of her succession. That April she co-authored Bill 21-25-S, which restructured SGA's Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Committee into the Action and Opportunity Committee and renamed Chief Diversity Officers to Chief Engagement and Opportunity Officers, telling the Herald the change followed President Trump's February 2025 executive order dismantling federal DEI mandates. She called the renaming "mostly a formality" and declined to say how it would affect WKU students, though she said the possibility of losing federal funding over resistance to the shift had been alluded to. The bill needed a two-thirds senate vote to pass as a constitutional amendment; when that week's meeting fell short of the 21 members required, absent senators were called in over Zoom so the vote could proceed, and it passed unanimously before going to a student referendum.

The secretaryship was recorded vacant at the first meeting on 27 August 2024, Speaker Vincent asking anyone interested to text her. Whipple, confirmed as Ogden College senator at that same meeting, held the post by March 2025 and was elected Speaker of the 25th Senate the following month.

Robinson, a senior from Benton, Kentucky triple-majoring in psychology, philosophy and sociology and a member of Sigma Phi Epsilon and Omicron Delta Kappa, won the SGA presidency in the 13-15 April 2025 general election on a turnout of 966, running with Savanna Kurtz for vice president and Gabriel Jerdon for chief financial officer. He also succeeded Sam Kurtz as WKU's student regent; the Board of Regents administered his oath of office on 8 August 2025, the same meeting at which it named the new Gordon Ford College of Business building Amy and David Chandler Hall and elected Jan West chair, Doris Thomas vice chair and Melissa Dennison secretary for 2025-26. Robinson ran on turning SGA away from national politics and toward direct student advocacy, saying the organization had sometimes echoed national political talking points and that he wanted it to act as "an advocate and resource for students" who could be pointed to the right contact in the administration. His cabinet - Kurtz as vice president, Jerdon as chief financial officer, Maggie Yelton as chief of staff, and Preston Jenkins, reappointed chief communications officer on 22 April 2025 and confirmed by the Senate - ran a legislative program heavy on small, direct-benefit measures: vouchers for CPR certification, dental cleanings, transcripts and identification cards, equipment to borrow such as umbrellas, calculators and hammocks, and a resolution urging accessible restroom stalls in Grise Hall. Jenkins also organized a student-painted mural for a column in the SGA chambers. In March 2026 SGA drew on its projects fund to host a baseball-game tailgate, a response to Athletics Director Todd Stewart's call for more student engagement. The Senate closed its final meeting on 14 April 2026 having passed 56 bills for the year, the most since 2018-19, with Jenkins also reporting that a new university Artificial Intelligence Committee was weighing bulk AI-product subscriptions for students. Robinson's most sustained policy push was on student mental health, working with Mental Health and Wellbeing Committee chair Veronica Butler on a year-long program backed by data from social work professor Jay Gabbard, who told SGA that 44 percent of WKU students reported depression symptoms and 10 percent had considered suicide in the past year. SGA co-organized Mental Health Week with the WKU Counseling Center and the campus NAMI chapter, ran a Toppers Talk About It awareness campaign, and had student recommendations - including relocating counseling services from Potter Hall to the Downing Student Union - reviewed by the Counseling Center Review Committee before forwarding them to administrators, though Butler said it was unclear whether they would be enacted. The push closed with an Out of Darkness suicide-remembrance walk on 18 April 2026, and successor Caden Lucas said the focus would continue "in a sustained and meaningful way." At the Senate's first meeting under his successor, Robinson opened by telling the mostly-new chamber they looked untainted by SGA's usual troubles, then handed president-elect Caden Lucas the red suit jacket passed president to president - the same jacket Sam Kurtz had given him the year before. His term as student regent outlasted his SGA presidency: at the Board of Regents' 5 June 2026 meeting, his last as regent, he cast the lone vote against a $204, 1.69 percent tuition increase, saying the board had "to do whatever we can to not raise the tuition" to preserve affordability. Afterward he planned to remain at WKU for an Ed.S. in school psychology, aiming for a career as a school psychologist in a school district.
Also student regent on the WKU Board of Regents.

Savanna Kurtz was elected a freshman senator in SGA's fall 2023 election, announced 20 September over an Instagram livestream and sworn in the following Tuesday. The Senate confirmed her as chair of the Student Experience and Enrollment Committee at the 24th Senate's fall opening meeting on 27 August 2024. That November she wrote Bill 20-24-F, funding a two-week toy drive with Student Activities for the Boys and Girls Club of Bowling Green with an extra $200 for toys, building on committee work she had done on the same drive the previous year. Kurtz was elected student body vice president unopposed on Rush Robinson's ticket with Chief Financial Officer Gabriel Jerdon in the spring 2025 general election, the same election in which 88% of students voted to rename the DEI Committee the Action and Opportunity Committee. As vice president she authored Bill 9-25-F, funding the 2025-26 SGA Pink Walk, which the Senate passed on 9 October 2025. At the 26th Senate's first meeting on 28 April 2026, as outgoing vice president, she reported that every scholarship offered in 2025-26 had been awarded and introduced two of the fifteen recipients of the Blue Grass Community Foundation Scholarship.

Gabriel Jerdon was elected chief financial officer on Rush Robinson's ticket, unopposed, alongside Vice President Savanna Kurtz, in the spring 2025 general election. As CFO he authored the Senate's fall organizational-aid appropriations bill, 10-25-F, which passed 16 October 2025; he told the Senate 78 organizations had applied, that groups could receive up to $500 a year and $250 a semester, and that the lowest-graded organizations would still get a $50 minimum, and the same meeting struck a separate bill that would have funded food pantries. In a February 2026 budget update, Jerdon reported SGA had written more bills that fall than in previous years but had not reached half its semester budget, spending $4,573.73, and told senators not to be afraid to ask for a large amount if the legislation was worth it. In March 2026 he reported organizational aid split among 33 registered student organizations; the Herald later corrected the story to renumber the bill and revise the funding figure to $580. In April 2026, as the discretionary fund neared zero, he said $71.17 would remain if the final week's bills passed as written. At the 26th Senate's first meeting on 28 April 2026, as outgoing chief financial officer, he reported $100 of organizational aid held in reserve and every other account, including office supplies, plaques and the year-end banquet, zeroed out.

President Rush Robinson appointed Maggie Yelton chief of staff at the 25th Senate's first meeting on 23 April 2025, alongside senator-at-large Amelia Tucker; former Speaker Sarah Vincent swore in the new Senate. Yelton told the Herald's editorial board on 11 September 2025 that a new Swipe It Forward programme, sponsored by the WKU Restaurant Group, would let students donate up to three meal swipes a semester from their meal plans, redeemable at the Fresh Food Company by students who requested them through a food-assistance form; President Robinson said he expected it to appear on the iWKU app within a couple of weeks. At the Senate's 17 February 2026 meeting, which passed a bill funding CPR-certification vouchers, Yelton reported seven dental, one ID and thirteen transcript vouchers still available in the voucher program.

President Rush Robinson reappointed him to the post on 22 April 2025, one of his first acts in office, and the Senate confirmed the reappointment unanimously; Jenkins kept the post through the 25th Senate's opening on 23 April 2025. In August 2025 Jenkins announced a plan to have four student artists each paint one side of a column in the SGA chambers, incorporating WKU campus elements, with entries due by 19 September. At the 25th Senate's final meeting on 14 April 2026, he reported that WKU's new Artificial Intelligence Committee, on which he sat, was in early talks about bulk subscriptions to AI products for students and a possible introductory AI course for freshmen; the Senate closed the year having passed 56 bills, the most since 2018-19.

Hadley Whipple was confirmed as the senate's Ogden College senator at SGA's first meeting of 2024-25 on 27 August 2024, the same meeting at which the secretary's post was announced vacant. She held the secretaryship by March 2025, and the following month the 25th Senate elected her Speaker over fellow nominees Caden Lucas and Sophia Bryant. "Since the day I came in, I knew I wanted to run for speaker," she said, adding that being the voice of the senate mattered to her and that she wanted to be approachable. As speaker into spring 2026 she chaired the senate's final meetings of the term, at one point urging senators running low on discretionary funds to be choosy and respectful about what they passed as bills competed for the last dollars. A graduating senior, she was succeeded as speaker after the senate's 28 April 2026 meeting, when it elected Veronica Butler to follow her.

Karlee Powell, a Gordon Ford College of Business ambassador, was elected Secretary of the Senate at the 25th Senate's first meeting on Aug. 19, 2025. She told the Herald she had joined SGA because friends were already members, and that she would have regretted leaving WKU without joining. She said she hoped to bring "fresh ideas and a new perspective" and to represent every student in the room. As secretary Powell also continued to author legislation from the floor: Bill 11-25-F, passed to fund $76.89 in chalk and fidget toys for the Senate's "Toppers Talk About It" Mental Health Awareness Week tabling in November 2025, and Bill 5-26-S, passed to fund $492.98 for an SGA International Women's Day tabling event in March 2026. At the Feb. 17, 2026 meeting she was one of three senators who spoke in favor of a bill creating CPR-certification vouchers for students, which passed unanimously.

Blake Graham served as chief justice of the Judicial Council for the 2025-26 Student Government Association, one of seven officers on President Rush Robinson's executive board when it met on 12 August 2025. At that meeting he reported five pending appointments to the Judicial Council to be sworn in at the Senate's first or second meeting, set 2 and 3 September as the dates for that fall's election code meetings with candidate packets due by 9 p.m. on the 3rd, and said the minimum GPA required of an SGA candidate had been lowered to 2.0. He did not finish the year in the office. The Judicial Council met on 12 November 2025 to choose a successor and elected Associate Justice Sophie Stirling 3-1 over Associate Justice Xavier Spiess; the Herald reported that Stirling would be sworn in at the SGA meeting of 18 November, the same meeting at which Graham stepped down.

holdings.what_they_did: Sophie Stirling was an associate justice on the Judicial Council under Chief Justice Blake Graham in the fall of 2025. Lucas entered SGA in September 2024 as its inaugural student senator for the Mahurin Honors College, a seat created as the college began a program revision; he was also an Honors Teaching Fellow for HON 251, working with first-year Honors students on civic engagement. A junior senator, WKU Spiritmaster, chairman of the Hilltoppers Vote Coalition and an employee of Bowling Green's Downtown Development Division, he won the SGA presidential election on April 15, 2026, with running mates Jakob Barker for vice president and Will Derryberry for chief financial officer. Running under the motto "Lead, build, deliver," his campaign centered on increasing awareness of SGA operations and outreach to the student body, and he defeated Jaden Marshall, who had sought to become the first Black male student body president. After the results were announced Lucas said he felt "electric" and that the "work starts tomorrow," beginning with thank-you cards to supporters. Lucas took office at the first meeting of the 26th Senate on April 28, 2026, where outgoing president Rush Robinson presented him with the traditional red suit jacket passed from president to president. Lucas thanked the new cabinet, nominated his defeated campaign opponent Jaden Marshall as an at-large senator, calling his campus work "phenomenal," and saw Gabi Pace and Cayden Bailey sworn in as chief of staff and chief communications officer. The meeting's speaker election deadlocked 9-9 between Amelia Tucker and Veronica Butler, a situation the governing documents did not address, and Butler won the seat in a re-vote. Days after taking office, Lucas was named a 2026 Truman Scholar, WKU's second in the award's history and Kentucky's only recipient that year, chosen from 781 candidates nationally; the scholarship funds $30,000 toward graduate or professional study for students committed to public service. A political science, legal studies and strategic communications major, he had spent that summer establishing the Civic Engagement Resource Center, a joint Mahurin Honors College, SGA and Housing and Residence Life initiative that opened 30 October 2024 with a lending collection on civic life, saying his goal was to get students "talking about what it means to be a good citizen." In May, WKU's Omicron Delta Kappa circle named him its Heather Strode Circle Leader of the Year, an award recognizing collaboration, inclusivity, integrity, scholarship and service. Before he was sworn in as student regent, Lucas told the Herald he was "generally concerned" by a proposed $210 tuition increase; the Board of Regents approved a $204 increase days later, with outgoing regent Rush Robinson casting the only dissenting vote before handing the seat to Lucas. After the results were announced Lucas said he felt "electric" and that the "work starts tomorrow," beginning with thank-you cards to supporters.
Also student regent on the WKU Board of Regents.

Jakob Barker served as a WKU SGA senator, first as a freshman and then as a sophomore, and chaired the Student Experience Committee, where he reworked its scholarship grading process and expanded the Bluegrass Leadership Scholarship to applicants from Tennessee. As a sophomore senator for 2025-26 he sponsored funding for an SGA "Meet n Greet" and resolutions on campus safety and a student experience survey. In April 2026 Barker ran for student body vice president on Caden Lucas's presidential ticket, with Will Derryberry for chief financial officer. At an executive-candidates town hall that month he said he planned to move scholarship applications from paper to digital and, as WKU transitioned from the Student Life Foundation to a public-private housing partnership, argued students still needed representation in decisions about it. The Lucas ticket won the election announced 15 April 2026, and Barker succeeded outgoing vice president Savanna Kurtz. At the new Senate's first meeting on 28 April 2026, Barker reflected on rising from a freshman senator to the vice presidency in two years; two years earlier, he said, he "didn't really know what was in store for me."

Will Derryberry, a sophomore senator, ran as chief financial officer on Caden Lucas's "Lead, build, deliver" ticket, which won the SGA presidential election on 15 April 2026 against a ticket headed by Jaden Marshall. He said he had never expected to hold the position when he first came to WKU, and that he did not plan to lower the executive branch's stipends. He took office after the senate's swearing-in of the new administration on 28 April 2026.

Gabi Pace was elected the Potter College of Arts and Letters senator in SGA's April 2026 election. At the senate's first meeting of the new term on 28 April 2026, she was sworn in as chief of staff to President Caden Lucas; the Herald's report of that meeting rendered her name as "Gabby Pace" in that instance, a spelling discrepancy unresolved in this record.

Working with outgoing President Rush Robinson, she helped build a year-long slate of mental health programming, including SGA-sponsored Mental Health Week events, and told the Herald that knowing when to seek help had been one of her own biggest struggles, and that much of it came down to whether students felt able to use the resources available and found them accessible. Called 'Mandy Coates'/'Mandy Coats' in weekly council reports, 'Amanda Coates' in special-order and award text; held the seat all year, gave a special-order speech on InfoRed (2 Mar 1999), and ran for President in spring 1999 on a 'Coates/Martin' ticket per the 6 April primary results. Contemporaneous records give her name as Amanda J. Coates. The SGA's own 2001 list of presidents records Amanda J. Coates of Brownsville as the 33rd president, serving 1999-2000, and marks her as having also served as student regent. The organization's website during and just after her term consistently refers to "President Amanda Coates." She won the presidency in a contested April 1999 race against Will Jones, in results so close the Coates-Martin ticket demanded a recount: the initial 616-611 tally over Jones and running mate Kara Yeckering narrowed to 614-611 on the recount. A write-in ticket, Dwight Campbell and Kerri Richardson, took 145 votes. The same election saw a bitter down-ballot fight for vice president of finance, where Joe Matheis beat Ryan Morrison 700-688 only after SGA's judicial council reviewed - and let stand - his victory over a campaign-flier violation, and a Herald letter to the editor questioned SGA's handling of an investigation into racially charged fliers that had targeted Jones, the first Black SGA presidential candidate in years. The Herald's pre-election issue had separately reported SGA questioning an election-eve pizza party Jones held, and a debate over dropping the rule requiring a year of SGA service before running for office. Her signature project was publishing faculty evaluations. From February 2000 she led meetings with the university president, the Faculty Senate chair and the senate's executive committee, and in April she co-authored Resolution 00-2-S with Adam Howard asking the Faculty Senate to approve a mandatory published evaluation beginning that fall. At the end of her term the SGA website opened with the words "What SGA has done for you," showcasing three things: the faculty evaluations project, the fight over the Vice President of Student Affairs position and the Provide-A-Ride service. It is as close to a self-written record of her administration's priorities as survives. As her term closed, the Herald ran an exit interview, "Amanda Coates Reflects on Year as President," in its April 25, 2000 issue. The election to succeed her, held in late March 2000, was contested between Cassie Martin and Duan Wright; Martin won, and by the following issue the Herald was asking the incoming president to "stand up on tough issues" while confirming that the faculty evaluations Coates had championed would be conducted and published starting that fall. The Herald introduced the incoming 1999-2000 president on April 22, 1999 under the headline 'New Student Government Association Leader Workaholic.' The paper's index records the new leader's name as Amanda Coates, and she took office in the aftermath of a spring election that SGA's Judicial Council had overturned two days earlier. Her congress spent the fall of 1999 building institutions: it created an Information Technology Director and website guidelines, established a senior awards banquet and hall of distinguished seniors, launched the toll-free Topline activity line, and publicly opposed an administrative move in Student Affairs while asking that Vice President Jerry Wilder be retained. Her public service continued past her SGA year at the state level. Kentucky's Council on Postsecondary Education carries a statewide student member, and the council's minutes of 13 November 2000 record a district judge swearing her in, introducing her as Amanda Coates, a graduate of Western Kentucky University then studying public policy at the University of Kentucky. The council's minutes of 30 July 2001 record Governor Paul Patton appointing Christopher J. Pace to replace the outgoing student member, named there as "Amanda Coates Lich." Those two records together are what tie the Coates who led WKU's SGA in 1999-2000 to the surname the SGA Chambers plaque uses for the same year. Won a recount, 614-611, over Will Jones and running mate Kara Yeckering.
people.sources: Herald 74:51, 15 Apr 1999; SGA Meeting Minutes, March 2, 1999; WKU SGA, Presidents 1966-Present (archived 2001)

people.all_offices: president (1989-90); Public Relations Vice-President (1988-89); Judicial Council Chairman (1990-91)
people.what_they_did: Amos Gott served as public relations vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1988-89. He announced the Vote America registration drive for Downing University Center on 4, 5 and 6 October 1988, and an ASG hotline running every Wednesday afternoon from 1 to 4, which he told Congress on 25 October would open the next day. He also wrote pieces for the Herald that year explaining the organization to students, including "Understand Associated Student Government" that November. He ran for the ASG presidency the following spring and won, taking office for 1989-90. Gott was a visible member before he was president, signing Herald letters on ASG's behalf, including a January 1989 piece promoting Campus Pride '89 and an earlier letter urging readers to understand the organization. He won the presidency in April 1989, edging Lynn Groemling in a race that had drawn candidate complaints about the brief primary. His presidency ran on correspondence: resolutions went out over his signature as memoranda to named administrators and answers came back. In spring 1990 he wrote to six administrators under Resolution 90-6-S seeking changes to the final exam schedule, part of a surviving file that also covers extended library hours, the Downing University Center flagpole, mace sales at the bookstore, AIDS education and larger diplomas. Gott was already writing on Associated Student Government's behalf before he led it, signing a January 1989 Herald piece promoting Campus Pride '89. That spring he ran for president, survived a primary that several candidates complained had been too brief, and then edged Lynn Groemling in the runoff to take the office for 1989-90. He started early. The Herald's second issue of the fall reported that Gott had gotten a jump on the ASG semester, running alongside a piece urging students to participate. The fall that followed was busy and money was tight: the paper reported ASG's budget was tiny compared with other schools, the congress approved a new statewide board before admitting it could not afford the dues, and it spent the semester picking up and putting down a proposed Public Interest Research Group. Gott opened the spring with a Herald letter asking students to become involved, and by February he was defending an Anti-Apathy Week in print after it drew criticism. The rest of his spring ran through the congress: opening Pearce-Ford Tower's windows, more parking on the lower end of campus, a revised WKU Glasgow constitution, and a vote to expand the congress so classes and student groups had more voice. He handed off to Michael Colvin in April 1990. After his term as ASG president ended in 1990, Amos Gott returned to Congress as chairman of the Judicial Council. He resigned in January 1991, when a new part-time university staff job made him ineligible for office under the ASG constitution. The Herald reported his departure, alongside that of public relations vice president Van Hodge, on 17 January 1991 under the headline "Two Associated Student Government Officers Step Down."
people.sources: ASG minutes, 27 September 1988 and 31 January 1989; Herald 66:33, 17 Jan 1991, "Two Associated Student Government Officers Step Down"; TopSCHOLAR - Gott correspondence

people.all_offices: president (2017-18); President (2017-18); MyCampusToo Committee Chair (2016-17); Senator (2015-16)
people.what_they_did: Gave a University Committee Report on a Campus Pride meeting on 20 October 2015 and was recorded voting in favor of Resolution 1-16-S on 2 February 2016. Chaired MyCampusToo through the spring of 2017, authoring or co-authoring at least seven bills and resolutions out of it, before being elected student body president in April 2017. Andi Dahmer, a Louisville sophomore who had served as a senator and chair of the MyCampusToo committee, was announced as the next student body president shortly after midnight on April 19, 2017, winning 930 of the 1,579 votes cast against Kenan Mujkanovic's 305 and Lily Nellans' 212. Her running mates Savannah Molyneaux and Kara Lowry were elected executive vice president and administrative vice president, and Dahmer entered office already drafting legislation aimed at improving retention, making study abroad more affordable and supporting sensitivity training. Her year in office was marked by internal division. The senate saw longer debates, more than 15 proposed constitutional amendments compared with about 10 the year before, and an emergency Judicial Council meeting on Jan. 29, with contention peaking around the DACA debates of October and November 2017, when the senate failed a clean DREAM Act resolution before passing a resolution supporting DACA students. Dahmer said the year had become "almost toxic in nature" and blamed partisan ideologies brought into what was supposed to be a nonpartisan organization. In April 2018 Dahmer told the Herald she had endured months of harassment as president and student regent, including senators cursing at her in the SGA office, a group message thread of eight people called the "Justice Friends" that wished her physical harm, and a profane note left on her car on Feb. 9 that prompted a police report. Of the note she said, "That's when I really started fearing for my life on this campus." Her residence hall director reported her case to the Title IX office, which found it did not meet the legal standard for harassment; it was processed instead through the Office of Student Conduct, which issued no-contact orders against two senators, and she did not seek reelection. In 2018 Dahmer, whose full name is Loandria "Andi" Dahmer, sued WKU, university president Timothy Caboni, director of student activities Charley Pride and assistant general counsel and Title IX coordinator Andrea Anderson, alleging sex-based discrimination and harassment by fellow SGA members, negligence by the university in responding to it, and that Caboni retaliated against her by declining to write a letter of recommendation for a Rhodes Scholarship application. U.S. District Judge David Hale granted the defendants summary judgment in March 2021, finding WKU had not been deliberately indifferent and that the incidents were not severe enough to constitute actionable harassment; the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals partially revived the case in 2022, directing the district court to consider whether student-on-student harassment had occurred before February 2018. The parties settled in January 2024, with WKU's insurance carrier paying Dahmer $10,000 and the university's attorney describing the payment as nominal and made without any admission of wrongdoing. Also served as student regent under the merged offices.
people.sources: Herald, 19 Apr 2017; SGA Bill 12-17-S; SGA Senate minutes, 12 Sep 2017; SGA Senate minutes, 2 Feb 2016

people.what_they_did: Andrea Ambam was a senator in WKU SGA's 2016-17 session. With fellow senator Brian Anderson, she authored Resolution 6-17-S, "Resolution to Support Reparations," which called on the university to acknowledge slavery as "a debt that will never be paid," asked for a task force to study test-optional and geographically weighted admissions, and called for full and free access to WKU for Black students. It passed the Senate 19-10-1 on second reading, 18 April 2017, and was modeled on legislation passed earlier that year at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, whose petition Tyriek Mack, a student activist there, helped write. The resolution drew national attention: Herald news coverage reported it reached the Associated Press, the Rush Limbaugh Show and the New York Post, and that Ambam was interviewed by Tucker Carlson on Fox News. The Herald's editorial board separately wrote that coverage also reached commentator Milo Yiannopoulos and The Blaze, and called the resolution a symbolic gesture that risked SGA's credibility. WKU President Gary Ransdell issued a statement saying the university would not adopt a free-tuition reparations policy. In Herald news coverage and in a letter to the editor written by Anderson, the authors said the resolution's language was largely symbolic, that they did not expect free tuition for Black students to result, and that their goal was to start a conversation about barriers facing Black students at WKU.
people.sources: SGA legislation: Resolution 6-17-S, Resolution to Support Reparations

people.what_they_did: Recorded in the archive so far only inside the year's senate note. She was Chief Justice the following year. Carlson served as associate chief justice of the Judicial Council for 2016-17, the year Cody Cox was chief justice, and was chosen by the council to succeed him as chief justice for 2017-18 in March 2017, pending Senate confirmation. As chief justice she swore in committee chairs, senators and cabinet members at the Senate's first meeting of the year on 29 August 2017, and in January 2018 chaired an emergency Judicial Council session on discrepancies in a fall referendum on constitutional amendments. In April 2018 she led the council through the most consequential ruling of her term: an emergency meeting disqualified the Mayer-Edmonds-Anderson presidential ticket, and separately senator candidate Anna McAvoy, for using a Pepe the Frog meme in campaign chalking that the council found violated the election code's ban on inappropriate depictions in sidewalk chalk and the constitution's anti-discrimination clause. Carlson told the Herald the whole ticket was held responsible because executive vice presidential candidate Garrett Edmonds had put the candidates' names on the chalking, and had been told the meme was used as a hate symbol but did not have it removed. After a senate meeting drew unusually large attendance from students objecting to the ruling, the Senate created a new appeal process, and the council itself voted 3-2 with one abstention to reduce the MEA ticket's penalty from disqualification to suspension with a required apology, later doing the same for McAvoy. The reinstated Mayer-Edmonds-Anderson ticket went on to win the election. Carlson's term ended in April 2018 when the Senate elected Associate Justice Jacob McAndrews to succeed her. Carlson returned to the council as an associate justice for 2018-19. In the spring of 2019 she argued against confirming President Stephen Mayer's nominee to a vacant council seat, saying the council itself preferred Erika Puhakka. In May 2019, in her final weeks as a graduating senior, an impeachment petition was brought against her alleging she had inconsistently listed spring 2019 candidates' preferred and legal names on the ballot and had overstepped her role during Wood Brown's confirmation hearing to advance Puhakka's candidacy instead. Carlson rebutted the naming allegation directly, saying names were checked for GPA eligibility, and more generally said that after four years in SGA she "would never intentionally jeopardize it." The Senate canceled the hearing for lack of attendance the day it was scheduled, and the archive found no record it was ever rescheduled. Carlson was chief justice in 2017-18 and an associate justice in 2018-19. In January 2018 she took the council into the dispute over whether the fall referendum had been properly advertised. In April 2018 the council she chaired disqualified the Mayer-Edmonds-Anderson ticket and a senate candidate over a Pepe the Frog image used in campaign chalking and suspended a third campaign under the election codes; she gave the Herald the minutes and rejected the suggestion that the meeting had been secret, and the council reversed the disqualification the following day. In April 2019 she opposed a presidential nomination to the council, saying another applicant was the better candidate, and the senate rejected it 17-11. In May 2019 an impeachment petition was brought against her over how candidates' names were listed on the spring ballot; she said the legal names had been used for a grade point check, and the hearing was cancelled for want of senators.

Annalise Finch was executive vice president of SGA for 2023-24, elected on Sam Kurtz's ticket in the spring 2023 election, which ran unopposed, alongside administrative vice president Salvador Leon. In January 2024 she appointed two campus-committee heads, Jaden Marshall to the Graduate Advisory Council committee and Chloe Ralston to the Colonnade General Education committee, both approved by the Senate. She was elected a senior senator in the spring 2024 election, listed as Annie Finch. Named as an author, with the seat title "Senior Senator," on Bill 13-24-F of 29 October 2024, the bill behind that autumn's Veterans Day 5K. The Herald's report of the race on 8 November 2024 gives its organiser as SGA senior senator and Community Relations head Annie Finch: the same seat, the same committee and the same event. SGA's own forms print the name both ways inside a single session, crediting Annie Finch as an author of Bill 24-22-F in 2022-23 and Annalise Finch as an author of three other bills that same session, and only one Finch sits anywhere in the record. On that evidence the archive now treats Annie and Annalise Finch as one person, the full-name/nickname variant this note previously left open. Speaker Vincent reported her resignation at the meeting of 28 January 2025. Approved as head of the Community Relations Committee at SGA's first meeting of the 2024-25 year on 27 August 2024. She organised SGA's second annual Veterans Day 5K at Kereiakes Park on 8 November 2024, a $15-entry race for WKU's ROTC with a raffle for an iPad and medals for the first ten finishers; she told the Herald the idea came from wanting to ease the ROTC's budget constraints, and that the previous year's race had raised about $2,000.

people.what_they_did: Moved the motion to adjourn the 15 April 1986 meeting. Appointed chair of Legislative Research on 2 September 1986 and also sat on the Judicial Council that year. He was Administrative Vice-President the following year. Before he joined the cabinet, Bill Schilling was already the most prolific bill-writer in Congress: a Herald feature by Lisa Jessie on 11 December 1986 named him the one Associated Student Government member who wrote most of Congress's bills, the same season he chaired the Legislative Research Committee. He wrote to the Herald under his own name that year too — a column headlined "Associated Student Government Has New Ideas" in March 1986, a letter backing Tim Todd's first run for the presidency the following month, and a separate letter, "College Heights Herald Abuses Rights." Schilling ran for the Interhall Council presidency in the spring 1987 elections; the Herald covered his signage under the headline "Candidate Using Big Red on Signs," and on 21 April 1987 reported that Delwin Cheek had defeated him for that council's presidency. He was then named Administrative Vice President of the Associated Student Government for 1987-88 under re-elected President Todd, and in that office reported to Congress on the Bowling Green City Traffic Commission and on a rise of more than 20 percent in campus crime, and handed down to Congress an official Judicial Council record to be implemented at the next election. His term turned contentious that fall. The Herald reported on 27 October 1987 that he had lost his Congress seat after the Residence Hall Association refused him a leave of absence — the report did not say which seat — and three weeks later, on 19 November, Congress opened an impeachment process against him. The proceeding did not go the distance: the Herald reported on 3 December that the impeachment request had been dropped, and the following week's issue described Schilling placed under the eye of a new watchdog committee, alongside a page of reader letters divided between defending the outcome and, in one case from Van C. Hodge Jr., insisting the issue was not closed. Schilling asked Congress for a leave of absence on 25 February 1988, and at the meeting of 1 March told the body he had been cleared by the university, that he would run for the ASG presidency, and that he would take leave from his office until after the election. A Herald item two and a half weeks later, on 17 March, reported the arrest of an Associated Student Government officer under the name William Byron Shilling; the surviving index preserves no charge. The Herald of 31 March 1988, the same issue that reported Shannon Ragland and Scott Whitehouse winning the presidential primary, carried the outcome: "Charge Against William Schilling Dismissed." He was not among the two candidates who survived that primary.
people.sources: ASG Meeting Minutes, 15 April 1986; ASG minutes, 2 and 9 September 1986; ASG minutes, 22 September and 17 November 1987, 1 March 1988

people.what_they_did: Sat on the Executive Committee as well as holding the Interfraternity Council seat, and was elected president of Associated Students in the May 1968 election. Straeffer ran for the Associated Students presidency against Charles Whitley in the 2 May 1968 election, the organization's second contested presidential race. He won 1,732 votes to Whitley's 1,098. Terry Gilpin was elected vice president in the same election, beating Bob Van Corbach 1,516 to 1,206. Total turnout was 2,894 votes, about 34 percent of the roughly 8,500-student enrollment - a turnout the Herald's coverage of the result treated as a persistent problem, running an editorial in the same issue headed 'Elections Illustrate Faults, Indifference'. A year later, the Herald's 8 May 1969 issue carried Straeffer and Gilpin's own review of their year in office, headlined 'Associated Students Produces Year of Advancement,' alongside a companion piece, 'Bill Straeffer, Terry Gilpin Review Their Year with Associated Students.' The archive does not yet hold the article text itself, only its headline and byline (Ellen Bennett), so the specifics of what the administration counted as advancement are not yet confirmed. Bill Straeffer vied with Charles Whitley for the Associated Student Government presidency in the spring 1968 election, the Herald carrying both hopefuls' ideas before the balloting, in a campaign that also saw Terry Gilpin and Bob Van Corbach contest the vice presidency. Straeffer won the presidency in the May 1968 vote, and in the same issue the Herald reported the new president making plans for 1968-69. Closing his term in May 1969, Straeffer and vice president Terry Gilpin reviewed their year with the Associated Students for the Herald, which credited the administration with a year of advancement.
people.sources: Herald 47:30, 9 May 1968; UA3/3/1 Associated Student Government Officers 1967-68; UA3/3/1 Memo Re: Results of Election, 3 May 1968

people.what_they_did: Recorded absent by full name on 22 February 2010. Billy Stephens joined SGA in the spring of 2009 and worked on organizational aid before being appointed director of academic and student affairs in the fall of 2010. He ran for SGA president in the spring 2011 election while holding the post, one of the candidates who presented platforms at a public debate in Downing University Center on 23 March 2011. His central proposal was a pre-finals "Dead Day" with classes canceled, which he called unfair to students left short of study time, noting other schools already did it. He also pledged to fix SGA's Provide-a-Ride service, which he said had been less dependable that year, by negotiating a better contract for a fixed route or more buses, and to improve SGA's public relations to raise awareness of the organization. He won the presidency the following month, detailed in his profile for 2011-12. Billy Stephens, a junior from Hawesville, was elected SGA president in the spring 2011 election, announced just after midnight on April 7. He defeated Diego Leal Ambriz, a senior from Monterrey, Mexico, with 56 percent of the 1,066 total votes. Outgoing president Colton Jessie called him "a fantastic candidate for the job," and Kendrick Bryan and Devon Hilderbrandt were elected unopposed as his executive and administrative vice presidents. Stephens opened his term in August 2011 with a revamped public relations campaign built around asking students what SGA could do for them. "I want PR to be visible on campus," he said, complaining that new students often did not hear about SGA until the second semester. The campaign aimed to raise turnout in the fall senate elections, produce contested races and fill all 36 senate seats. The fall brought open conflict: the senate voted down, 19-8, a resolution to rename Downing University Center that campus improvements chair Keyana Boka had written, the Herald editorial board told Stephens to focus on his own platform promises instead, two senators were dismissed for absences, and SGA was surprised by a $15,000 bill for the prior administration's unpaid Provide-A-Ride service. Chief of Staff Katie Stillwell resigned before the spring semester was out; Stephens replaced her with Eric Smiley, who had held the same post two years earlier under his brother's administration. The senate passed a spring budget of $50,026 in February 2012, down from $54,000 in fall spending. The full account of Stephens's year - the public relations relaunch he opened it with, the resolution to rename Downing University Center that the senate voted down, the unpaid Provide-A-Ride bill left behind by the previous administration, the resignation of his chief of staff and the spring budget - is under his leader entry for this year.
people.sources: Herald, 25 Mar 2011; Herald, 7 Apr 2011; SGA Senate minutes, 22 Feb 2010

people.what_they_did: The first person to hold the Mahurin Honors College seat, one of five senators the Senate approved unanimously at its opening meeting of the year on 27 August 2024. He was made the Senate's parliamentarian that October, went on to chair the Legislative Operations Committee, and was elected student body president for 2026-27. Named as an author on eleven pieces of SGA legislation in the 2025-26 session: Resolution 6-25-F (Resolution to Support the WKU “Food for Fines” Initiative Between the Student Government Association, WKU Food Pantry, and WKU Parking & Transportation Services); Bill 7-25-F (Funding for “Birthday Boxes” for the Office of Sustainability’s Food Pantry); Bill 10-25-F (Organizational Aid Funding Fall 2025); Bill 24-25-F (Funding for the Reestablishment of the SGA Transcript Voucher Program); Resolution 1-26-S (Resolution to Reaffirm Campus Safety and Security); Resolution 8-26-S (Resolution to Support Increased Awareness and Strategic Enhancement of Existing Signage and Navigation Resources in Downing Student Union (DSU)); Bill 9-26-S (Funding for Additional SGA Student ID Vouchers); Bill 11-26-S (Funding for the Expansion of the Adirondack Chair Project at Western Kentucky University); and two further measures. Resolution 2-26-S amended SGA's constitution or bylaws. Authored the transcript voucher bill among other legislation. Lucas entered SGA in September 2024 as its inaugural student senator for the Mahurin Honors College, a seat created as the college began a program revision; he was also an Honors Teaching Fellow for HON 251, working with first-year Honors students on civic engagement. A junior senator, WKU Spiritmaster, chairman of the Hilltoppers Vote Coalition and an employee of Bowling Green's Downtown Development Division, he won the SGA presidential election on April 15, 2026, with running mates Jakob Barker for vice president and Will Derryberry for chief financial officer. Running under the motto "Lead, build, deliver," his campaign centered on increasing awareness of SGA operations and outreach to the student body, and he defeated Jaden Marshall, who had sought to become the first Black male student body president. After the results were announced Lucas said he felt "electric" and that the "work starts tomorrow," beginning with thank-you cards to supporters. Lucas took office at the first meeting of the 26th Senate on April 28, 2026, where outgoing president Rush Robinson presented him with the traditional red suit jacket passed from president to president. Lucas thanked the new cabinet, nominated his defeated campaign opponent Jaden Marshall as an at-large senator, calling his campus work "phenomenal," and saw Gabi Pace and Cayden Bailey sworn in as chief of staff and chief communications officer. The meeting's speaker election deadlocked 9-9 between Amelia Tucker and Veronica Butler, a situation the governing documents did not address, and Butler won the seat in a re-vote. Days after taking office, Lucas was named a 2026 Truman Scholar, WKU's second in the award's history and Kentucky's only recipient that year, chosen from 781 candidates nationally; the scholarship funds $30,000 toward graduate or professional study for students committed to public service. A political science, legal studies and strategic communications major, he had spent that summer establishing the Civic Engagement Resource Center, a joint Mahurin Honors College, SGA and Housing and Residence Life initiative that opened 30 October 2024 with a lending collection on civic life, saying his goal was to get students "talking about what it means to be a good citizen." In May, WKU's Omicron Delta Kappa circle named him its Heather Strode Circle Leader of the Year, an award recognizing collaboration, inclusivity, integrity, scholarship and service. Before he was sworn in as student regent, Lucas told the Herald he was "generally concerned" by a proposed $210 tuition increase; the Board of Regents approved a $204 increase days later, with outgoing regent Rush Robinson casting the only dissenting vote before handing the seat to Lucas. Caden Lucas, a junior senator, WKU Spiritmaster, chairman of the Hilltoppers Vote Coalition and an employee of Bowling Green's Downtown Development Division, won the SGA presidential election on April 15, 2026, with running mates Jakob Barker for vice president and Will Derryberry for chief financial officer. Running under the motto "Lead, build, deliver," his campaign centered on increasing awareness of SGA operations and outreach to the student body, and he defeated Jaden Marshall, who had sought to become the first Black male student body president. After the results were announced Lucas said he felt "electric" and that the "work starts tomorrow," beginning with thank-you cards to supporters. Also student regent on the WKU Board of Regents.

people.what_they_did: Elected to Freshman Council on 3 Feb 1998 (OCR renders the surname 'Manin'). She took over the Coming Home and Bowl for Kid's Sake events and handled SGA's advertising in the College Heights Herald. Coates's running mate; elected SGA president the following year, 2000-01. Cassie Martin, a junior from Glasgow, was elected SGA president in April 2000 to lead the association for 2000-2001. With running mate Leslie Bedo, she defeated the ticket of Duan Wright and Dwight Campbell by 654 votes to 541, and the win also made her the student representative on Western's Board of Regents. The race followed weeks of Herald coverage of proposed SGA election-code reforms meant to close loopholes and set spending limits, and the Martin-Wright contest itself was covered from the candidacy announcement in late March through a pre-election issues debate. Her most visible stand of the year came at the Board of Regents meeting on October 27, 2000, when the board voted 8-2 to raise the student athletic fee by $80 in two installments. Martin was one of only two dissenters, alongside Faculty Regent Mary Ellen Miller. She said she understood the need for the additional funding but questioned the timing and the amount, and disagreed with raising student fees in the middle of an academic year. SGA's congress in 2001 passed legislation putting $13,000 toward a campus gazebo that was never built. In October 2002 the Herald reported that the money had mistakenly gone back into SGA's general fund and been spent on other things, including computers, and SGA's finance vice president said leaders from the past two years, including former presidents Martin and Leslie Bedo, were all partly responsible for not properly earmarking it. people.what_they_did: Active as a senator throughout 2011-12, frequently speaking in floor debate and moving procedural motions. The Senate elected him speaker for 2012-13 at the meeting of 17 April 2012, where President Stephens congratulated "Chris Costa" by name, tying this document's "Senator Costa" to the full name Christopher Costa already recorded as 2012-13 speaker. Christopher Costa was elected to the senate in the fall 2011 election with 977 students voting. By spring 2012 he had joined the four SGA members who traveled to the Rally for Higher Education in Frankfort to protest a proposed 6.4 percent cut to the state's postsecondary education budget. On 18 April 2012 the senate elected him speaker of the student senate for 2012-13, over fellow senator Poorvie Patel and public relations committee head Mallory Treece; he told senators his time in the Army had taught him to follow before he learned to lead, and he was sworn in at SGA's end-of-year banquet on 9 May 2012, receiving the gavel from outgoing speaker Kaylee Egerer. As speaker, Costa presided over a year in which SGA rewrote its own constitution, restructuring senate seats by college rather than class year and adding representation for the Glasgow and Owensboro regional campuses. During floor debate in September 2013 he spoke against a separate proposal, opposing a dedicated Navitas/ESL international senate seat even though he supported the broader goal of international student involvement, arguing the seat would function as a band-aid; the amendment passed anyway. Throughout his term Costa said his hardest task was remaining impartial as speaker, saying it was hardest "when there were issues present which I had a strong position or opinion on." Costa chose not to seek a second term, and the senate elected Paige Settles to succeed him as speaker on 16 April 2013. He said at the time that the responsibilities of the office had grown difficult to balance with his coursework as he entered his senior year, and that he intended to return to an ordinary senate seat after the spring semester ended.
people.sources: Herald, 14 Nov 2012; SGA Senate minutes, 17 Apr 2012

people.all_offices: president (1976-77); Administrative Vice President (1975-76); Congress Member (1974-75)
people.what_they_did: Vogt sat in the ASG Congress in 1974-75 and resigned from it on 28 January 1975. The Herald reported that both the student affairs chairpersonship and a representative-at-large seat were vacated by her resignation and were filled the following week by presidential appointment. She returned the next year as administrative vice president, and the archive already records that term. Before she became administrative vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1975-76, Christy Vogt had already spent two years working her way up through ASG. A Talisman profile of Vogt recorded that she came to Western from Angela Merici High School in Louisville, where she had served four years on student council and been both its vice president and president; as a Western freshman she ran for and won freshman vice president, then as a sophomore was elected an ASG representative-at-large before President Jeff Consolo appointed her student affairs chairman. She ran for administrative vice president with about a week left before the spring 1975 election and won. In office, Vogt ran the book exchange ASG co-sponsored with Veterans on Campus from 12 to 26 January 1976, reporting that the two groups had covered their expenses by 21 January on sales of more than 600 books at a margin of 25 cents a book. She said the year's executive officers were closer than in any administration she had witnessed, crediting President Steve Henry for not minding which officer brought him ideas directly. She told the Talisman there was a 90 percent chance she would run for the ASG presidency in 1976-77; she did, and won. Her term as president is recorded separately, under 1976-77. Christy Vogt entered the spring 1976 Associated Student Government campaign with an endorsement from Herald columnist John Butchko, in an issue whose front section also covered the start of impeachment hearings against congress member Gerard Faulk and an editorial warning the university's new Faculty Senate away from ASG's own troubles. Vogt and Bruce Smith survived the 2 April primary as the Herald reported 527 ballots cast, then Vogt won the presidency outright, the paper reporting the result on 9 April 1976 under the headline "Christy Vogt Wins Election," with her own note of thanks to voters in the same issue - the same week Faulk was acquitted. In office for 1976-77, Vogt's congress created a constitutional revision committee within its first month (Bill 2, 7 September 1976) and kept revision on its agenda all year. It asked the university for a minimum wage policy for student employees (Resolution, 26 October 1976), recommended preregistration for all students, and opposed a proposed tuition increase (Bill 9, 8 March 1977) while creating a Complaint Committee to field student grievances the same meeting. A resolution on discrimination failed in February 1977 with fourteen members abstaining. The fall Seals and Crofts concert lost the organization $3,800, a recurring sore point ASG had wrestled with under Vogt's predecessors as well. Vogt wrote her own case for the office in the Herald - "Urges Involvement," 12 April 1977, days before Bob Moore won the presidency to succeed her by a 26-vote margin. She closed her term on 26 April 1977 with a letter to Congress thanking its members and recommending four items to the administration: constitutional revision, extended hours for student buildings, open visitation, and advance registration - the same four causes her congress had pushed all year. WKU's own archive later indexes her, alongside her maiden name, as Christy Vogt Mollozzi, and separately as Christy Mollozzi in President's Office records tied to Marketing & Promotions - evidence, though not a documented statement, that she went on to a career on the university's own staff.
people.sources: 1976 Talisman, ASG; Herald 50:35, 7 Feb 1975, 'ASG congress hears treasurer's budget explanation'; TopSCHOLAR - SGA Documents
