Elected an associate justice at the same Judicial Council meeting that elected Amber Daniel chief justice; Chief Justice himself the following year. Cox was elected an associate justice of the SGA Judicial Council alongside Amber Daniel's election as chief justice, a Judicial Council meeting reported to the Senate on 2 February 2016, and moved up to chief justice himself for 2016-17. As chief justice he reviewed that fall's election codes with the Senate on 6 September 2016 and told senators to report any justice seen campaigning for a candidate. On 11 October 2016 he told the Senate the council had received a complaint that several SGA members had made racist remarks, and that the council would meet the next day to decide whether to investigate. Cox told senators such conduct "is not tolerated in the Student Government Association ... whatsoever." The investigation was dropped when the members concerned resigned that morning; because no investigation was held, SGA did not release their names or the nature of the remarks. In November Cox reported that justice Amarah Reed had stepped down and that the council was looking for a replacement. In March 2017 Cox announced the council had chosen Annalicia Carlson to succeed him as chief justice and Lane Hedrick as associate chief justice, both pending Senate confirmation. That spring he ruled on eligibility questions in a crowded presidential race, and in April the council split 5-2 on granting freshman candidate Kenan Mujkanovic a late exemption to run without a full year of Senate service, with Cox and Carlson in the minority against allowing it.
people.sources: SGA Judicial Council page, archived 1 Nov 2016 (last modified 29 Aug 2016); SGA Senate minutes, 2 Feb 2016

people.what_they_did: Appointed 'Senator at large' and approved by acclamation in the 16 November 2010 minutes.

Named as an author on eight pieces of SGA legislation in the 2021-22 session: Resolution 2-21-F (Resolution to Support students and faculty members of Western Kentucky University who have served our country in the armed forces); Bill 8-21-F (Funding for the Intercultural Student Engagement Center Homecoming 2021 events and activities); Bill 12-21-F (Funding for 3 of the Spring WKU College Job Fair Scholarships: STEM, Business, and Spring); Bill 1-22-S (Relief funding for the food pantry in the WKU Office of Sustainability); Resolution 2-22-S (Resolution to Support The Swipe-Out Hunger Initiative); Resolution 10-22-S (Resolution to Support the addition of a food insecurity related clause to Course Syllabi); Bill 15-22-S (Funding for the Intercultural Student Engagement Center (ISEC) Women’s History Month Tabling). Bill 21-22-S amended SGA's constitution or bylaws. Cole Bornefeld came to the presidency by an unusually fast route. He transferred to WKU from Volunteer State Community College as a junior, emailed then-President Matthew Wininger during his first week on campus, and was appointed a senator-at-large at their first meeting. He had not planned to run for president, but after senators urged him to, he formed a ticket the week of the filing deadline and won. He campaigned on programs he backed as a senator, including the Share-A-Swipe meal donation program and growing SGA's scholarship budget, which rose by $3,500 during his presidency. Adjusting to the office, he said it felt like "drinking out of a fire hose," and he sought advice from former student body presidents weekly. Bornefeld opened the 2022-23 year with an executive retreat on Aug. 29 at the Cliff Todd Center, where his team set three priorities: a one-stop resource guide for students, a push to represent WKU's five regional campuses, which he said was "an area that I really don't think SGA has ever touched," and financial assistance for students as the year's underlying goal. He had met with the director of regional campuses the week before to start that work. His spring semester was dominated by fallout from anti-LGBTQ Instagram posts he had liked. After the judicial council unanimously declined to censure him, the Queer Student Union removed SGA meetings from its list of campus safe spaces and said it would not associate with SGA until a public apology was released. Addressing the senate on Feb. 21, Bornefeld, who also served as student regent, said he "always commits to loving thy neighbor" but could not commit to always agreeing, tying his position to his Christian values and offering to meet any student over coffee or breakfast to discuss disagreements.
people.sources: Herald - censure hearing; SGA legislation: Bill 15-22-S, Funding for the Intercultural Student Engagement Center (ISEC) Women’s History Month Tabling

people.what_they_did: Sworn in with the incoming freshman senators on 25 September 2012, the first year of a senate career that continued into 2014-15 and 2015-16 as secretary of the senate. Appointed a senator by the President and, the same night, named Secretary of the Senate by the Speaker. Cole McDowell was sworn in as a freshman senator in September 2012, representing the incoming class alongside Barrett Greenwell, Paige Settles and Gatton Academy senator Linda Cruz. As a senator in 2014-15 he authored a resolution objecting that SGA had not been consulted before Housing and Residence Life decided to move Gatton Academy students into Bates-Runner Hall, introduced and reported to the senate on 11 November 2014, where it was postponed to await a joint SGA, Gatton and Housing meeting; he said the resolution was not a judgment on the decision itself, but a statement that senators could not represent student views on decisions they were never told about. SGA's cabinet minutes also name him secretary of the student senate that year, though the senate's own leadership page rendered the name "Patrick Mcdowell" for the same office — a discrepancy the archive has left unresolved rather than guessed at. The Senate reappointed McDowell secretary for 2015-16, this time named by Speaker Paige Settles and approved at the senate's first meeting on 1 September 2015; he asked fellow senators that December to tell him if they did not plan to return in the spring. In that capacity he argued in February 2016 for lowering SGA's own senator GPA requirement from 2.5 to 2.0, saying "if a 2.0 is good enough for the university, then it's good enough for me" — the amendment failed. The same spring he brought a resolution asking WKU to include a faculty and staff salary increase in the 2016-17 budget and to guarantee raises in future years, citing a Herald report that administrators were considering the idea; President Gary Ransdell had already expressed support for a raise, though the archive has found no record of the resolution's ultimate fate. Appointed by Speaker Paige Settles and approved by the Senate at its first meeting on 1 September 2015. He asked senators in December to tell him if they were not returning in the spring.

people.what_they_did: Colton Jessie served as clerk of the Judicial Council under Chief Justice Stuart Kenderes in 2009-10, before winning the SGA presidency for 2010-11. By 28 May 2010 the clerkship had passed to Eliana Martinez. Jessie opened the 2010-11 year having spent the summer preparing with his executive board, which attended the Kentucky Leadership Academy at Barren River State Park alongside SGAs from Kentucky's other public universities. His early priorities included building a closer relationship with international students, whom SGA hosted at a dinner during orientation, planning a study away program for students to study elsewhere in the country, and setting up a forum for South Campus concerns. "We are trying to reach out to South Campus," he said, and he and Executive Vice President Kendrick Bryan reallocated the budget to fund scholarship and study abroad programs. By the end of his term, SGA had given out more scholarship money than ever, with the scholarship fund raised by $8,000 and organizational aid increased to $40,000, and the senate had passed first-of-their-kind bills reimbursing CLEP exam fees and buying test prep books for libraries. Jessie called the DUC renovation "one of the biggest things SGA has done in a while," and Ransdell credited him with taking the initiative to start the renovation talks. A senior, Jessie handed the office to Billy Stephens and left for Chicago after graduation to work for Teach for America. Colton Jessie served as SGA president for 2010-11, the year after he was clerk of the Judicial Council. His full term — the Kentucky Leadership Academy retreat, the DUC renovation talks, and the increases to scholarship and study-abroad funding — is recorded under his leader entry for this year.

people.what_they_did: Hounshell authored the constitutional amendment requiring the administrative vice president to report executive discretionary spending, passed 29-0-1 on 4 April 2017, and co-authored the parking ticket forgiveness resolution, passed 31-0-0 a fortnight later. He also sat on the organizational aid committee. He became chief of staff the following year. Hounshell served on the organizational aid committee, which reviewed student organisations' applications and brought the funding bills to the floor; he is recorded among its members on Bill 22-16-F of November 2016. His legislative work this year is set out under his senate officer entry. Hounshell served as SGA's Chief of Staff in 2017-18 and ran for president that April on a ticket with Executive Vice President Savannah Molyneaux and Administrative Vice President Kara Lowry, both seeking re-election. Days before the vote the Judicial Council disqualified, then suspended, the rival Mayer-Edmonds-Anderson ticket over a Pepe the Frog meme in its campaign chalking. Hounshell's ticket won 33 percent of the presidential vote to Mayer's 35 percent; all three were elected senators instead. In February 2018 he co-authored Resolution 3-18-S with President Andi Dahmer, Molyneaux and Lowry, opposing the scale of a renegotiated Aramark dining-fee increase on students without meal plans. He had recommended Garrett Edmonds, whom he met when Edmonds joined SGA in fall 2017, for the chair of the Campus Improvements committee, but by the following fall told the Herald his opinion of Edmonds had completely changed after the chalking controversy. The Herald's account of that criticism, and Edmonds's own answer to it, are in the article cited here; the archive does not restate one side of it in the other man's record. Hounshell returned to the senate after a year as chief of staff and co-authored Bill 1-18-F, the bylaw change that set up a way of tracking senate and executive office hours; it passed on 11 September 2018. Named on the document as senator.

A Connie Hoffman — almost certainly the same person, given the continuity of interest — was writing about student government before she took office: a September 1983 Herald letter, 'And Old Tricks,' and, ahead of the spring 1984 ASG elections, an April 1984 letter defending a proposal from ASG's own Student Rights Committee (both bylined 'Hoffman' in the Herald's own index, one N; the ASG minutes and a later Herald letter about her spell it with two). The identification rests on the matching name and the continuous ASG involvement, not on a source that states the two are the same; it is recorded here as likely, not certain. As Secretary in 1984-85 she announced the vacancies on Congress week after week and, on 16 October 1984, the openings on the Judicial Council as well; she signed the minutes for the year. She sought further ASG office in the spring 1985 election: the Herald of 2 April 1985 carried a full slate of candidate-endorsement letters, one backing her ('Supports Connie Hoffmann'), alongside letters for Mitchell McKinney, Greg Elder, Loree Zimmerman, and Stan Reagan, plus a joint endorsement of Caroline Miller and Donna Holloway written by Elder himself. The Herald does not say which office any of the letters' subjects were seeking. Only McKinney's result is established elsewhere in this archive; it does not yet record who won the 1985-86 secretary, treasurer or vice-president races, so Hoffmann's absence from the recorded 1985-86 leadership does not establish that she lost — only that which office she sought, and how the race came out, is not yet established here.

people.all_offices: president (2012-13); President (2012-13); Director of Information Technology (2010-11); Director of Information Technology (2011-12)
people.what_they_did: Cory Dodds, then a sophomore, was SGA's director of information technology in 2010-11. In February 2011 the Herald reported he would build and maintain an off-campus housing listings website in-house using open-source software, after Executive Vice President Kendrick Bryan said SGA lacked a "one-stop shop" for such listings. An earlier attempt to build the site through an outside vendor, considering options including a company called Off Campus Partners, had stalled over cost and fit for the Bowling Green market, Dodds said. He aimed to have the site functional by the end of April 2011 and said he planned to maintain it himself until he graduated. He went on to be elected SGA president for 2012-13, detailed in his own presidential profile. Launched SGA's off-campus housing site earlier in the autumn of 2011 and rebuilt the SGA website in December to match WKU's new university template, a change mandated because SGA sits under the Student Activities Office. He was an author of the transcript voucher bill and one of four WKU members at the February 2012 Frankfort rally. Cory Dodds, a junior political science major from Smithland, Kentucky, was elected SGA president for 2012-13 in spring 2012 over Austin Wingate and Corey Johnson, after two years as SGA's director of information technology, during which he built a legislation and minutes archive for the SGA website that he said promoted transparency and accountability. Under the merged offices, Dodds also served as the student regent representing students on WKU's Board of Regents. In office, Dodds led SGA in unanimously opposing an administration proposal to shift tuition to a per-credit-hour, bi-term model, which Provost Gordon Emslie dropped in February 2013 after student and faculty pushback. His administration also drafted a teaching assistant evaluation program the senate passed in February 2013, worked to restart a dormant student government at WKU's Glasgow campus, donated cameras to the Teaching and Learning Resource Center, and passed a resolution opposing a new $150 Study Abroad application fee; a Dodds amendment to bar SGA members from receiving SGA-awarded study-abroad scholarships, after 11 of 125 such awards had gone to SGA members that year, failed. Dodds's term ended amid a contested succession: his successor, Keyana Boka, was elected in April 2013 but disqualified five days later by the Judicial Council 3-2 over a campaign email, then reinstated after appealing to Vice President for Student Affairs Howard Bailey. Later in 2012 Dodds was named a finalist for the Harry S. Truman Scholarship and, that November, WKU's first finalist for the George J. Mitchell Scholarship, the only Kentuckian among 20 national finalists. He went on to earn a law degree from Georgetown University, worked as directing attorney of the Children's Law Center and as a legal services staff attorney representing low-income clients in public benefits, housing and family law matters, and by the mid-2020s was a visiting professor at the University of Kentucky's J. David Rosenberg College of Law teaching Civil Procedure and Children and the Law, with research on rural "legal deserts" and the attorney shortage. Also served as student regent under the merged offices.
people.sources: Herald, 15 Feb 2011; Herald, 30 Mar 2012; Herald, 9 Dec 2011

people.what_they_did: Daniel Rodriguez, a senior from Barquisimeto, Venezuela, served as the Associated Student Government's Public Relations Vice President in 1986-87 and chaired its Public Relations committee. At the opening Congress meeting of 2 September 1986 he distributed the year's new ASG brochures and announced the Weekend in the Woods leadership retreat, held at Camp Decker 12-14 September 1986. Rodriguez helped organize that retreat starting in March, lining up speakers and camp reservations, then promoting it with letters to freshmen, newspaper ads and brochures mailed to campus organizations. Rodriguez told the 1987 Talisman that the lower-than-expected turnout, 45 of a possible 75, actually helped attendees participate more. When the closing speaker, university president Kern Alexander, could not make the retreat, he invited the attendees to breakfast at his home the following week instead; Rodriguez called it "a great way to finish."

Daniel Shaw resigned his Senate seat at the meeting of 20 October 2009, one of three senators — alongside Michel Stephens and a third member the Herald and SGA's own minutes recorded under conflicting names, "Emmett Stephens" and "Emmitt" respectively — who stepped down that night. Michel Stephens said the resignations followed President Kevin Smiley's nomination of Greg Capillo to the Student Publications Committee, which helps choose the Herald's editor-in-chief, calling the pick unmerited; Smiley called the accusations of favoritism unfounded. SGA's own Senate minutes of 22 February 2010 separately record a Daniel Shaw serving as Parliamentarian; the sources searched for this profile do not explain how the October resignation and the February record of him in office relate, and both are given here as printed, unreconciled. The 7 December 2010 minutes record 'Senator Shaw' motioning to table the DUC Renovation Resolution (04-10-F) indefinitely; his full name appears elsewhere in the same minutes corpus (e.g. the 21 September 2010 minutes name him 'Daniel Shaw'), and by 8 February 2011 he was recorded as Public Relations Committee 'Chair Elect.' A "Senator Shaw" is one of the most frequent speakers in floor debate throughout 2011-12, moving amendments and questioning bills at nearly every meeting.

Danielle Williamson served as Secretary of the Associated Student Government in 1987-88, under President Timothy Todd. The Herald's coverage of the spring 1987 campaign that put that year's officers in place, in its issue of 14 April, carried a letter backing her under the headline "Danielle Williamson Best" — the same issue in which Kim Summers wrote in support of Todd's re-election as president. As Secretary, Williamson signed Congress's minutes through the year, including those recording the opening of impeachment proceedings against Administrative Vice President Bill Schilling in November 1987. Carwell sat on the Associated Student Government's lecture committee in 1976-77, one of the student members the 1977 Talisman pictures hosting visiting speakers backstage. The archive separately records a David Carwell as ASG's activities vice president two years later, in 1978-79, negotiating the Sunshine Promotions concert contract. David Carwell was elected ASG activities vice president unopposed in the April 1978 election and put in charge of the year's concerts and lectures, saying he wanted more mini-concerts and fewer large shows. That fall ASG moved to sign the Indianapolis firm Sunshine Promotions as an outside concert promoter; Carwell told the 1979 Talisman that Sunshine met the university's three tests for such a firm, having an office within 500 miles of Western, having promoted at least 75 major concerts, and having grossed at least $2 million on them. Shortly before the 3 November 1978 Player and Exile concert it emerged that the contract with Sunshine had never actually been signed, because the firm balked at a $100,000 performance bond; Sunshine later posted a letter of credit instead. On 7 December 1978 the Herald reported colleagues' claims that Carwell was neglecting an office that carried an $800 salary, saying he had missed five ASG meetings and that lecture committee members and a Herald reporter had been unable to reach him. President Steve Thornton said one more missed meeting would bring him before the executive council to explain himself; Carwell replied that much of his work was done by telephone from home and defended his record. This archive has found no later report of an executive council hearing, of any removal, or of a successor taking the office before the year ended. That spring the Board of Regents voted to move some responsibility for lecture and concert programming out of ASG's hands and into a rebuilt University Center Board, effective that fall.
people.sources: 1977 Talisman, lecture series, p. 92 photograph caption; Herald 54:30, 7 Dec 1978

He was elected ASG treasurer the following spring and served in 1975-76 and again in 1976-77. David Payne was treasurer of the Associated Student Government for 1975-76, a job he described to the 1976 Talisman as "simple record keeping": reviewing the past year's records, planning a budget, getting it approved, vouching for payments, advising the ASG president on finances and preparing an expenditure report each semester. Congress member Marc Levy brought charges against him that year for spending before budget approval had been given, and appeared twice before the Judicial Council to press the case; Payne argued the ASG constitution provided for such spending, and the council ruled in his favour. Note for the editor: years.json separately carries a David Payne who succeeded Marcel Bush as ASG president in January 1982, filed under 1981-82 (not 1982-83) with year_confidence "corrected" - Board of Regents minutes of 30 January 1982 already confirm that identification, so he is not simply an unresolved name. This Payne was re-elected treasurer for a second term in 1976-77, recorded there. Whether the 1981-82 president is the same person as this 1970s ASG treasurer is not established by any source found so far, and this archive should not merge them without one that links them. David Payne returned as treasurer of the Associated Student Government for 1976-77, one of two officers, along with activities vice president Rick Kelley, beginning a second consecutive term that year, the 1977 Talisman recorded. Note for the editor: years.json separately carries a David Payne who succeeded Marcel Bush as ASG president in January 1982, filed under 1981-82 (not 1982-83) with year_confidence "corrected" - Board of Regents minutes of 30 January 1982 already confirm that identification, so he is not simply an unresolved name. Whether the 1981-82 president is the same person as this 1970s ASG treasurer is not established by any source found so far, and this archive should not merge them without one that links them. David Payne first appears in the indexed record in February 1981 with a Herald letter titled 'Apathy Erased.' By October 1981, before he held the presidency, he was writing on the Associated Student Government's behalf, declaring that ASG was rallying for higher education as budget cuts loomed. Payne became ASG's president after Marcel Bush resigned on 14 January 1982; Board of Regents minutes from the January 30 meeting name him the new SGA president. In early February the Herald reported that Payne wanted another adviser for ASG, and its editorial page attacked his judgment, while a report the next week said Payne considered certain resolutions misdirected. Later that month, letter writers to the Herald argued that Payne had been made a victim in the affair; the indexed headline does not state what precipitated it. His name does not appear in the indexed headlines of the April 1982 election that chose Margaret Ragan for the 1982-83 term, nor in the 1982-83 issues examined - consistent with his presidency ending with Bush's original term. Succeeded Bush; named in Board of Regents minutes 30 Jan 1982.
people.sources: 1975 Talisman, Greeks (Alpha Kappa Psi); 1976 Talisman, ASG; 1977 Talisman, ASG, pp. 50-51; Herald 57:12, 12 Oct 1981; WKU Board of Regents minutes, 30 Jan 1982

David Porter was elected vice president of Associated Students for 1969-70, beating John Lyne by 1,751 votes to 1,725, the closest of the four officer races that spring, under president Larry Zielke. The Herald had covered the two candidates' contest that March under the headline 'John Lyne, David Porter Square Off in Race for Second Spot,' and after the result ran Zielke and Porter's account of the coming administration on 22 May 1969. As vice president, Porter wrote to WKU faculty on 15 May 1970 about ASC Bill No. 3, which created an Environmental Commission. The Herald of 24 April 1970, the issue reporting that Congress was seeking ratification of four constitution changes, separately carried an item naming Porter the Associated Students unsung hero. Porter's defeated opponent, John Lyne, returned the following spring and was elected president unopposed for 1970-71.

people.what_they_did: Sworn in as a senator by President Jessie on 8 February 2011, alongside Brittany Crowley and Chad Winston. David Spalding was SGA's chief justice in 2011-12. That November he ran the semester's judicial reviews after nearly a third of the senate's 36 members were called up for excessive absences; two senators, Kevin Adams and Kevin Preston, were dismissed after failing to attend their own review hearings, which he said the judicial council read as an intention to resign. Spalding said the rest were given the sternest of warnings and that the branch would administer oaths to their replacements, calling the episode a "very minor speed bump" and noting some senators flagged for review had simply had trouble submitting absence excuses to the right place on SGA's website. In February 2012, after President Billy Stephens moved to reappoint Adams to the senate, Spalding said Stephens had not needed the judicial branch's sign-off but the two had discussed the situation; he noted SGA's constitution has no rule barring a removed senator's return, so long as they affirm they again have the time for it.
people.sources: Herald, 15 Nov 2011; SGA Senate minutes, 8 Feb 2011

The Executive Council slate approved on 25 August 1992 named Donald Smith chair of the Legislative Research Committee, a post he still held that February, ahead of the spring election in which he won the SGA presidency for 1993-94. Smith won the April 1993 election decisively. The Herald's headline was "Student Government Association Election: Donald Smith Rolls to Victory." Interviewed by the Herald in 2022, he said that while the structure had changed over the years, "the fundamental principle for SGA to be a voice for the students has remained unphased," and that if SGA improves over time the WKU experience improves with it.

people.what_they_did: Accepted as Public Relations co-chair on 20 September 1988, having been sworn in as a Representative At-Large a fortnight earlier. Dwight Adkins was sworn in as an Associated Student Government representative at-large on 6 September 1988, alongside Ron Hennig, and was accepted as co-chair of the Public Relations Committee two weeks later, on 20 September 1988. The following year Congress approved Adkins as Student Rights chairman on 29 August 1989, the same meeting at which it accepted him as junior class vice president. His committee reported to Congress on 10 October 1989 that it had reviewed the university's alcohol policy with the campus lawyer and discussed expanding co-ed housing and 24-hour visitation; Adkins himself was recorded absent from that meeting. He resigned from the organization altogether at the 5 December 1989 meeting, citing schedule conflicts, and Congress replaced him as Student Rights chairman with Heather Falmlen. Adkins ran for the Associated Student Government presidency the following spring: the Herald's coverage on 5 April 1990 named him and Michael Colvin as the field, and the paper ran further pieces backing his campaign over the following week. Colvin won the 19 April 1990 election and took office for 1990-91, not Adkins. On the absence roll 23 Oct 1990, 27 Oct 1990, and 13 Nov 1990.
people.sources: ASG Minutes, 23 Oct 1990; ASG Minutes, 29 Aug 1989 and 10 Oct 1989; ASG minutes, 6 and 20 September 1988

Jordan ran for the Associated Student Government presidency on a platform the Herald's Roger Miller labeled progressivism, profiled a week before the vote. Congress had separately voted to place his opponent, Bob Hatfield, on the ballot after a dispute over Hatfield's eligibility. Jordan beat Hatfield in the 20 April 1972 election; the Herald reported his win on 25 April under the headline 'Ed Jordan Wins Top Office,' in the same issue as an editorial by Pence and Carter arguing the new ASG president needed cooperation and support. Edward Jordan's name entered the Herald's letters columns on November 7, 1972, when he and Charles Boteler urged readers to restore ideals. The digitized index does not label the ASG office Jordan held. On April 10, 1973, as top ASG offices went on the line in the spring election, a letter praising Ed Jordan ran in the Herald. Jordan stayed in student politics after his year: in April 1974 he wrote to the Herald judging Steve Henry the most qualified candidate in that spring's races.

people.what_they_did: Sat as Potter College senator. Co-author with the Administrative Vice President and the Legislative Research chair of Bill 25-17-F, the Go With the Flow programme. Elected Executive Vice President for 2018-19. Edmonds had chaired campus improvements the year before, funding the Go With the Flow programme that put free menstrual products in Grise Hall, the campus safety seminar and Mission: Thank You Veterans. He was elected executive vice president with 54 percent against Savannah Molyneaux, after the Judicial Council disqualified and then suspended his ticket over a Pepe the Frog image used in its campaign chalking and reversed the disqualification the next day. In office he led the delegation of twenty-four SGA members to the 2019 Rally for Higher Education in Frankfort and co-authored Resolution 10-18-F denouncing the white nationalist group Identity Evropa's recruiting on campus, which passed 28-0 on 4 December 2018. Signed as J. Garrett Edmonds on legislation. He worked over the summer of 2019 with the Student Life Foundation on the WKU Commons and the green space by the new First Year Village, defended the executive special projects fund through the September budget fight, and co-authored Bill 3-20-S committing $5,000 to hammock areas across campus. Edmonds, a senior from Island, Kentucky, spent his freshman year as chair of the Campus Improvements Committee, working with Vice President of Student Affairs Brian Kuster on projects including a campus safety walk, before winning election as executive vice president in April 2018 on a ticket with Harper Anderson and Stephen Mayer. He served two years as executive vice president under President Will Harris, pushing for a budget model geared toward campus amenities and recreational life and working to diversify Senate appointments with seats for underrepresented students. He ran for the presidency in fall 2020 on the Edmonds-Norvell ticket, after his original running mate for administrative vice president, Nathan Terrell, dropped out and was replaced by Abbey Norvell. The campaign centered on a pledge to create a Director of Outreach position to close the communication gap between campus organizations and SGA, and the Sept. 24 Herald town hall covered WKU's COVID-19 response and the summer's Black Lives Matter protests on campus. Voting ran Sept. 28-29 on TopNet; Edmonds defeated senator MJ Mayo, becoming SGA president and, since the two offices had merged by then, student regent on the WKU Board of Regents. Norvell was elected administrative vice president alongside him, with the Herald reporting no decision yet made on a separate executive vice president post. Taking office amid the pandemic, the senate confirmed Isaac Keller to a vice-president post 29-1 in October after Edmonds said he wanted a deputy willing to challenge him; the Herald's report on that vote first called the office executive vice president, then ran a correction changing it to administrative vice president -- the same title the Herald had given Norvell in September, a conflict the record does not resolve. Matt Barr, Ashlynn Evans, Kody Okert and Paul Brosky rounded out the executive and Shelby Robertson served as non-voting speaker of the senate. Early cabinet business set up officer office hours, an ad hoc outreach committee chaired by Me'Lon Craighead and a push toward inclusive pronoun language in Senate proceedings. That fall SGA petitioned WKU to restore Pass/D/Fail grading for COVID-disrupted students; Associate Provost Rob Hale initially rebuffed the request, calling the university's extended drop deadline sufficient, but by December the petition -- more than 3,500 signatures in three days -- had succeeded, and Edmonds thanked senators for the work behind it at the semester's final meeting alongside bills funding campus safe-driving signage and several student organizations. In the spring his senate passed the organization's largest-ever organizational aid bill and a resolution seeking a codified vetting process for campus dining vendors after a controversial social media post by a local pizzeria owner, alongside legislation backing WKU's Naming and Symbols Task Force in renaming buildings tied to racism, a community garden, and a diversity-event push by DEI chair Fatin Yaro. Near the end of his term he declined to fill the chief justice seat vacated by Erika Puhakka, saying the choice belonged to his successor: "I think that's the only thing that is right in this scenario." He also worried publicly that only 13 students were running for senate in the April election, and closed his term addressing the Class of 2021 at the delayed Fall 2020/Spring 2021 commencement, telling graduates their perseverance through "this past year" had brought them to their day of celebration. Also student regent on the WKU Board of Regents.
people.sources: Herald, 31 Mar 2021; SGA Bill 25-17-F; SGA Senate minutes, 10 Sep 2019; SGA Senate minutes, 4 Sep 2018; WKU Talisman, Voter's Guide, 28 Sep 2020

Midway through the fall 1974 semester, Herald writer Al Cross profiled the new regent under the headline 'Greg McKinney Feels Regents Can Aid Western's Progress,' as McKinney settled into his seat on the Board of Regents. After his term as student regent, McKinney stayed on at WKU as a graduate assistant in Student Affairs. The university's own file on him, opened in 1983, holds correspondence between McKinney and President Donald Zacharias and a paper he wrote titled "Student Affairs: An Analysis" - the record of a former student regent moving into the administration whose board he had once sat on.

people.what_they_did: Accepted by floor motion (with Darla Roof) as On-Campus Representative and sworn in, 29 August 1989; absent 10 October 1989. Chosen Sophomore Class President 24 October 1989, succeeding John Seiber (resigned 17 October). Accepted by floor motion as Chairman of Student Rights, 5 December 1989, succeeding Dwight Adkins (who resigned from ASG that meeting citing schedule conflicts). Absent 27 February 1990; nominated for the Kerrie Faye Stewart award, 3 April 1990. Falmlen served as Administrative Vice-President in 1990-91, the year before she was elected president. She met individually with that year's committee heads, drove a campus recycling programme she reported should be solidly under way by the end of November 1990, and discussed the possibility of adding one or two more co-educational dormitories with Dave Parrott. She was elected Associated Student Government president for 1991-92 the following spring. Falmlen won the Associated Student Government presidency in results the Herald reported on 11 April 1991 under the headline "Heather Falmlen Wins Amid Associated Student Government Election Protests." A Herald "Meet the Candidates" feature on 2 April had previewed four contenders for the race: Falmlen, Rob Evans, Van Hodge, and Dan Knowles. The same 11 April issue reported a rival group urging students to boycott the vote, an editorial calling the contest's "immature antics" a disappointment, and a published complaint that the Herald's own election coverage had been biased. In office, her administration fought a running battle over the makeup of the Board of Regents. On 29 October 1991 the Associated Student Government passed Resolution 91-6-F asking that Joe Iracane not be re-elected chair of the board; the Herald covered the vote the same day under "Associated Student Government Opposes Joseph Iracane." The board went ahead and re-elected him a week later, the university's own "On Campus" newsletter reported on 6 November. On 30 January 1992 the Herald reported the Associated Student Government was separately planning a committee aimed at student access to the regent, in the same issue that carried an editorial cartoon, "Ventriloquist's Dummy," targeting Falmlen. On 4 February 1992 the body passed Resolution 92-7-S, declaring its support for the WKU football program in spite of budget cuts; the Board of Regents voted that May to keep the program. That fall the body passed Resolution 91-2-F, asking for a change to Big Red Shuttle bus fares, and held its regular fall senate elections in October, including a separate freshman senator election on 15 October. The signature action of her term was procedural: on 7 April 1992 the Associated Students voted to rename itself the Student Government Association, a change students ratified in a referendum a week later, effective that autumn. WKU's own "On Campus" newsletter had confirmed on 22 May 1991, at the start of her term, that Falmlen held both the presidency and the student regent seat - the same dual role held by the presidents before and after her in this period. The archive does not preserve further detail of her regency or of what she did after her term. Other legislative business that fall included Resolution 91-7-F, backing the renewal of President Thomas Meredith's contract by the Board of Regents; a bill funding a "President for a Day" fundraiser (Bill #91-09-F); a bill funding renovation of the ASG chambers (Bill #91-03-F); and a bill proposing a new organizational slogan (Bill #91-11-F), introduced the same season the body renamed itself from the Associated Students to the Student Government Association. Held both offices at once, as was standard for this period.
people.sources: ASG Minutes, 16 Oct 1990 and 12 Feb 1991; ASG Minutes, 29 August 1989; Herald 66:54, 11 Apr 1991, "Heather Falmlen Wins Amid Associated Student Government Election Protests"; On Campus 1:7, 22 May 1991, "Heather Falmlen is Student Regent, Associated Student Government President"

people.all_offices: president (1983-84); President (1983-84); president (1984-85); Administrative Vice President (1982-83)
people.what_they_did: Jack Smith was serving as Administrative Vice President by the Congress meeting of 29 April 1982, where he went over how to write a resolution and its stages; the same minutes name him chairperson of both the Student Affairs Committee and the Legislative Research Committee. A candidate also named Jack Smith ran in that spring's ASG presidential primary and was eliminated on 6 April 1982, and a Jack Smith went on to win the ASG presidency the following year, in April 1983 — already recorded elsewhere in this archive. No source found ties this Administrative Vice President directly to either the 1982 candidate or the 1983 president, and the archive does not merge them: this record is kept deliberately separate rather than assumed to be the same person. Jack Smith first ran for the Associated Student Government presidency in spring 1982, drawing repeated endorsement letters in the Herald, and though Margaret Ragan won that race, Smith and Lonnie Sears took awards as the year closed. He returned as a candidate in March 1983, when 68 students filed for ASG positions and his supporters again filled the letters pages. Smith won the presidency of the Associated Student Government in the April 12, 1983 election, in which students also approved constitutional revisions. His victory came after roughly 500 students had voted in the primary the week before. His presidency was colorful and contentious: the fall brought a discount card controversy, letters accusing him of partying while committees waited and others defending him, and a December cartoon that he wrote in to protest. In April 1984 the Herald caught him impersonating a bunny as his ASG ran a low-turnout poll on beer and a campus pub. Smith's plaque term runs two years, 1983-85, and the Herald's own account of his exit backs that up: its April 11, 1985 issue reported him ending his term as ASG president in an article headlined 'Jack Smith Ends Term as Associated Student Government President,' alongside a companion piece crediting his enthusiasm with reviving interest in the organization. Smith's 1983 campaign drew an unusual run of supporting letters in the Herald. The issue of 7 April 1983 carried two, from Dorothy Metzmeler and Sarah Hein, following one from Tony Johnson the week before; the same issue reported that about 500 students had voted in the ASG primary. Jamie Morton reported on 14 April 1983 that Jack Smith had won the presidency of the Associated Student Government. The same issue reported that students had also voted in favor of the ASG constitutional revisions worked out that spring. His first term drew heavy comment. In December 1983 the Herald reported that ASG had voided its own procedures even as it saw growth in membership and took up fourteen proposals, and the same issue carried Stanley Reagan's letter headed "Jack Smith, Associated Student Government Thrown Away" along with another Lou Bloss cartoon on ASG. He filed for re-election in February 1984 and stayed in office through a second year, ending his term in April 1985. Jack Smith held the presidency of the Associated Student Government in 1983-84, the first of two years on a single plaque plate. He won the election of 12 April 1983 after about 500 students voted in the primary the week before, in a campaign carried by an unusual run of supporting letters in the Herald; the same ballot approved that spring's constitutional revisions. He chaired a Congress whose officers were administrative vice president Tony Whalen, treasurer Kelly S. Smith, secretary Teresa Anthony and public affairs vice president Happy Chandler, succeeded during the year by John Holland. The year brought a discount card controversy, letters accusing him of partying while committees waited and others defending him, a December cartoon he wrote in to protest, and a December report that ASG had voided its own procedures even as membership grew and fourteen proposals came forward. Smith filed for re-election in February 1984 and stayed in office a second year. In April 1984 the Herald caught him impersonating a bunny while his ASG ran a low-turnout poll on beer and a campus pub. The paper marked the end of his term on 11 April 1985 with a report headlined that he was ending his term as ASG president and a companion piece crediting his enthusiasm with reviving interest in the organisation. Smith presided over a productive opening to the 1984-85 year. By the third week of September the Herald reported that four ASG proposals had been made reality, and the congress had begun studying a student book exchange, which became the signature project of his final year. By mid-year the record was mixed. The book exchange venture appeared likely to take a summer pause, and the organization was weighing whether to fight cuts to education funding. His term ended in April 1985. The Herald covered his exit with a news story headlined that Smith was ending his term as ASG president, an editorial crediting his enthusiasm with reviving interest in the organization, and an editorial cartoon. The SGA plaque records him on a two-year 1983-85 plate. Jack Smith first won the presidency of the Associated Student Government in a race the College Heights Herald reported under the headline "Jack Smith Wins Presidency of Associated Student Government," in the paper's fifty-eighth volume. That win put him in the office he would go on to hold across more than one term. Smith and the Herald did not always get along. One issue in the paper's fifty-ninth volume indexed an item headed "Jack Smith, Associated Student Government Thrown Away" together with a letter written by Smith himself under the title "Cartoon Aggravates," showing that he answered the paper's cartoonists in print rather than letting the criticism stand. His time in office closed in April 1985, when Mack Humphreys wrote up Smith ending his term as Associated Student Government president. The Herald ran a second piece in the same issue crediting Smith's enthusiasm with reviving interest in ASG, and Kevin Knapp marked the departure with an editorial cartoon on Smith and the organisation.
people.sources: ASG Minutes, 29 Apr 1982; Herald 58:49, 24 Mar 1983; Herald 58:55, 14 Apr 1983; Herald 60:7, 20 Sep 1984

people.what_they_did: Jaden Marshall served as a senator at large in SGA's 23rd Senate in 2023-24, co-authoring, with Administrative Vice President Salvador Leon and others, the bill funding Neurodiversity Acceptance Week. He returned to the Senate for 2024-25, reappointed to a senator-at-large seat and confirmed by unanimous voice vote on 11 February 2025, and again for 2025-26 as an ISEC senator (Intercultural Student Engagement Center), where he co-authored a bill funding the Go With the Flow menstrual-product program together with a WKU Food Pantry donation drive, a Black History Trivia Night held with Why Knot Us and Black Women of Western, graduation cords for transfer students, and resolutions supporting the installation of drinking-water dispensers, printers and computers in residence halls and an accessible 24-hour space on campus. In April 2026 Marshall ran for SGA president on a ticket with Kaden Blankenship and Miles VanRude, against Caden Lucas, Jakob Barker and Will Derryberry, taking questions at a town hall in the DSU auditorium. On 13 April 2026 the Judicial Council, acting on its own initiative rather than a complaint, found the Marshall ticket guilty 4-0 of breaching the election code's ban on distributing perishable food within 48 hours of an election, after Red Bull cans were handed out at their campaign table and photographed for their campaign's social media story; the council issued a formal censure but declined to remove the ticket from the ballot. Two days later, on 15 April 2026, the council found the same ticket guilty 5-0 on a separate, unrelated complaint of campaigning in the Commons while voting was open; it censured and disbanded the ticket's campaign team rather than issuing a second censure to the ticket itself. Lucas's ticket won the election, with turnout up 66 percent over the previous year's uncontested race. Marshall was sworn into a new role at the first meeting of the 26th Senate on 28 April 2026, alongside Gabby Pace, Cayden Bailey and Maggie Phelps. Named as an author on one piece of SGA legislation in the 2023-24 session: Bill 4-24-S (Funding for the Neurodiversity Acceptance Week). Reappointed to a Senator-at-Large seat and confirmed by unanimous voice vote on 11 February 2025, having served SGA in an earlier capacity. Named as an author on six pieces of SGA legislation in the 2025-26 session: Resolution 4-25-F (Resolution to Support the Installation of Drinking Water Dispensers, Printers, and Computers within Residence Halls); Resolution 5-25-F (Resolution to Support an Administrative Commitment to Establish and Maintain an Accessible 24-Hour Space on Campus); Bill 10-25-F (Organizational Aid Funding Fall 2025); Bill 17-25-F (Funding for the Go With the Flow Program and WKU Food Pantry Donation Drive); Bill 1-26-S (Funding for the Black History Trivia Night in Partnership with Why Knot Us, Black Women of Western, and Student Government Association); Bill 22-26-S (Funding for SGA to purchase Graduation Cords for Transfer Students). Sworn in as a new at-large senator at the 26th Senate's first meeting, 28 April 2026, then ran for Speaker of the Senate the same night.

people.what_they_did: James Line chaired SGA's public relations committee in 2014-15, one of five new committee chairmen named at the first senate meeting of the year on 3 September 2014, alongside Josh Knight, Kasey Glasgow, Paige Settles and Tyler Scaff. James is also the person that will advise the entire executive cabinet throughout the entire year." Line himself said the MyCampusToo initiative, meant to broaden student involvement in SGA, would be "the centerpiece" of the coming year's work. As chief of staff, Line met with WKU's Counseling and Testing Center in March 2016 about its Sexual Assault Awareness Month programming. He continued as chief of staff into 2016-17, and in April 2017 he co-authored, with Administrative Vice President Hannah Neeper, a senate resolution urging WKU to prioritize future faculty salary increases over new construction, citing WKU's near-last ranking in faculty pay among its benchmark institutions. The 2016 Talisman profiled him under the headline "The President's Keeper." Line was appointed chief of staff by Jay Todd Richey and sworn in at the first meeting of September 2015, saying the MyCampusToo initiative to widen SGA's membership would be the centrepiece of the year. He worked through the spring on a policy for student parents, telling the senate SGA had nothing on its books about student mothers, and met the Counseling and Testing Center about Sexual Assault Awareness Month. He was one of the authors of the resolution setting out what SGA wanted from WKU's tenth president. In his second year as chief of staff Line ran SGA's voter work: Richey gave him the job of registering students and getting them to the polls, and on 8 November 2016 he ran the Ride To Vote shuttle from three campus pick-up points. He authored the bill co-sponsoring the 2016 Presidential Debate Fest, the constitutional amendment lowering SGA's membership requirement from a 2.5 to a 2.0 grade point average, which passed 24-7, the organizational aid inclusivity pledge, and, with administrative vice president Hannah Neeper, the resolution asking WKU to put faculty salaries ahead of new construction.

people.all_offices: president (2002-03); President (2002-03); Executive Vice President (2001-02); Congress member (membership shown by committee-meeting assignment and award nominations, not a swearing-in record among the minutes checked) (2000-01)
people.what_they_did: Assigned to attend a Parking and Transportation Committee meeting, 30 Jan 2001; named Outstanding Congress Member nominee twice (27 Feb, 10 Apr 2001). Jamie Sears served as executive vice president of the Student Government Association for 2001-02, alongside president Leslie Bedo; the Herald reported the pair preparing to move into the executive offices on 5 April 2001. She was named in the officer-report roll call of every Congress meeting checked across the year, from 28 August 2001 through 9 April 2002. She was elected SGA president the following spring and took office for 2002-03. Sears, a junior public relations major from Melber, won the presidency in a landslide, defeating senior Sam Stinson 1,284 votes to 594 in the April 2002 general election that also seated her incoming executive team: John Bradley as executive vice president, Ross Pruitt as vice president of finance, Anna Coats as vice president of public relations, and Brandon Copeland as vice president of administration. Sears opened her 2002-03 term as SGA president under immediate scrutiny. Seventeen months after congress passed a bill putting about $5,000 of leftover budget money toward an on-campus gazebo, members discovered the gazebo was never built and the money was gone. When three members petitioned congress in September over $28,000 they said was unaccounted for, Sears told the Herald, "I have absolutely no idea where that money went." The petition was withdrawn only after her executive council created an ad hoc financial review committee. By October the money had been traced: it had slipped back into SGA's general fund and been spent on other things, including computers for the SGA office. Sears acknowledged that she and former student activities director Scott Taylor had decided during the summer where the leftover money, which included the gazebo funds, would be allocated, saying other executive council members were consulted through email. She said the financial review committee would explain the budget findings to congress, and no move was made to set aside new gazebo money. Sears finished the year on stronger footing. She traveled with about 20 Western students to Frankfort to oppose state budget cuts to higher education, calling the trip one of SGA's greatest accomplishments: "That was a great feeling seeing students from everywhere rallying for the same cause." Under her leadership congress debated more than 55 pieces of legislation and passed the first student referendum in SGA history, a $3 fee for radio station Revolution 91.7 that students approved in the spring election. Her final meeting as president came on April 22, 2003.
people.sources: College Heights Herald 77:51, 11 Apr 2002 - "Jamie Sears Wins Election in Landslide" (O'Connor, Molly); SGA Meeting Minutes, August 28, 2001; SGA Meeting Minutes, January 30, 2001; WKU News, 11 Apr 2002

people.what_they_did: Appointed Chair of the Legislative Research Committee 11 February 2014. On 15 April 2014 the outgoing 12th Senate elected him to serve as Speaker of the incoming 13th Senate for 2014-15. Sat on the Executive Cabinet as Speaker through the year, then won the student body presidency in April 2015. Richey opened his first term in fall 2015 "leaving behind the Postergate controversy" of the spring election, saying he had "about a hundred things" he wanted to do. His priorities included MyCampusToo, a campaign initiative to bring underrepresented students into SGA, more outreach to international students and the regional campuses, and stronger communication between the executive cabinet and senate. He also oversaw a student competition to name the new pub coming to the Garrett Conference Center, a product of the alcohol-policy change SGA had supported the previous year. In September he championed the senate's resolution disapproving of how the Confucius Institute building was approved, writing in a letter to the Herald that the contract was signed in China before the Board of Regents voted and that many controversial details were never disclosed. He rejected warnings that the vote made "powerful enemies," saying he hoped it sent a message that "accountability and transparency should always be top priorities" at WKU, while noting he respected Ransdell and would keep working with him. In April 2016 Richey won reelection with 1,497 of 2,341 presidential votes, becoming a two-term president in a high-turnout election announced after midnight in the Downing Student Union senate chambers. "It's a tremendous honor to be elected the first time," he said, "but a second time is verification of promises kept." His running mate Kate Hart won executive vice president and MyCampusToo chairwoman Hannah Neeper won administrative vice president, keeping his allies in the executive branch for 2016-17. A March 2017 Herald profile noted the win made him WKU SGA's first two-term president since 1988 and one of only three since 1974. Also served as student regent under the merged offices. His re-election made him WKU SGA's first two-term president since 1988 and one of only three since 1974. Over his two terms he led the creation of three new committees, Sustainability, MyCampusToo and SAVES (Standing Against Violence and Ending Self-harm), revamped SGA's website, authored nine bills and resolutions, and represented students on the Board of Regents, the University Senate and the presidential search committee that chose WKU's 10th president. A Herald profile in March 2017 described a president who arrived late to office hours from overrun meetings, fielded budget questions and calls from the chief of police, and admitted he still struggled with low self-esteem. In a farewell letter published as his term ended, Richey wrote that fighting for college affordability had been a personal priority: SGA rallied at the Kentucky Capitol and lobbied the General Assembly against university budget cuts, and he chaired the Board of Student Body Presidents of Kentucky. He cited expanded services for military and veteran students, the Rave Guardian safety app, WKU's first eSports program, an SGA Voter Empowerment Initiative that registered hundreds of voters, new SGA scholarships including one for students with disabilities, and helping select president Tim Caboni. His successor Andi Dahmer took the oath of office on May 2, 2017. Also served as student regent under the merged offices.

people.what_they_did: Elected Speaker at the 6 December 2005 meeting over Josh Collins and Josh McCubbins after nominees spoke and were escorted out for the debate; she had chaired Campus Improvements that autumn and told senators in April to stop bringing legislation that had to be amended or rescinded. The 8 December 2005 Herald issue names her directly as the new speaker. Appointed chair on 6 September 2005; her committee met a Lexington design firm that autumn and she authored Bill 07-05-F, defending its cost as a service to the whole campus rather than to one organisation. Chaired in the fall by Jeanne Johnson (before she became Speaker), then by Tori Theiss in the spring; vice-chairs Christa Wilcox (fall) and Ben Redmon (spring, from 28 Feb 2006). Jeanne Johnson was executive vice president when Rob Watkins resigned the presidency and the student regent seat in November 2006. The senate minutes for 28 November record his resignation being read to the chamber and senators being told she would be sworn in at the Winter Banquet on 5 December; the minutes of that meeting list the executive vice presidency as vacant because she had moved up. The regent seat did not pass with the presidency, and Western went about two months without a student on its governing board. At the Board of Regents meeting of 26 January 2007 she spoke against the size of a 7.8 per cent tuition increase for online and distance learners without holding a vote, saying tuition increases were inevitable but that distance learners should not carry the burden. She won the special election for the seat the following week with 688 votes, 41 per cent of those cast. She was elected to a full term in her own right and sworn in as president and student regent at the SGA banquet on 1 May 2007, where she also received the Dero Downing Award. Jeanne Johnson was one of the candidates the Herald introduced in its 15 March 2005 special election edition ahead of that spring's SGA vote. By December 2005 she had risen to speaker of the senate, elected by her fellow senators at the meeting of 8 December that year, and in April 2006 she and Amanda Allen ran against each other in that spring's election, under a Herald headline arguing "Experience Helps Jeanne Johnson." She took office as executive vice president for 2006-07 and gave the office's report at the season-opening senate meeting on 5 September 2006. Her seat was vacant by the 5 December 2006 meeting because she had moved up to the presidency after Rob Watkins's resignation; the fuller account of that succession is in her presidential profile for 2006-07. Johnson was already SGA's sitting executive vice president when she presided over the senate as president pro tempore at the 28 November 2006 meeting, the session at which Rob Watkins's resignation was read into the record. She was sworn in as president the following week, at the Winter Banquet on 5 December 2006. Jeanne Lynn Johnson, a Marion senior and Kappa Delta member, had served as SGA's president pro tempore after Rob Watkins's November 2006 resignation and won the February 2007 special election for the vacant student regent seat with 688 votes. She became SGA president and student regent for 2007-08 in her own right, sworn onto the Board of Regents on April 27, 2007, and installed as president at SGA's May 2007 banquet. That fall her administration reported record interest in the senate election, 25 candidates for 20 seats, and she and Executive Vice President Johnathon Boles helped organize a mock gubernatorial election that drew 127 student voters. She pushed a senate resolution asking the state for more funding after Western received only 54 percent of its recommended budget increase, and organized Walk Out Western, an Oct. 25 class walkout protesting state budget cuts that President Gary Ransdell said he could not condone. As student regent, Johnson voted against the scale of the board's 9 percent tuition increase at the April 24, 2008 quarterly meeting, seconding Louisville regent Larry Zielke's motion to cap the increase at 6 percent and push the General Assembly for more funding instead; the motion died with only two votes. At the same meeting she argued the $370,000 budgeted for the Honors College should be cut, saying the college "only benefits 900 students" and other students should not have to pay for it; Ransdell defended it as part of the university's strategic plan. In the spring, as her administration ran the election to choose her successor, Johnson defended the one-week campaign window written into election codes she said were inherited from past administrations, warning that longer campaigns could hurt candidates' schoolwork and that "too much PR hurts." She pointed to new turnout efforts her administration tried, including holding the debate during SGA week and adding candidate profiles and questionnaires to the SGA website. Johnathon Boles won the March 2008 election and was installed as SGA president at the spring banquet, but Johnson kept the Board of Regents seat until the board's next quarterly meeting; a resolution read there on July 18, 2008 thanked her for "able leadership, faithful service, and dedication" and Boles took the oath as student regent the same day. In the spring, as her administration ran the election to choose her successor, Johnson defended the one-week campaign window written into election codes she said were inherited from past administrations, warning that longer campaigns could hurt candidates' schoolwork and that "too much PR hurts." She pointed to new turnout efforts her administration tried, including holding the debate during SGA week, arranging extra credit for students who attended it, and adding candidate profiles and questionnaires to the SGA website. Also held the Board of Regents' student seat; sworn onto the board 27 Apr 2007 and continued as regent through 18 Jul 2008, past the end of her presidency.

Joe Rains served as treasurer of the Associated Student Government for 1991-92, under president Heather Falmlen. He presented the 1991-92 budget for acceptance at the first Congress meeting on 3 September 1991, reported a running budget summary of $794.98 a fortnight later, and ran the organizational aid process that year, setting a 14 February 1992 application deadline with interviews set for 17 to 28 February. He was elected president for 1992-93, running against Mistianna Holcomb in the April 1992 vote; the same election carried a referendum on renaming the Associated Student Government the Student Government Association, and the organization went by the new name from that year. Joe Rains was elected Associated Student Government president on 14 April 1992, a contested race the Herald's election-day issue covered with dueling opinion pieces: an editorial headlined "Associated Student Government Needs Joe Rains" ran alongside a cartoon depicting him as Darth Vader, and the paper carried separate profile pieces on candidates Mark Miller, Mistianna Holcomb and Melony Jones. The same ballot carried the referendum that renamed Associated Students as the Student Government Association; Rains took office that autumn as the first president to serve under the new name. In office, Rains argued that SGA should support a campus student escort service (Herald, 10 December 1992) and took part in a rally at the state capitol in Frankfort urging the legislature to stop cuts to higher-education funding, for which the WKU University Senate commended him in Resolution R92.11. The archive does not preserve further detail of how the term ended. Rains ran for the presidency in April 1992 against Mistianna Holcomb, in the same election week that students voted on a referendum to rename the Associated Student Government as the Student Government Association. The Herald covered both races in a single issue, so his campaign and the rename were decided together. On election day the Herald's opinion pages carried a letter headlined "Associated Student Government Needs Joe Rains" alongside a Patrick Richardson editorial cartoon depicting Rains as Darth Vader, a sign of how visible the race had become on campus. The SGA's own list of presidents, published on its website in 2001, records Joe Rains of Nashville, Tennessee as the organization's 26th president, serving 1992-93, and marks him as having also served as student regent. The digitised record of his year does not name him directly in any indexed description, but it carries one distinctive trace: the minutes for December 1, 1992 record plans for a call-in radio show the association titled 'Just Ask Joe,' alongside Project Western and President for a Day. The same year's minutes show a congress preoccupied with state budget cuts, tuition increases, student health insurance and repeated plans for a rally in Frankfort. Approved as Foreman of the Judicial Council on 31 August 1993. He had been SGA president in 1992-93 and treasurer in 1991-92.

John "Jack" McKinney served as an Associate Justice on WKU SGA's Judicial Council beginning in fall 2016. At the SGA meeting of 11 October 2016, Chief Justice Cody Cox said he had received a complaint that several SGA members had allegedly made racist remarks, and the Judicial Council met the next day to decide whether to open an investigation. McKinney and senator Braxton Powell both resigned from SGA that Wednesday morning, 12 October 2016; Powell's resignation letter cited scheduling conflicts, and Associate Chief Justice Annalicia Carlson said McKinney resigned for "personal reasons." The Herald reported that neither man confirmed or denied the allegations, or said their resignations were connected to them, and that SGA did not release the names of those accused or describe the alleged remarks. The Herald also reported that the Judicial Council did not go forward with an investigation because the students it would have examined had already left SGA, without identifying those students as McKinney and Powell. The record does not show the allegation being confirmed, denied or otherwise resolved.
people.sources: SGA Judicial Council page, archived 1 Nov 2016 (last modified 29 Aug 2016)

Lyne first ran for Associated Students office in the March 1969 election, contesting the vice-presidential ('second spot') race against David Porter and losing; Porter went on to serve as Larry Zielke's vice president for 1969-70. A year later, no one filed against Lyne for the 1970-71 presidency, and the Herald reported on 13 March 1970 that he had 'won the presidency before the race begins.' Doug Alexander won the vice presidency the same election cycle, beating Steve Tichenor, in a vote held the following week. The term began against the backdrop of the Kent State shootings that May: the Associated Student Congress's October 1970 resolution on the women's curfew ran in a Herald issue whose letters page was dominated by students arguing about Kent State, and the same fall the Board of Regents seated eight students on the Academic Council. Beyond the curfew resolution, the Congress passed a lecture bill on 6 November 1970 funding campus appearances by William Kunstler and Bernadette Devlin, and separately endorsed a proposed new constitution two weeks later; a study committee kept refining it, reaching judicial-reform provisions by February 1971. John Lyne was one of the most visible students on the Hill before taking office, writing a steady stream of Herald columns through 1969-70 and representing Kentuckians in the national draft lottery drawing in December 1969. Lyne won the Associated Students presidency in March 1970 without opposition, the Herald reporting that he had captured the office before the race began. Through 1970-71 Lyne fought his administration's corner in the Herald's letters column, complaining in January that he had been kept in the dark about an appointment and defending the Associated Students lecture series against attack that April, in the issue that reported W.S. Moss taking the oath as regent. Unopposed.

people.all_offices: president (2008-09); Executive Vice President (2007-08); Speaker of the Senate (2006-07); Senator; SGA archivist (2005-06)
people.what_they_did: Sworn in as a Senator 27 Sep 2005; prolific spring author (Professor of the Year, Camera Purchase, SGA Portrait, Election Forum) and appointed SGA archivist 14 Mar 2006. Gave Academic Affairs reports when the chair was absent but is never named vice-chair in the minutes. Nominated Committee Member of the Semester (minutes-222); he was not nominated Speaker of the Senate or Senator of the Semester. Johnathon Boles served as executive vice president for 2007-08. He sat on a faculty advisory committee for athletics and helped arrange a November 2007 consultation with athletics director Wood Selig on increasing football attendance. In March 2008 he ran to succeed Jeanne Johnson as president, facing Tedde Harden in a Herald-hosted candidate forum on 25 March, and published campaign op-eds on 27 March and 3 April arguing that a diverse student body needed "one voice" through SGA and asking students to use their vote as "an instrument for your voice." He won that election and served as president for 2008-09, detailed in his own presidential profile. Johnathon Boles ran for SGA president in spring 2008 on the "Red Towel Party" ticket, a slate that also carried Theodore Harden, Reagan Gilley, Skylar Johnson, Kayla Shelton and Kevin Smiley as candidates for other executive and senate offices. After Boles's ticket won, Skylar Jordan filed a complaint against the Red Towel Party; the SGA council took no action on it on 22 April 2008, and the result stood. Boles, a junior from Elizabethtown, served as SGA president and student regent for 2008-09. In November 2008, Gov. Steve Beshear appointed him and fellow SGA member Kevin Smiley to the student committee of the governor's College Access Work Group on college affordability, and Boles traveled to Frankfort for its first meeting, where he raised the burden of textbook costs. "I'm honored the governor chose me to represent WKU," he said. In December 2008, Boles led SGA through its first mid-year budget cut, after a state shortfall required the university to trim about 4 percent. He and Administrative Vice President Reagan Gilley cut $4,100 from SGA's $110,000 budget while protecting scholarships and Provide-A-Ride, and Boles addressed the senate about the cuts, saying he would keep fighting for the affordability of higher education. He also worked to arrange charter buses to a Feb. 3 rally in Frankfort against cuts to higher education. Boles resigned on Jan. 30, 2009, for health reasons, midway through his term. Executive Vice President Kayla Shelton took his place as president but not as student regent, and the student body went 26 days without a regent until Reagan Gilley won a special election on Feb. 25. Gilley said he planned to contact Boles the day after his win to get up to date on Board of Regents business.
people.sources: Herald, 1 Nov 2007 (Wayback); SGA Meeting Minutes, 27 Sep 2005; SGA Senate minutes, 28 Nov 2006, TopSCHOLAR; TopSCHOLAR - Frankfort rally reflections

people.what_they_did: Josh Collins, a junior from Jackson studying geography and Spanish, joined SGA in 2003 and was sworn in as a justice of the judicial council in September that year. When president-elect Nick Todd was accused in April 2004 of misusing more than $600 from the SGA Dining Dollars account, it was Collins who drafted the articles of impeachment against Todd's finance vice presidency, though the judicial council ruled a two-week impeachment could not be finished before Todd left that office anyway. Collins told the Herald the organisation would “be hearing echoes of this for a while.” That March he had run for administrative vice president, campaigning on clarifying university policies for students and building a searchable database of past SGA legislation, and calling the previous autumn's rally against plus/minus grading “the clearest, most recent event that was SGA working, making our voices be heard.” He lost that race to Evelina Petkova, 692 votes to 481. In February 2005 the Herald reported that he and Katie Dawson had announced plans to run for SGA president; Dawson was elected that spring. Chaired the Academic Affairs Committee in 2004-05, per the WKU SGA legislative branch page's list of standing committee chairs. The chair was still unfilled when the rest were appointed on 6 September 2005; Collins was chairing by December, reporting that all legislation had to pass through his committee. Speaker Jed Conrad ran LRC until Josh Collins was appointed chair 4 Oct 2005; Josh Collins chaired it for the rest of the year, with Jonathon 'J.P.' Roy as spring vice-chair.

people.what_they_did: Held the chair by April 2019 in place of Trevor Huffman, and kept it through the following year. Zaczek was confirmed as chair of SGA's Legislative Research Committee in the first meeting of the 2019-20 year, on 3 September 2019, and for the term's first month was the Senate's only confirmed committee chair, which led him to insist that his own sponsorship of a bill and his committee's approval of it be treated as separate steps and that all legislation clear his committee before a first reading. He was a persistent skeptic of executive spending plans that fall. During a September 2019 budget standoff over whether to fund scholarships or a special-projects fund for sand volleyball and hammock space in the new First Year Village, Zaczek argued the recreational spending did little more for student engagement than students already got from picnicking or playing frisbee, and the following week warned that halving campaign spending caps could shut low-income students out of running for office. When the hammock bill returned in March 2020, he pressed the executive board for a full accounting of how the money would be spent before he would vote for it, saying he wanted to know the funds were being used "in an all-inclusive way." On legislation, Zaczek proposed an amendment during February 2019 debate on a study-abroad-scholarship bill, and after it was pulled and rewritten by its authors he remained critical of the revised version, saying it was "detracting from a merit-based scholarship" and questioning how SGA could verify applicants' answers. In October 2019 the Senate struck "removal from campus" from the title of a resolution seeking penalties against a sorority chapter over members' use of a racial slur in a video; Zaczek's friendly amendment put "suspension from Greek affairs" in its place, and the resolution passed 24-7. Already recorded as Legislative Research Committee Chair; the 3 March 2020 Senate minutes separately call him "Senator Zaczek" twice during floor debate on Bill 3-20-S — first asking about the project's timeline, then about its funding source — confirming he held a Senate seat in addition to chairing the committee.
people.sources: SGA Senate minutes, 10 Sep 2019; SGA Senate minutes, 16 Apr 2019; SGA Senate minutes, 3 Mar 2020

people.what_they_did: Listed among the Judicial Council members on the SGA judicial page as archived 21 Jan 2022. Goins held the associate chief justice's seat on the Judicial Council at the start of 2022-23, under Chief Justice Holden Schroeder, and is recorded in that office in the council's minutes of 16 September 2022. He left it in January 2023 on being elected chief justice in Schroeder's place, and nominated Isaac King to succeed him as associate chief justice at the meeting of 24 January 2023. Goins served as an associate justice on the Judicial Council in 2021-22, then moved up to associate chief justice under Chief Justice Holden Schroeder at the start of 2022-23. After Schroeder left the council, the Senate elected Goins chief justice on 17 January 2023, in a vote Parliamentarian Meghan Pierce moved up the agenda; President Cole Bornefeld swore him in and he then swore in that meeting's new senators. He went on to nominate Isaac King as his associate chief justice. On 17 February 2023 Goins presided over a Judicial Council hearing on Speaker of the Senate Julie Mishchuk's censure complaint against President Bornefeld, who had liked several Instagram posts Mishchuk said were transphobic; Mishchuk read the council a letter from the Queer Student Union about the visibility given to transgender students and said the group had removed SGA from its list of safe spaces; QSU's president said the same to the Senate four days later. The council heard both sides and voted unanimously against censure, and Goins announced the decision, saying the justices "could not find any basis for discrimination in the current WKU constitution."
