people.what_they_did: Won $50 Big Red Dollars for Congress attendance on 20 April 2004 and moved to suspend the bylaws on 2 March 2004 to seat Dana Lockhart on the Judicial Council. She was sworn in on 2 September 2003 as a committee head, a separate class from Congress members, but the Congress attendance award names her as a Congress member. Sworn in as a committee head on 2 September 2003; defended the committee's private-information-security, hooded-sweatshirt and broadband-expansion-fee legislation that year. Tim Howard is named alongside her in the committee's 2 December 2003 report; his specific role is not stated in the minutes. Katie Dawson held the SGA presidency for about two months in the summer of 2004 without having been elected to it. She had come up through the cabinet as Nick Todd's running mate in the March election and was his executive vice president when he resigned in July amid the Dining Dollars investigation. She acted in the office until students voted in a special election that September. Hers is the only one of the archive's four mid-year vacancies filled this way. In 2004 the presidency was treated as vacant and put back to the students, with the executive vice president acting until they had voted. When Rob Watkins resigned in November 2006 and when Johnathon Boles resigned in January 2009, the executive vice president succeeded to the office instead, Jeanne Johnson being sworn in as president at that year's Winter Banquet. The same organisation met the same kind of vacancy in two different ways within five years. She was elected president in her own right for 2005-06, and the Chambers wall carries her for that year alone. Elected Todd's running mate in March 2004; acted as interim president during the summer 2004 vacancy and continued as Johnson's EVP through the year before winning the presidency herself for 2005-06. Dawson served as both SGA president and student regent during Western's centennial year. When the university launched its 14-month centennial celebration on Nov. 19, 2005, she spoke at the dedication of Centennial Plaza, offering her own meaning for the school slogan: "Find what you love and carry it with you your whole life through." Her spring semester was dominated by a proposed $46-per-semester fee for three campus construction projects. At a student forum with President Gary Ransdell she suggested exempting the next year's seniors, who would graduate before any project was finished; the Board of Regents rejected the exemption 10-1 at its April 7 meeting and approved the fee 9-1. Dawson cast the lone abstention, saying that although she supported the fee, she could not vote for it with so many seniors counting on the exemption. Her term ended at Western's 159th commencement on May 13, 2006, where the Radcliff native graduated with a degree in corporate and organizational communication and addressed her 1,797 fellow undergraduates as SGA president. She charged the graduates to have courage, endurance, strength, patience and character, saying success was knowing "when to throw in the towel and when to wave it around and cheer."

people.what_they_did: Sworn in to the Student Senate 3 October 2006 under the minutes' own "Senate Swearing In" heading — but she had already been approved Student Affairs Committee chair on 12 September and reported again as chair that same 3 October night, before her recorded oath. The record does not explain the sequencing; an earlier, untranscribed swearing-in is possible but unconfirmed. Unfilled at the 5 Sep. 2006 opening meeting; Shelton chaired it by the 28 Nov. and 5 Dec. 2006 meetings. Presided from the first meeting of the sixth Senate on 4 September 2007 through the spring; she announced Cacy Schooler's resignation and Jacob Miers's succession as Secretary on 4 December 2007 and questioned all three candidates for her own successor in April. Kayla Shelton ran on Johnathon Boles's "Red Towel Party" ticket in the spring 2008 SGA election and served as executive vice president for 2008-09. When Boles resigned as president and student regent on 30 Jan. 2009 for health reasons, Shelton succeeded him as president but not as student regent, leaving the regent seat vacant. As president, Shelton backed the SGA Judicial Council's 2-1 decision to hold a special student regent election rather than leave the seat vacant, over the dissent of Executive Vice President Skylar Jordan, saying "That's what they decided, so I support it" and that her main focus remained serving the student body. She also accepted Chief Justice Lisa Kappler's resignation in mid-February, which came with the regent election two weeks away. Administrative Vice President Reagan Gilley won that special election on 25 Feb. 2009, taking over the regent's seat while Shelton continued as president through the rest of the term. Shelton presided over the senate through the spring, including a Feb. 24 meeting where senators debated and rejected, 13 votes to 9, a bill to cover an extra $82.27 for water bottles SGA had earlier agreed to fund as prizes for a Housing and Residence Life energy-saving contest. Shelton said she thought it was great that the senate debated something it felt passionate about rather than casting "just a general yes or no." Shelton did not continue as president into 2009-10; Kevin Smiley won the regular spring election for that term on 16 April 2009. Kayla Shelton, who had been executive vice president, became SGA president after Johnathon Boles resigned, serving out the rest of the 2008-09 year. She inherited a dispute over whether to hold a special election for the vacant student regent seat, and when the Judicial Council voted 2-1 in February to hold one despite objections from other executives, she backed the decision. "That's what they decided, so I support it," Shelton said, adding that her main focus remained serving the student body. Kayla Shelton ran for executive vice president alongside presidential candidate Johnathon Boles in the spring 2008 election, running against Kevin Smiley, and took office for 2008-09. She reported to the senate's first meeting of the year, on 26 August 2008, on the fall retreat she was organizing, and represented SGA that year on the Academic Quality Committee and the parking ticket appeals board. When Boles resigned the presidency in January 2009, Shelton succeeded him as president for the balance of the term - the fuller account is in her presidential profile for 2008-09 - and in April 2009 she was a candidate in the election for a full term as president, which Kevin Smiley won.

people.what_they_did: Boka, the outgoing executive vice president, was elected 2013-14 SGA president on 4 April 2013 with 626 votes (47 percent), beating administrative vice president Cain Alvey (419 votes) and Austin Wingate (300). Five days later the Judicial Council voted 3-2 to disqualify her after Alvey, the runner-up who stood to become president if she were removed, complained that a self-promotional email had gone to Honors College students at her request. Boka appealed to Howard Bailey, WKU's vice president for Student Affairs, who reinstated her; the Judicial Council declined to contest his ruling in an emergency meeting on 16 April, with Chief Justice Seth Church calling the intervention "a serious infringement on our autonomy" and Boka countering that the council itself had conflicts of interest. In office, Boka's fall 2013 senate created a new international student senate seat for Navitas/ESL students and finalized a $125,000 budget, part of which sent her and executive vice president Mark Reeves on a Washington, D.C. higher-education lobbying trip. She fielded student anger over new two-tier priority registration rules at a November open forum with Provost Gordon Emslie, and announced the permanent closure of Thompson Complex North Wing, long slated for demolition. A senate attempt to reverse SGA's support for the Talisman's student fee was struck down by the Judicial Council as unconstitutional, as was the underlying 2005 policy. In spring 2014 Boka organized a Frankfort rally against a $1.8 million state budget cut to WKU and opposed a senate amendment stripping the president's sole power to appoint Judicial Council justices, which was sent back to committee after the council found too few senators had been present to pass it. At the year's final meeting she announced a 4.8 percent tuition increase for the coming year, and the senate passed a resolution backing a Good Samaritan policy to protect students who called 911 during drug or alcohol overdoses.

Some minutes and one Herald headline spell the forename Kristin; the spelling here follows the archive's other records and is not settled. Miller had been a Herald columnist and an SGA officer before winning the presidency; her letters in the paper defending the organization date to 1994. In her first weeks as president in August 1996 she made a plan to drive party-goers home, the beginning of what became the Provide-A-Ride service. As student body president she was the student representative on the committee searching for WKU's ninth president. Interviewed in 2016, she recalled serious talk of cutting football or academic programs, saying "there was one pot of money everyone was fighting over," and described how a late-arriving alumnus candidate named Gary Ransdell impressed the committee by pulling out a binder full of plans after his interview. In March 1997 the Herald ran "Kristen Miller Reflects on Year as Student Government Association President" as her term wound down. The SGA's 2001 list of presidents records Kristen L. Miller of Louisville as the 30th president and marks her as having also served as student regent. Miller won the SGA presidency in April 1996 at the end of a four-way race, with the Herald's news coverage declaring 'It's Kristen Miller's Time.' A week earlier the paper had profiled her campaign under the headline 'Kristen Miller Focuses on Experience in Student Government Association.' Days into the fall semester, the Herald reported 'Kristen Miller Makes Plan to Drive Party-Goers Home.' The idea became Provide-a-Ride, the safe-ride program that appears in SGA's minutes throughout 1996-97 and was still being funded by the congress years later. Near the end of her term, the Herald ran 'Kristen Miller Reflects on Year as Student Government Association President,' looking back on a year that included the creation of a Technology Committee, the Provide-a-Ride launch and SGA's narrow vote to back adding sexual orientation to Western's anti-discrimination policy.

Called the Congress meeting of 13 April 1999 to order while the president and executive vice president were counting election ballots. Leslie Bedo served as vice president of the Student Government Association for 2000-01, elected on the ticket with president Cassie Martin. She went on to run for SGA president herself the following spring alongside vice-presidential candidate Jamie Sears; the Herald reported on 5 April 2001 that the two were preparing to move into the executive offices, and she took office as president for 2001-02. Leslie Bedo, a senior corporate communications major from Bowling Green, served as SGA president for 2001-02 after three years in the organization, having previously been parliamentarian, public relations committee chair and executive vice president. Her stated priorities for the year were tuition, student health and online course syllabi, and she described SGA as run "by the students, for the students." As student regent, Bedo pushed back in August 2001 when the Board of Regents raised tuition 9 percent at a meeting held before fall classes officially began. She said the timing sent "a message to students" that the increase would pass before they could weigh in, though she ultimately joined the board's unanimous vote approving it. That November, Bedo wrote a Herald op-ed titled "Meeting Goals of Student Government Association, But Not Students'", questioning the organization's effectiveness; fellow member Troy Ransdell responded in the same issue with a piece headlined "Action, Not Complaints." The same paper reported SGA was buying Christmas presents for children at Potter Children's Home that season. In March 2002, near the end of her term, Bedo publicly challenged the university after a land deal meant to add 400 to 500 parking spaces fell through while the Diddle Arena renovation was removing about 200 spaces. She noted regents had raised the student athletics fee on the expectation of more parking, said "the parking has been put on hold," and called added parking imperative because more students parked on campus than attended basketball games. As her term wound down, an April 30, 2002 Herald profile by Molly O'Connor reported renewed interest in SGA under Bedo's leadership. Jamie Sears was elected to succeed her that April; Bedo's own former rival for vice president of administration, Patti Johnson, went on to become SGA president herself in a September 2004 special election. Already recorded as president/regent for this year from other sources; corroborated here as the officer presiding over the President's report at Congress's first meeting of the year.

people.what_they_did: Linda Jones is listed as secretary of the Judicial Committee in the 1971 Talisman's Associated Students section, serving under committee chairman David Eyler and vice-chairman Michael E. Freville, in the same year that Carol Gray held the separately elected office of ASG secretary. A different Linda Jones was elected Associated Students president in April 1971, but the archive holds no source connecting the two, and this record does not merge them. Jones was elected the first woman president of the Associated Student Government on 6 April 1971; the Western Alumnus photographed her being sworn in with faculty regent Lowell Harrison by Georgia Bates. That fall, on 14 September 1971, the Herald reported the Associated Students affiliating with a wider student association, though the article index alone does not identify which body. By 1 February 1972, four years after the student regent seat was created, the Herald was still reporting the seat had no vote. Through February and March 1972, Jones's Congress pushed a rewritten constitution: it voted section by section on 22 February, when the Herald printed the executive branch's full text, and the Herald reported the executive branch accepted on 29 February. The same 29 February issue reported the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union planning court action connected to Associated Students and The Fly, a separate WKU underground newspaper, and carried Jones's own piece, 'Associated Students Corrects Herald', a public correction of the paper's coverage of the organization. The archive does not yet hold the text of either the KCLU piece or Jones's correction, so the underlying dispute and what she corrected both remain unconfirmed. Days earlier, the Herald's 25 February 1972 issue ran under the headline 'Chaos Reigns at Associated Students Meeting', alongside a separate piece arguing that student interest in the organization had collapsed and the Associated Students had followed it down. The constitution went to referendum at the end of March: the Herald's 28 March issue urged students to 'Vote Yes' ahead of a two-day vote, and Associated Students formally endorsed the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union's lawsuit in the same issue. The archive does not yet show the referendum's result or turnout. Her term closed on 28 April 1972 as a Mass Action Committee called for a strike over dorm visitation and the Associated Students installed its next officers; the same issue reported students had won six votes on a university council, and carried Jones's own reflection on her year in office.
people.sources: 1971 Talisman, Associated Students, pp. 68-69; Herald 51:50, 28 Apr 1972

people.all_offices: Administrative Vice President (2014-15); Administrative Vice President (2015-16)
people.what_they_did: Liz Koehler served as SGA's administrative vice president for 2014-15, taking office that August alongside President Nicki Seay and Executive Vice President Nolan Miles. Koehler won a second term in the spring 2015 election, taking 66 percent of the vote over J. William Berry, in the same election that made Jay Todd Richey president and returned Miles unopposed for a second term as executive vice president. That September, after SGA's budget fell $19,500 — largely because a one-time $15,000 private donation was not repeated and the university cut a further $4,500 — she reallocated $4,000 from organizational aid back into scholarships to soften the loss. The following February she reported an expected 4.5 percent cut to SGA's own budget, a loss of $1,301.27, amid the senate's debate over a state tuition-freeze bill. Koehler was elected administrative vice president in April 2015 with 66 percent of the vote against J. William Berry, and kept the budget through a year in which SGA's money fell by $19,500 after a $15,000 private donation was not repeated. She moved $4,000 out of organizational aid back into scholarships and warned that fewer organisations would be funded; in February 2016 she reported a further 4.5 percent cut worth $1,301.27. At the executive cabinet on 1 December 2015 she moved the $600 that kept the library open longer through finals week, argued against a separate Judicial Council adviser and a code of conduct, and proposed that SGA take up suicide awareness after a student's death.
people.sources: Herald, 28 Aug 2014; SGA Executive Cabinet minutes, 1 Dec 2015

Logan Hornback was a senator-at-large in WKU SGA's 2017-18 session. With senator Amanda Harder, Hornback co-authored Bill 15-18-S, allocating $300 to the newly formed WKU Students for Breast Cancer Awareness for its #WhyIFight fundraising campaign, and was among six senators and officers named on Bill 17-18-S, which put $500 toward Take Back the Night event T-shirts during Sexual Assault Prevention Month. Both bills passed on second reading in March 2018. Student Body President Stephen Mayer nominated Hornback to fill a vacant at-large Senate seat at the meeting of 16 October 2018. A vote-counting software error initially reported that the confirmation vote had failed; the error was found and corrected later that night, and it was ruled Hornback had in fact been elected to the seat, the Herald reported two months later when a second contested nomination revived the story. Hornback continued serving into spring 2019 and spoke in favor of a $5 student fee to fund the Herald at the 23 April 2019 meeting, saying that although the fee would add to tuition, "at least we know it will benefit the rest of the students." Hornback sat on SGA SAVES. He authored the resolution asking the Counseling and Testing Center to take appointments online, $300 for the newly formed WKU Students for Breast Cancer Awareness, and $500 for T-shirts for Take Back the Night during Sexual Assault Prevention Month. Nominated by President Mayer to fill a vacant Senate seat, confirmed 18-14-2 and sworn in at the same meeting, 16 Oct. 2018, after a motion out of the bylaws so she could join the debate. She is not named in the minutes of the previous meeting, 2 Oct. 2018.
people.sources: SGA Bill 15-18-S, 2017-18 session; SGA Senate minutes, October 16, 2018; SGA legislation: Bill 15-18-S, Funding for the WKU Students for Breast Cancer Awareness

Marc Levy served as an ASG Congress member in 1974-75 and again in 1975-76, and was one of the Herald's most frequent student critics through both years, writing letters attacking Associated Student Government, the Herald itself, the Academic Council and the ASG constitution in issue after issue. In a letter printed in the Herald of 4 October 1974, Levy wrote that he had hoped the year's meetings would differ from what he called the previous year's "invisible congress." He reported that a roll call at the meeting of 1 October 1974 showed a good number of members missing, and that three of the four committee reports were delivered by president Jeff Consolo himself rather than by the committee chairs. In the fall of 1975 Levy brought a complaint against ASG treasurer David Payne over spending ahead of budget approval. The Judicial Council heard the case and cleared Payne of fund misuse, reported in the Herald's 21 November 1975 issue (51:25) under the headline "Judicial Council Clears David Payne of Fund Misuse"; the same issue separately reported Levy had been picked "top legislator" at a recent intercollegiate meeting, without the archive confirming which one. Who's Who profile states he was active in the Academic Council, Associated Student Government (ASG) and Forensics Union, and made student government his major concern at Western. He also appears on the ASG Attendance Roll, and a separate ASG-related item describes him bringing spending-violation charges against ASG treasurer David Payne before the Judicial Council (council ruled for Payne).
people.sources: 1975 Talisman, Associated Student Government; 1976 Talisman, Who's Who, p. 63

people.what_they_did: Marcel Bush won the Associated Student Government presidency in April 1981, defeating David Sturgeon after a campaign the Herald said saw candidates "playing big time politics." Close races elsewhere on the ballot prompted recounts. In office that fall, ASG raised its own campaign spending limit and vetoed a plan to pay an education lobbyist, days after rallying publicly for higher education funding. Bush later listed the fall rally as one achievement of his term. Bush resigned the presidency on or shortly before 14 January 1982, reported the same week as the retrospective on his term. David Payne succeeded him; Board of Regents minutes from 30 January 1982 name Payne the new SGA president. Resigned 14 Jan 1982.

people.what_they_did: Chairs the Complaint and Suggestion committee from 7 Oct 1980; appointed student member to the University Academic Complaint Committee by President Fuller with the consent of Congress, 17 Feb 1981; nominated for Outstanding Congress Member, 31 Mar 1981. Name spelled Ragan, Ragen, Raden and Racan across different scans, all the same committee chair. nothing in either year's sourced record connects the two directly, so no identity is asserted here. Reporting for the committee by 7 October 1980 and after, succeeding Debbie Thomas. Margaret Ragan survived the April 1982 Associated Student Government presidential primary along with Glenn Sargent, emerging from a five-way field. Endorsement letters for her ran in the Herald through both rounds of the election. After the first general election was voided, Ragan won the presidency in the repeated election held April 20, 1982. She and the other new officers were sworn in before the month was out. Midway through her term Ragan used the Herald's pages to explain that the ASG presidency and the student regent seat were now separate positions. Her spring saw a grade plan, a student shuttle vote, and a contested rewrite of the ASG constitution before Jack Smith was elected to succeed her. Ragan's presidency came out of a disrupted spring. The Associated Student Government repeated its general election on 20 April 1982, after the Herald had reported the previous week that the first round's results were void. She set out her agenda at the start of the fall term. Monica Dias reported in the Herald's second issue of the year that major ASG changes were envisioned by Margaret Ragan, and over the following months the congress took up a campus Wall of Fame, a joint coed housing poll with the Interhall Council, and a coed housing bill it approved in November. Ragan also argued in print for keeping the two student offices distinct. In February 1983 the Herald carried her statement that the Associated Student Government and the student regent position were separate, in the same issue that reported the ASG shuttle service. Won a repeated general election 20 April 1982 after the first was voided; succeeded by Jack Smith in April 1983.
people.sources: ASG Minutes, 7 Oct 1980; Herald 57:53, 8 Apr 1982; Herald 57:57, 22 Apr 1982

people.what_they_did: Clark was a senator in fall 2017, later confirmed as a senator at large by early 2018, co-authoring Resolution 7-17-F with Lily Nellans and student Francisco Serrano, backing a proposed Bowling Green Fairness Ordinance protecting LGBTQ residents from discrimination; it was sponsored through the Committee for Diversity and Inclusion and read 14-28 November 2017. He co-authored Bill 5-18-S with Administrative Vice President Kara Lowry in February 2018, proposing funding for a recycled computer for the Pride Center. He became chair of the Committee of Diversity and Inclusion in February 2018, replacing Corey Newsome, who had stepped down over scheduling conflicts. The same week, on 13 February, the senate unanimously passed Resolution 1-18-S, which Clark co-authored with Chief of Staff Conner Hounshell and Kara Lowry, supporting an integrated LGBTQ-health curriculum at WKU. As chair, he authored Bill 7-18-S, funding food for CDI's first spring meeting, and co-authored Bill 13-18-S with Hounshell and Jayden Thomas, funding $250 in stoles for the Lavender Recognition Ceremony honoring LGBTQ graduates; it passed 28-5 on 20 March 2018. After Senator Dallas McKinney cited his reading of the Bible as his reason for voting against the bill, LGBTQ students and SGA members addressed the senate on 3 April, and Clark, speaking as Diversity and Inclusion chair, told the meeting that people in the room had demonstrated discrimination towards the LGBTQ community while a harmless funding bill was being passed. Clark authored or co-authored the year's LGBTQ legislation: the resolution backing a Bowling Green fairness ordinance, which he wrote with Lily Nellans and Francisco Serrano and which passed 34-2 at the meeting of 28 November 2017; the resolution for an integrated LGBTQ+ health curriculum in medical education; $150 for a recycled computer in the Pride Center; $250 for the stoles at WKU's first Lavender Graduation, passed 28-5 on 20 March 2018, a figure the Herald printed the morning after the vote and again a week later, though its recap of 4 April gave it as 26-5; and $150 for the first meeting of the new Committee of Diversity and Inclusion, which he chaired. Clark had set up the Committee of Diversity and Inclusion as its first chair in spring 2018 and took the chair again in October 2018. In September 2019 he co-authored the bill that put $500 into the Bowling Green Pride Festival, which passed on its second reading on 10 September. Named on the document as senator.
people.sources: SGA Bill 7-18-S, Funding for the First Meeting of the Committee of Diversity and Inclusion; SGA Senate minutes, 23 Oct 2018; SGA legislation: Bill 13-18-S, Funding for Lavender Graduation Stoles; SGA legislation: Bill 2-19-F, Funding for the Bowling Green Pride Festival

people.all_offices: Executive Vice President (2013-14); Senator, Graduate Students (2012-13)
people.what_they_did: Sworn in as a graduate senator on 25 September 2012, before running for and winning executive vice president the following spring for 2013-14. Mark Reeves, a Louisville graduate student, was sworn in as a graduate senator in September 2012 before running for executive vice president the following spring. He won the April 2013 general election with 632 votes, 57 percent, defeating Brad Cockrel's 485; asked how it felt, he said he was "really privileged and honored that the students chose this" and that he appreciated the chance to serve. As executive vice president in 2013-14, Reeves co-authored with President Keyana Boka a constitutional amendment creating a senate seat for Navitas and English-as-a-second-language international students; the Judicial Council initially struck the wording down as unconstitutional before the senate passed a revised version. He also introduced a resolution opposing WKU athletics' automatic annual fee increase ahead of the move to Conference USA, arguing that WKU paid $80,000 in Sun Belt Conference dues but received only $40,000 back in revenue sharing. A Herald editorial later criticized him for voting for a new priority-registration policy at the University Senate without first bringing it to SGA for debate. Reeves also spoke to senators about the state budget, warning in February 2014 that further cuts were likely, and joined Boka on a Washington, D.C. lobbying trip that year. At a South Campus forum that November he said WKU had made the same mistake it made when it closed the South Campus food court, again failing to consult South Campus students before closing the campus store there.
people.sources: Herald, 26 Sep 2012, "SGA welcomes new senators"; Herald, 4 Apr 2013

people.what_they_did: Mark Wilson was elected to a top Associated Student Government office on 24 April 1980, reported alongside president-elect Steve Fuller and Activities Vice President-elect Greg Zoeller. ASG's own minutes name him Administrative Vice President giving officer reports in meetings read from 7 October 1980 through 17 February 1981, and record him chairing the Legislative Research committee, one of two committee chairmanships Congress approved by name at the year's first meeting. Marshall Galloway sat in the Associated Students Congress in 1971-72, under president Linda Jones, vice president Reginald Glass, secretary Nancy Pape and treasurer Joe Glasser. The Congress group photograph on pp. 272-273 of the 1972 Talisman is the only record of the term found: it names the members and gives no office, seat or committee. The same pages record the Congress's year - elections for class officers, Who's Who and Homecoming queen, an October mock election for governor, an autumn symposium at which students questioned administrators, a renewed attempt at constitutional revision, and the revival of the Kentucky Student Association among the state's student governments.

people.what_they_did: Approved by unanimous Congress vote as Parliamentarian on 16 September 2003, after being announced for swearing-in that night. Chaired the Legislative Research Committee in 2004-05, per the WKU SGA legislative branch page's list of standing committee chairs. Mason Stevenson, a Princeton junior double-majoring in broadcasting and political science, joined SGA as parliamentarian in fall 2003, a non-voting post he said taught him parliamentary procedure; he had previously served as treasurer of the Southwest Hall Council and was a resident assistant at Bemis Lawrence Hall, and had earlier helped start a College Republicans chapter at Paducah Community College. He ran for one of the new senate's elected seats that March, saying he wanted a vote in decisions rather than the parliamentarian's advisory role, and won; that fall he chaired the senate's Legislative Research Committee. In March 2005 Stevenson and Melissa Paris were elected to SGA's two vice presidencies unopposed, alongside Katie Dawson's contested win for president. As executive vice president in 2005-06, he read a letter to the 2 March 2006 SGA meeting airing a rift between the executive and legislative branches, saying some members protecting their own political interests had “thwarted” the organization's mission to improve Western; the Herald headlined its report “We’ve Got Problems.”

people.what_they_did: Distinct from David Bastin, below: each recurs under his own first name across several separate documents rather than as a one-off slip, so they are kept as two people under this archive's rule against merging by surname alone. Took the dead week proposal to Academic Council and authored Resolution 97-15-F on announcing syllabi in the schedule bulletin, passed unanimously on 18 November 1997. In December 1998 Bastin circulated that fall's record of passed legislation to SGA's adviser, its officers, committee heads and the Herald's editor, answering a charge that the organization had done nothing that semester. He closed the term by writing to university president Gary Ransdell in April 1999 to press SGA's concerns about student health services. Matt Bastin won the 1999 race for vice president of public relations, defeating Duan Wright 806 votes to 570. That November, with Congress already on record asking the university to keep Jerry Wilder as vice president of Student Affairs, Bastin wrote his own letter to the Herald making the same appeal.

people.all_offices: president (1990-91); President (1990-91); Administrative Vice-President (1989-90); Congress member (1988-89)
people.what_they_did: Named absent at roll call 15 Nov, 6 Dec 1988 and 7, 14, 21 Mar 1989. Announced he was taking applications for an oozeball team, 28 Feb 1989. Michael Colvin served as administrative vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1989-90, under president Amos Gott. At the first Congress meeting of the year, 29 August 1989, he walked members through the congressional notebook and how to write a resolution, set out the attendance policy, and raised a resolution for a stop light at the corner of Regents Avenue and Normal Drive. He was elected president for 1990-91, succeeding Gott. Michael Colvin won the Associated Student Government presidential election in results the Herald reported on 19 April 1990 under the headline "Michael Colvin Aces Associated Student Government Election." The 1991 Talisman independently lists him as Associated Student Government President for 1990-91. In office, the Herald reported ASG considering a four-day class week (7 February 1991) and covered concern inside the organization over a change affecting student insurance (15 January 1991). The archive does not preserve further detail of how the term ended or what Colvin did afterward. Colvin took office in August 1990, introduced by the Herald as a new leader who wanted to make ideas reality. He had been active in the organization at least since September 1989, when he signed a Herald piece soliciting help for ASG. His spring 1991 agenda was the widest of the era: in a single February week ASG moved to cap tuition boosts, proposed overhauling the Detrex registration system, and planned lobbying to protect student financial aid. Letters he signed under Resolution 91-7-S survive in the SGA records, pressing administrators Kemble Johnson and Debby Cherwak for improvements to Detrex Field. Legislative records fill out the year beyond what the Herald's brief items captured. In fall 1990 the body introduced bills for a roundtable of student organization presidents (Bill #90-2-F) and for microwaves in the cafeterias (Bill #90-4-F). On 29 November 1990 it passed Resolution 90-10-F asking for a left-handed desk in every classroom, and killed Resolution 90-12-F, which had asked that absences tied to Iben Browning's widely publicized New Madrid Fault earthquake prediction be excused; no earthquake came. In the spring the Senate suspended and amended its own by-laws in a short cluster of bills, including Bill #91-6-S changing the procedure for overriding a presidential veto - a procedure tested weeks later when the emergency-kit resolution survived a veto on 14 March 1991. The spring term also produced a resolution asking the university to improve Detrex Field, the intramural field, and bills on joining the Hilltopper Athletic Foundation, recognizing presidential scholars in the Herald, and a book exchange board for Grise Hall.
people.sources: 1991 Talisman (Western World), "Sitting In & Speaking Up"; ASG Minutes, 15 November 1988; ASG Minutes, 29 Aug 1989; Herald 65:55, 19 Apr 1990, "Michael Colvin Aces Associated Student Government Election"

people.all_offices: regent (1972-73); Activities Vice President (1972-73); Sophomore class president (1971-72)
people.what_they_did: Named in the 1972 Talisman's sophomore class pages as sophomore class president for 1971-72. The 1972 Talisman's class pages record that the class structure carried no separate power of its own, leaving its officers to direct their attention at the Associated Students Congress. The archive separately records a Michael Fiorella as the student regent for 1972-73; the name-aliases file already treats Mike and Michael Fiorella as one person, and this entry follows the yearbook's spelling. In September 1972 the Herald profiled Michael Fiorella, the Associated Student Government vice president, under the headline that he was anti-apathy. A week later the Herald reported that Fiorella had won the student seat on the Board of Regents. Fiorella was sworn in on September 26, 1972, alongside Gerald Edds and Chalmer Embry, the board's two other new members. This archive's leader record names Michael Fiorella only as the 1972-73 student regent, but the sources say he held both offices at once. The 1973 Talisman states that the newly revised ASG constitution created two vice presidents, one for administrative duties and one for activities, and that Charles Boteler and Mike Fiorella held them respectively; the Herald of 1 September 1972 likewise calls him vice president for activities, and the 1974 Talisman says he was elected ASG activities vice-president in his junior year and was also student regent. As activities vice president he headed the Activities Committee, which the 1973 Talisman credits with the greatest number of nationally known groups yet booked at Western, naming Chicago, Jethro Tull and the Beach Boys among five concerts that year. The same volume records him arguing for a higher student activity fee than the $1.50 a semester then charged. Fiorella went on to the voting student seat on the Board of Regents that year; the 1973 Talisman's own account of how he came to hold it is not fully consistent, crediting his selection in one place to Ed Jordan's disqualification as an out-of-state student and in another to election by the student body. He was sworn in on 26 September 1972.
people.sources: 1972 Talisman, sophomore class pages; 1973 Talisman, Associated Students, pp. 74-75, and Profile, p. 237; Herald 52:6, 15 Sep 1972

In April 1974 the Herald ran the contest for the student seat on the Board of Regents over four issues. The issue of 19 April, whose lead reported that five students had filed for the seat, printed a letter under his name headlined "Inman Announces". The archive has not been able to read the letter and cannot say what he announced or whether he was one of the five.

people.what_they_did: Mike Inman completed three consecutive years in the Associated Student Government Congress by way of class office, elected senior class president for 1974-75 with Pam Stewart as vice-president. The 1975 Talisman recorded that only the two of them attended the meeting called to organise the class's Homecoming contribution, for a class of 1,865, and that they rented the Harrodsburg Heritage mobile history unit rather than build a float. The yearbook printed his own account of why he sought class office: he said it was the easiest route to a seat in the student government. He held the office itself to be of little consequence, since seniors had little class unity by then, and proposed a bill to abolish class officers and create congress representatives for each class instead. Student government president Jeff Consolo opposed the bill. Inman allowed that class officers carried slightly more standing than representatives-at-large, but argued there should be no distinction among members. He was elected to Who's Who and was president of the Omicron Delta Kappa National Leadership Society. He was a member of the Scabbard and Blade military honour corps, and the same page records him as second runner-up for a national scholarship award the yearbook prints as Mayer-Raebum. Asked to name his chief accomplishment from a list that included the presidencies of his junior and senior classes, the vice-presidency of his sophomore class and a series of military science awards, he chose his involvement in ROTC, and said his campus activities had taught him more than his classes.

McKinney was appointed Parliamentarian on 18 September 1984, a year before he was elected president; the minutes of that meeting record his name as Mitch McKinney. He also chaired the Student Affairs committee that year, and on 9 April 1985 commended its members for their work. Before he was a candidate, McKinney wrote a Herald op-ed on 21 March 1985 headlined 'Associated Student Government Shouldn't Force Bill,' one of a pair of dueling pieces the paper ran on the same question - a sign he was already active in ASG's legislative debates a week before he entered the presidential race. McKinney won the spring 1985 primary on a ticket with Chris Watkins on March 28, the Herald's headline saying the pair rode experience to their primary victory over a field that included candidate Stan Reagan. He was announced as the new Associated Student Government president in the Herald of April 4, in the same issue that reported an unnamed legislative group rejoining ASG. The record found so far does not confirm what office, if any, Watkins went on to hold. In office, the congress abolished its own Finance Committee that September and, the following spring, wrote a Financial Advisory Council into the ASG bylaws in its place. The spring 1986 session was especially active: bills created major/minor college representative seats, revised the membership application process, asked Board of Regents members to attend an SGA meeting, sought chains for Pearce-Ford Tower windows, and pushed for a welcome sign at Normal Drive and University Boulevard. In March 1986 McKinney pulled out of the race for a second term. The same issue carried a piece arguing that student government needed a strong leader, and the field he left behind grew to four candidates before Tim Todd won the presidency that April. The outgoing congress commended McKinney's work in Bill 86-13-S on April 3, and the WKU Board of Regents included a resolution honoring him, alongside outgoing president John D. Minton, at its meeting of August 8, 1986. A 1986 presidential proclamation he signed honoring English professor Thomas Jones survives in the SGA records. Ran on a primary ticket with Chris Watkins in spring 1985; the record found so far does not confirm what office, if any, Watkins held afterward. Withdrew from re-election in March 1986 and was commended by the outgoing congress that April.

Confirmed at all four meetings checked in 2003-04; reported on the budget on 2 and 16 September 2003. Nick Todd, a Henderson senior and SGA's outgoing vice president of finance, won the presidency in March 2004 with 772 of the 1,232 votes cast. Days before the new officers were sworn in on 27 April, the judicial council found $611 missing from the SGA Aramark Dining Dollars account, which had opened the year with $5,000. A senator drafted articles of impeachment against the finance post Todd was about to leave, and the council ruled a two-week process could not finish before he left it anyway. Only Todd, outgoing president John Bradley and the adviser held cards to the account. He submitted his resignation in July, citing personal conflicts within the association. In May the university's internal auditor had reported more than $800 of questionable purchases from the account between August 2003 and May 2004, mostly small buys at campus restaurants with no receipts, and recommended he reimburse the money along with $71 charged on the SGA purchasing card after a spring break car rental. Campus police determined no police action was necessary. In September the dean of Student Life said Todd had been sanctioned by judicial affairs in July, disputing Todd's public account that losing the card was the only action taken against him. Executive vice president Katie Dawson acted as president until the special election of 14 and 15 September. Patti Johnson, the previous year's executive vice president, was the only student to come forward for the office, saying she ran because of the turmoil within the organization, and was sworn in on 23 September. The Herald noted at the time that a re-election for SGA president is rare.

Nicki Seay was appointed SGA's parliamentarian in February 2012 and later served as legislative research chair in 2012-13 before she was elected administrative vice president for 2013-14, alongside presidential candidate Keyana Boka and executive vice president Mark Reeves, in the April 2013 election. By the time she ran unopposed for president in April 2014, the Herald reported she had been on SGA for three years and wanted to use Adobe Connect to broadcast SGA meetings to students who could not attend in person. Asked at an executive candidates' debate on 2 April 2014 whether she could balance the presidency with a double major, she said she planned to take 12 hours with no Friday classes that fall. She won the presidency in that election; the year opened under "Nicki Seay" before her name changed partway through to "Nicki Taylor," and the fuller account is in her presidential profile for 2014-15. Nicki Seay had been SGA's Legislative Research Chair in 2012-13 and ran successfully for administrative vice president in the spring 2013 election. She took office as SGA president in August 2014, a Crofton senior, alongside Administrative Vice President Liz Koehler and Executive Vice President Nolan Miles, and named student involvement, retention and graduation her priorities. Her administration opened the year by expanding SGA's summer and winter need-based scholarship program from $6,000 to $21,000. By the middle of October 2014 the Herald was referring to the same sitting president as Nicki Taylor; no election or resignation separates the two names in the paper's coverage. As Taylor, she presided over a fall senate that voted down a nonsectarian prayer resolution, saw its smoke-free campus resolution vetoed by the Executive Cabinet and sustained on a failed override vote, and passed a resolution backing changes to the campus alcohol policy. She addressed WKU's December 2014 commencement as SGA president, telling graduates, "You have the rest of your life to look forward to." In the spring semester the senate under Taylor passed a limited-smoking-campus resolution and a resolution backing a $10 million parking garage funded by a new student fee; President Gary Ransdell responded formally to both. She also sat, by virtue of the office, on the WKU Board of Regents, and abstained from an Executive Council vote on the smoking measure because of that seat. Her term ended with the 2 April 2015 election of Jay Todd Richey as her successor. Took office in August 2014 as Nicki Seay; called Nicki Taylor in coverage from mid-October 2014 on.

Congress unanimously elected Pat Long parliamentarian at its first meeting of the 1972-73 year, 31 August 1972; the Herald described him as a senior speech major from Franklin, Ohio. The 1973 Talisman also names him, together with Gary Whitfield, as head of the Legal Rights Committee, which worked on a bail-bond fund for arrested students, on the appeal of the 'Fly' movie-censorship case, and pressed the university over the expulsion of students charged but not convicted of drug violations. Long had run for ASG president that spring and lost. A 31 March 1972 Herald feature profiled him under the headline "Pat Long: Activism is Associated Student Government," and on election day the paper urged support for Ed Jordan over him, while a student action group declined to endorse Long. Jordan won and served as president for 1972-73, the year Long instead held the parliamentarian post and the Legal Rights co-chairmanship. That same spring, Long and Charles Boteler led a group of Western students into the McGovern-for-president campaign, running a voter-registration drive and taking part in the Warren County Democratic caucus that chose delegates to the party's national convention; the 1973 Talisman later names Long president of Western's Young Democrats club. Long ran for ASG president again in April 1973, one of four candidates -- with Henry Davis, Mike Fiorella and Steve Yater -- whose platforms the Herald covered that spring. Yater won and served as president for 1973-74. The archive has found no further record of Long's activity in student government after that election.

people.what_they_did: Nominated for the year-end "Stewart" and "Committee" awards, 9 Apr 2002 (minutes_835.pdf). Confirmed as Executive Vice President, chairing Congress, at all four meetings checked (2 Sep, 16 Sep, 2 Dec 2003, 13 Apr 2004). Patti Johnson, a senior from Marion, had been active in SGA for over three years and served on committees including public relations and athletics before becoming executive vice president in 2003-04. Nick Todd, the vice president of finance, was elected president for 2004-05 in March 2004, but before the new officers were sworn in on April 27, SGA's judicial council fielded an allegation that $611 was missing from the SGA Dining Dollars account, an account that had started the year with $5,000. Senator Josh Collins drafted articles of impeachment against Todd's vice presidency, but the judicial council ruled a two-week impeachment process could not finish before he left that office anyway. Johnson had not planned to run for president herself, but after Todd's resignation that July she entered the September 2004 special election as the only candidate to show interest, saying she stayed on because of "the turmoil within the organization" and that she knew "what it takes to get the job done." Johnson ran unopposed for president and student regent in the Sept. 14-15 online election, the group having been without an elected president since July. She said she was disappointed that students would not "really get to make a decision," but still planned light campaigning, and she wanted to continue reviewing the plus/minus grading proposal and to make faculty evaluations available to students. Johnson received 1,291 votes in the two-day uncontested election and was sworn in as president at SGA's fall reception on Sept. 23, 2004, one week after her election. She said committees had been formed and members had begun proposing legislation, and she looked forward to being sworn in as student regent at the Oct. 29 Board of Regents meeting, declaring it was "back to business." She served through the year until Katie Dawson was elected to succeed her in the March 2005 spring election. Johnson served as the Board of Regents' student member from August 2004 to July 2005, a term confirmed by the resolution of appreciation the board read into its July 22, 2005 minutes when Katie Dawson, the executive vice president who had served alongside her all year, was sworn in to replace her. Dawson had come up through the cabinet as Todd's running mate in the original March 2004 election and had acted as interim president during the summer vacancy before Johnson's win. Also held the Board of Regents' student seat from August 2004 to July 2005.

people.what_they_did: Deom, a junior from Boonville, Indiana, was an Associated Student Government member and Judicial Council representative in 1980-81 when he broke with ASG over the university's dormitory room-inspection policy. After Congress defeated a resolution against the inspections 16-13, he contacted the Kentucky Civil Liberties Union and asked it to investigate, and, working with campus KCLU chapter president Michael Taylor, joined the effort to build a broader Bowling Green chapter of the group drawing in non-student residents. ASG did not follow him. After the KCLU took up the matter, Congress defeated a second resolution against the inspections and re-endorsed the university's policy; the 1981 Talisman's own account of the vote is inconsistent, giving the tally as both 24-9, with three abstentions, and separately as 29-4. Administrative vice president Mark Wilson argued in the debate that fire-safety checks should not be equated with search and seizure, and that if the resolution passed, dorm residents' rights would be waived. By February 1982 Deom was no longer on the Judicial Council. The Herald's 4 February 1982 issue carried a letter from him, headlined "Former Judicial Council Member Irked," and two further letters followed in reply: M. A. Baker's "Paul Deom Honorable" on 9 February and Winston Stevenson's "Paul Deom Defended" on 18 February. people.all_offices: regent (2008-09); Administrative Vice President (2008-09); Senator (2006-07); Director of Academic and Student Affairs (2007-08)
people.what_they_did: One of eighteen sworn in to the Student Senate 3 October 2006, printed "Reagan Gilley". Also recorded later as an executive officer for 2007-08 and 2008-09. Reagan Gilley was director of academic and student affairs for 2007-08. He authored Resolution 07-07-S, which named SGA's study abroad scholarship, passed at the year's first senate meeting on 4 September 2007, and that year he also worked toward opening the university library for 24-hour hours and on the study abroad and film scholarships. In the spring 2008 campaign he ran for administrative vice president against Skylar Johnson, and co-wrote a 27 March Herald op-ed with presidential candidate Theodore Harden and executive vice-presidential candidate Kevin Smiley arguing that student representation needed a change. Harden was running against Johnathon Boles, so the three op-ed signatories stood as a slate opposed to Boles; the same issue carried a report on a Red Towel Party seeking to energize SGA, and in April a complaint was filed against that party, but the surviving index does not state which candidates belonged to it. Gilley won his race and served as administrative vice president for 2008-09. Reagan Gilley was a Pineville senior and the Student Government Association's administrative vice president when he won the special election for student regent held 25-26 February 2009, filling the seat left empty for 26 days after President Johnathon Boles resigned on 30 January for health reasons. He beat Fairdale senior Nate Eaton, the speaker of the senate, 477 votes to 224 of the 701 cast, and Chief Justice Corey Bewley announced the verified result at 12:17 a.m. Thursday in the SGA office. Gilley had campaigned on short notice through a Facebook group, announcements in classes and a YouTube video built around the Rick Astley song "Never Gonna Give You Up," and after the count he handed Eaton a plaque he had bought at Kroger that day. He said he planned to contact Boles the next day to catch up on Board of Regents business and then to contact Faculty Regent Patricia Minter, and that he wished more students had voted. "I am very relieved but excited for things to come," he said. Gilley took the constitutional oath of office from Board Chair Lois Gray at the second quarterly meeting on 24 April 2009, where President Gary Ransdell presented him with the regent's pin, and he answered the roll call as student regent. He seconded Larry Zielke's motion to approve the naming of designated facilities and rooms, and seconded Yevette Haskins's motion to accept the 2008-09 second quarter statement of revenues and expenditures for filing. On the 2009-10 tuition and fees schedule, which carried a 4 percent increase, Gilley asked to amend the motion to strike the proposed per credit hour fee on course loads above 15 hours; the amended motion was seconded by Zielke and carried unanimously. He then moved to add a drop/add fee of $50 per transaction to the schedule, which Zielke seconded and which also carried unanimously, and afterwards told the Board that tuition increases were a major concern of the student body and that "for the record, I meant to vote in opposition to the tuition increase." During a long exchange over personnel actions and campus morale, in which the faculty and staff regents described resignations and low morale, Gilley said that on behalf of the student body there was concern about fewer staff being available for classes. The minutes list the Board's next meetings as a special budget meeting on 19 June 2009 and the third quarterly meeting on 31 July 2009. His time on the Board was over by the summer. The minutes of the special budget meeting of 19 June 2009 record the constitutional oath of office being administered to Kevin Smiley as student regent, again by Chair Lois Gray and with the regent's pin presented by President Ransdell, and the roll call for that meeting lists Smiley rather than Gilley. Gilley's name does not appear in those minutes at all, so the quarterly meeting of 24 April 2009 was the only Board meeting that fell within his tenure, and the record of his service as student regent runs to that single day of votes. Gilley's name does not appear in those minutes, so the handover had happened by 19 June 2009, earlier than the 31 July roll call previously recorded here. Reagan Gilley served as administrative vice president for 2008-09, alongside Executive Vice President Kayla Shelton, though the two had run in the spring on opposing slates. He presented the year's budget to the senate line by line at its first meeting, 26 August 2008 - $8,000 for two student workers, $9,050 for executive stipends, $1,000 for travel and $5,000 for senate programming - and told senators the budget was now in their hands. He represented SGA that year on the Budget Council, Faculty Welfare and the University Calendar Committee. When President Johnathon Boles resigned in January 2009, Gilley won the special election for the vacant student regent seat that February; his time on the Board of Regents is recorded in his separate regent profile for 2008-09.
people.sources: Herald 84:35, 26 Feb 2009 - Gilley elected student regent; SGA Minutes, 3 October 2006; SGA Senate minutes, 26 Aug 2008, TopSCHOLAR; SGA Senate minutes, 4 Sep 2007, TopSCHOLAR

people.what_they_did: Reginald Glass was elected vice president of the Associated Students for 1971-72 under president Linda Jones, becoming, the 1972 Talisman says, the first Black vice president of the body and the first Black student to hold a top student leadership post at Western. As vice president he sat on the Academic Council as one of its two voting student members and chaired the activities committee; a yearbook caption shows him signing a speaker contract, placed beside the note that Dr. Benjamin Spock was A.S.'s first sponsored speaker, though the volume does not state outright that this was Spock's own contract. Glass was also active in Black campus life outside ASG: he belonged to Alpha Phi Alpha fraternity, chartered nationally at Western on 31 October 1971, and the Herald reported him named the campus's outstanding Black Greek that November. He remained involved in student government after his year as vice president ended. By the fall of 1973 he sat in the ASG Congress as the representative from the Graduate College, and the Herald reported him pressing for better representation of minority students in student government and on the Academic Council. On 4 December 1973 the Herald reported that he had resigned that seat in protest; the 1974 Talisman records his reasoning as the harm he said the absence of Black and foreign students from ASG and the Academic Council did to the minorities and to the University. Resigned from Congress in protest in the section covering 1973-74, having asked for better representation for minority groups in student government and the Academic Council; the text says he argued the lack of black and foreign students in those bodies was harmful to both minorities and the University. His prior 1971-72 Associated Students vice-presidency is not sourced to this citation.

people.all_offices: Activities Vice President (1975-76); Activities Vice President (1976-77)
people.what_they_did: Rick Kelley was activities vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1975-76, the first of two consecutive terms in the office. In October he introduced a bill creating a student activities committee; members were chosen in December from open applications, and the committee ran three subcommittees covering concerts, lectures, and special events and publicity, meant to bring more student input into the entertainment program after controversy over past concert bookings. The 1976 Talisman credits the Homecoming concert by Linda Ronstadt, on 1 November 1975, with a $4,300 profit for ASG, calling it a tremendous financial success that kept ASG in the black; an earlier concert that September by Kenny Loggins and Jim Messina, by contrast, lost about $7,000 to poor attendance. His surname is printed both Kelley and Kelly in the same volume; the spelling is not settled. Rick Kelley was re-elected activities vice president of the Associated Student Government on 6 and 7 April 1976, beating Robert Tackett 705 votes to 496 for a second term running Western's concert program. He presided over the 6 April 1976 Congress meeting in President Steve Henry's absence. A 1977 Talisman feature on his two years in the office, published as his term ended, described how Kelley worked with the concert selection committee and assistant dean of student affairs Ron Beck to book acts. When an agent representing Chicago called offering the band for a $25,000 show, Kelley discussed it with Beck, found a private promoter willing to cover the cost, then took the arrangement to the concert committee for approval; the show, a first for Western with a privately promoted act, set an advance-ticket sales record; Kelley said the show sold out of advance tickets and grossed over $50,000, while the Talisman's own concert report noted that the concert itself was not a sellout despite the record advance sales. The Seals and Crofts homecoming concert that same year drew about 5,200 people but lost roughly $3,800, which assistant dean of student affairs Ron Beck attributed to a Saturday date competing with other homecoming events. Kelley told the yearbook that Beck bore the brunt of student criticism over concert choices, and that students who complained about a show rarely wrote in when one succeeded. His surname is printed both Kelley and Kelly across these volumes; the spelling is not settled.

Moore was one of four candidates - with Tom Blair, Kirt Grubbs and Mark McChesney - who opened the 1977 Associated Student Government presidential race on April 1. The archive does not yet show what Moore's administration did over the winter and into the spring beyond the ordinary business of readying his succession - see the 1978 election events below. By September 1978, after his term had ended, the Herald reported that Moore had been found ineligible for another Associated Student Government job; the archive does not yet hold the article's account of why. By the 12 September meeting, an opening for Judicial Council chairman had appeared and Congress confirmed Steve Wilson in the position, 30 votes in favour with 3 abstaining. Neither source explicitly ties the ineligibility ruling to the chairmanship, but the dates align and no other ASG post for Moore is recorded that year, so his tenure as chairman appears to have run under two weeks.

people.what_they_did: Robert Watkins, a Bowling Green sophomore, was serving on Congress in October 2003 when he authored a resolution recommending students vote in the 4 November election, moving to suspend the by-laws so it could pass without the usual delay; it passed unanimously. The following spring Watkins wrote the new three-branch constitution as chair of the Legislative Research Committee, and Congress elected him the senate's first speaker on 13 April 2004, defeating Brittany Fausey 9 votes to 8 with 17 of 20 members present. The result was disputed immediately because the new constitution did not make clear whether two-thirds of eligible voters or of the full membership was required, and three members present had been barred from voting by a judicial council ruling; one member warned of a “semester of frustration” if the dispute went unresolved. Abby Lovan had withdrawn from the race before the ballot, and Fausey declined to challenge the result. Watkins went on to win the SGA presidency in April 2006 and served until his resignation that November; his full term is recorded under his leader entry for 2006-07. Wrote and defended the new three-branch constitution and bylaws (Bill 03-10-F) as the committee's chair in fall 2003, before his election as speaker of the senate the following April. Robert "Rob" Watkins, a Bowling Green student, wrote the SGA constitution adopted in 2004 and was elected the first speaker of the senate under it on 15 April 2004, defeating Brittany Fausey 9 votes to 8 in a result immediately contested over what quorum the new constitution required; the vote was upheld later that month. Watkins won the SGA presidency in the 13 April 2006 online election, defeating Berea junior Kara Ratliff after more than a week courting TopNet voters, with results announced at a crowded Revolution 91.7. He took office for 2006-07 alongside Administrative Vice President Amanda Allen, who by October was tightening the budget after the prior administration left roughly $24,000 unspent. Watkins resigned as SGA president and student regent on 28 November 2006, with the resignation read into the senate's own minutes at that day's regularly scheduled Tuesday meeting, after senators had aired concerns about him at an unannounced 10 p.m. meeting the evening before. (A Herald account this site had followed gave the date as 30 November; the primary senate minutes are treated as authoritative here.) A Herald editorial the same week was headlined "SGA actions an embarrassment to Western." The resignation left students without a voting voice on the Board of Regents for at least a month and put junior Jeanne Johnson, already serving as his executive vice president since the 5 September season-opening meeting, in as a fill-in leader for the rest of the term, formally sworn in as president at the 5 December Winter Banquet. Robert Watkins served as SGA president for 2006-07 after winning the 13 April 2006 election over Kara Ratliff. He resigned as president and student regent on 28 November 2006. The full account of his election, administration and resignation is recorded under his leader entry for this year.

people.what_they_did: Listed as "Member of Organizational Aid" alongside the Senator title. Named as an author on six pieces of SGA legislation in the 2023-24 session: Bill 1-23-F (Funding for the SGA Pink Walk); Resolution 3-24-S (Resolution to Encourage Sustainability Initiatives by Charging a $5.00 Sustainability Fee to Students); Bill 6-24-S (Funding for the Office of Sustainability); Bill 7-24-S (Funding for Gift Bags for WKU Students); Bill 33-24-S (Organizational Aid Funding Spring 2024); Bill 34-24-S (Funding for the WKU Unplugged Scholarship Initiative). Named as an author on six pieces of SGA legislation in the 2023-24 session: Bill 1-23-F, Resolution 3-24-S, Bill 6-24-S, Bill 7-24-S, Bill 33-24-S and Bill 34-24-S. Thanked the senators who turned out for the campus safety walk, trailed legislation for an SGA poll-ooza and Earth Day work. He was elected student body president the following month. Robinson, a senior from Benton, Kentucky triple-majoring in psychology, philosophy and sociology and a member of Sigma Phi Epsilon and Omicron Delta Kappa, won the SGA presidency in the 13-15 April 2025 general election on a turnout of 966, running with Savanna Kurtz for vice president and Gabriel Jerdon for chief financial officer. He also succeeded Sam Kurtz as WKU's student regent; the Board of Regents administered his oath of office on 8 August 2025, the same meeting at which it named the new Gordon Ford College of Business building Amy and David Chandler Hall and elected Jan West chair, Doris Thomas vice chair and Melissa Dennison secretary for 2025-26. Robinson ran on turning SGA away from national politics and toward direct student advocacy, saying the organization had sometimes echoed national political talking points and that he wanted it to act as "an advocate and resource for students" who could be pointed to the right contact in the administration. His cabinet - Kurtz as vice president, Jerdon as chief financial officer, Maggie Yelton as chief of staff, and Preston Jenkins, reappointed chief communications officer on 22 April 2025 and confirmed by the Senate - ran a legislative program heavy on small, direct-benefit measures: vouchers for CPR certification, dental cleanings, transcripts and identification cards, equipment to borrow such as umbrellas, calculators and hammocks, and a resolution urging accessible restroom stalls in Grise Hall. Jenkins also organized a student-painted mural for a column in the SGA chambers. In March 2026 SGA drew on its projects fund to host a baseball-game tailgate, a response to Athletics Director Todd Stewart's call for more student engagement. The Senate closed its final meeting on 14 April 2026 having passed 56 bills for the year, the most since 2018-19, with Jenkins also reporting that a new university Artificial Intelligence Committee was weighing bulk AI-product subscriptions for students. Robinson's most sustained policy push was on student mental health, working with Mental Health and Wellbeing Committee chair Veronica Butler on a year-long program backed by data from social work professor Jay Gabbard, who told SGA that 44 percent of WKU students reported depression symptoms and 10 percent had considered suicide in the past year. SGA co-organized Mental Health Week with the WKU Counseling Center and the campus NAMI chapter, ran a Toppers Talk About It awareness campaign, and had student recommendations - including relocating counseling services from Potter Hall to the Downing Student Union - reviewed by the Counseling Center Review Committee before forwarding them to administrators, though Butler said it was unclear whether they would be enacted. The push closed with an Out of Darkness suicide-remembrance walk on 18 April 2026, and successor Caden Lucas said the focus would continue "in a sustained and meaningful way." At the Senate's first meeting under his successor, Robinson opened by telling the mostly-new chamber they looked untainted by SGA's usual troubles, then handed president-elect Caden Lucas the red suit jacket passed president to president - the same jacket Sam Kurtz had given him the year before. His term as student regent outlasted his SGA presidency: at the Board of Regents' 5 June 2026 meeting, his last as regent, he cast the lone vote against a $204, 1.69 percent tuition increase, saying the board had "to do whatever we can to not raise the tuition" to preserve affordability. Afterward he planned to remain at WKU for an Ed.S. in school psychology, aiming for a career as a school psychologist in a school district. Also student regent on the WKU Board of Regents.

people.what_they_did: Named as an author on two pieces of SGA legislation in the 2021-22 session, both amendments to SGA's constitution or bylaws (Bill 4-22-S and Bill 6-22-S). Named as an author on two pieces of SGA legislation in the 2021-22 session: Bill 4-22-S and Bill 6-22-S. Sole author of the year's organizational aid bills, including 20-22-F, 21-22-F, 22-22-F and 48-23-S. He introduced the 2022-23 budget at the first meeting on 30 August 2022 and reported roughly $7,000 given out to organizations by January. Sam Kurtz, then the outgoing administrative vice president, was elected student body president in results announced early on April 19, 2023 in the Downing Student Union senate chambers, after voting opened on TopNet on April 17. His KFL ticket, with Annalise Finch as executive vice president and Salvador León as administrative vice president, ran unopposed, and Chief Justice Justin Goins read the results. In a statement, Kurtz said the ticket would "listen to students' concerns, represent their voices, lead with integrity, and promote transparency." At the 23rd Senate's first fall meeting on Aug. 29, Kurtz nominated Ashley Ranger, Anna Kate Hardin, Ellen Henderson, Morgan Gammons and Garrison Reed to the Judicial Council from what he called a record number of applicants, and named seven committee heads, including Rush Robinson for Campus Improvements and Sustainability and Karley Solorzano for Diversity, Equity and Inclusion. The Senate's first bill of the year, passed unanimously that September, funded the SGA Pink Walk breast-cancer event. That November the senate backed moving DSU fire drills from 5 a.m. to 2 a.m. and funded a Boys and Girls Club toy drive. Speaker of the Senate Sydney Denney wrote or co-wrote several of the year's bills, including a resolution capping student parking fees at $50, a $700 fund to help students pay parking fines, and voucher funding for the Dental Hygiene Center and ID Center. In February 2024 Kurtz and Chief of Staff Donté Reed rolled out a 450-voucher Uber giveaway aimed at student safety and outreach, followed in March by a need-based scholarship awarding Uber vouchers and a Community Builder Excellence Scholarship for incoming Bowling Green-area freshmen; that month the senate also planned a Frankfort trip for the Rally for Higher Education. The year's fight was internal. In February 2024 the Judicial Council voted 6-0 to censure Administrative Vice President Salvador León after a hearing brought by Denney and the executive cabinet, which alleged León had spent SGA funds - including a $425.25 Preston Center deposit for Neurodiversity Acceptance Week - before the Senate passed the funding bill, in violation of the constitution's clause 2.5.3 requiring the administrative vice president to expend funds only as the Senate authorizes. Chief Justice Isaac King said the cabinet, excluding León, had asked for the censure after León spent the funds despite Kurtz's condition that he wait for Bill 22-23-F to pass, and after he pushed PR Director Preston Romanov to promote the week on SGA social media ahead of the vote, effectively forcing the Senate's hand. León countered that text messages showed Kurtz had signed off on the spending in advance; the council found the spending improper but recommended no discipline beyond the censure itself. In January 2024 Chief of Staff Lindsey Kelly and enrollment director Donte Reed both resigned, with Reed moving up to chief of staff. That April, Kurtz ran for a second term with Reed as his executive vice president candidate and junior senator Ethan Taylor for administrative vice president; the ticket again ran unopposed on a ballot of more than 60 legislative candidates, and the three were re-elected as the 24th Senate's 34 members were announced the night of April 16-17, 2024. Before that, SGA partnered with WKU Red Wave for a final Red Wave tailgate on April 9, with a student-DJ contest winner earning a $500 scholarship. The 23rd Senate held its last meeting on April 16 with no legislation on the agenda, and Kurtz thanked senators in his final report for what the group had accomplished that year. Elected student body president in the spring 2023 election on an unopposed ticket with Salvador León as administrative vice president and Annalise Finch as executive vice president, the results being read out in the senate chambers in the early hours of 19 April 2023 by Chief Justice Justin Goins. Kurtz had been administrative vice president the year before. Kurtz opened the 2024-25 year presiding over the 24th Senate, which passed SGA's $100,000 budget at its first meeting on Aug. 27. Sitting down with the Herald editorial board alongside his executive cabinet, he described SGA as "a vessel for good" and a group of 45 to 50 people advocating for students, and credited President Caboni with keeping the budget untouched for several years. Through the spring he presided over a run of student-welfare legislation, including the Gordon Wilson Hall elevator resolution and a resolution seeking 24/7 library hours during finals week. In February he announced a POLLapalooza push to raise election participation, telling the Senate, "My goal is that 3,000 students vote in our election." Kurtz closed his term at the 24th Senate's final meeting on April 15, having served as student body president for two years and holding executive branch positions for most of his college career, and prepared to graduate at the end of the semester. He received a standing ovation after his last report, and his parting words to senators were "Please be for the students." Re-elected without opposition to a second term.

people.what_they_did: Nominated to the senate by President Jay Todd Richey and approved by unanimous consent, 29 September 2015. Molyneaux wrote most of the sustainability committee's legislation: the bill renewing the committee in autumn 2016, the constitutional amendment making it permanent, the resolution to take Styrofoam out of every WKU campus, the resolution supporting an end to printed paper by 2030, which passed 21-6-2, and Bill 8-17-S, which sent $1,314.03 to the Office of Sustainability - $500 of it matching Double Dollars at the Community Farmers Market and $814.03 to Big Red Bikes - and passed 16-10-1. She was elected executive vice president for 2017-18. Under Molyneaux the sustainability committee went from a body renewed each year to a permanent one written into the constitution. It brought reusable takeout containers to Fresh in September 2016, ran a panel on social justice and sustainability in April 2017 for $20, staged the Earth Day festival in Centennial Mall, and funded the Double Dollars matching programme at the Community Farmers Market and the Big Red Bikes scheme. Molyneaux chaired SGA's Sustainability committee in 2016-17 before running for re-election as executive vice president in April 2018 on a ticket with presidential candidate Conner Hounshell and Administrative Vice President Kara Lowry. Days before the vote, the Judicial Council disqualified, then suspended, the rival Mayer-Edmonds-Anderson ticket over a Pepe the Frog meme in its campaign chalking; Stephen Mayer's ticket was reinstated to run and won, with Hounshell's ticket placing second. Molyneaux, Lowry and Hounshell were all elected senators instead. In February 2018 she joined President Andi Dahmer, Lowry and Hounshell in writing Resolution 3-18-S opposing the scale of a renegotiated Aramark dining-fee increase, which would have raised a per-semester fee on students without meal plans from $75 toward $350 over ten years; the Senate passed it unanimously. At the Senate's final meeting of the year, Molyneaux spoke about what she called an "awful" year for the executive board, describing sexism and misogyny within the Senate and backing Dahmer's account, reported the same week, of harassment she said she had faced as president. Molyneaux cited the threatening note left on Dahmer's car and the derogatory names used in the SGA offices, and told senators who had taken part in it to think about what they had done.
