people.what_they_did: Whitehouse won the March 1988 ASG presidential primary alongside Shannon Ragland, emerging from a field of seven candidates in a year when only two of 32 congress positions were contested. He won the presidency on 7 April 1988, in an election the Herald's own editorial pages said had been marred by oversight and closed minds, and amid coverage of votes for a write-in candidate that the congress was told it could not ignore. The disputed election shadowed his term into the fall: Bruce Cambron, who had demanded a new election in April, took his complaint to university president Thomas Meredith in October 1988, weeks after the congress banned future write-in campaigns. His year also produced ASG's formal written reaction to the General Education Task Force proposal. Scott Whitehouse came through the Associated Student Government primaries in the spring of 1988. Dorren Klausnitzer reported that Whitehouse and Shannon Ragland were the winners, in an issue that also covered what a losing campaign cost candidates in money and in feeling. By the middle of his year in office the Herald had settled on a running characterisation of him. Rebecca Fullen's feature called him the "Peddling President" who sold Associated Student Government to students, and the same issue reported that university president Thomas Meredith had come to speak to the organisation. The following week the paper printed "Scott Whitehouse Selling Good Government" together with a John Chattin editorial cartoon drawing him as a salesman. people.what_they_did: Seth Church served on SGA's Judicial Council, becoming chief justice by April 2013 after having been an ordinary justice as of the previous August. As chief justice he announced the council's 3-2 vote disqualifying president-elect Keyana Boka after runner-up Cain Alvey complained that a self-promotional campaign email had gone to Honors College students at Boka's request. When Howard Bailey overruled the disqualification and reinstated Boka, the council voted unanimously not to challenge his decision but registered its disapproval; Church called Bailey's intervention "a serious infringement on our autonomy" and said it set a bad precedent. Church remained chief justice for 2013-14. In April 2014 he delivered the council's Opinion 2014SP-002, holding that senators who abstain neither vote yes nor no but concur with the majority of those voting, and that they still count toward quorum; Julia Payne and Jackie Stewart joined the opinion, and Megan Lemmons took no part. He moved into the executive branch as chief of staff for 2014-15 under President Nicki Taylor. Church wrote the resolution supporting private spaces on campus for expressing breast milk, prompted by a non-traditional student who had just had her third child and found the existing unlocked room uncomfortable; it passed unanimously without debate. He proposed and chaired a new Cultural and Diversity Affairs Committee developed in collaboration with Taylor, and wrote the resolution rewriting the Glasgow regional campus's constitution after Glasgow struggled to keep members. He also argued against a smoke-free campus resolution that the senate passed and the Executive Cabinet then vetoed, saying a ban was unfair to students required to live on campus for two years, and objected that a proposed $10 million parking garage had moved too fast and left out the regional campuses. Chief justice for 2013-14 on SGA's own judicial branch roster, last modified 27 August 2013. Already recorded in the archive but filed under the executive; SGA's own site puts the chief justice in the judicial branch. Church proposed the Cultural and Diversity Affairs Committee with President Nicki Taylor and chaired it in its first term, taking it into the Campus Pride Index and into work with Housing and Residence Life on gender-neutral housing and on letting applicants identify as transgender. He opposed the smoke-free campus resolution, arguing it was unfair to students required to live on campus for two years, and signed the executive cabinet's veto of it in November 2014; he then wrote with senator J. William Berry the limited-smoking resolution that passed 13-11 in February 2015. He authored the resolution on private space for breastfeeding students, brought to him by a non-traditional student, which passed unanimously in March 2015; co-authored with senator Zach Jones a resolution to publish SGA's attendance and voting records; and argued against the $10 million parking structure resolution on the ground that regional campus students would pay the $30 fee without using it. In April 2015 he wrote to the Judicial Council opposing the disqualification of president-elect Jay Todd Richey over misplaced campaign posters.

people.what_they_did: Held the office by 4 April 2006, when he reported on the Distinguished Senior awards and the opening of the Student Success Center; the minutes of that meeting give his name as Ricky Skylar Jordan. Appointed with Whitfield on 6 September 2005 and sworn in by Katie Dawson. A Ricky Skylar Jordan appears as Director of Academic and Student Affairs by April 2006; the constitution barred a justice from serving in another branch, so the move implies he left the council, but no minute of his resignation was found. Reported on 6 February 2007 that he had met Dr Minter about textbook ordering at the University Bookstore, was looking into space for the Gay and Lesbian Resource Center, and was going to the Kentucky Building to read SGA's old files and minutes. Laid groundwork for the Listen Up Legislators spring lobbying campaign after the traditional February Frankfort rally alone had not worked. Skylar Jordan first held SGA office in 2005-06 as director of academic and student affairs, reporting by early April 2006 on the Distinguished Senior awards and the opening of the Student Success Center; the Senate minutes of that meeting give his full name as Ricky Skylar Jordan. He held the same post in 2006-07, reporting in February 2007 that he had met with the university about textbook ordering at the bookstore, was looking into space for a Gay and Lesbian Resource Center, and was researching SGA's own history in the Kentucky Building archives. Jordan moved to chief of staff for 2007-08, laying groundwork that fall for the "Listen Up Legislators" spring lobbying campaign after a February Frankfort rally alone had failed to move the legislature. That April, after Johnathon Boles's "Red Towel Party" ticket won the SGA election, Jordan filed a complaint against the party; the SGA council took no action on it on 22 April 2008, and the result stood. He returned to serve as Boles's chief of staff again in 2008-09, nominated on 26 August 2008 after serving in the role pro tem, and built a master schedule of every SGA committee's meeting time for senators to consult. In September 2009, after Boles had resigned and been succeeded by Kevin Smiley, Jordan publicly criticized Smiley's decision to nominate his own brother, Eric Smiley, as chief of staff. The Herald identified him in that report as "former executive vice president Skylar Baker-Jordan" — a title and surname variant not otherwise recorded for him in SGA's own minutes, which consistently give his office as director of academic and student affairs and then chief of staff, never executive vice president. Active on the floor at the 6 October 2009 meeting, questioning a committee report and moving procedural votes; also active, per the Senate's 29 September 2009 minutes, in debate on Bill 01-09-F, the Florence Schneider mural bill.

people.what_they_did: Named as Academic Affairs chair on the spring 2017 constitutional amendment bill and on Bill 29-17-S; the autumn chair had been Amy Wyer. Elected student body president for 2018-19. Mayer was elected SGA president and student regent in April 2018 on the MEA ticket with Garrett Edmonds and Harper Anderson, taking 35 percent of 2,378 presidential votes against Conner Hounshell's 33 percent and Kenan Mujkanovic's 32 percent; 2,447 students voted overall. His ticket won only after the Judicial Council reversed a disqualification it had imposed days before the election over the campaign's use of a Pepe the Frog meme chalked on campus sidewalks, downgrading the penalty to a campaign suspension. A biology and chemistry double major who had served three semesters as a senator and studied at Harlaxton College, Mayer opened his term in September 2018 promising greater transparency from both the Board of Regents and SGA, and required senators to log a weekly office hour. As student regent he was an outspoken critic of WKU's fee structure, especially the $450 online academic fee, and opposed that year's 4 percent tuition increase, saying he did not see the need to put the financial burden "on the students' backs." Also served as student regent under the merged offices.
people.sources: Herald, 18 Apr 2018; SGA Bill 29-17-S; SGA Senate minutes, 4 Sep 2018

The Sigma Alpha Epsilon chapter page in the same volume calls the freshman class president Pledge Steve Harvey; the Classes section spelling is followed here. A Herald report would give the vote; the archive has not read it. The Sophomores section says active class members included seven sophomores who were members of the ASG congress, and names Steve Henry as class president in text and in a photo caption of Henry and Jeff Wampler checking notes before an ASG meeting. A Sigma Alpha Epsilon chapter page in the 1975 Talisman records Henry and Stan McDivitt as elected members of the Associated Student Government. He was elected ASG president the following spring and served in 1975-76. Steve Henry appeared in ASG coverage as early as September 1972, when the Herald reported his view that the Associated Student Government had lost respect. Henry won the spring 1974 election on a ticket with Jeff Consolo, and resigned his post running the student discount program after the victory. As president in 1975-76 Henry moved in November to change ASG's concert proposal after a money-losing fall season, while a student group urged support for his energy awareness plan. At year's end the Herald summed up his tenure with a piece on how the role had required balancing the twin jobs of student regent and ASG president, which he held at the same time. A Wikipedia biography of Stephen L. Henry, later the 52nd Lieutenant Governor of Kentucky (1995-2003), describes an orthopedic surgeon and WKU alumnus who was elected Student Body President on his second attempt after an earlier loss, and who sat on the WKU Board of Regents as president - a career arc that lines up point for point with this record's own Herald sourcing, though no WKU archive document has yet been found that states the identification directly.

people.what_they_did: Fuller was elected Administrative Vice President on 17 April 1979, defeating Tom Jecker, a Louisville senior, 973 votes to 574, the same election that sent Jamie Hargrove to the presidency. At the Congress's 24 April 1979 swearing-in he urged the incoming members to think about which committees they wanted to serve on. He was elected Associated Student Government president the following spring, taking office for 1980-81. Steve Fuller entered the April 1980 Associated Student Government presidential race against David Rue and Tim Irons; the Herald covered ASG hopefuls debating the issues at an April 3 candidates' forum before reporting the three-way field on April 10. Fuller won the presidency in the April 24 election, reported under the headline "Persistence Pays Off in Steve Fuller Campaign." Mark Wilson and Greg Zoeller were elected to other top ASG offices the same day; Tim Irons's loss was covered separately. Fuller's fall term was consumed by a running fight over dormitory room inspections. A September 4 inspection measure was voted down amid criticism of how the vote was conducted; a September 11 bill calling for a ban on bugs in the dorms drew a mocking editorial cartoon and an editorial calling the university's protective inspection policy unnecessary; and by November 13 the Herald reported ASG had nearly slept through its own vote before re-endorsing inspections, followed a week later by a bill proposing a stricter room-entry rule. In office, ASG under Fuller also proposed a change to the organization's own title in October 1980 and asked the state to evaluate higher education funding in February 1981, as budget worries dominated the legislative session. His successor, Marcel Bush, was elected that April. Fuller entered the Associated Student Government presidential race in the spring of 1980 as one of three candidates. Michele Wood's Herald report was headlined "3 Running for Associated Student Government President," naming Steve Fuller, David Rue and Tim Irons. During the 1980-81 year the Associated Student Government pressed the state on the condition of higher education, with Robert Pillow reporting in February 1981 that the body had asked the state to conduct an evaluation. The request came as the campus argued over budget cuts, including cuts to athletics. Steve Fuller held the presidency of the Associated Student Government in 1980-81, elected on 24 April 1980 over David Rue and Tim Irons in a race the Herald reported under a headline about persistence paying off; Mark Wilson and Greg Zoeller took the other top offices the same day. He chaired Congress through the year and made its appointments: Jeff Morris and then Kevin Strader as parliamentarian, M. A. Baker, Charles Bussell, Perry Hines and Jim Payne as representatives, Patti Davis and Lonnie Sears as on-campus representatives, and Margaret Ragan to the University Academic Complaint Committee. The 1980 Talisman records that the ASG president was also sworn in as student regent that year, so Fuller sat on the Board of Regents as well. His term was dominated by the fight over dormitory room inspections, which ran from a defeated measure on 4 September 1980 to Congress's approval of stricter room-entry rules on 4 December, and by the state's cuts to higher education: ASG asked the state for an evaluation of higher education in February 1981, and Fuller circulated a petition to Governor John Y. Brown, finance secretary George Atkins and the Council on Higher Education, saying many students did not realise the cuts meant dismissing faculty. He opened the year telling the Herald that ASG wanted a stronger voice in policy making, and spent much of it complaining of the opposite: he was reported disappointed by attendance at his own meetings in October 1980, and the student opinion poll committee's first survey found 29 per cent of students said they would recognise him while 28 per cent thought the university centre director was the ASG president. Marcel Bush succeeded him in April 1981.
people.sources: Herald 54:56, 19 Apr 1979; Herald 55:51, 10 Apr 1980; Herald 55:55, 24 Apr 1980

Sophomore class president the year before he was elected student body president. Thornton beat Ed Johnson for the Associated Student Government presidency in the 6 April 1978 election, campaigning on his experience; Johnson contested the result, and the ASG Judicial Council denied his appeal on 18 April 1978 after a long debate. In office that fall, Thornton's ASG tabled an open house bill rather than act on it, the Herald reported on 28 September 1978. By January 1979 the government faced a fight to keep control of student activities funding and was pressing for a student seat on a state-level council, both reported in the same 25 January 1979 issue. In March 1979 the Herald reported Thornton and fellow WKU student Terri Craig elected to the executive council of the Student Government Association of Kentucky, a state-level body - the kind of state seat ASG had been pressing for two months earlier. In the last full week of his term, Thornton's ASG approved resolutions on campus housing and parking policy, reported 26 April 1979, the same week voting closed in the election for his successor. The archive does not otherwise show how the January activities-funding fight was resolved, and no further Herald coverage of the Thornton administration has been found before his successor, Jamie Hargrove, was profiled as the new ASG head at the start of the 1979-80 year.
people.sources: Associated Student Government organization chart, March 1978; Herald 53:54, 6 Apr 1978

people.what_they_did: Steve Yater led the Associated Student Government through 1973-74. Early in his term he publicly commended the Board of Regents in the Herald, weeks after the board had increased ASG's budget allotment. Yater's win was reported in the Herald's 13 April 1973 election returns; the same issue profiled him as making a good impression in his first contact with Congress and stressing a calm approach to the office. Carter Pence's companion article covered new officers being installed at a Congress party the same week, though the archive index does not yet name who besides Yater took office. In April 1974, stung by election-season criticism, President Yater defended his administration in a letter to the Herald. His final weeks in office stayed argumentative: the Herald of April 30 carried dueling letters under the heading 'Linda Jones vs. Steven Yater' as the student regent race closed out the year. The Herald's own retrospective on his term, by Al Cross, ran 16 April 1974 under the headline 'Presidency Ends for Steve Yater; One Major Program Started' - the archive does not yet hold the article's text, only its headline crediting his administration with a single major accomplishment.

As a senator in 2018-19, Whalin ran for administrative vice president on a ticket with presidential candidate Asha McWilliams and Jacob McAndrews in the spring 2019 election; the ticket lost, with Kenan Mujkanovic defeating her for the AVP seat. That February she co-authored, with Kara Lowry and Conner Hounshell, Resolution 1-19-S calling for the relocation of a campus marker identifying Bowling Green as the Confederate capital of Kentucky; it passed 29-1 and moved the marker into a Kentucky Museum display rather than removing it. In autumn 2019, by then Diversity and Inclusion committee chair, she and Senator Anthony Survance authored Resolution 4-19-F seeking Alpha Xi Delta's suspension from Greek affairs after chapter members sang a racial slur in a song posted online, and organized an October 2019 protest at Kappa Delta's Shenanigans philanthropy event to press the point after SGA voted to cancel that week's Senate meeting for the same event. "Their inaction just proved that students have to do action," she said of the university's response. On 22 October the Senate amended the resolution's title from "Removal from Campus" to "Suspension from Greek Affairs" and passed it 24-7; the executive board vetoed it 4-0 the following week, and the Senate confirmed the veto rather than overriding it, so Whalin and Survance had to draft a new resolution. She also secured a floor amendment raising the funding in a 2020 tampon-access bill from $1,176 to $1,300. Already recorded as Diversity and Inclusion Committee Head; the 11 February 2020 Senate minutes separately call her "Senator Symone Whalin" as she offered a friendly amendment to Bill 1-20-S, confirming she held a Senate seat in addition to chairing the committee.

people.what_they_did: Recorded absent at Congress roll call, 12 October 1993, the year before she was elected Administrative Vice President. Tara Higdon was elected Administrative Vice President in April 1994, running alongside presidential candidate Rob Evans against Scott Sivley, and served in that office through 1994-95. A year later she was elected to succeed Evans as president and student regent for 1995-96. The Herald reported that result on 11 April 1995 under "Tara Higdon Moves Up; Voting Down," and SGA's own 2001 roster of former presidents records Tara D. Higdon of Slaughters as the 29th president. Her term is recorded on this site under the plaque's form of her name, Tara (Higdon) Howard. Higdon's path to the presidency ran through the campus security debates of 1995. During the spring campaign the Herald reported that her experience of being stalked had influenced her, under the headline "Campus Security: Stalking Influenced Tara Higdon." After a year as part of the elected leadership alongside Robert Evans, she won the presidency, and the Herald marked the transition with "Tara Higdon Sees New Beginning." Her term brought new emergency phones, a skywalk proposal, a campus store proposal and a push for longer visitation hours. The SGA's 2001 list of presidents records Tara D. Higdon of Slaughters as the 29th president, serving 1995-96, and marks her as having also served as student regent. Higdon won the presidency in April 1995, with the Herald reporting the result under the headline 'Tara Higdon Moves Up; Voting Down' - she moved up to the top office even as voter turnout fell. The paper's year-end editorial the following week argued that visibility would be the key to the association's success. Her year ended in a contested, four-way race to succeed her, and Higdon took a public side: her letter 'Vote for Kristin Miller' ran in the Herald's April 16, 1996 issue, in the same election-week pages as the candidates' debate coverage and the campaign for SGA's constitutional amendments. The spring of her term was the stormiest stretch in the association's decade of Herald coverage: within a single week in February 1996 the paper carried both SGA's skywalk proposal for the bottom of the Hill and a letter dismissing the association as a 'puppet' group, and by late April a columnist was asking whether students cared about student government at all. A Slaughters junior; had served as Administrative Vice President and student regent in 1994-95 before moving up to the presidency.
people.sources: Herald 69:52, 21 Apr 1994, "Rob Evans & Tara Higdon Ready to Lead Students"; Herald 70:51, 11 Apr 1995; Herald 70:51, 11 Apr 1995, "Tara Higdon Moves Up; Voting Down"; SGA Minutes, 12 Oct 1993

people.all_offices: Activities Vice President (1973-74); Activities Vice President (1974-75)
people.what_they_did: Thomas LaCivita was elected activities vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1973-74 in what the 1974 Talisman calls one of the most controversial elections in the school's history, serving under president Steve Yater alongside administrative vice president Glenn Jackson, treasurer Lee Goodpaster and secretary Pam Stewart. He was re-elected to the post for 1974-75, one of the few ASG officers of the decade to serve two consecutive years; that second term is recorded under his 1974-75 entry. Early in his first year LaCivita clashed publicly with Ron Beck, the assistant dean of student affairs who administered concert bookings through ASG. LaCivita charged that Beck put too little creativity into the entertainment program, did not weigh LaCivita's opinions, and did not keep up with the music scene; he also argued that concerts should be advertised beyond Bowling Green to draw more ticket revenue. Beck, who at first declined to respond to the specific charges, said cost, student appeal and any tendency of an act to encourage drug use were what determined which acts were booked, telling the Herald's reviewer, 'If I haven't heard of a group, they won't go on this campus.' The dispute eased as the year went on, and the two ran an entertainment program that turned a profit after a rocky start. Thomas LaCivita, elected unopposed to a second consecutive term as activities vice president of the Associated Student Government for 1974-75, chaired the ASG Activities Committee on a roughly $42,000 entertainment budget, of which $27,000 went toward two free concerts. His full account, including the 1973-74 dispute with assistant dean of student affairs Ron Beck over concert booking, is recorded under his first term the year before. After students picketed the poorly received Doc Severinsen Homecoming concert on 11 October 1974, a newly formed Student Action Committee pressed to give LaCivita more say in negotiating with prospective acts; he absorbed the committee into his own rather than cede ground, though Kentucky law kept the activities vice president's role advisory, since a student could not control university funds outright. When a booked Al Stewart mini-concert fell through after Stewart's United States tour was cancelled under immigration law, LaCivita booked the New York hard rock group Kiss to replace him. President Jeff Consolo credited LaCivita afterward with running a more diversified entertainment series that year.
people.sources: 1974 Talisman, Associated Student Government, p. 56; 1975 Talisman, Associated Student Government

people.all_offices: president (1986-87); president (1987-88); Chairman, Student Rights Committee (1985-86)
people.what_they_did: Tim Todd chaired the Student Rights Committee in 1985-86, the year before Associated Student Government elected him president. The one set of that year's minutes the archive holds, from the closing meeting of 15 April 1986, records a single remark of his: he wished the body a good summer. Todd reached the April 1986 runoff against Greg Elder after Mitchell McKinney's withdrawal left the presidential field open. The Herald reported the two-man race on 3 April, with the general election the following week. Days after an election week the Herald described as marred by pranks and accusations, the paper identified Todd as the new ASG president in a sharply critical opinion piece headlined that he lacked knowledge of his own issues. Todd answered in print the following issue, criticizing the paper's reporting. His first fall opened with an approved budget of $12,100, a plan to reach students by phone for their ideas and needs, and an ASG retreat featuring university president Kern Alexander. Todd's first year leading Associated Student Government opened with ordinary organisational business. The Herald of 11 September 1986 reported that ASG approved a $12,100 budget, planned to telephone students to collect their ideas and needs, and scheduled a retreat that was to feature Kern Alexander. By the end of the spring term the body was still working through routine legislation, tabling a phone bill after an amendment was raised, while a student government conference was set for that weekend. The same issue of 26 March 1987 covered the election for the following year, in which Todd stood again and Bill Fogle said he had entered the presidential race to help Todd rather than to win it. Todd sought a second term in spring 1987 in a rematch against Greg Elder, the man he had beaten the year before. The Herald reported the two would battle again in its 19 March issue. On election day the Herald endorsed Elder as the better choice and indexed the race itself under the headline no contest. The vote was then re-run, and Todd won it: the paper carried the result on 16 April 1987. The SGA plaque lists him on a single 1986-88 plate, and no other president appears in the 1987-88 record. The 1987-88 year under the two-year plate ended with the election of Scott Whitehouse on 7 April 1988, closing out the era of the Todd presidency. Todd stood for a second term in the election held in March 1987. The Herald reported that Bill Fogle had entered the presidential race to help Todd rather than to win it, and the same issue recorded a shortage of candidates across the races and an appeal by a disqualified candidate. His second year drew harder coverage. The Herald of 29 October 1987 reported that Associated Student Government was considering required course evaluations, and carried a separate article saying apathy was killing both ASG and the Residence Hall Association.

Tom Blair was elected administrative vice president of the Associated Student Government on 6 and 7 April 1976, beating John David Evans by 570 votes to 552 in one of the closest races that spring; the 1977 Talisman lists him among the year's officers as already having ASG experience. About a year earlier, the Herald's 1 April 1975 issue had reported that Blair wanted a president's council formed, with no indication in the sources checked that he then held ASG office himself. At the 6 April 1976 Congress meeting, before a vote on the impeachment of congressman Gerard Faulk, Blair moved to drop the proceedings without a vote on removal, then withdrew the motion at the urging of several other congressmen. The Herald's 13 April 1976 issue separately reported that Blair withdrew charges he had brought against President Steve Henry; the archive records those charges, one of the two cases behind Faulk's impeachment, as an allegation that Henry had obstructed an advisory intramurals committee. Blair ran for the ASG presidency himself the following April and lost to Bob Moore, 562 votes to 536.

Veronica Butler was elected a junior senator in SGA's April 2026 election and chaired the senate's Mental Health and Wellbeing Committee. Working with outgoing President Rush Robinson, she helped build a year-long slate of mental health programming, including SGA-sponsored Mental Health Week events, and told the Herald that knowing when to seek help had been one of her own biggest struggles, and that much of it came down to whether students felt able to use the resources available and found them accessible. Victor Click co-signed the same 2 April 1987 Herald letter with Hollie Hale endorsing Tim Todd for the Associated Student Government presidency. Todd won the race, in a re-run of the election the Herald reported on 16 April 1987. By the fall of 1987 Click chaired the Associated Student Government's Student Affairs Committee, which ran the Book Exchanger — a free listing service through which students advertised used textbooks to each other instead of selling them back to the bookstore. Click told the Herald in November 1987 that the exchange had raised about $60 the previous fall and nothing that spring against roughly $653 in printing costs, against a $750 budget for the service, and said he would recommend dropping the project if that semester's run failed too. Click continued in student government the following year as co-chair of the Student Affairs Committee, accepted by Congress on 13 September 1988 alongside chair Brad Cooper.

Victor Jackson, an accounting major from Clarksville, Tennessee, chaired ASG's faculty evaluation committee in 1978-79. That year ASG approved a questionnaire for a student evaluation of the faculty, called the Purdue Cafeteria System, under which instructors chose questions from a list of several hundred, each form built around a set of core questions common to all of them. Jackson said only the core questions would be published, citing printing costs, and put the first year's cost at about $6,500 and about $5,000 a year after; the evaluations were due to begin in fall 1979. Jackson had earlier been the only Black student to run in a campus election for a seat on the Board of Regents' presidential screening committee, an October 1978 vote called after roughly forty Black students, most of them members of the campus NAACP chapter and the United Black Students, asked ASG to secure minority representation on the committee. Two students were to be chosen for the committee in a campus election, and NAACP chapter president Anita Orr said at the October meeting that Jackson had little chance of winning, since minority students made up only about 6.5 percent of the student body. The regents in the end appointed a Black elementary school principal from Russellville and a female WKU associate professor of home economics and family living to the committee, at the request of ASG president and student regent Steve Thornton. The 1979 Talisman also credits Jackson with serving on several ASG committees that year and being, in the words of Herald reporter Tom Beshear, 'very active.'

people.what_they_did: Harris authored Bill 12-17-F, the constitutional amendment binding the president to a set process when appointing senators to vacant seats. He managed the Mayer-Edmonds-Anderson campaign in the April 2018 election and was one of those the Judicial Council called to speak about the Pepe the Frog image used in its chalking. He was elected SGA president in 2019. Harris authored Bill 12-17-F, the constitutional amendment setting a fixed process for appointing senators to vacant seats. His wider part in the year is under his senate officer entry. Elected student body president for 2019-20 the following spring. Harris won the student body presidency in April 2019 at the head of the WGK ticket with Garrett Edmonds and Kenan Mujkanovic, defeating Asha McWilliams. After the results were announced at SGA's election party, he said he looked forward to "making a positive impact for all students here at WKU" and to collaborating with the opposing ticket. He took office at SGA's annual banquet and presided over his first meeting the following Tuesday. The defining controversy of his fall semester was Resolution 4-19-F, the senate's push to punish Alpha Xi Delta after a video showed members singing a racial slur. Harris abstained when his executive board vetoed the resolution 4-0, explaining that the discrimination claim would have to come from the Student Code of Conduct and that no violation had been noted by the Office of Student Conduct. When senators suggested his position as a knight of Alpha Xi Delta motivated him, he rejected the charge and said he wanted to reach an amicable outcome with the resolution's authors. Opened the eighteenth Senate on 3 September 2019 by moving his own slate of executive nominations, all five of which were confirmed that night, and warned that the Judicial Council had four vacancies to fill. Recorded as President William Harris in the following week's minutes.

people.all_offices: Chair, Public Relations (2017-18); Senator At Large (2016-17); Senator At Large (2017-18)
people.what_they_did: William "Will" Hurst was already sitting as a senator at large in 2016-17. He co-authored Bill 13-17-S, which the Senate passed 19-11-1 on March 21, 2017 (after being tabled two weeks) to buy a $225 portable whiteboard for SGA committees and events, and he authored Bill 26-17-S, a constitutional amendment to strip the Executive Branch of its power to propose legislation to the Senate; it failed 7-22-1 on April 4, 2017. Later that month he was returned as one of twelve at-large student senators in the April 2017 election, serving through the 2017-18 year and chairing the Public Relations Committee. As a senator at large in 2017-18 he co-authored a bylaws amendment fixing set election windows for constitutional amendments (with Lucas Knight, passed) and a resolution asking WKU to add a required sexual-assault-education course (with Ashlyn Jones, Annabelle Ford, Garrett Edmonds and Alex Sergent). At the Sept. 12, 2017 meeting, as Public Relations Committee Chair, he said LGBTQ rights were "fundamental rights as Americans" in supporting funding for Bowling Green's inaugural Pride Festival. On Jan. 23, 2018 he voted against, and spoke against, the reappointment of former senator Stephen Mayer, calling it "hypocritical" for the executive board to nominate a second fraternity member after criticizing SGA's Greek overrepresentation. Hurst walked out of an emergency Judicial Council meeting on Jan. 29, 2018 amid a tense stretch in the Senate. He did not attend the March 20, 2018 meeting, where fellow senator Alex Sergent, the Public Relations Committee's vice chair, sat in his usual seat at the front of the chamber as interim chair; SGA President Andi Dahmer said at the time that "nothing is official" about Hurst's status. By the following week's Herald coverage of Senate tensions, he was being described as "former Public Relations Committee Chair." Hurst chaired public relations and authored fourteen pieces of legislation, a total matched that year only by administrative vice president Kara Lowry. Most of it rewrote SGA's own rules: a constitutional and bylaw pair creating constitutional amendment elections at the end of each semester, a limit on the executive branch's power to propose legislation, a standing emergency committee to fill senate seats out of cycle, new senate debate procedure, and the office of parliamentarian. He also funded a $500 voucher scheme with the Counseling and Testing Center, a $230 camera for the public relations committee, a $250 SGA tailgate and $300 for a political forum run jointly by Young Americans for Freedom, the College Republicans and the Young Democrats, and wrote the resolution standing with the College Heights Herald in its lawsuit with the university. In January 2018 he alleged the executive board had failed to advertise the fall election; the Judicial Council found the board had complied and censured him, and censured him again on 4 February over his conduct at the emergency meeting, which he apologised for. Censured by the Judicial Council in January 2018 over an election-discrepancy complaint.
people.sources: SGA legislation: Bill 13-17-S, Funding for a Portable Whiteboard for SGA; SGA legislation: Bill 14-17-F, A Bill to Amend the Bylaws of the Student Government Association of Western Kentucky University

people.all_offices: president (1967-68); Senior Class President (1966-67); Associated Students President (1967-68)
people.what_they_did: A senior from Dawson Springs on the first Congress. He was elected president of Associated Students for 1967-68. Menser headed the Associated Student Government from the start of the 1967-68 year, appearing alongside President Kelly Thompson in a 14 September 1967 Herald article welcoming students back to campus. That fall the idea of a student seat on the Board of Regents was already circulating: a 2 November 1967 Herald article headlined 'Ward Favors Student on Board of Regents' reported support for the idea four months before an enabling bill reached committee. That December the Herald reported an Associated Students survey of student activity preferences and, in the same 8 December 1967 issue, ran a piece by Dennis Jaffe commending the government's efforts; the same issue covered the Kentucky Intercollegiate Press Association backing a proposal for student representation. In February 1968 Western sent lobbyists to Frankfort for a bill to seat a student on the Board of Regents; on 4 April 1968 the Herald reported Menser had assumed duties as the board's first student regent, a non-voting seat. As his term closed, the Herald's 29 April 1968 issue - the same one covering the Straeffer-Whitley presidential race to succeed him - carried both a piece headlined 'Menser Discusses Head Fee' and a separate retrospective, 'Past Performance of Associated Student Government Analyzed'. The archive does not yet hold the text of either article, only their headlines. Menser opened his year in office in September 1967 sharing the front page with President Kelly Thompson, in a piece headlined "Dr. Kelly Thompson, William Menser Welcome Students." The same first issue of the year set out the Associated Student Government's schedule of events. Menser's correspondence with President Kelly Thompson survives in the WKU Archives, filed under student fees. The file is described as correspondence about the assessment of student fees and the Associated Student Government budget for 1968-1969. Heads the 1967-68 officers and congressmen roster and its Executive Committee list. The 1968 Talisman's Associated Students page describes the body in its second year of existence pushing student proposals through legislation and expanded activities.

people.what_they_did: Already an active senator by 30 September 2014; voted in a roll-call vote on 24 February 2015. Jones chaired campus improvements and ran the annual campus safety walk, which in spring 2016 he said would concentrate on the outside of buildings because of the time it took. He took to the International Student Office the difficulty Nigerian students were having getting money out of their country. In debate he was cautious about SGA co-sponsoring the 'I Am a Kentuckian' event, telling the senate it was being rushed into a vote on a contentious subject. Jones chaired the Campus Improvements Committee for 2015-16 and continued in the post into 2016-17 as a senior senator. In his report to the Senate on 13 September 2016 he announced that year's Campus Safety Walk, an annual inspection of campus for locations needing safety improvements, would be held two days later. The following month, as the Public Relations committee polled students on where they felt least safe on campus, Jones told the Senate that some areas had a reputation for being unsafe that the university's actual safety record did not support, saying "there's the impression that we're unsafe, but truly we are safe." Also chaired the Campus Improvements committee. Jones's committee ran the campus safety walk each semester, starting from Centennial Mall on 15 September 2016, and polled students on where they felt unsafe; he told the senate some places were thought unsafe that were not. In March 2017 he sat on the university's food service bid and said he had tried to represent the whole student body in the vote that gave Aramark a new letter of intent.

people.most_senior_office: Campus Improvements and Sustainability Committee Chair
people.all_offices: Campus Improvements and Sustainability Committee Chair (2021-22); Senator At Large (2021-22)
people.what_they_did: Zachary Skillman was elected a WKU SGA senator-at-large in September 2021, one of two Skillmans (with fellow business economics junior Jacob Skillman, no relation established in the sources) sworn in on 14 September. A junior majoring in business economics and a Gordon Ford College of Business ambassador, he said Matthew Wininger had encouraged him to run and that he wanted to continue the recycling and sustainability initiatives Wininger had started as head of the sustainability committee, including off-campus recycling, a used-WKU-apparel recycling program and an adopt-a-highway effort. By 2021-22 Skillman chaired the renamed Campus Improvements and Sustainability Committee. In April 2022 he won Senate approval of $570.02 for an e-waste recycling bin on WKU's main campus, saying the project would earn WKU 0.25 credits toward Gold certification from the Association for the Advancement of Sustainability in Higher Education. He also co-authored Resolution 12-22-S, adding benches to South Lawn, and authored Bill 41-22-S, funding an Earth Day tie-dye tabling event. Named on the document as senator at large.
people.sources: SGA legislation: Bill 3-21-F, A Bill to Amend the Student Government Association Bylaws; SGA legislation: Resolution 12-22-S, Resolution to Support the Addition of Benches on South Lawn

Zoe Martin sat as a senator at-large in 2025-26 and worked with the Student Mental Health and Wellbeing Committee. She co-authored Bill 11-25-F, funding the "Toppers Talk About It" Mental Health Awareness Week tabling, and Resolution 3-25-F, supporting "Flipping the Script," a two-part faculty-student mental wellness panel held 6 November 2025 in which staff from the Counseling Center, SARC and the Psych Clinic answered student questions before pre-selected student leaders took the stage to answer questions of their own. Named as an author on two pieces of SGA legislation in the 2025-26 session: Resolution 3-25-F (Resolution to Support “Flipping the Script”: Faculty-Student Mental Wellness Panel); Bill 11-25-F (Funding for the “Toppers Talk About It” Mental Health Awareness Week in November 2025).
